title: Software
text:
Software research and analysis. Software design is the broad concern of how software is structured; architecture is a part of design — the decisions that are hard to change — but not all design is architecture.
This section organizes software design into:

Architecture — the part of design concerned with module boundaries and system-level structure.
Cohesion — cohesion as correctness relative to a partitioning rule; the (purity, completeness) pair; the knowledge-embodiment theorem.
Coupling — coupling as access to a shared resource; coupling as a consequence of cohesion; the coupling floor.
Languages — the design of, and analysis of, programming languages.

The five CUPID properties are assessed separately: CUPID tests them against the assessment requirement their author set, and against the standards that define engineering. The consolidated ledger of what IVP diagnoses about styles and sets is in Verdicts.
The change-management account of module structure that informs the software analysis is published in the paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1].


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

The Independent Variation Principle — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.20794332

title: SOLID
text:
SOLID names five heuristics for object-oriented design — Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion — assembled and taught by Robert C. Martin [1], [2]. The same body of work adds six packaging heuristics — Reuse/Release Equivalence, Common Closure, Common Reuse, Acyclic Dependencies, Stable Dependencies, Stable Abstractions — presented as the architecture-scale companion to the five [2].
The five have been criticised for thirty years as vague, overlapping, or arbitrary [3], [4], [5], [6], [7]. This page does not add another judgement of taste. It asks of each heuristic the questions an engineering discipline asks of any rule: what exactly does it assert, can a design be checked against it, and is the assertion true? It then asks the same of the set as a whole, because the heuristics are taught and applied together.

title: SOLID
text:
1 At a glance








Heuristic
What it asserts
Status




SRP
a module has one reason to change
False: the adapter has two, under Martin’s own reading of his terms [8]


OCP
entities are open for extension, closed for modification
Vacuous: “extension” has no independent test


LSP
a subtype substitutes for its supertype
A definition of the subtype relation, not a design rule [9]


ISP
no client depends on methods it does not use
A corollary of DIP applied per client [10]


DIP
depend on abstractions; the client owns the interface
A placement directive with no criterion for which abstractions


REP, CCP, CRP, ADP, SDP, SAP
six constraints on package structure
Jointly unsatisfiable in general [11]

title: SOLID
text:
2 Single Responsibility: false
The heuristic is stated as “a class should have only one reason to change” [1], and restated as a grouping rule: gather together the things that change for the same reasons, and separate those that change for different reasons [2]. Martin grounds the reason in people: a reason to change is a person or a group whose requirements can independently force a modification.
The adapter refutes the cardinality claim under that grounding. A Stripe payment adapter implements an internal payment port and calls Stripe’s API. Two groups can require it to change independently: the group that owns the internal port, and Stripe. The count of reasons to change is therefore two, and the adapter violates the heuristic. The counterexample is not marginal: every façade, bridge, API gateway, protocol translator, and anti-corruption layer that mediates between two independently governed interfaces has the same shape [8].
The prescribed remedy fails as well. Splitting the adapter is supposed to give each part one reason to change, but mediation requires both domains’ knowledge in the same reasoning step: a part that knows only one interface can no longer map between them. The paper examines the three natural salvage attempts — a data-transfer object, a mapping table, and delegation — and each either leaves the two domains’ knowledge in one module or destroys the mapping [8].
The grouping half miscounts too. Two stakeholders whose requests trace to one document force a false split; one stakeholder whose requests trace to two documents forces a false merge [8]. What survives is the grouping form re-grounded on documented sources of change — which is not Martin’s definition. The vocabulary is part of why the error survived: “concern” and “responsibility” carry a cardinality assumption into the sentence before any reasoning starts [12].
For practice, the consequence is direct: the heuristic demands a split that removes the element’s function, and a reviewer who invokes it cannot be satisfied without damaging the design.

title: SOLID
text:
3 Open/Closed: vacuous
The heuristic is stated as “software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification” [1], [13].
The defect is in the word extension. Nothing fixes which changes count as extension and which as modification, and for any change both descriptions are available. Adding a branch to a conditional is a modification of the conditional; it is also an extension of the set of cases the conditional handles. Extracting a strategy is an extension of the entity’s behaviour; it is also a modification of the entity, which now delegates. A change to a configuration file modifies no code at all and can be described as an extension of the system’s behaviour.
The situation the heuristic addresses is real, and the mechanisms it points at are ordinary. A design must eventually serve requirements the team does not have yet, and the constructs that admit later code without editing earlier code are the ones every programmer knows: inheritance, composition, event handling, callbacks, higher-order functions. Each of them is a way of writing today’s code so that tomorrow’s code can attach to it. What the heuristic asks, however, is that this be done before the requirement exists — that the entity be made open for a change nobody has specified. That request cannot be met by method, because future domain knowledge is not available at design time. A designer either waits for the requirement and modifies the entity, or guesses; the heuristic treats the guess as compliance and the wait as violation, yet it supplies no test that separates a guess that will pay from one that will not.
So every design satisfies the heuristic under some description, and every design violates it under another. A rule with that property does not rank designs, because the description is chosen after the design and after the change. It cannot be checked in review — the reviewer and the author can always disagree about which description applies, and neither is wrong. It cannot be refuted: no program is a counterexample, because no program is required to be anything in particular. And it cannot decide a design question, including the question it appears to answer, which is when the cost of an extension point is justified [2].
What the heuristic names is a real observation — that some changes are cheap after a boundary exists and expensive before it, and that ordinary constructs can buy that cheapness. It converts the observation into no criterion: it licenses whatever was built, describing it afterwards as open or closed as needed, and it cannot say which of the available mechanisms should be put in place now.

title: SOLID
text:
4 Liskov Substitution: a definition
Liskov and Wing define the subtype relation behaviourally: S is a subtype of T if an object of type S can be used wherever an object of type T is expected, without altering the desirable properties of the program [9].
That sentence defines what “subtype” means. It is a criterion of correctness for the claim “S is a subtype of T”, not a prescription about which types should exist, which hierarchies are worth building, or where a boundary belongs.
Applying it classifies and stops. If a square cannot stand in for a mutable rectangle, then the square is not a subtype of the rectangle — the modelling claim is false, and the defect is in the claim, not in the definition. The definition does not say what to do next: remove the hierarchy, separate the types, or keep the hierarchy and change the invariant. That choice is a design decision the definition does not reach.
The example that made the rule famous — a square inheriting from a rectangle — is one instance of that classification, and no more. Type substitution fails when it is done incorrectly, and the square is the standard demonstration: a client that sets width and height independently receives a square it did not ask for. What the example does not show, and Martin does not say, is that the modelling choice behind it is contingent. In drawing software a square is commonly modelled as a shape with a single side length rather than as a rectangle under a constraint, because the operations that matter are move, resize, and rotate, and neither width nor height exists on its own. Modelled that way, the substitution question never arises. The definition cannot choose between the two models: both describe their objects correctly, and the choice turns on which operations the domain requires.
A definition is also not the kind of thing that can be falsified or improved by evidence, which is why the substitution rule is best read as the boundary of a vocabulary rather than as guidance. The actionable content usually attributed to it is contractual — preconditions, postconditions, invariants [13] — and that discipline checks a relation the designer has already chosen. It is not a criterion for choosing it.

title: SOLID
text:
5 Interface Segregation: a corollary
The heuristic says that no client should be forced to depend on methods it does not use [1].
DIP contains an ownership clause: the client owns the interface it depends upon [2]. Apply that clause once per client of a shared provider. Each client receives its own interface, the provider implements all of them, each client sees only its own slice, and no client depends on a method it does not use — which is the structure ISP prescribes. At the class level the two procedures produce the same classes, the same interfaces, and the same dependency and implementation relations, and the converse holds as well: any interface segregation is structurally indistinguishable from per-client application of the ownership clause [10].
ISP is therefore a corollary, not an independent fifth letter. Naming it has pedagogical value — it directs attention to the per-client reading of DIP, which the textbooks underemphasise — but it prescribes no design action that DIP does not already prescribe. The count of five overstates the independence of the set, and the acronym’s shape has been mistaken for its structure [10].

title: SOLID
section: 6 Dependency Inversion: a directive without a criterion
text:
6 Dependency Inversion: a directive without a criterion
The heuristic says that high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules, that both should depend on abstractions, and that abstractions should not depend on details [1], [2]. Its ownership clause adds who writes the abstraction: the client.
What it fixes is the direction of a dependency that already exists. What it does not fix is which abstractions should exist, where a boundary belongs, or whether a given dependency is justified at all.
The gap is not a matter of interpretation. Pushed towards packaging, the heuristic admits three readings, and they disagree: a co-location reading, an examples reading, and an ownership reading [11]. The co-location reading contradicts Reuse/Release Equivalence; the examples reading contradicts Interface Segregation; the ownership reading, the only one that survives, places no constraint on package structure at all [11].
So the heuristic directs the arrow once the abstraction is chosen, and is silent on the choice. The choice is the design question.

title: SOLID
text:
7 ISP and DIP are conditional
These two are neither false nor vacuous, which is why they survive where the others do not. Interface segregation states a real constraint on who may see which operations, and dependency inversion states a real constraint on the direction of a dependency and on who owns the interface [2], [10].
They are wrong when applied blindly, because the structure they prescribe is right only when the two sides of the interface are governed independently. Where the client’s needs and the provider’s needs move together, a client-specific interface adds an indirection with no boundary behind it: the provider must still change when the client changes, and the interface is one more place to edit. Where they move apart, the indirection is the boundary, and the dependency points at the part that changes less. The heuristics name the structure but not the condition, which is whether the two sides are driven by independent change drivers [14]. Applied uniformly, they produce an interface for every use and an abstraction for every collaborator — indirection without a boundary.
That is the sense in which these two are conditionally true: their conclusion holds under a hypothesis neither of them states, and the hypothesis is a fact about the domain’s sources of change.

title: SOLID
text:
8 The packaging heuristics: jointly unsatisfiable
The six packaging heuristics are stated as follows [2]. Reuse/Release Equivalence (REP): the unit of reuse is the unit of release, so a package must be a viable unit of reuse for everyone who depends on it [2], [11]. Common Closure (CCP): elements that change for the same reasons belong in the same package. Common Reuse (CRP): elements used together belong in the same package. Acyclic Dependencies (ADP): the package dependency graph has no cycles. Stable Dependencies (SDP): depend in the direction of stability. Stable Abstractions (SAP): a stable package should be abstract.
Take the minimal configuration that DIP and ISP together endorse: one provider implementing two client-specific interfaces, serving two clients [11]. Fifty-two partitions of the five elements are possible, and the heuristics are supposed to narrow them. They do not narrow them to anything, because CCP and REP cannot both hold. CCP puts each client interface with its client, since they change for the same reasons. REP then condemns the result: the provider must implement both interfaces, so the provider’s package must depend on both client packages, including one whose elements it never uses [11].
The escape hatches do not escape. Martin presents CCP, CRP, and REP as a tension triangle in which the architect chooses a vertex to sacrifice; dropping REP or CRP does not restore satisfiability for this configuration, only dropping CCP produces any solutions at all, and then five partitions survive with no heuristic left to select among them [11]. The three natural placements — with the client, with the provider, in its own package — each have principled support and principled condemnation from inside the same corpus [11].
The consequence is stronger than “these heuristics conflict sometimes”. Every system with a provider serving two or more clients through client-specific interfaces violates at least one packaging heuristic at every point in its history. The notion of technical debt assumes a principled ideal that the debt departs from; for packaging, no such ideal exists [11].

title: SOLID
text:
9 Against the standards of engineering
Two standards define engineering practice: grounding in a theory or a model, and falsifiability [15], [16], [17], [18]. Both are absent here.
On grounding, the heuristics are selected, not derived. They respond to symptoms their authors observed, and no model of the domain, theory of change, or empirical result selects this set rather than another [3], [4], [5]. The corpus is presented as five rules, but the rules were developed separately, and their five-letter arrangement is an acronym rather than a structure [2], [3]. The packaging heuristics were added later, at a different scale, and are not consistent with the earlier set when both are pushed [11].
On falsifiability, the set splits into four kinds, and none of them is a tested engineering claim. SRP is false: it makes a countable assertion, and the count comes out wrong [8]. OCP is unfalsifiable: no observation can violate it, because the description of the change is chosen to suit the verdict. LSP is a definition: it fixes the meaning of a term, and definitions are not refuted by evidence [9]. ISP is a corollary of DIP: it follows by derivation and predicts nothing that DIP does not [10]. DIP is underdetermined: it constrains a direction, not a structure [11]. The packaging heuristics are jointly contradictory: there are configurations for which no assignment satisfies them [11].

title: SOLID
section: 10 The missing criterion: the domain’s change structure
text:
10 The missing criterion: the domain’s change structure
Each heuristic classifies by something internal to the code: a responsibility, an extension point, a type relation, an interface shape, a dependency direction, a package metric. None of them classifies by the domain’s sources of change.
Those sources are external and independent. A regulator, a payment provider’s API, a customer segment, or an accounting standard each force changes on its own schedule, and their reach cuts across the categories the heuristics use [14]. A boundary drawn by technical role therefore cuts through a source of change: one required change then reaches several modules, and each module mixes pieces that change for unrelated reasons. A boundary drawn to keep a source of change whole would avoid that, and none of the heuristics can express the difference, because none of them has a term for an external source of change.
That is the missing criterion, and it is why the heuristics cannot answer the question they are consulted for. They can report a symptom — two things in one class, a dependency pointing down, a package that is hard to reuse — but a symptom is not a boundary rule. Two decompositions can score identically on every heuristic and differ completely in how much work one change costs.

title: SOLID
text:
11 What remains
Not nothing. The substitution contract is sound as a definition of subtyping and useful as a check on a hierarchy the designer has already chosen [9]. Interface segregation is sound as the per-client application of interface ownership [10]. Dependency inversion is sound as a statement about the direction of a chosen dependency, and its ownership clause says who should write the interface [2]. Acyclicity is a structural property worth enforcing, and the observation that some changes are cheap after a boundary exists is real. The SRP grouping form also survives in a corrected version — grouping by documented sources of change — which is not the heuristic as stated [8].
What does not survive is the claim that these are a method. One is false, one is vacuous, one is a definition, one is a corollary, one is a directive without a criterion, and the packaging set is unsatisfiable as a set. What is left is practitioner advice: memorable names for symptoms, with no model that selects them, no test that refutes them, and no procedure that decides a boundary [7]. That is a legitimate thing to write and to teach. It is not engineering, and it should not be presented as the discipline’s foundation.

title: Layered Architecture
text:
Layered architecture — the classic horizontal, or “N-tier,” style — divides the system into horizontal layers by technical role: presentation, application or business logic, and persistence or data access. Each layer calls the layer beneath it; the call graph descends. A common discipline forbids skipping a layer: the presentation layer reaches the database only through the business layer.
The style has no single author. It is the default arrangement of a great many systems, taught as the natural way to separate a user interface from business logic from storage. So the question is not whether it admits to being a design. It is the commonest one. The question is which parts of it embody the domain’s knowledge and which parts it invents.
This page applies the same test used for onion architecture, clean architecture, and hexagonal architecture: does the domain’s change-driver structure mandate the cut?

title: Layered Architecture
text:
1 At a glance








Underlying principle
Succeeds when
Fails when




Layers group elements by technical role: presentation, business logic, persistence.
Each change is confined to one layer.
A single change driver crosses layers — a rule edit touching presentation, logic, and persistence.

title: Layered Architecture
text:
2 The claim
The layers are technical roles: presentation (controllers, views), application (coordinating logic), business logic, and persistence (repositories, data access). Each layer depends on the layer below it. The claim is that a change to a technical concern stays within its layer: a change to the interface touches presentation, a change to storage touches persistence.

title: Layered Architecture
text:
3 Layers divide by technical role
Layering’s axis is technical role. Elements are grouped by what they technically are — a controller, a service, a repository — not by what they change for. The rule that fixes the depth is a direction claim: each layer calls the one below.
IVP does not group by technical role; it groups by which change activates an element. Technical role and change-driver class are different axes [1]. A business rule and its persistence code may share a change driver while sitting in different layers; a controller and a repository may share nothing. So layering’s stated axis — presentation versus logic versus storage — is a proxy. It can coincide with the partition, when a domain’s change drivers happen to be technical; it does not determine it.

title: Layered Architecture
section: 4 The layers are not in the domain’s analysis
text:
4 The layers are not in the domain’s analysis
No business analysis or functional analysis organises knowledge as presentation, business logic, and persistence. Analysis names capabilities, processes, rules, entities, and decisions. It does not name “the controller layer” or “the data-access layer.” Those categories appear when a designer lays out code; they are a technical encoding. Absence from the analysis is evidence, not the test; the test is coincidence with the partition.

title: Layered Architecture
section: 5 A layer is not independently replaceable
text:
5 A layer is not independently replaceable
Layering’s strongest claim is replaceability: swap the database layer, or the presentation layer, and the others stand. That is a claim about the direction of reference. Layering exists to isolate change — a technical change stays in its layer — so the coupling at issue is change coupling.
Under the framework’s reading, a single business-rule change commonly drives the controller, the service, and the repository together: the rule is edited, its endpoint changes, its stored form changes. Then those elements carry the same change-driver assignment, and the layer boundaries run through one Γ-equivalence class. Each boundary that separates them splits a class — a Unit Completeness failure. The rule is scattered across layers, and the change must cross every boundary between them. Replaceability holds for the layer’s mechanism; it does not hold for the rule.

title: Layered Architecture
section: 6 What layering embodies, and what it invents
text:
6 What layering embodies, and what it invents
Two parts are worth separating.

The descending dependency rule is a claim about direction, not about the cut. Direction is domain-determined only where the domain itself orders the elements: where one element’s requirement is chosen to satisfy another’s. Layering’s rule points every dependency down, whether or not the domain orders them that way. Where they align, the rule adds no structure; where they do not, it asserts a direction the domain does not have.
The layers are a claim about the cut. Presentation, business logic, persistence: the stratification is not in the analysis.

A representation is unavoidable. What is not unavoidable is inventing a concept — a named kind, boundary, or category — that the knowledge does not contain. A layer is such an invention exactly when it does not coincide with a change-driver class. If the layer groups elements with different change-driver assignments, it invents a unity; if its boundary splits elements with the same assignment, it invents a division. Only a layer that coincides with a Γ-equivalence class is not an invention, and then it is a redundant name for a real class. Layers rarely so coincide, because a domain’s rules do not divide by technical role.
By IVP’s foundational claim, the change-driver partition is the domain’s only organising knowledge [1]. Faithfulness admits no concept that does not correspond to a Γ-equivalence class; any structure beyond the partition is deviation, and deviation is the accidentality. Layering’s layers are that deviation: the business layer usually holds rules with several distinct change drivers, and its boundary separates each rule from the persistence code that shares the rule’s change driver.

title: Layered Architecture
section: 7 The split is not the style
text:
7 The split is not the style
The proof is in the artifacts. Grouping by change driver yields the partition; an engineer who embeds the domain faithfully, and who has never heard of layering, arrives at the partition. She may separate concerns — interface, logic, storage — because that is a natural impulse, but the strict layer discipline, each layer calling only the one below, is a convention. She groups by what changes together, not by what an element technically is.
Non-spontaneity is evidence, not proof, that a structure is a convention and not knowledge. Layering fails wherever a layer straddles a Γ-equivalence class — the ordinary business-rule feature, for example. The encoding is the designer’s, the partition is the domain’s.

title: Layered Architecture
text:
8 The IVP account
IVP groups elements by change-driver assignment: elements with the same assignment belong together. A module is pure when all its elements share one change-driver assignment set [1]. Judged by that standard, layering’s layers are correct where no class straddles them and no two non-equivalent elements are grouped.
For the ordinary feature, they are not correct; off the partition, the decomposition is wrong under the change-driver criterion.

title: Layered Architecture
section: 9 When layering is beneficial, and when it is harmful
text:
9 When layering is beneficial, and when it is harmful
The theory is not maintenance-only. Each concern the system must respect — logical structure, security, deployment, platform, a latency budget — is, once modelled as knowledge governed by change drivers, a partitioning rule over the same element set. IVP is one such principle, and not the only one: grouping by the full change-driver set (Γ-equivalence) is the common refinement of the concerns’ rules, correct under every one at once [2]. The claim is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists. So layering answers to one decomposition, not one per concern.
Layering does no harm only where its layers coincide with that decomposition. Where they do not, every change crosses a boundary the domain did not set: a class split across layers scatters one change, and a layer that groups non-equivalent elements couples what the domain keeps apart.
Two caveats bound the claim. The cost model is separate, and it models maintenance cost: the partition minimises total maintenance cost under the coefficient condition the model states, unconditional only in the pure, disjoint change-driver case [3]; whether the metric matches real economic cost is empirical. And the theory does not discover the rule: identifying the domain conditions and building the partition is a separate domain-analysis task [2]. A concern left out of the model is a requirements gap, not a cohesion judgement.
Beneficial, here, means only that layering does no harm: its layers coincide with the change-driver decomposition. It still adds no decomposition of its own. Outside the band, layering is harmful wherever its layers do not coincide with the partition.

title: Layered Architecture
text:
10 Beyond placement: faithful embodiment
The theory separates three properties: placement — the right knowledge in the right modules — which is what cohesion measures; faithful embodiment — each piece realised as it requires; and dependency parsimony — the dependencies are the ones the purpose requires. The three are independent [2].
Correctness is the second alone. A system satisfies an obligation exactly when every knowledge piece the obligation constrains is correctly embodied by some element; placement does not enter. So cohesion governs the cost of achieving and maintaining correctness — the scope to read and the radius to change — not whether it holds. A module can be placed exactly right and still compute a rule with the wrong formula.
Layering can clear placement and fail this. Nothing in a layer checks whether the code realises the knowledge it carries, and the layer diagram looks the same.
Layering is fully sound only when it clears every bar: its layers coincide with the change-driver decomposition, and the code realises the domain’s knowledge faithfully. Alignment without embodiment is a system placed correctly and still wrong about its domain.

title: Layered Architecture
text:
11 Summary

Layered architecture divides the system into horizontal layers by technical role, each calling the one below. Its stated axis is technical role.
IVP does not group by technical role; it groups by change driver. The role axis is a proxy.
The layers — presentation, business logic, persistence — appear in no analysis artifact.
A layer is not independently replaceable: under the framework’s reading, a rule and its persistence code carry the same change-driver assignment, so the layer boundaries split one class (a Unit Completeness failure).
Where the layers coincide with the partition, layering adds nothing; where they do not, it invents structure the domain did not mandate.
The strongest defensible claim: layering’s layers are invented concepts except where they coincide with the partition. Its decomposition value is the partition, which one can obtain without it.
Layering does no harm only where its layers coincide with the change-driver decomposition; it is harmful where they do not. Placement is not faithful embodiment.
IVP is one modularising principle among those the system’s concerns induce; Γ-equivalence is the common refinement of them. The theory is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists.

Compare vertical slice architecture, which cuts the other way, and hexagonal architecture.
Back to the verdict ledger.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
text:
Hexagonal architecture — Ports and Adapters — puts an application core at the centre and surrounds it with ports and adapters. A port is an interface the core defines; an adapter is the mechanism that fits it — HTTP, a message queue, a database, a payment rail. The core does not know the adapters; the adapters know the ports. Cockburn’s stated goals are that the application can run with no user interface and no database, for testing, and that mechanisms can be swapped [1].
Cockburn is explicit that the hexagon is a drawing convention — the shape is “not a hexagon because the number six is important,” but to leave room to draw the ports around the edge; and what a port is “is largely a matter of taste” [1]. So the question is not whether it admits to being a design. It does, openly. The question is which parts of it embody the domain’s knowledge and which parts it invents.
This page applies the same test used for onion architecture, clean architecture, and layered architecture: does the domain’s change-driver structure mandate the cut?

title: Hexagonal Architecture
text:
1 At a glance








Underlying principle
Succeeds when
Fails when




Hexagonal treats the core and the integration mechanisms as two disjoint change-driver sets, with a port between them.
The core’s change drivers are disjoint from the adapters’.
A change driver reaches across the port — a persisted entity’s field, whose state and mapping carry the same assignment. The port then splits one class.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
text:
2 The claim
The core holds the application’s rules. The ports are the interfaces it defines for what it needs. The adapters are the mechanisms that implement the ports: a web controller on one side, a repository on the other. Dependency direction is the point: the core does not import an adapter; the adapter imports the port.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
section: 3 Hexagonal’s axis is core versus mechanism
text:
3 Hexagonal’s axis is core versus mechanism
Hexagonal’s axis is a structural split: core domain versus integration mechanism. It is not a frequency ordering or a policy ordering; it is a claim that the core’s elements and the mechanism’s elements are two kinds.
Cockburn’s justification is engineering: test the core without a database or a user interface, and swap mechanisms without touching the core. Those are goals, not domain knowledge. IVP groups by which change activates an element. Core-versus-mechanism is a proxy for that: the core’s change drivers differ from the adapters’ when the domain separates them, and only then [2]. So the axis can coincide with the partition. It does not determine it.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
section: 4 The ports are not in the domain’s analysis
text:
4 The ports are not in the domain’s analysis
No business analysis or functional analysis organises knowledge as a core with ports and adapters. Analysis names rules, entities, processes, events, and decisions. Cockburn derives the inside from the outside and places the ports from the use-case context; but a use-case set names operations, not ports. The port — the interface, and the indirection it carries — appears when a designer lays out code; it is an encoding. Absence from the analysis is evidence, not the test; the test is coincidence with the partition.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
section: 5 The core is not independent of the mechanism
text:
5 The core is not independent of the mechanism
Hexagonal’s strongest claim is that the core is independent of the mechanisms. That is a claim about the direction of reference. Hexagonal exists to isolate change, so the coupling at issue here is change coupling.
Under the framework’s reading, if recording a new domain fact is taken as one change driver covering the field, the column, and the wire field, then a persisted entity’s state and its mapping carry the same change-driver assignment. Hexagonal puts the entity type in the core and its mapping in an adapter. The port boundary therefore runs through one Γ-equivalence class. It separates the entity type from its mapping and splits that class — a Unit Completeness failure. It is exactly the failure the core-is-independent claim is meant to prevent. The core is not quiescent: under the framework’s reading, it is coupled to the very mechanism the port was meant to hold away.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
section: 6 What hexagonal embodies, and what it invents
text:
6 What hexagonal embodies, and what it invents
Two parts are worth separating.

The dependency direction — the core owns the port, the adapter implements it — is a claim about direction, not about the cut. Dependency inversion changes placement only; it adds, removes, and transmutes no change driver. Direction is domain-determined only where the domain itself orders the elements: where one element’s requirement is chosen to satisfy another’s. Where it aligns, the rule adds no structure; where it does not, it asserts a direction the domain does not have.
The ports and adapters are a claim about the cut. The port, the adapter, and the core/mechanism boundary are not in the analysis; they are concepts the designer adds.

A representation is unavoidable; what is not unavoidable is inventing a concept — a named kind, boundary, or category — that the knowledge does not contain. A port is such an invention exactly when it does not coincide with a change-driver class. If the boundary groups elements with different change-driver assignments, it invents a unity; if it splits elements with the same assignment, it invents a division. Only a boundary that coincides with a Γ-equivalence class is not an invention, and then it is a redundant name for a real class.
By IVP’s foundational claim, the change-driver partition is the domain’s only organising knowledge [2]. Faithfulness admits no concept that does not correspond to a Γ-equivalence class; any structure beyond the partition is deviation, and deviation is the accidentality.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
section: 7 The split is not the style
text:
7 The split is not the style
The proof is in the artifacts. Grouping by change driver yields the partition; an engineer who embeds the domain faithfully, and who has never heard of hexagonal, arrives at the partition. She may isolate the core from the mechanism because that is a natural impulse, but the port-and-adapter scheme, and the inversion it carries, are a taught pattern.
Non-spontaneity is evidence, not proof, that a structure is a convention and not knowledge. Hexagonal fails wherever the port straddles a Γ-equivalence class — the persisted entity, for example. The encoding is the designer’s, the partition is the domain’s.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
text:
8 The IVP account
IVP groups elements by change-driver assignment: elements with the same assignment belong together. A module is pure when all its elements share one change-driver assignment set [2]. Judged by that standard, the core/mechanism cut is correct where no class straddles it and no two non-equivalent elements are grouped.
For a persisted entity, it is not correct; off the partition, the decomposition is wrong under the change-driver criterion.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
section: 9 When hexagonal is beneficial, and when it is harmful
text:
9 When hexagonal is beneficial, and when it is harmful
The theory is not maintenance-only. Each concern the system must respect — logical structure, security, deployment, platform, a latency budget — is, once modelled as knowledge governed by change drivers, a partitioning rule over the same element set. IVP is one such principle, and not the only one: grouping by the full change-driver set (Γ-equivalence) is the common refinement of the concerns’ rules, correct under every one at once [3]. The claim is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists. So hexagonal answers to one decomposition, not one per concern.
Hexagonal does no harm only where its port boundary coincides with that decomposition. Where it does not, every change crosses a boundary the domain did not set: a class split across the boundary scatters one change, and a boundary that groups non-equivalent elements couples what the domain keeps apart.
Two caveats bound the claim. The cost model is separate, and it models maintenance cost: the partition minimises total maintenance cost under the coefficient condition the model states, unconditional only in the pure, disjoint change-driver case [4]; whether the metric matches real economic cost is empirical. And the theory does not discover the rule: identifying the domain conditions and building the partition is a separate domain-analysis task [3]. A concern left out of the model is a requirements gap, not a cohesion judgement.
Beneficial, here, means only that hexagonal does no harm: its port boundary coincides with the change-driver decomposition. It still adds no decomposition of its own. Outside the band, hexagonal is harmful wherever its boundary does not coincide with the partition.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
text:
10 Beyond placement: faithful embodiment
The theory separates three properties: placement — the right knowledge in the right modules — which is what cohesion measures; faithful embodiment — each piece realised as it requires; and dependency parsimony — the dependencies are the ones the purpose requires. The three are independent [3].
Correctness is the second alone. A system satisfies an obligation exactly when every knowledge piece the obligation constrains is correctly embodied by some element; placement does not enter. So cohesion governs the cost of achieving and maintaining correctness — the scope to read and the radius to change — not whether it holds. A module can be placed exactly right and still compute a rule with the wrong formula.
Hexagonal can clear placement and fail this. Nothing in a port checks whether the code realises the knowledge it carries, and the port diagram looks the same.
Hexagonal is fully sound only when it clears every bar: its boundary coincides with the change-driver decomposition, and the code realises the domain’s knowledge faithfully. Alignment without embodiment is a system placed correctly and still wrong about its domain.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
text:
11 Summary

Hexagonal architecture puts a core behind ports and adapters, with the core owning the interfaces and the adapters implementing them. Its stated axis is core versus mechanism.
IVP groups by change driver, not by core versus mechanism. The axis is a proxy; dependency inversion changes placement only.
The ports and adapters appear in no analysis artifact; a use-case set names operations, not ports.
The core is not independent of the mechanism: under the framework’s reading, a persisted entity’s state and mapping carry the same change-driver assignment, so the port boundary splits one class (a Unit Completeness failure).
Where the boundary coincides with the partition, hexagonal adds nothing; where it does not, it invents structure the domain did not mandate.
The strongest defensible claim: hexagonal’s ports and adapters are invented concepts except where they coincide with the partition. Its decomposition value is the partition, which one can obtain without it.
Hexagonal does no harm only where its boundary coincides with the change-driver decomposition; it is harmful where it does not. Placement is not faithful embodiment.
IVP is one modularising principle among those the system’s concerns induce; Γ-equivalence is the common refinement of them. The theory is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists.

Compare onion architecture, clean architecture, and layered architecture.

title: Clean Architecture
text:
Clean Architecture puts enterprise rules at the centre and rings the rest around them. The rings are Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, and Frameworks and Drivers. One rule governs every dependency: source-code dependencies point inward, and only inward. The centre holds the highest-level policy; the rim holds the mechanisms — the web, the database, the frameworks [1].
Martin presents Clean Architecture as a synthesis: it gathers the concentric-ring family — hexagonal, onion, and others — under one rule and one picture [1]. So the question is not whether it admits to being a design. It does. The question is which parts of it embody the domain’s knowledge and which parts it invents.
This page applies the same test used for onion architecture and hexagonal architecture: does the domain’s change-driver structure mandate the cut?

title: Clean Architecture
text:
1 At a glance








Underlying principle
Succeeds when
Fails when




Clean nests a role partition (Entities, Use Cases, Adapters, Frameworks) inside a stability ordering: depend toward the stable core.
The domain has one capability, the core is genuinely stable, and providers are substitutable — role tracks the change driver and ring position tracks real stability.
Role does not track the change driver (the use-case ring aggregates independent capabilities); ring position does not track real stability (a volatile domain core, a concrete-but-inert framework); or the client depends on a provider’s specifics.

title: Clean Architecture
text:
2 The claim
Clean draws four rings. At the centre sit Entities, the enterprise-wide business rules. Around them sit Use Cases, the application-specific rules. Around those sit Interface Adapters, which convert data between the use cases and the outside. At the rim sit Frameworks and Drivers: the web, the database, the devices. Martin’s rule is that source-code dependencies point only inward. An inner ring knows nothing of an outer one.

title: Clean Architecture
section: 3 Clean is a role partition plus a stability ordering
text:
3 Clean is a role partition plus a stability ordering
Clean is the composition of two ingredients. The first is a partition criterion: group every element into one of four rings by its role in the application flow. The second is a dependency-direction constraint: enforce the Stable Dependencies Principle across ring boundaries — depend toward the stable core.
The stability ordering rests on Martin’s metrics. Instability is I(P)=Ce(P)/(Ca(P)+Ce(P))I(P) = C_e(P) / (C_a(P) + C_e(P)), the ratio of efferent to total coupling: I=0I = 0 is maximally stable (many depend on it, it imports nothing); I=1I = 1 is maximally volatile. Abstractness is A(P)A(P), the fraction of abstract types. The Main Sequence A+I=1A + I = 1 is the optimal locus; the entity ring sits near I=0I = 0, the framework ring near I=1I = 1 [1].
The stability here is structural self-containment on the import graph, not actual change frequency. An element counts as “stable” because nothing imports force it to change, not because an external authority changes rarely. Clean’s axis therefore couples a role partition to a structural stability ordering, and asserts that ring position determines stability for every element, whatever actually governs it.
IVP groups by which change activates an element. Role and ring-position stability are proxies for that. They can coincide with the partition — in a domain where role tracks the change driver and ring position tracks real stability. They do not determine it [2].

title: Clean Architecture
section: 4 The rings are not in the domain’s analysis
text:
4 The rings are not in the domain’s analysis
No business analysis or functional analysis organises knowledge as Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, and Frameworks. Analysis names rules, entities, processes, events, decisions, responsibilities, and policies. “Entity” and “use case” are domain-near; the ring stratification is not. The rings appear when a designer lays out code; they are an encoding. Absence from the analysis is evidence, not the test; the test is coincidence with the partition.

title: Clean Architecture
section: 5 Entities are not coupled only to themselves
text:
5 Entities are not coupled only to themselves
Clean’s strongest claim is that Entities — the centre — are the most stable rules, encapsulating the most general business rules, and that outer rings depend on them and never the reverse. That is a claim about the direction of reference. Clean exists to isolate change, so the coupling at issue here is change coupling.
Under the framework’s reading, if recording a new domain fact is taken as one change driver covering the field, the column, and the wire field, then an entity’s state and its mapping carry the same change-driver assignment. Clean puts the entity at the centre and its mapping in an outer ring. The ring boundary therefore runs through one Γ-equivalence class. It separates the entity type from its mapping and splits that class — a Unit Completeness failure. It is exactly the failure the entity-at-the-centre claim is meant to prevent. The entity is not quiescent: under the framework’s reading, it is coupled to the very mechanics the rings were meant to isolate.

title: Clean Architecture
section: 6 What Clean embodies, and what it invents
text:
6 What Clean embodies, and what it invents
Two parts are worth separating.

The Dependency Rule is a claim about direction, not about the cut. Direction is domain-determined only where the domain itself orders the elements: where one element’s requirement is chosen to satisfy another’s. Clean’s blanket rule points every dependency inward, whether or not the domain orders them that way. Where they align, the rule adds no structure; where they do not, it asserts a direction the domain does not have.
The rings are a claim about the cut. Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, Frameworks and Drivers: the stratification is not in the analysis.

A representation is unavoidable. What is not unavoidable is inventing a concept — a named kind, boundary, or category — that the knowledge does not contain. A ring is such an invention exactly when it does not coincide with a change-driver class. If the ring groups elements with different change-driver assignments, it invents a unity; if its boundary splits elements with the same assignment, it invents a division. Only a ring that coincides with a Γ-equivalence class is not an invention, and then it is a redundant name for a real class.
By IVP’s foundational claim, the change-driver partition is the domain’s only organising knowledge [2]. Faithfulness admits no concept that does not correspond to a Γ-equivalence class; any structure beyond the partition is deviation, and deviation is the accidentality. Clean’s rings are that deviation, most sharply in the Use Case and Interface Adapter rings: the split between “application rules” and “adapters” is a code distinction the domain does not name.

title: Clean Architecture
section: 7 The split is not the style
text:
7 The split is not the style
The proof is in the artifacts. Grouping by change driver yields the partition; an engineer who embeds the domain faithfully, and who has never heard of Clean, arrives at the partition and not at the rings. The rings are not a structure a developer arrives at on their own: the impulse to keep business rules out of the database is common, but the four-ring scheme is a taught pattern.
Non-spontaneity is evidence, not proof, that a structure is a convention and not knowledge. Clean fails wherever a ring straddles a Γ-equivalence class — the persisted entity, for example. The encoding is the designer’s, the partition is the domain’s.

title: Clean Architecture
text:
8 The IVP account
IVP groups elements by change-driver assignment: elements with the same assignment belong together. A module is pure when all its elements share one change-driver assignment set [2]. Judged by that standard, Clean’s rings are correct where no class straddles them and no two non-equivalent elements are grouped.
For a persisted entity, they are not correct; off the partition, the decomposition is wrong under the change-driver criterion.

title: Clean Architecture
section: 9 When Clean is beneficial, and when it is harmful
text:
9 When Clean is beneficial, and when it is harmful
The theory is not maintenance-only. Each concern the system must respect — logical structure, security, deployment, platform, a latency budget — is, once modelled as knowledge governed by change drivers, a partitioning rule over the same element set. IVP is one such principle, and not the only one: grouping by the full change-driver set (Γ-equivalence) is the common refinement of the concerns’ rules, correct under every one at once [3]. The claim is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists. So Clean answers to one decomposition, not one per concern.
Clean does no harm only where its rings coincide with that decomposition — that is, where role tracks the change driver and ring position tracks real stability. That is the single-capability, substitutable-provider domain Clean was calibrated against: one capability, a genuinely stable core, genuinely interchangeable providers. There, role happens to track the change driver and ring position happens to track stability.
Outside that domain, Clean is harmful in three ways. Role does not track the change driver: the use-case ring aggregates independent capabilities, and every capability’s changes propagate through it. Ring position does not track real stability: a domain core that is volatile, or a framework that is concrete but inert, inverts or flattens the assumed gradient, and the Dependency Rule then points dependencies toward the most volatile elements. And the inversion is unconditional: where the client’s correctness depends on a provider’s specifics, the abstraction the pattern demands is fabricated — it claims a substitutability the domain does not grant.
Two caveats bound the claim. The cost model is separate, and it models maintenance cost: the partition minimises total maintenance cost under the coefficient condition the model states, unconditional only in the pure, disjoint change-driver case [4]; whether the metric matches real economic cost is empirical. And the theory does not discover the rule: identifying the domain conditions and building the partition is a separate domain-analysis task [3]. A concern left out of the model is a requirements gap, not a cohesion judgement.
Beneficial, here, means only that Clean does no harm: its rings coincide with the change-driver decomposition. It still adds no decomposition of its own. Outside the band, Clean is harmful wherever its rings do not coincide with the partition.

title: Clean Architecture
text:
10 Beyond placement: faithful embodiment
The theory separates three properties: placement — the right knowledge in the right modules — which is what cohesion measures; faithful embodiment — each piece realised as it requires; and dependency parsimony — the dependencies are the ones the purpose requires. The three are independent [3].
Correctness is the second alone. A system satisfies an obligation exactly when every knowledge piece the obligation constrains is correctly embodied by some element; placement does not enter. So cohesion governs the cost of achieving and maintaining correctness — the scope to read and the radius to change — not whether it holds. A module can be placed exactly right and still compute a rule with the wrong formula.
Clean can clear placement and fail this. Nothing in Clean checks whether the code realises the knowledge it carries, and the ring diagram looks the same.
Clean is fully sound only when it clears every bar: its rings coincide with the change-driver decomposition, and the code realises the domain’s knowledge faithfully. Alignment without embodiment is a system placed correctly and still wrong about its domain.

title: Clean Architecture
text:
11 Summary

Clean Architecture rings Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, and Frameworks around a centre, with all dependencies pointing inward. It is a role partition plus a stability ordering.
The stability ordering uses Martin’s metrics — instability, abstractness, the Main Sequence — which measure structural self-containment on the import graph, not real change frequency.
The rings — entity, use-case, adapter, framework — appear in no analysis artifact; the use-case/adapter split is a code distinction the domain does not name.
Entities are not coupled only to themselves: under the framework’s reading, a persisted entity’s state and mapping carry the same change-driver assignment, so the ring boundary splits one class (a Unit Completeness failure).
Clean does no harm only where its rings coincide with the partition — where role tracks the change driver and ring position tracks real stability; it is harmful where they do not.
The strongest defensible claim: Clean’s rings are invented concepts except where they coincide with the partition. Its decomposition value is the partition, which one can obtain without it.
IVP is one modularising principle among those the system’s concerns induce; Γ-equivalence is the common refinement of them. The theory is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists.

Compare onion architecture and hexagonal architecture, which reach the same conclusion by different routes.

title: Scala (3.8 / 3.3 LTS)
text: This assessment applies the coupling account — coupling as access to a shared resource, and the coupling floor [1], [2] — and the knowledge-embodiment theorem [3]; the language is assessed against its official reference [4].

title: Scala (3.8 / 3.3 LTS)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Scala in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 50/100 · Ecosystem coupling 72/100 · Engineering readiness 85/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Traits enable composition: Multiple trait inheritance without diamond problem
✅ Implicit parameters decouple: Can pass context without threading parameters
✅ Higher-kinded types: Generic over type constructors (Map, List, Option)
⚠️ Implicits can create hidden coupling: Action-at-a-distance when implicit resolution is not obvious and resolution order matters
❌ Complexity allows many ways to couple: Language flexibility means discipline required



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Case classes separate data from construction: Immutable, auto-generated constructors
✅ Apply methods decouple construction syntax: Person("Alice", 30) instead of new Person(...)
⚠️ Can use Java-style mutable constructors: Interop allows coupled patterns



1.1.3 Memory

✅ JVM GC decouples memory: Generational GC handles deallocation
✅ Immutable collections reduce GC pressure: Structural sharing, persistent data structures
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Stop-the-world pauses, though modern JVM GC improves (ZGC, Shenandoah)
⚠️ Object allocation overhead: Boxing/unboxing couples primitives to heap allocation
⚠️ Closure captures can extend lifetimes: Function closures hold references, preventing collection



1.1.4 Error

✅ Try/Either/Option separate concerns: Multiple error handling approaches
✅ For-comprehensions make error composition clear: for { a <- tryA; b <- tryB } yield f(a, b)
❌ Exceptions still common: Scala culture uses exceptions more than Haskell-style Result



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Futures decouple async: Future[T] separates async from sync
✅ Akka actors separate concurrent operations: Message passing prevents shared state
✅ Immutable collections by default: Prevents concurrent modification coupling
⚠️ Can use Java threads: Interop allows traditional coupling



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Portable JVM target: Scala runs wherever a JVM runs — Linux, macOS, and Windows — rather than on one vendor’s runtime
✅ Multiple JVM implementations: OpenJDK builds from Oracle, Eclipse Adoptium, Amazon, and Azul all run Scala, so no single vendor controls the runtime
✅ Open-source compiler: The Scala 3 compiler is Apache-2.0-licensed and developed by EPFL’s Scala Center with the community
✅ Three backends, not one platform: Scala compiles to JVM bytecode, to JavaScript through Scala.js, and to native code through Scala Native



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Expressiveness vs. Simplicity: Multiple ways to solve problems couples team to arbitrary choices
Implicits as Magic: Implicit resolution hides dependencies, creating action-at-a-distance coupling
Compile Time vs. Development Speed: Type-level programming couples fast iteration to long compile times
OOP + FP Hybrid: Can use both paradigms, but mixing couples code to dual mental models
Library Fragmentation: Cats vs. Scalaz vs. ZIO couples projects to ecosystem factions




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ JVM performance: JIT optimization, fast steady-state
⚠️ GC pauses: Inherits JVM GC characteristics (R2)
❌ Slow compilation: Couples development velocity to compiler speed
✅ Immutable collections optimized: Persistent data structures perform well
⚠️ Runtime reflection overhead: Implicits and type classes have runtime cost



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ JVM ecosystem: Access to massive Java library ecosystem
✅ sbt/Mill build tools: Standardized (though complex)
⚠️ IDE support mixed: IntelliJ good, others struggle
❌ Slow build times: Compilation couples to wait time, so build time affects iteration speed
✅ Active ecosystem: Libraries for most use cases



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ Scala 2 → 3 breaking changes: Major version couples code to rewriting effort
⚠️ Library fragmentation: Scala 2.12 vs 2.13 vs 3 couples to version matrix
✅ Active development: Regular improvements
❌ Binary compatibility issues: Cross-version compatibility couples deployment



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for backend/distributed systems: Akka, Spark, Play
✅ Strong for data engineering: Spark is industry standard
✅ Great for functional programming: Full FP support
⚠️ Less common for frontend: Scala.js exists but niche
✅ JVM deployment: Runs anywhere Java runs



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Very steep: Implicits, type system complexity, multiple paradigms
❌ Too many ways to do things: Couples productivity to knowing “the right way”
⚠️ Scala 2 vs 3 differences: Learning couples to version
✅ Good books/resources: “Functional Programming in Scala” et al.



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Expressive: For comprehensions, pattern matching, case classes
❌ Symbol overload: =>, <-, _, * used in many contexts
⚠️ Implicit complexity: Hard to understand what’s happening
✅ Concise when done right: Less boilerplate than Java



1.2.7 Testing

✅ ScalaTest, Specs2: Mature testing frameworks
✅ Property testing: ScalaCheck available
⚠️ Debugging implicits hard: Stack traces couple to implicit resolution
✅ JVM tooling: Profilers, debuggers work



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: JVM GC prevents memory bugs
✅ Type safe: Strong static typing
⚠️ Java interop: null, exceptions can leak through
✅ Immutability by default: Prevents mutation bugs (if used)




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.3 Observability

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [5]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [6].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [7].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

title: Haskell (GHC 9.12)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Haskell in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 76/100 · Ecosystem coupling 56/100 · Engineering readiness 53/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Pure functions separate side effects from pure logic: The type system (IO monad) keeps effects isolated, preventing hidden coupling to global state
✅ Type classes enable polymorphism without inheritance coupling: Abstraction through type classes (Functor, Monad, etc.) decouples interface from implementation
✅ Parametric polymorphism prevents coupling to concrete types: map :: (a -> b) -> [a] -> [b] works for any types without knowing their internals
⚠️ Monad transformers can create coupling: Stacking monads (ReaderT, StateT, ExceptT) creates order-dependent coupling
❌ IO monad couples all effects: Can’t separate file IO from network IO from randomness at type level (without effect systems)
❌ Global type class instances couple: Orphan instances create action-at-a-distance coupling



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Data constructors separate shape from creation logic: ADTs (Algebraic Data Types) decouple data structure from construction
✅ Smart constructors enable validation without coupling: Can wrap raw constructors to add invariants
✅ No shared mutable state: Construction doesn’t couple to global state



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Garbage collection decouples memory from logic: Don’t think about deallocation
✅ Immutability simplifies GC: No cyclic references from mutable structures
⚠️ GC pauses couple to runtime: Non-deterministic pauses affect real-time requirements
⚠️ Space leaks from lazy evaluation: Thunks accumulate, so evaluation strategy and computation order couple to memory usage
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free or double-free bugs



1.1.4 Error

✅ Either/Maybe separate success from failure: Either Error Result makes error path explicit and separate from success path
✅ Exceptions are typed: IO exceptions are contained in IO monad, preventing hidden coupling
⚠️ Partial functions (head, tail) can couple: Runtime errors bypass type system unless avoided



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ STM (Software Transactional Memory) decouples concurrency from logic: Composable transactions separate concurrent coordination from business logic
✅ Immutability prevents temporal coupling: No shared mutable state means concurrent operations don’t interfere
✅ Async/threading is explicit in types: Concurrency concerns are separate via type signatures



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No vendor owns the language: The Haskell 2010 report is a community standard, and GHC — the de facto reference compiler — is open source under a permissive BSD-style licence
✅ Native-code targets: GHC emits native executables for Linux, macOS, and Windows, so no virtual machine must be installed on the target host
✅ Free, redistributable toolchain: GHC, Cabal, and Stack are open source and freely redistributable, with no vendor licence gate
✅ Open package distribution: Hackage and Stackage index open-source packages under open licences, so dependencies are not gated by a vendor registry



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Performance vs. Abstraction: Lazy evaluation optimizes for composability but couples performance to evaluation strategy
Purity vs. Practicality: IO monad is all-or-nothing—can’t separate different IO types without mtl/effect systems
Type Class Coherence vs. Modularity: Only one instance per type globally couples modules that define instances
Laziness vs. Predictability: Space/time behavior depends on evaluation order, creating hidden coupling
Monad Transformer Order: ReaderT (StateT (ExceptT ...)) ≠ StateT (ReaderT (ExceptT ...)), order matters




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Lazy evaluation couples performance to evaluation strategy: Space/time behavior is non-obvious, creating coupling between logic and performance
⚠️ GC pauses unpredictable: Non-deterministic pauses couple timing-sensitive code to runtime behavior
✅ Immutability enables parallelism: No data races, can parallelize without coupling to synchronization
❌ Thunk accumulation: Space leaks couple memory usage to evaluation order



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Cabal/Stack standardized: Build system is consistent
⚠️ Package ecosystem smaller than mainstream: Library availability couples to niche community
✅ GHC is excellent: Compiler quality decouples from platform-specific quirks
❌ Dependency hell with base library versions: Breaking changes couple code to GHC version



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ GHC extensions allow gradual adoption: Can opt into new features without breaking existing code
⚠️ Extensions create fragmentation: Different codebases use different language subsets
✅ Haskell 2010 standard stable: Core language doesn’t break compatibility
❌ Extension proliferation: Code couples to specific GHC versions and extension combinations



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for parsers, compilers, DSLs: Type system supports these domains naturally
⚠️ Struggles with I/O-heavy, stateful systems: IO monad creates friction for imperative domains
❌ Poor for systems programming: GC, unpredictable performance couples to domain requirements
✅ Strong for financial, formal verification: Correctness guarantees match domain needs



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Very steep: Monads, functors, type classes couple productivity to deep expertise
❌ Lazy evaluation surprises: Space leaks require expertise to debug
✅ Excellent documentation: Books, tutorials decouple learning from trial-and-error
⚠️ Multiple ways to do things: Mtl vs. transformers vs. effect systems couple to architectural choices



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Concise, expressive: Minimal boilerplate
⚠️ Type signatures can be verbose: :: Monad m => (a -> m b) -> ... couples readability to type system knowledge
✅ Function composition natural: f . g . h decouples steps
❌ Operator overload: Custom operators (<$>, <*>, >>=) couple readability to library knowledge



1.2.7 Testing

✅ QuickCheck property testing: Built-in support for generative testing
✅ Pure functions easy to test: No setup/teardown coupling
❌ Debugging lazy code hard: Stack traces don’t show evaluation order
⚠️ GHCi debugger limited: Couples debugging to printf-style techniques



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents use-after-free, buffer overflows
✅ Type safety prevents many bugs: Can’t mix incompatible types
✅ Immutability prevents mutation bugs: No race conditions on shared state
⚠️ Timing attacks possible: Lazy evaluation can leak information through timing




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ A change pays a slow build.



1.3.5 Interop

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].

What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].

What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

title: Nim (2.2)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Nim in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 43/100 · Ecosystem coupling 64/100 · Engineering readiness 72/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Distinct types: Create new types from existing without coupling
✅ Concepts: Generic constraints like Rust traits
✅ Method call syntax: Uniform function call, decouples OOP from functional style
⚠️ Macros powerful but complex: Can create coupling in generated code, and can hide it behind opaque expansion



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Objects, tuples, refs separate: Multiple data representation strategies
⚠️ GC for refs: Garbage collection couples to runtime
✅ Destructors for non-GC: Can manage resources explicitly



1.1.3 Memory

⚠️ Multiple GC modes: Can choose GC strategy (ARC, Boehm, etc.)
✅ Ref vs value types: Can choose between GC (ref) and stack (value)
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Depends on the GC mode, so allocation timing cannot be controlled precisely
✅ Destructors for deterministic cleanup: =destroy hook for custom cleanup
⚠️ ARC mode has cycles: Automatic reference counting needs manual cycle breaking
✅ No GC mode available: Can compile without GC for embedded
⚠️ Manual memory management possible: alloc/dealloc available but error-prone



1.1.4 Error

⚠️ Exceptions exist: Not as explicit as Result types
✅ Can return Option/Result: Libraries support explicit errors
⚠️ Effect system planned: Future feature for tracking errors/effects



1.1.5 Concurrency

⚠️ Multiple models: Threads, async/await, channels
⚠️ GC complicates: Shared heap couples concurrent operations (K2)
✅ Async/await separates: Explicit async functions



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Compiles through C, C++, or JavaScript: Nim emits source for a language the target platform already supports, so it reuses that platform’s compiler and libraries instead of requiring its own runtime
✅ No vendor owner: The compiler is developed in the open by the Nim project, so no company controls the language
✅ No platform-specific build service: The standard library ships with the compiler and Nimble fetches packages directly, so a build needs no vendor infrastructure
✅ Runs on every mainstream platform: One source base targets Linux, macOS, Windows, and embedded devices through the portable C and C++ backends



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Indentation is significant: Blocks are marked by layout, a syntax decision that shortens code and makes the parser and the editor extra important
seq and string copy on assignment: The built-in containers have value semantics, trading accidental aliasing for a copy unless a move or sink parameter is used
The default memory manager changed: Nim 2.0 moved the default to the ARC/ORC family, so code from the 1.x era assumed a different collector — a project decision with a migration cost
The language spans two levels: High-level abstraction sits beside raw pointers and alloc, a deliberate breadth whose cost is that a codebase may mix idioms
The manual is the specification: Nim’s behaviour is defined by its manual and its compiler rather than by a separate standard — a scope decision




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Compiles to C: Good performance
⚠️ GC overhead: Non-deterministic pauses (but tunable)
✅ Zero-cost abstractions: Templates compile away
✅ Predictable: C backend makes performance transparent
⚠️ GC tuning needed: Couples performance to GC configuration



1.2.2 Ecosystem

⚠️ Small ecosystem: Nimble packages limited
✅ Nimble package manager: Works well
⚠️ IDE support: Limited (Nimsuggest, VSCode)
⚠️ Small community: Fewer resources
✅ Good docs: Manual is comprehensive



1.2.3 Evolution

⚠️ Breaking changes: v1.0 to v2.0 had issues, and language evolution couples code to a version
✅ Stable now: Post-1.0 more stable
⚠️ Small team: Development pace couples to resources
✅ Active: Regular improvements



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Good for systems: Compiles to C, performance
✅ Great for scripting: Python-like syntax
✅ Strong for CLI tools: Single binary
⚠️ Limited adoption: Niche use cases
⚠️ Web backend: Possible but uncommon



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Python-like syntax: Familiar, gentle
⚠️ Macro system: Powerful but complex
✅ Good docs: Tutorial, manual
⚠️ Small community: Fewer learning resources



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Clean, readable: Python-influenced
✅ UFCS: Uniform function call syntax elegant
✅ Expressive: Macros, templates
⚠️ Indentation-based: Not everyone’s preference



1.2.7 Testing

✅ unittest module: Built-in testing
⚠️ Debugging: Gdb works but not ideal
⚠️ Limited tooling: Fewer profilers
✅ Compile-time checks: Good error messages



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents memory bugs
⚠️ C interop: FFI can introduce unsafety
✅ Type safe: Static typing
⚠️ Exceptions: Less explicit than Result types
