title: C (C23)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses C in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 25/100 · Ecosystem coupling 73/100 · Engineering readiness 65/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Structs separate data: Pure data, no methods
✅ Function pointers enable polymorphism: Can pass behavior as data
❌ No encapsulation: Everything is public
❌ No generics: Void pointers couple to type casting
✅ No inheritance: Can’t create coupled hierarchies
❌ Header files couple: Includes create compilation dependencies
❌ Macros couple: Preprocessor doesn’t respect scope
❌ No namespaces: Global namespace pollution



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Explicit memory management: Allocation separate from initialization
✅ Designated initializers: Can initialize specific fields
❌ No constructors: Manual initialization couples to usage
❌ Global state common: Static variables couple modules



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Manual control enables precise memory strategy: Can separate memory management from logic
✅ Explicit allocation/deallocation: malloc/free make lifetime visible
❌ No safety: Use-after-free, double-free, memory leaks all possible
❌ No RAII: Must manually track and free resources
✅ Predictable: No GC pauses, deterministic performance
❌ Pointer arithmetic couples to memory layout: Buffer overruns couple to hardware, with no abstraction over memory
✅ Custom allocators: Can decouple allocation strategy (arena, pool, etc.)
❌ Undefined behavior on errors: Buffer overruns, null derefs, and other memory-safety violations are UB



1.1.4 Error

✅ Explicit error codes: Return values make errors visible
❌ No enforcement: Can ignore return values
❌ errno couples: Global error state couples functions
❌ NULL everywhere: Pointer errors couple all code



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ pthreads manual: All synchronization explicit
❌ Shared mutable state default: No protection
❌ Data races are undefined behavior: No prevention
⚠️ Explicit is predictable: At least coupling is visible



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No platform owner: The language is standardised by ISO/IEC and implemented independently by GCC, Clang, and MSVC, so no single vendor controls it
✅ No required platform runtime: A conforming program depends only on the C standard library, not on a vendor runtime
✅ Every mainstream platform has a C compiler: Linux, macOS, Windows, and embedded targets all have conforming implementations, and operating systems expose a C ABI to other languages
✅ No single-implementation dependence: Source compiles under more than one compiler, so the loss of one implementation does not strand the code



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Power vs. Safety: Complete control couples to complete responsibility for safety
Simplicity vs. Safety: No abstractions means manual discipline required to control coupling
Performance vs. Correctness: Optimization couples to unsafe patterns (buffer tricks, pointer arithmetic)
Portability vs. Platform Access: Platform-specific code couples to hardware/OS
Manual Memory Management: Must couple resource acquisition to every usage site
Undefined Behavior Everywhere: Memory errors couple entire program to runtime environment
Header Dependencies: Changes to one header couple to all files that include it (transitively)




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Maximum performance: No abstraction overhead
✅ No GC: Deterministic, predictable
✅ Full control: Manual everything
✅ Predictable: What you write is what runs
✅ Minimal runtime: Runs anywhere



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Ubiquitous: Available on every platform
⚠️ Build systems: Make, autotools, CMake fragmentation
✅ Mature tooling: GCC, Clang, debuggers
⚠️ No package manager: Manual dependency management
✅ Stable ABI on a given platform: A platform’s C ABI is long-stable, so binaries built by ABI-compatible compilers interoperate on that platform (the C standard itself defines no ABI, and compatibility is not guaranteed across compilers or targets)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Extremely stable: C89/C99/C11/C17/C23 all backward compatible
✅ No breaking changes: Code from 1980s still compiles
✅ Conservative: Changes are minimal
⚠️ Slow evolution: New features take decades



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for systems: OS kernels, drivers
✅ Great for embedded: Minimal footprint
✅ Strong for performance: No overhead
✅ Good for portability: Runs everywhere
⚠️ Not for application dev: Too low-level



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Simple language: Small, learnable
❌ Hard to master: Undefined behavior, pointers
✅ Lots of resources: K&R, tutorials
❌ Many footguns: Easy to shoot yourself



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Simple, direct: Minimal syntax
❌ No abstractions: Manual everything
❌ Pointer syntax: int *(*fp)(void) confusing
✅ Explicit: Clear what’s happening



1.2.7 Testing

⚠️ Testing frameworks: Check, Unity, cmocka
✅ Excellent debuggers: Gdb, lldb
❌ Manual memory tracking: Valgrind needed
⚠️ UB makes debugging hard: Anything can happen



1.2.8 Security

❌ Memory unsafe: All memory bugs possible
❌ Buffer overflows: No bounds checking
❌ Undefined behavior: Security vulnerabilities
❌ No protection: Manual everything




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [8], [9].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

✅ A standards-qualified toolchain or an established safety standard covers this language.

title: Zsh (5.9)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Zsh in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 43/100 · Ecosystem coupling 68/100 · Engineering readiness 64/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Values are strings with no static check: A scalar, an array element, and an associative-array value all hold text, and no declaration states what kind of thing a name holds (T1)
❌ No sum types: An alternative is a word plus a convention, and typeset -A gives a mapping rather than a tagged choice (T4)
❌ No generics and no dispatch by type: A routine is specialised only by its positional arguments, and behaviour is selected by the command name (T5, T9)
❌ One flat namespace: Functions and parameters share the global space, and local only narrows a name inside a function body, so nothing hides a library’s internals from the process (T6, T11)
❌ An unset name expands to nothing by default: setopt nounset turns the reference into an error, but the option is off unless it is requested, and an empty value still passes (T10)
✅ typeset -T ties two parameters together: typeset -T PATH path makes the scalar PATH and the array path one value in two shapes, so colon-separated data is edited as a list



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Global by default and mutable by default: An assignment writes the global unless local or typeset narrows it, and no binding is immutable unless readonly is applied (C1, C2)
❌ No constructor or validation on a plain parameter: Nothing checks a value when it is bound; validation exists only where setopt or an explicit test is applied (C4)
✅ local in a function body is a real scope: A parameter declared local is restored when the function returns, so working state stays with the routine
✅ autoload -Uz separates definition from call: A function body is loaded from $fpath on first reference, so the name is declared without the implementation being read
✅ Configuration files are layered and sourced by role: .zshenv, .zprofile, .zshrc, .zlogin, and .zlogout each hold one kind of setup, so interactive configuration does not reach a script
✅ emulate -L zsh fixes the option set inside a function: The options are reset for the function’s duration and restored on return, so a routine does not inherit settings from the caller



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No allocation or free in the language: There is no pointer and no deallocation builtin; parameters are allocated and released by the shell
✅ Scope and unset bound a lifetime: A local parameter disappears when its function returns, so working state does not persist by accident
✅ Associative arrays are managed by the shell: typeset -A allocates and grows its own storage, so no capacity handling is written
⚠️ Assignment copies the value: An array is duplicated on assignment, and referencing one without copying requires an explicit indirection
⚠️ Command substitution is materialised whole: $(cmd) collects the entire output before the enclosing command runs, so a large result is held in memory
⚠️ always blocks hold their state until the block ends: The try and always blocks are kept for the duration of the construct, so a long-running trap delays release



1.1.4 Error

❌ No structured error path: $?, TRAPZERR, and the always block are the apparatus, with no exception and no error value (Er1)
❌ The error trap is global and undifferentiated: TRAPZERR runs for the whole script, it receives no description of the failure, and it fires only where a non-zero status is not consumed (Er3)
❌ Errors cannot be returned: A function’s outcome is an exit status, so an error carries no payload and cannot be combined with another (Er4)
✅ { ... } always { ... } guarantees cleanup: The always block runs after an error, a break, or a continue, so teardown is attached to the construct rather than to a global trap
⚠️ The always block does not survive a parse error: A syntax error in the try list aborts during parsing, so the always list never runs
⚠️ setopt errexit is fragile: The option does not fire inside && and || chains, in conditions, or after a negation, so a wrapper that suppresses it changes error behaviour



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ No concurrency primitives: There is no lock, channel, mutex, or await; the only parallel construct is a background job (K5)
✅ zmodload zsh/system adds real synchronisation: The module provides a zsystem builtin with file locking and a sysread/syswrite pair, so a race over a shared file can be avoided in the language
✅ Processes are the unit of parallelism: Concurrency is expressed with pipes and background jobs, so no shared address space has to be reasoned about
✅ Coprocesses give two-way communication: coproc starts a child that print -p and read -p can drive, so a long-running program is not restarted per iteration
⚠️ Background jobs inherit the environment: A & job shares every global parameter, the umask, and the current directory, so ordering is unspecified unless the script waits
⚠️ wait returns a status, not a value: A result must travel through a file, a pipe, or a coprocess



1.1.6 Platform

❌ One implementation defines the language: Zsh exists as the zsh project’s own C implementation, with no independent implementation of the same specification to compare against (P2)
✅ zsh is packaged for every UNIX-like system: Linux distributions, the BSDs, and macOS all ship it, and it is the default interactive shell on macOS
✅ The implementation runs on POSIX systems and Windows: The same code base builds on Linux, the BSDs, Solaris, and through Cygwin or MSYS2 on Windows
⚠️ emulate sh is a compatibility mode, not POSIX compliance: The shell can be invoked as sh or ksh and behave closer to them, but the mode is offered for convenience rather than as a conformance claim
⚠️ Open-source governance is project-led: The language is directed by its maintainers in a public repository, with no standards body and no formal change process
⚠️ No second implementation is likely: With a very large option and module surface, an independent implementation would be a research project



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The large option set is a deliberate design: setopt lets a user choose behaviour that other shells fix, and the price is that a script must state which behaviour it expects
The completion system is a language of its own: compinit, _arguments, and zstyle make completion programmable, which is a feature rather than a coupling mechanism
Modules are optional capability: zmodload adds zsh/mathfunc, zsh/datetime, and zsh/system on demand, so a script chooses its own surface
1-indexed arrays were a compatibility decision: The offset differs from Bash and ksh, and KSH_ARRAYS exists for users who want the other convention
oh-my-zsh is a distribution, not the language: The framework owns configuration and the prompt, so its coupling is to the user’s setup rather than to zsh itself
zsh is not a general-purpose language: The model is a shell over external commands, which is a scope decision




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Interpreted with no compilation: Each command is parsed and executed as text, and there is no artifact and no JIT (R1)
✅ A native implementation with a fast path for common work: Expansion, globbing, and arithmetic are executed in C rather than by calling an external command
✅ Floating-point arithmetic is built in: (( ... )) handles real numbers, so a numeric calculation does not need awk or bc
✅ zmodload zsh/mathfunc adds the C math library: Trigonometric and logarithmic functions are available inside arithmetic expressions
⚠️ Start-up sources several configuration files: An interactive shell reads .zshenv, then .zprofile or .zshrc, so a large oh-my-zsh setup costs time on every new shell, which zsh/zprof can measure
⚠️ The completion system builds a cache: compinit scans $fpath and writes ~/.zcompdump, so the first shell after a change pays for the scan



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ No package manager in the language: There is no dependency resolver, so plugins arrive through third-party frameworks such as oh-my-zsh, prezto, zinit, or antigen (Ec1)
✅ The plugin ecosystem is one of the largest in the shell world: Prompt themes, completions, and syntax-highlighting plugins exist for most command-line tools
✅ The bundled completion system is extensive: _arguments definitions ship for hundreds of commands, and compinit makes them all available without an add-on
✅ vcs_info provides a git-aware prompt in the standard distribution: Version-control state is read by a shipped module instead of a script
✅ Documentation is complete and versioned: The manual is shipped as man pages and as a searchable HTML manual
⚠️ Frameworks own the configuration: oh-my-zsh and its alternatives take over .zshrc, so a user’s setup depends on a third-party project



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ No breaking-change culture: New releases add features, and the project documents the few changes that affect existing configuration
✅ emulate pins behaviour: A script can fix the option set with emulate -L zsh, so a change of defaults does not silently alter it
✅ The project ships regular releases: The 5.x series has been maintained for many years with ongoing fixes
✅ Options are the compatibility mechanism: A new behaviour is normally introduced behind a setopt, so the old behaviour remains available
⚠️ Change depends on the maintainers: The language is directed by its project team rather than by a committee with a published process
⚠️ Frameworks must track the language: A plugin that depends on internal behaviour can break when a release changes it, which is a risk of the ecosystem rather than of the language



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for interactive use: The completion system, prompt substitution, and vcs_info make the terminal the primary domain
✅ Strong for text and path processing: Glob qualifiers such as *(.) for plain files, recursive **/, and setopt extendedglob express selection that other shells delegate to find
✅ Arrays and associative arrays fit scripting that needs structure: typeset -A and array slicing cover indexed and keyed data inside the language
✅ Emulation covers other shells when needed: emulate sh and emulate ksh run foreign syntax in a nested scope
⚠️ A zsh script needs zsh: An interpreter that is not installed on every host, so a portable bootstrap script cannot be written in zsh
⚠️ The most useful features are interactive: Completion, prompt themes, and autosuggestions do not travel into a script



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Bash knowledge transfers: The core syntax, expansions, and pipelines are familiar to a Bash user
✅ Documentation is complete and searchable: The manual covers the language, the builtins, the options, and the modules
⚠️ Parameter expansion is more complex than in Bash: ${(flags)name} and the setopt-controlled variations each have their own rule
⚠️ The option set is very large: The behaviour of a script depends on which options are set, and a reader must know the current set
⚠️ Framework configuration hides the setup: An oh-my-zsh user learns the framework before the language



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Arrays are first-class with slicing: $a[2,-1] expresses a range that other shells express with a loop
✅ Glob qualifiers replace external tools: *(.), *(/D), and **/*.c select files by kind and recursion in the pattern itself
✅ No word splitting by default: An unquoted $var expands as one word even when it contains spaces, so fewer quotes are needed
⚠️ Parameter expansion flags are dense: ${(q)var}, ${(j:,:)a}, and ${(k)assoc} pack quoting, joining, and keys into a short notation
⚠️ setopt changes the reading of the text: The same script behaves differently under shwordsplit, nomatch, or extendedglob
⚠️ Arrays may be 0-indexed or 1-indexed: The default is 1-indexed while KSH_ARRAYS changes it, so an array index is not always portable between zsh configurations



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No test framework in the language: A test is a script that checks $?, with no assertion, fixture, or reporting facility (G1)
❌ Faults appear only on the branch that runs: With no static check, a mistyped parameter or a bad array index is found during the run (G3)
✅ A syntax check runs without execution: zsh -n parses a script and reports errors without running it
✅ functions -T traces a selected function: Tracing can be limited to the function under test instead of the whole script
✅ TRAPDEBUG gives a debugger hook: A function bound to the DEBUG trap runs before each command, which supports a stepping harness
✅ The test set can be isolated with emulate -L zsh and a subshell: Each case runs with known options in a child process



1.2.8 Security

❌ Dynamic typing removes a check the shell cannot make: A value that should be a path, a number, or a flag is a string, and only the command that receives it can object (Q2)
⚠️ Text can re-enter the interpreter: A value assembled from data and passed to eval, or interpolated into a substituted command, becomes code
⚠️ nomatch controls a failure mode rather than removing it: An unmatched glob either errors or expands literally, so the script must choose which surprise it prefers
✅ setopt nounset turns an unset reference into an error: A misspelled parameter is reported instead of expanding to nothing
✅ ${(q)var} quotes a value for re-input: The expansion flag makes safe quoting explicit instead of leaving it to hand-written escaping
✅ setopt noclobber protects existing files: The option makes > refuse to overwrite a regular file

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

title: PowerShell (7.6)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses PowerShell in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 43/100 · Ecosystem coupling 65/100 · Engineering readiness 61/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ A typed variable or parameter is checked at the boundary: [int]$n and a typed param() block make the binder convert and reject a bad call
✅ Object-oriented: Everything is an object (not strings like Bash)
✅ Classes: PowerShell 5+ has classes
❌ Dynamic typing is the default (T1): A variable takes its type from the value assigned, so a type error is reported only when the statement runs
✅ Interfaces: Can use .NET interfaces
⚠️ Module scope pollution: Import-Module can overwrite commands
❌ Verb-Noun naming: While helpful, couples to conventions



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Constructors: Classes have constructors, [PSCustomObject] for ad-hoc
✅ Factory patterns: Common with New-Object cmdlets
✅ Pipeline objects: Objects flow through pipelines
⚠️ Hashtables: Often used for construction, less structured
⚠️ Global scope: Can create global variables



1.1.3 Memory

✅ .NET GC: Automatic garbage collection
✅ Dispose pattern: IDisposable for resources
⚠️ GC pauses: Non-deterministic .NET GC
⚠️ Disposal is explicit: There is no using block for a resource, so a value is released with try/finally, or by the clean block that a PowerShell 7.3 function runs when it ends



1.1.4 Error

✅ Try/Catch/Finally: Structured exception handling
✅ Typed exceptions: Can catch specific .NET exceptions
⚠️ Terminating vs non-terminating: Two error types, confusing
✅ $ErrorActionPreference: Control error behavior
⚠️ Silent failures: Default is to continue on errors



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Jobs: Background jobs with Receive-Job
⚠️ Workflows are Windows PowerShell only: The workflow keyword is not implemented in PowerShell 7
⚠️ Runspaces: Low-level threading, complex
⚠️ No async/await: The language has no await keyword, even in PowerShell 7
✅ ForEach-Object -Parallel: PowerShell 7+ parallel pipelines
⚠️ Pipeline variable: $_ implicit like Perl



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The runtime is open source under the MIT licence: PowerShell 7 is developed in the open at github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell and has no proprietary runtime component
✅ The engine is .NET: PowerShell 7 runs on .NET (formerly .NET Core), so one runtime assembly runs on every platform .NET supports
✅ Builds ship for Windows, macOS, and Linux: Microsoft publishes a Windows installer, a signed macOS package, and packages for Debian/Ubuntu, RHEL, and Alpine
✅ A module is a portable .NET assembly: A cmdlet written in C# against the .NET API loads on any host running the Core runtime
✅ Nothing in the core language names a Windows API: The built-in cmdlets cover files, processes, and text, so a script that avoids WMI, COM, and the registry providers runs unchanged off Windows



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The type system is borrowed: The types are .NET types, so the language adds convenience syntax and inherits .NET’s type behaviour rather than defining a model of its own
The language ships with a host and a remoting layer: PowerShell is a shell, a session, and a language in one product, so its scope reaches past programming into administration
Help is part of the runtime: Get-Help and Get-Command read metadata from the loaded modules, a design decision that ties documentation to the session rather than to a separate manual
Aliases ship as part of the surface: ls, cd, and cat map to cmdlets, a convenience whose meaning depends on what the session has loaded
Two products share the name: Windows PowerShell 5.1 ships with Windows while PowerShell 7 is the cross-platform line, so a script states which one it targets — a version split, not a language dependency




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Interpreted: Slower than compiled
⚠️ .NET overhead: JIT warmup, GC pauses
✅ Object pipelines: More efficient than text parsing
⚠️ Startup time: Slow to launch



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ PowerShell Gallery: Central repository
✅ Excellent Windows integration: WMI, COM, .NET
✅ VSCode: PowerShell extension excellent
⚠️ Smaller than npm/PyPI: But growing
✅ Cross-platform: PowerShell Core runs everywhere



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Active development: Regular improvements
✅ PowerShell Core: Open source, cross-platform
⚠️ Windows PowerShell frozen: v5.1 last version
✅ Mostly compatible: Migration path exists



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for Windows administration: Best-in-class
✅ Good for DevOps: Configuration management, automation
✅ Azure/Office 365: First-class support
⚠️ Linux: Works but less common
❌ Not for applications: Scripting language



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Discoverable: Get-Command, Get-Help
✅ Consistent: Verb-Noun naming
⚠️ Large surface area: Many cmdlets to learn
⚠️ .NET knowledge helps: But not required



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Readable: Verb-Noun is clear
⚠️ Verbose: Get-ChildItem vs ls
✅ Aliases: Shortcuts available
⚠️ Pipeline syntax: | familiar but object-based



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Pester: Testing framework mature
✅ Debugger: Set-PSBreakpoint, step-through
✅ ISE/VSCode: Integrated debugging
✅ Verbose/Debug streams: Good diagnostics



1.2.8 Security

✅ Execution policy: Script signing available
✅ .NET security: Inherits .NET protections
⚠️ Code injection: Still possible with Invoke-Expression
✅ Constrained language mode: Restrict capabilities




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.

title: Fish (4.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Fish in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 43/100 · Ecosystem coupling 49/100 · Engineering readiness 68/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Values are strings with no declaration: set x 10 and set x abc are the same operation, and nothing states what a name holds (T1)
❌ No sum types: An option that may be absent, numeric, or textual is a list of words, and the reader decodes the convention from the calling code (T4)
❌ No generics: A function is specialised only by its positional arguments, so the same logic is written again for each shape of data (T5)
❌ One namespace for every name: Functions and variables share one flat space, so collisions are avoided by convention — the __fish_-prefixed helper names in the bundled completions are the visible result (T6, T11)
❌ An unset name expands to an empty list: set -q tests whether a name is set, but nothing forces it to be, so a mistyped variable silently expands to nothing (T10)
✅ Lists are values, not strings to be re-split: set a 1 2 3 and $a expand to exactly three arguments, so element structure survives expansion without quoting



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Global is still the default: An assignment without a scope flag reaches the innermost existing scope or the global one, so an accidental write into the caller is easy (C1)
❌ No immutability by default: There is no read-only binding, so any visible name can be reassigned (C2)
✅ set -l gives block scope: A variable declared local inside a function, a begin/end block, a for, a while, or an if disappears at the end of that block
✅ alias is sugar over function: An alias becomes a real function, so the invocation name and the body are separated instead of textually substituted
✅ argparse validates options at the boundary: A function declares its own option spec, so callers do not hand-roll a getopts loop and a bad option fails before the body runs
✅ Configuration lives outside scripts: ~/.config/fish/config.fish, the conf.d/*.fish snippets, and the universal-variable file separate shell setup from script logic



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No allocation syntax: There is no pointer, no address, and no free; lists and strings are allocated by the interpreter
✅ Block scope bounds a value’s lifetime: A set -l list is released at the end of its block, so storage does not leak past the code that created it
✅ Export joins a list on the way out: A list assigned to an exported variable is joined with :, so PATH is edited as a list without building a string by hand
⚠️ Assignment copies the list: set b $a duplicates every element, and there is no way to reference a list without copying it
⚠️ Command substitution is materialised whole: (cmd) builds the entire output before the enclosing command runs, so a large output is held in memory
⚠️ Universal variables outlive the process: set -U writes to fish_variables, so a value persists after the shell exits until it is erased deliberately



1.1.4 Error

❌ No structured error path: A command reports success through $status and text on stderr; there is no exception and no error value (Er1)
❌ Errors are not composable: and and or chain status codes, but a status carries no payload and cannot be returned from a function as data (Er4)
❌ A non-zero status is easy to ignore: A function reports the status of its last command, so a failure in the middle of a block is discarded unless or return follows it (Er3)
✅ $pipestatus reports every stage: Each stage of a pipeline keeps its own status, so a failure is not hidden by a successful last stage
⚠️ Syntax errors are reported with a source position: Fish names the file, line, and column, but only for text it has parsed, so a fault inside a function body is reported when the function is defined
⚠️ An unknown command is a hookable event: fish_command_not_found runs when a command is missing, so the message can be replaced, but the failure remains a status code



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ No concurrency primitives: There is no thread, lock, channel, or await; the only parallel construct is backgrounding with & (K5)
✅ Event handlers decouple producer from consumer: function --on-variable NAME, --on-event, --on-process-exit, and emit let a consumer subscribe without the producer knowing it exists
✅ Processes are the unit of parallelism: Concurrency is expressed with pipes and background jobs, so no shared address space has to be reasoned about
⚠️ Process events are the only synchronisation: A script coordinates jobs by watching exit events or by wait, and no value can be returned from a job
⚠️ Background jobs share the environment: A & job inherits every global and universal variable, so ordering between jobs is unspecified unless the script waits
⚠️ No coprocess: Fish cannot keep a two-way conversation with a child, so an interactive child must be driven through files or a while read loop



1.1.6 Platform

❌ Not a POSIX shell: Fish does not implement the POSIX shell language, so a #!/bin/sh script is a different language and sh -c calls a separate program (P2)
✅ One implementation defines the language: With no standard to satisfy, behaviour is fixed by the fish manual and its release notes
✅ Runs on every Unix-like target: Fish ships on Linux, the BSDs, and macOS, and is packaged by every major distribution
⚠️ Windows support is through an emulation layer: Fish relies on Unix APIs and their semantics, so Windows use goes through WSL, Cygwin, or MSYS2 rather than a native port
⚠️ One implementation is one point of failure: There is no second implementation to test the language’s contract against
⚠️ fish is the default login shell nowhere: A user installs it and sets it as their shell, so availability depends on the host’s configuration



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Fish is deliberately not POSIX: Giving up sh compatibility buys the design freedom that removes word splitting and most quoting noise
Universal variables are a convenience with a lifecycle cost: Persisting a value outside the shell trades reproducibility for ergonomics
Aliases became functions because functions are better: The change breaks the textual-substitution habit from other shells, which is the point of the change
The web-based configuration UI is a front end: fish_config writes plain files under ~/.config/fish, so the browser is not a runtime dependency
Autosuggestions and highlighting are interactive features: They cost start-up work and terminal capability, and they are not part of the scripting language
The Rust port is an implementation change: The language contract is unchanged; the gain is in the codebase, not in what a script may rely on




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Interpreted with no compilation: Every command is parsed and executed as text, and fish offers no ahead-of-time path (R1)
✅ The core is native code: Fish was written in C++ through the 3.x series and was ported to Rust for 4.0, so parsing, expansion, and completion run in compiled code rather than in script
✅ Command substitution does not re-split: (cmd) performs no word splitting or globbing, so a large result is not re-parsed argument by argument
✅ Start-up can be profiled and trimmed: fish --profile-startup measures configuration work and --no-config skips it
⚠️ Start-up runs the configuration snippets: An interactive shell sources config.fish and every file in conf.d, so a heavy prompt or completion setup costs time on each new shell
⚠️ for over a substitution materialises the output: A large (cmd) result is held in memory before the loop starts



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ No package manager in the language: There is no dependency resolver, so plugins are copied into ~/.config/fish by third-party managers such as Fisher or Oh My Fish (Ec1)
⚠️ The ecosystem is small but growing: Completions and prompt themes exist for popular tools, and there are far fewer fish libraries than sh libraries (Ec3)
✅ The bundled completion system is large: complete -c declarations ship with fish and cover hundreds of commands, so everyday completion needs no add-on
✅ fish_config gives a built-in UI: Prompts and themes are edited in a browser against files under ~/.config/fish
✅ Documentation is first-class: The manual, the tutorial, and help <builtin> are maintained with each release
⚠️ Third-party plugin managers own the plugin ecosystem: Fisher and Oh My Fish are unofficial, so the plugin supply chain is not part of the language



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ No breaking-change culture: Fish adds features and documents the few incompatible changes in the release notes
✅ Release notes record every incompatibility: The manual lists removals and behaviour changes for each version, so an upgrade is inspectable
✅ The project ships on a regular cadence: Fish 4.0 was released in February 2025, and further 4.x releases followed it
⚠️ No standards body: The direction of the language follows its maintainers rather than a committee
⚠️ Non-POSIX means the language may keep diverging: With no standard to align to, fish is free to change and is not compelled to hold sh semantics



1.2.4 Domain

❌ It is not a POSIX shell: A fish script runs only under fish, so portable system scripts, configure scripts, and #!/bin/sh entry points cannot be written in fish (D2)
✅ Strong for interactive work: Syntax highlighting, autosuggestions, and completion make the terminal the primary domain
✅ Good for personal automation on a fixed host: Where the interpreter is guaranteed, a fish script is shorter and clearer than its sh equivalent
✅ Lists map to the filesystem naturally: $PATH and command output are lists of paths, and path and string split operate on them directly
⚠️ Weak for distribution: A fish script cannot be shipped to a host without fish, which rules fish out for bootstrap, packaging, and installer code
⚠️ Not a general-purpose language: The model is a shell over external commands, so real data processing moves to other tools



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The tutorial and manual are written for newcomers: Fish ships a tutorial and an FAQ, and each builtin has its own help page
✅ Error messages name the file, line, and column: A beginner sees where the problem is rather than a bare failure
✅ The language is smaller and more regular than sh or zsh: One end closes every block, set is the only binding command, and there is no word splitting to learn
⚠️ Quoting habits from other shells misfire: "$var" and [ -f x ] do not apply, and $var is not split where an sh user expects it to be
⚠️ The builtin vocabulary is large: string, math, path, set, argparse, complete, and status each carry their own option set



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ No word splitting means fewer quotes: $var expands as written, so a path containing a space needs no quoting to survive
✅ One block terminator: end closes if, for, while, switch, and function
✅ One binding form: There is no =, no setenv, and no typeset to choose between
⚠️ and and or begin a line: A boolean continuation puts the operator at the start of the next command, which reads unusually
⚠️ Piping a block needs a wrapper: A multi-command producer must be written as begin ... end before it can be piped
⚠️ switch has no fallthrough: A case ends at the next case, so an intentional fallthrough must be written as a second case



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No test framework in the language: A test is a function that calls the code and checks $status, with no assertion or reporting facility (G1)
❌ Debugging is breakpoint and fish_trace: Fish can pause with breakpoint and print a stack with status stack-trace, but it has no debugger with breakpoints, stepping, and inspection (G2)
❌ Faults appear only on the branch that runs: With no static check, a mistyped variable or a bad list index is found during the run (G3)
✅ fish --no-execute checks syntax without running: A script can be parsed before it is executed
✅ fish_indent --check fails on unformatted code: A shipped formatter gives a cheap consistency gate in a test path
✅ fish --private isolates a test from user state: Configuration, history, and universal variables are left untouched, so a test run is reproducible



1.2.8 Security

❌ Text can re-enter the interpreter: Input assembled from untrusted data and passed to eval, or interpolated into a substituted command, becomes code (Q3)
✅ No word splitting removes a whole class of injection: An unquoted $var does not split or glob, so a value with spaces or * cannot become several arguments or an unexpected path list
✅ string escape and string collect make quoting explicit: Output can be quoted for re-input instead of being concatenated by hand
✅ argv and argparse keep options out of the parser: A function receives its arguments as a list, so a value beginning with - is not silently taken as an option
✅ No memory-safety surface: Lists and strings are interpreter-managed, so a fish script has no buffer to overflow
⚠️ History and universal variables are unencrypted state: Command history and set -U values are written to disk in the user’s configuration, so a secret typed at the prompt is recorded by default




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No general foreign-function interface.
⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Every operation starts a process: time, and therefore energy, is dominated by process startup.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [5].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Fish lowers the coupling that a scripting shell normally imposes on construction and on text handling: set -l gives block scope, $var never splits, lists are first-class, and functions replace textual aliases. Its core score still stops at 43, because the value model has no types, every name is global by default, and an error remains a status code rather than a value. The price is paid elsewhere: fish is not a POSIX shell, so a fish script runs only where fish is installed, and start-up configuration, an unofficial plugin supply chain, and the absence of a test framework hold the platform and ecosystem score to 49.

title: Bash (5.3)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Bash in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 43/100 · Ecosystem coupling 53/100 · Engineering readiness 68/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Everything is strings: No type system whatsoever
❌ No abstractions: Shell functions are commands with positional parameters, and there are no interfaces
⚠️ Associative arrays: Bash 4+ has hashes, but limited
❌ No encapsulation: All variables global unless explicitly local
❌ No modules: Sourcing scripts pollutes namespace
❌ Word splitting: Unquoted variables couple to IFS



1.1.2 Construction

❌ No objects: Not an object-oriented language
❌ No constructors: Everything is imperative scripting
⚠️ Functions: Can simulate construction with functions
❌ No validation: Can’t enforce invariants
❌ Global variables: All variables global unless local
❌ Environment variables: Implicit dependencies everywhere



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Automatic: Shell manages memory for variables
✅ Process-based: Each script is a process, cleaned up on exit
⚠️ File descriptors: Must manually close, can leak
✅ No manual management: Can’t segfault (unless calling C programs)



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exit codes only: Return 0-255, no typed errors
❌ Ignores errors by default: Must use set -e to fail on errors, and a failure is otherwise silent
❌ No exceptions: Can’t catch/throw
⚠️ trap: Can handle signals, but limited



1.1.5 Concurrency

⚠️ Background jobs: & runs in background
❌ No coordination: No semaphores, mutexes in pure bash
⚠️ Pipes: Pipeline concurrency, but limited
❌ Race conditions: Easy to create, hard to avoid
⚠️ Process-based: Fork/exec model, heavyweight



1.1.6 Platform

❌ Path dependencies: Couples to external commands availability
❌ Platform coupling: Bash version, coreutils differences
✅ A POSIX subset is portable across systems: A script limited to POSIX sh runs under dash, ash, ksh, and zsh, and the standard is a published specification
✅ The script is the artifact: A Bash program is a text file that needs only an interpreter on the target, so nothing of the language is deployed with it
✅ The shell is a GNU project with no vendor owner: Bash is developed in the open by the GNU Project under the GPL
❌ The dialect is defined by one implementation: The extensions beyond POSIX ([[ ]], arrays, local, mapfile) are Bash’s own, so a script that uses them depends on Bash and its version (P2)
⚠️ The installed Bash version varies by platform: MacOS ships Bash 3.2 while Linux distributions ship Bash 5.x, so a script that uses newer features fails on the older interpreter



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Interactive use shapes the syntax: History expansion, aliases, and prompt escapes are features for a terminal session, and they are why the language reads oddly inside scripts
The pipeline is the composition model: Programs combine as processes joined by pipes, so composition happens between executables rather than inside one program — a design boundary
Arithmetic is integer-only: $(( )) computes on integers, so decimal work calls an external program — a scope decision rather than a dependency
Universal availability is the goal: The language keeps to what an interpreter can supply on any Unix system, which is why new features arrive slowly




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

❌ Very slow: Interprets every line, with no JIT and no compilation
❌ Process spawning: Fork/exec for every command
❌ String manipulation: Terribly inefficient
✅ Good for orchestration: Fast when calling other programs



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Ubiquitous: On every Unix system
⚠️ No package manager: Manual dependency management
✅ shellcheck: Excellent linter
❌ No IDE support: Basic syntax highlighting only
✅ Coreutils: Standard Unix tools available



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Stable: Bash 3/4/5 mostly compatible
⚠️ Slow evolution: Conservative changes
❌ Fragmentation: Sh, bash, zsh, fish differ
✅ POSIX: Standard helps portability



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for shell automation: Perfect use case
✅ Good for CI/CD: Build scripts, deployment
✅ System administration: Natural domain
❌ Terrible for applications: Not designed for this
❌ No cross-platform: Windows support poor



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Easy to start: Simple commands work
❌ Hard to master: Quoting, word splitting, and unquoted variables are footguns
✅ Good resources: Advanced Bash Scripting Guide



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Quirky: [ vs [[, quoting rules
❌ Verbose: if [ "$x" = "y" ]; then
✅ Pipe-oriented: Natural for Unix philosophy
❌ Special variables: $?, $!, $@, $$



1.2.7 Testing

✅ bats: Bash Automated Testing System exists
⚠️ set -x: Trace execution, but noisy
❌ No debugger: Just echo/printf
✅ shellcheck: Catches many errors



1.2.8 Security

❌ Code injection: Easy with eval, command substitution
❌ Path injection: $PATH manipulation dangerous
❌ No input validation: Everything is strings
❌ Shell injection: Major attack vector




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No general foreign-function interface.
⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.

Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Every operation starts a process: time, and therefore energy, is dominated by process startup.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [5], [6].

Verdict: Bash is a scripting language that trades nearly all separation-of-concerns enforcement for universal availability. Everything is a string, all variables are global by default, and errors are ignored unless explicitly checked. Its main strength is that it runs everywhere and excels at gluing Unix tools together. Its main weakness is pervasive coupling to the platform, the environment, and the availability of external commands. Use Bash for small automation, not for application development.

title: The Criteria: Every Mechanism, Its Harm, and Its Points
text:
Companion to: The Great Language Smackdown · the Scoreboard and the full per-language data · the scoring model

Every language on this site is measured against one inventory of 75 mechanisms — the same list, with the same weights, and the same arithmetic, for all 65. The inventory has three parts: Core coupling (34 mechanisms), Ecosystem coupling (29), and Engineering readiness (12). No language gets a private criterion, and no mechanism is applied to one language and then set aside for another. That is what makes the comparison a comparison: a difference between two scores is a difference in which mechanisms are present, never a difference in how strictly the two languages were judged.
This page explains each criterion. For every mechanism it gives what the mechanism is, the kind of coupling it imposes and why, how harmful it is — the weight tier that removes the points — and a concrete example. The Scoreboard publishes the other half: which mechanisms each language has, and the score that follows. The scoring model gives the arithmetic and the tests that decide presence.


Two parts of a program are coupled where they must agree about one shared thing: a type, a heap, a lock, a name space, a platform ABI, a runtime. The agreement is the cost. It has to be established when the code is written, it has to be maintained while the code lives, and it has to be re-established whenever either side changes.
A language mechanism is a coupling criterion when it forces agreement that the programmer cannot refuse. Three properties decide how much that costs:








Property
Question
Effect on the weight




Breadth
How much of the program has to agree — one call site, one module, or the whole program?
A wider agreement costs more


Escape
Can a programmer opt out of the mechanism locally?
No escape costs more


Silence
Does the language say so, or must a reader discover it?
A silent obligation costs more



A mechanism that makes the whole program agree, with no local way out, and nothing in the language that records the agreement, is High. A mechanism that forces agreement across ordinary code, escapable only by a convention that the whole codebase must keep, is Moderate. A mechanism whose agreement is confined to a boundary, and removable by a contained workaround, is Minor.
That is the whole rationale for the weights. The tier is a judgment about breadth, escape, and silence — not a count of incidents, and not a substitute for measurement.
Every entry names its coupling. After the tier, each entry states the kind of coupling the mechanism imposes and why it cannot be refused: which two parties must agree, what they must agree about, and which property of the language forces the agreement. The kind is the name of the shared resource — a type, a call target, a heap, a schedule, a version, a supply — so the entries read as a catalogue of shared resources rather than as a list of complaints.












Tier
Weight
What the tier asserts
What saturates a dimension




High
−15
Agreement across the whole program, no local escape, and nothing in the language that records it
One High mechanism, alone


Moderate
−8
Agreement across ordinary code, escapable only by a whole-codebase convention
Two Moderate mechanisms


Minor
−4
Agreement confined to a boundary, removable by a contained workaround
Four Minor mechanisms, clamped to −15



Within one dimension the present weights are added and the total is clamped at −15, the weight of one High mechanism. The dimension score is 100 minus that clamped total. The clamp is a rubric choice, not a measurement: it keeps the scores bounded (a dimension never costs more than one severe mechanism), monotone (adding a mechanism never improves the score), and comparable (no score collapses to zero). It is deliberate, and it is arbitrary.



Each entry gives the mechanism’s code and tier, what the mechanism is, the kind of coupling it imposes and why, an example, and — where the criterion is easy to misread — what its presence does not mean.
Presence is a factual question about the language: does the language hand the programmer this construct? It is not a judgment about the code. Every language permits a global; C1 asks whether a global is the default home for state.
A check behind a project switch. Some mechanisms depend on a compiler switch. The mark uses the configuration the language’s own project initialiser writes for the version shown, because that is what a new project gets without a decision. tsc --init writes "strict": true (which sets strictNullChecks), so TypeScript is not charged T10; dotnet new writes <Nullable>enable</Nullable>, so C# is not charged T10; Visual Basic’s compiler default is Option Strict Off and the SDK template sets no OptionStrict, so the narrowing conversion is charged T2. Where the initialiser writes no switch, the compiler default governs. A check that only a separate tool supplies is never counted — that is what T1 already says about mypy in CI.
A mitigation is not an absence. Some languages offer an opt-in construct that avoids a mechanism — @CompileStatic in Groovy, try-with-resources in Java, reified in Kotlin, a lint rule, or a flag the initialiser does not set. The mechanism stays charged, because the default code still pays it and avoiding it needs knowledge the language does not force. The model measures what the language imposes, not what a disciplined team can achieve. If a mitigation lowered the score, two teams on the same language would score differently, and the language would have no score. The mitigation is recorded on the language page as a strength or a trade-off, never as a discount. The line between a mitigation and an absence is the project-switch rule above.
Core (34) Type (14) — T1 · T2 · T3 · T4 · T5 · T6 · T7 · T8 · T9 · T10 · T11 · T12 · T13 · T14 Construction (4) — C1 · C2 · C3 · C4 Memory (4) — M1 · M2 · M3 · M4 Error (4) — Er1 · Er2 · Er3 · Er4 Concurrency (5) — K1 · K2 · K3 · K4 · K5 Platform (3) — P1 · P2 · P3
Meta (29) Performance (3) — R1 · R2 · R3 Ecosystem (7) — Ec1 · Ec2 · Ec3 · Ec4 · Ec5 · Ec6 · Ec7 Evolution (4) — V1 · V2 · V3 · V4 Domain (3) — D1 · D2 · D3 Learning (3) — L1 · L2 · L3 Syntax (3) — S1 · S2 · S3 Testing (3) — G1 · G2 · G3 Security (3) — Q1 · Q2 · Q3





What the Type dimension asks: can the language keep the meaning of a value in one place, or must every reader reconstruct it?


High · −15. A value carries its type at run time, so nothing checks that an operation suits its operand until the operation runs. The meaning of every value becomes a shared agreement between the site that produces it and every site that consumes it, and no tool holds that agreement: it lives in the tests and in the reader’s memory.
Coupling imposed. Type-identity coupling across the whole program: producer and consumer agree on what a value is, and on every operation that may apply to it, and nothing in the source records that agreement. Because the check happens when the operation runs, the agreement survives only while both sides are read together, so a change to one reaches all the others at once.
Example. Python accepts n = 1 and then n = "one", and n + 1 fails only on the path that reaches it, and only for the inputs that take that path. MATLAB, R, SAS, Lua, and every POSIX shell behave the same way.
Presence does not mean a checker is unavailable. The criterion asks whether the language enforces a check. A program that runs mypy --strict in CI has a check the language did not give it, and the score still records the language.



Moderate · −8. The compiler knows the types, but it converts between them implicitly, so a check that would catch a mistake becomes a silent conversion. The conversion rules become the shared resource: every expression depends on a table that nothing forces a reader to know.
Coupling imposed. Conversion coupling: every expression that mixes types agrees with the language’s conversion table rather than with its neighbour. The table is the shared resource, so a reader who does not hold it cannot tell a checked expression from a silently narrowed one, and an implicit conversion hides the moment the meaning changed.
Example. C compiles int i = 3.7; and discards the fraction, and lets an integer stand in for a pointer. COBOL converts between two different PICTURE clauses on a MOVE without complaint. Visual Basic’s Option Strict Off default admits a narrowing conversion and a late-bound call.



Moderate · −8. Which code a call reaches is decided by the value’s run-time type rather than by a declared contract. The set of operations a value must answer becomes a shared agreement that no declaration holds, so a rename in one module breaks a caller in another — and only at run time.
Coupling imposed. Call-target coupling: a caller and a callee agree on a name and an arity that no declaration enforces, and the agreement must hold for every type that can arrive at the call site. Because the target is chosen from the value, the coupling spans types the author of the call never named.
Example. Erlang resolves Mod:Fun(Args) when it is called, so a missing function fails there; Elixir and Clojure choose a protocol or a pattern clause from the value they receive; Ruby and Python resolve an attribute at the moment of the call.
Presence does not mean T1. Objective-C is statically typed at the pointer level and still dispatches every message at run time, so it is charged T3 and not T1. TypeScript is statically typed and still reaches a method through the prototype at run time, so it is charged the same way. Duck typing is about which code runs; T1 is about what a value is.



Minor · −4. The language cannot declare that a value is one of several alternatives and have the compiler track which one. The alternatives are encoded by convention, so the tag and its payload are a shared resource that every consumer re-derives, and the compiler cannot prove that a consumer handles every case.
Coupling imposed. Encoding coupling: producer and consumer agree on how an alternative is written down — a tag beside a payload, a nil, a nullable column — rather than on the alternative itself. The encoding is the shared resource, so a new case has to be taught to every reader of it, and exhaustiveness stays a convention.
Example. Go has no sum type, so “a value or a failure” is a pair and a nil check stands in for a match. SQL models an alternative as nullable columns, and the caller must know the encoding. Rust’s enum and C++’s std::variant are the constructs whose absence is charged.
Minor because it is containable. A constructor plus its accessors can confine the cost to one place — but never to zero, because exhaustiveness stays unchecked.



Minor · −4. The language cannot write an algorithm once over a type parameter, so it duplicates the code per type or falls back on one universal representation. That representation becomes the shared resource, and every user casts out of it, so the type is known by convention.
Coupling imposed. Representation coupling: every use of the algorithm agrees on the one representation it can carry — void *, Object, interface{} — and casts back out by hand. The universal representation is the shared resource, so the real type of a value becomes knowledge held by the programmer rather than a fact held by the compiler.
Example. Pre-generics Java needed (String) list.get(0) from an Object container; C passes void * with a callback; Go before 1.18 used interface{}; SQL has no type parameter at all and generates DDL per column type instead.
Presence does not mean the checking half of generics. A language with generics whose parameters cannot be constrained still leaves a gap — but that gap is charged under T2 or T3. T5 records only the absence of the type parameter itself.



Moderate · −8. The language has a single flat name space, so two declarations with the same name collide whichever module they live in. The global name space is the clearest shared resource there is: every name is a claim on it, and a new module can break an unrelated one.
Coupling imposed. Name coupling over one flat space: every declaration competes for the same set of identifiers, so two modules that never call each other are coupled through the name they both want. The name space is the shared resource, and nothing local bounds a claim on it, which is why the convention that resolves it — a prefix — must be kept by the whole codebase.
Example. Two C libraries that both define init cannot be linked without renaming one, which is why C libraries prefix their symbols (gl_, png_). Lua keeps every global in one shared table. An assembler puts every global symbol in one flat symbol table.
Presence asks about the mechanism, not the idiom. MATLAB is not charged, because +pkg folders scope a name, and R is not charged, because a package declares a NAMESPACE. C is charged, because a header’s declarations all land in one translator-level name space.



Minor · −4. The type parameter is present in the source and gone from the artifact, and the program can inspect and alter its own structure at run time. The erased type is a shared resource that no longer travels with the value, so a consumer must recover it by convention — and reflection turns every private field into a reachable one.
Coupling imposed. Type-recovery coupling at the boundary: the consumer agrees with the producer on a type argument that the artifact no longer carries. The agreement sits where the cast is written, so it holds per call site and cannot be checked back at the place the value was made.
Example. Java’s List<String> is a List at run time, so get(0) returns Object and the cast is unchecked. Objective-C’s id carries no compile-time type at all. TypeScript’s types exist in the editor and the build, and not in the running program.
Minor because the cost sits at the boundary where the type is recovered — a cast, a Class<T> token, an isKindOfClass: test — not in the body of the algorithm.



Minor · −4. A symbol such as +, ==, or [] takes its meaning from the operand types. A symbol is a shared resource with one meaning by default, and overloading makes that meaning depend on a lookup the reader has to perform.
Coupling imposed. Symbol-meaning coupling: the reader agrees with the definer on what + or == does for the type at hand. The meaning is resolved by a lookup at the use, so the coupling is real but bounded to one expression — the reader resolves one type and the answer arrives.
Example. C++’s << both shifts and inserts into a stream. Scala’s + on a Set performs a union. Racket’s + accepts exact and inexact numbers and returns whichever type the operands dictate.
Minor because the operator still carries a type signature, so its meaning is discoverable by resolving one type — unlike a macro, which can mean anything at all.



Minor · −4. The only way to use two types through one interface is to place both in an inheritance chain. The base type becomes a shared resource that the types must be placed into, which forces an “is-a” commitment wherever the domain has only “does-this”, and a change to the base changes every subtype.
Coupling imposed. Hierarchy coupling: a type agrees to be placed under the interface it will be used through, so it inherits its base’s identity and its base’s future changes. The chain is the shared resource, so a change at the root reaches every leaf, and an unrelated type must be moved into the chain before it can play the role.
Example. Eiffel’s polymorphism runs through its inheritance and genericity rules. C approximates it with a struct holding function pointers, or with a void * and a convention. TclOO expresses a shared protocol as a class or a mixin rather than a declared type.
Minor, and the cheapest to remove. Go’s implicit interfaces, Rust’s traits, and Elixir’s protocols supply polymorphism without a chain, so those languages are not charged.



Moderate · −8. Any reference can be the absent value, and nothing in the type says whether it is. “May be absent” becomes a shared resource that every consumer must guard, and no signature records the guard, so each reader repeats the check or forgets it.
Coupling imposed. Absence coupling: every consumer agrees with every producer about whether a reference may be missing, and no signature records the answer. The unwritten agreement is the shared resource, so each guard is written per use and each omission stays invisible until the missing value arrives.
Example. Java compiles String s = null; s.length(). SQL’s NULL is compatible with every domain and propagates through three-valued logic, so IF x = 5 is not true when x is NULL. In PL/SQL a variable that is never assigned is NULL. A null pointer in Assembly is a zero register, and a load from it is an ordinary instruction.
Presence does not mean “the language has an absent value”. Kotlin’s String? against String, Swift’s optionals, Rust’s Option<T>, and TypeScript’s string | null under strict are exactly the construct whose absence is charged, which is why those languages are not charged T10.



Moderate · −8. There is no construct that declares what a module exposes and what it keeps. The boundary is the shared resource, and its absence means every declaration is reachable by every consumer, so an internal change can break an unrelated caller.
Coupling imposed. Visibility coupling in its total form: every declaration is a public fact, so a consumer may depend on anything a producer contains. The missing boundary is what makes the coupling unbounded — a change to an internal name travels to callers the module never intended to have.
Example. A C header makes everything it declares public, and static is the only file-scoped boundary. A POSIX shell script sources another script into the same variable space. VBScript’s ExecuteGlobal writes into the same global scope. Scratch exposes every sprite’s blocks with no declared interface.
Presence does not mean “no files”. Splitting code across files is not a boundary. Go is not charged, because a package-level unexported name is a real boundary, and neither is MATLAB, whose +pkg and private folders hide what they do not export.



Moderate · −8. A call’s signature says what it returns, not what it does. The effects a call may perform — input and output, mutation of shared state, exceptions, randomness — are a shared resource that no declaration carries, so every caller learns them by reading the body or by testing. A change to an effect is invisible to every caller [1].
Coupling imposed. Effect coupling: a caller agrees with a callee on what the call may do, and reads that agreement from the body rather than from the signature. Because the effect set is unwritten, every caller is exposed to every effect the implementation may later acquire.
Example. Haskell’s IO, PureScript’s Effect, and Unison’s abilities put the effects in the type, so a function cannot hide a socket behind a pure signature. In Java, Python, Go, and C a function that writes a file, mutates a global, and throws looks like any other function.
Held at Moderate, not High. The breadth is the whole program — any call may perform any effect — but nothing breaks when the effect set is wrong. The cost is the reading and refactoring work an untracked effect adds, not a missed check, so the mechanism does not carry a High mechanism’s weight.
Presence records whether the type states the effects. Every language has effects. Haskell, PureScript, Unison, Lean 4, and Rocq carry them in the type; so do Nim (its raises and tags lists are part of a proc type) and D (pure, nothrow, and @nogc are constituents of the function type). Java’s throws clause is a signature annotation, not part of the method type, so Java is charged.



Moderate · −8. The language has two kinds of function — one that may suspend and one that may not — and the two do not compose. A synchronous function cannot call an asynchronous one without a bridge, so the kind spreads outward through the call graph and every caller must agree on it. The kind is a shared resource that a change in one function imposes on the whole chain [2].
Coupling imposed. Function-kind coupling along the call chain: a caller must share the kind of its callee, so the kind propagates from the smallest suspending leaf to the entry point. The kind is the shared resource, so adopting it at one site is a decision that the whole chain must repeat.
Presence records a function-kind split, not the existence of concurrency. Go’s goroutines and Erlang’s processes are concurrency without a second function kind, so neither is charged.
Example. In JavaScript, C#, and Dart an async function returns a future, and a plain function that calls it must itself become async or block. Rust’s async fn returns a Future that only an executor drives, Nim’s {.async.} proc can be awaited only inside another async proc, and Python’s async def and Kotlin’s suspend draw the same line.



Minor · −4. The language can call code outside its own type system, and nothing checks that the two sides agree. The foreign interface — argument order, ownership, layout, lifetime, and error convention — is a shared resource held by a hand-written declaration, so a mismatch is found at run time or not at all.
Coupling imposed. ABI coupling at the foreign boundary: the two sides agree on argument order, layout, ownership, and error convention through a hand-written declaration that neither compiler validates. The declaration is the shared resource, so the agreement holds until run time and then fails as corruption rather than as a diagnostic.
Example. Rust’s extern "C" block is an unchecked promise. Python’s ctypes and Ruby’s Fiddle accept any signature. JNI requires the C side to agree by hand, and a Java exception that crosses the boundary unwinds nothing on the other side.
Minor because the boundary is containable to one module — but never zero, because the compiler cannot check across it.
Covers the native boundary, not a boundary inside one runtime. Unison 1.0 added a C FFI, so it is charged. PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server can load native code through a user-defined function, so the procedural SQL dialects are charged with them. Solidity calls only inside the EVM, and a shell reaches foreign code by starting a process, so neither is charged. The readiness axis prices the other side of the same boundary, under Y9: a language is charged there for having no interface, and here for the interface being unchecked. Both can be charged at once.




What the Construction dimension asks: can the language keep state local, and can a value only come into existence through a path that establishes its invariant?


High · −15. The default home for a value is a global that any code can read and write; state is local only when the programmer asks for it. The global is the widest shared resource there is — the whole program is its consumer — so any module can change it, and any change can surprise any reader.
Coupling imposed. State coupling to one cell: every reader and every writer of the global agrees on its meaning at each instant, and the whole program is a party to that agreement. Because the cell has no owner, no module can change its own behaviour without the possibility of changing another’s.
Example. Python’s module-level names and global. MATLAB’s base workspace, and R’s global environment with <<-. A POSIX shell, where x=1 inside a function can write the caller’s variable. COBOL’s WORKING-STORAGE. A PL/SQL package variable, which lives for the whole session.
Presence asks whether a global is the default. Every language permits a global. Kotlin and Rust make top-level state immutable unless it is declared otherwise, so neither is charged.



Minor · −4. A binding, and the value behind it, can be changed unless the programmer says otherwise. “Who may write this?” then has no default answer, so every reader has to trace the writes.
Coupling imposed. Write-permission coupling: every holder of a binding must know which other holders may change it, and the language states no default answer. The permissive default makes the coupling silent at the definition and forces it to be reconstructed at every read.
Example. Java fields are mutable unless they are final; C++ members unless they are const; a MATLAB array is mutable with no const at all; a SAS DATA step may overwrite the dataset it is reading.
Minor because immutability is usually a local decision. A language that inverts the default — Rust’s let with mut, Haskell’s bindings — is not charged.



Minor · −4. Creating a value and obtaining its storage are one act, and the construction cannot be redirected to different storage. The storage site becomes a shared resource, so a caller cannot choose where a value lives, and the code that builds a value cannot be separated from the code that reserves it.
Coupling imposed. Storage coupling: the constructor and the caller must agree on where the value will live, because the language offers no way to separate the act of construction from the act of reservation. The agreement is narrow — one allocation site — which is why a single indirection removes it.
Example. In C a value exists only because storage was reserved and then filled, and a constructor is a naming convention over malloc. In Assembly the reservation is a register or a stack slot, and nothing constructs.
Minor because one indirection restores the separation. C++’s placement construction and allocator-aware containers, and Rust’s Box and Vec::with_capacity, build in storage that already exists, so those languages are not charged.



Minor · −4. A value of the type can exist without having passed any validating path. The invariant becomes a shared resource that nothing enforces, so every consumer either re-validates or simply trusts.
Coupling imposed. Invariant coupling: every consumer must agree with every producer that a value is valid, because no constructor stands between the type and its instances. The agreement is silent — a consumer cannot tell a validated value from an unvalidated one.
Example. A C struct is uninitialized memory until each field is assigned. A Fortran variable can be referenced before it is set. A Solidity contract without a constructor is deployed with whatever the default state is. In a POSIX shell a variable comes into existence on first assignment, and no construct can state an invariant about it.
Minor because the invariant can often be re-established cheaply — a smart constructor, a factory, a private field plus a validating entry point. The criterion is the same either way.




What the Memory dimension asks: can the language state when storage and other resources are released, and who owns them?


High · −15. The programmer decides when storage is released, and the program is wrong if the decision is wrong in either direction — a missed release leaks, and a doubled release corrupts. The heap becomes a shared resource, and “who frees this, and when” is a question that every path through the program must answer identically.
Coupling imposed. Lifetime coupling: every path that holds a value must agree on when it stops being valid, because the decision is written per path rather than once for the value. The agreement is global in effect and local in expression, so one divergent path corrupts what the others still trust.
Example. malloc and free in C. A stack frame plus malloc plus free in Assembly. New and Dispose in Turbo Pascal. Zig’s allocator.free. In Fortran, allocate and deallocate are written by hand for a pointer, and a missing statement leaks.
Presence follows the ordinary path. A language with an optional collector for one allocation class is charged when the ordinary path is manual, because the ordinary path carries the cost.



Moderate · −8. Memory returns when the collector decides, not when the last reference goes away. The heap becomes a shared resource whose release schedule the program cannot name, so a latency-sensitive path is coupled to a component it never calls.
Coupling imposed. Schedule coupling: every path that depends on latency and the runtime must agree on when memory returns, because the release is the collector’s decision and not the program’s. The agreement is unavoidable and unnamed: no declaration states the schedule that the path is relying on.
Example. The JVM family (Java, Kotlin, Scala, Groovy, Clojure), the CLR (C#, F#), Go, Crystal, D, Nim, OCaml, Haskell, Dart, Unison, and the Lisp family (Common Lisp, Racket, Scheme). Elixir, Erlang, JavaScript, and Ruby each collect on their own runtime’s schedule, and TypeScript inherits the JavaScript runtime’s.
Presence does not mean “the language has a collector for one thing”. Reference counting is deterministic and is not M2: Swift’s ARC and Delphi’s strings and interfaces release at the last reference, and Delphi on Windows frees objects explicitly, so neither is charged. Objective-C is charged, because an autorelease pool defers a release past the last reference and a Core Foundation handle is released by hand.



Minor · −4. Nothing runs automatically when a scope ends, so a resource is released in a finally, by a project convention, or not at all. The resource — a lock, a file, a connection — is shared, and its release depends on every path remembering.
Coupling imposed. Release coupling: every exit path must run the same release, because no scope boundary runs it for them. The agreement is duplicated on every branch, so its cost grows with the number of paths rather than with the resource.
