title: Smalltalk (ANSI Smalltalk)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Smalltalk in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 47/100 · Ecosystem coupling 72/100 · Engineering readiness 57/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ No static type check: A variable has no declared type, and a message send is resolved when it executes, so a mismatch is reported at run time (T1)
❌ A receiver’s type is a protocol, not a class: Any object that answers a selector is acceptable, and the compiler checks no such promise (T3)
❌ No sum types and no generics: An alternative is a class hierarchy or a Symbol and a collection holds Objects, so both the branch and the element type are conventions (T4, T5)
❌ No namespaces: A class is entered in the one global system dictionary, so a class name collision is a system-wide event (T6)
❌ nil is an object, not an absent type: A send to nil raises MessageNotUnderstood rather than failing a static check (T10)
✅ Message passing separates a request from its implementation: A send names a selector, and the receiver chooses the method that runs



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Global mutable state is the default: A class variable, a class instance variable, or a Smalltalk at: global is reachable from every method, so construction couples to shared state (C1)
❌ Objects are mutable by default: An accessor writes a field in place, and nothing in the language makes an object immutable (C2)
✅ Every operation is a message: +, new, and size are all sends, so a call site does not distinguish an operator from a method
✅ The class object holds the constructor and its initialize hook: new and new: are class-side methods and a subclass can override the setup that follows
⚠️ The class browser compiles into the running system: A change is made in the live image, and the deployed artifact is the image rather than the source files
⚠️ Open classes allow a change from anywhere: Any tool or package can add a method to Object, so a change has system-wide reach



1.1.3 Memory

❌ A garbage collector reclaims memory: Collection runs on the virtual machine’s schedule, so the program cannot choose when a pause happens (M2)
❌ No RAII: A resource is released by an explicit message, though ensure: or ifCurtailed: runs a release block on the way out (M3)
❌ No ownership model: A reference is an untracked alias, and only the virtual machine knows when an object is unreachable (M4)
✅ No manual deallocation: An object becomes garbage, and no free message exists
✅ ensure: binds a release to a protected block: The block runs on a normal return and on a signal that unwinds through it
✅ Collection is invisible in the source: An instantiation is new, and no deallocation is ever written



1.1.4 Error

❌ Failures are signals and no selector describes them: A send may raise any Error subclass, so the failure set is not readable from the method name (Er2)
✅ on:do: installs a structured handler: A handler is bound to a class of signal for the duration of a block, and it returns a value to the sender
✅ ensure: and ifCurtailed: separate the normal path from the cleanup path: The cleanup runs however the block exits
✅ MessageNotUnderstood is a defined signal: A send that no method implements raises it with the receiver and the selector
✅ resume:, return:, and retry state the recovery: A handler can resume the signal, return a value, or re-run the block
⚠️ No handler is checked to exist: The compiler does not know which signals a send raises, so the handler is written from documentation



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Process and Semaphore are part of the class library: A scheduler multiplexes processes, and a semaphore is the synchronisation primitive
✅ Monitor and SharedQueue are in the class library: The common coordination patterns ship with the environment
✅ Delay suspends a process for a stated time: The scheduler resumes it, so a timed wait is a library call rather than a system call
⚠️ Every object is reachable from every process: The class library supplies the synchronisation primitives, and the discipline that keeps two processes apart from one shared object is the programmer’s
⚠️ The classic virtual machine decides when a process runs: Priority decides which process resumes, and the switch points belong to the interpreter, so a process at the same priority can hold the CPU through a tight loop



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The language is standardised independently of a vendor: ANSI INCITS 319-1998 fixes the syntax and the protocols of the standard class library
✅ Several independent implementations exist: Squeak, Pharo, VisualWorks, GNU Smalltalk, and GemStone/S each run the language
✅ GNU Smalltalk runs a text file as an executable: gst file.st needs no image, so a program can be deployed as source
⚠️ The deployment unit is a virtual-machine image: An image carries the classes, the methods, and the live state, so a deployment couples to one virtual machine
⚠️ The image format is not standardised: A program moves between dialects through source, not through an image file
⚠️ Portability stops at the dialect’s tools: Monticello, Metacello, and Seaside are dialect packages, so a portable program stays within the ANSI subset



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The image is a deliberate development model: A running system is editable and the image is the artifact, which is the point of the environment
Live coding is a workflow choice: A change is compiled into the running system; the compiler is the mechanism, and the workflow is the choice
Open classes are deliberate flexibility: A method can be added to any class, and the global reach of that change is the price
The absent static typing is a design choice: No annotation is required, so the discipline is the programmer’s
Everything is an object by design: Classes, blocks, and nil are objects, and the uniformity is the language’s identity
Niche adoption is an outcome: The language predates and influenced the mainstream object-oriented languages




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Modern dialects compile the hot path: The Cog virtual machine of Pharo and Squeak compiles a method to machine code once it becomes hot
✅ The virtual machine is the optimisation boundary: The runtime optimises a method, so no source-level tuning is needed to reach the native path
✅ In-line caches make a polymorphic send cheap: A send site caches the receiver’s class and its method, so a repeated send costs one lookup
⚠️ Steady-state speed is below a statically compiled language: A dynamic send is a polymorphic call site, so a numeric inner loop is slower than in Ada or C
⚠️ Warm-up precedes peak speed: The interpreter runs a method until the runtime decides to compile it



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is small and centred on a few communities: Pharo and Squeak carry most of the active library work, and commercial Smalltalk is a niche (Ec3)
✅ Pharo and Squeak are active open-source communities: Each ships a maintained image with tools, a package manager, and libraries
✅ The commercial implementations are long-lived: VisualWorks, VA Smalltalk, and GemStone/S have decades of use
✅ Metacello and Monticello give package management and versioning: A package is loaded from a repository with a version map
✅ Seaside and Glamorous Toolkit add depth: A continuation-based web framework and a moldable development environment are both maintained
⚠️ A library is often image- or dialect-specific: A package loaded into one dialect usually needs adaptation for another



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Pharo releases on a regular cadence with a migration guide: A release names the changes to the image and the tools
✅ A file-in of source is the migration unit across dialects: A program’s classes and methods load into another image
✅ The ANSI standard is a stable foundation: The standardised language does not move under a program that stays within it
⚠️ Later work is dialect-specific: Each community extends the class library and the tools on its own, so the dialects diverge
⚠️ A dialect fork is the usual form of a break: Squeak and Pharo diverged from a shared image, so a program may target one community only
⚠️ The image carries its own history: An old image can hold classes and methods that the source no longer describes, so a migration needs care



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for prototyping and live systems: The image, the class browser, and the debugger let a system be built and changed while it runs
✅ A strong fit for exploratory modelling: The uniform object model and the interactive debugger support a step-by-step design
✅ A web application has a framework: Seaside serves a deployed web application with continuations, and GemStone/S adds a transactional object store
✅ The environment is the development tool: A refactoring browser, a debugger, and a test runner are part of the image
⚠️ Commercial product work is rare today: A new product team usually picks another language, so precedents and hiring are scarce



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The image-based workflow is unfamiliar and steep: A program is edited inside a running system, and a newcomer must learn the browser, the debugger, and the image at once (L1)
❌ The uniform message model must be internalised: Control flow is a message (ifTrue:, whileTrue:) and class creation is a message, which is unlike an expression-based language
✅ The debugger teaches by inspection: A MessageNotUnderstood opens on the failing frame with the receiver and the selector in view
✅ The browser shows the whole system: A method, its senders, and its implementors are reachable from one tool
⚠️ Little feedback arrives before run time: With no static check, a mistake appears when the path executes



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ A message send has three small forms: Unary (size), binary (+), and keyword (at:put:), and all three are sends
✅ Blocks give inline control flow: [:x | x + 1] is a closure in the same syntax as everywhere else
✅ Cascades group several sends to one receiver: a add: 1; add: 2 sends both messages to a
✅ The grammar is small: The language is famously described in a few lines, and the class library carries the rest
⚠️ A keyword message can nest confusingly: a b: c d: e parses by fixed rules, so a reader must recall them



1.2.7 Testing

❌ A selector or type error appears only when the line runs: With no static check, the first execution of a path is the first check of it (G3)
✅ TestCase and the SUnit runner ship with the environment: A test class with test-prefixed methods is run by the test runner
✅ The debugger opens on the failing test frame: A failure can be inspected and fixed in the running system
✅ should:raise: asserts on a signal: A test states the error class it expects
✅ The test suite lives in the image with the code: A test is a class beside the class it tests
⚠️ An unexecuted path is untested and unchecked: A test covers the branches it runs, and a dynamic mistake in another branch waits



1.2.8 Security

❌ The absent static typing is a security-relevant gap: A selector error, a wrong argument, or a type confusion is detected at run time, and an unexecuted path is not checked (Q2)
✅ Memory safety is the virtual machine’s responsibility: The machine manages references, so a buffer overflow or a use-after-free is not expressible in Smalltalk source
✅ The standard class library exposes no address: There is no pointer value in the language for a program to misuse
⚠️ The image persists running state to a file: An image is a serialised object graph, so a value that should not be saved can be written into the deployed artifact
⚠️ perform: reaches a method by a computed selector: A selector built from input invokes code the source does not name
⚠️ Compiler evaluate: compiles a string into the running system: An untrusted string must never reach it




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [5]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [6].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [7].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

The core score is nevertheless in the middle band, because the language’s own constructs force coupling elsewhere: no static type check, no namespaces, no module boundary, no ownership model, global mutable state by default, and open classes that let any tool change any class. title: Rocq (9.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Rocq in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 85/100 · Ecosystem coupling 69/100 · Engineering readiness 49/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Dependent types decouple a specification from its implementation: A type may mention a value, so a sorted list or a length-indexed vector is a type and a term of that type is the proof that the specification holds
✅ The Curry–Howard correspondence equates propositions with types: A proposition is a type and a proof is a program, so logic and computation are written in one language
✅ Inductive types define the data and the proofs over it together: An Inductive declaration fixes the constructors, and recursion over them is checked for coverage
✅ The universe hierarchy stratifies types: Prop holds propositions, Set holds program data, and Type holds types, so a type cannot contain itself
✅ Type classes and records express an interface: A Class or a Record states a structure and instance resolution selects the implementation, so reuse does not require inheritance
⚠️ Definitional equality is the checker’s equality: Two terms that are equal only up to a lemma are not interchangeable without a rewrite, so an implementation must be shaped to compute the way the checker reduces



1.1.2 Construction

✅ The logic core is pure: A Gallina term has no side effect, so building a value cannot change shared state
✅ The tactic language is separate from the term it builds: A proof script constructs a Gallina term, and the kernel checks that term, so the proof strategy and the proof object are distinct artifacts
✅ Definitions are checked terms: Definition and Fixpoint each name a term that the kernel type-checks before it is used
✅ Modules and functors confine names: A Module Type states a signature and a Module implements it, so a name is reachable only through its path
✅ Extraction separates verified construction from the runtime: Extraction emits OCaml, Haskell, or Scheme, so verification is decoupled from the implementation language
⚠️ Totality is required: Every Fixpoint must be shown to terminate, so a construction that is correct but not obviously decreasing needs a measure or a well-founded relation



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The logic core names no memory: A Gallina term has no address, no allocation, and no free operation, so a proof cannot couple to a memory layout
✅ Collection belongs to the runtime: The checker is an OCaml program with its own collector, and the extracted program uses its target language’s collector
✅ Reduction strategy is a tactic choice: cbn, cbv, lazy, vm_compute, and native_compute select how a term is reduced, so checking cost is stated where it is needed
⚠️ A large reduction consumes memory without a visible allocation: A vm_compute or native_compute over a large term can exhaust memory while the source names no allocation
⚠️ native_compute compiles a module through OCaml: It evaluates the term through code the OCaml compiler produced at proof time, trading the kernel’s own reduction for speed



1.1.4 Error

✅ A wrong proof is a type error: A term that does not inhabit the goal is rejected when it is checked, before any extracted code runs
✅ Tactic failure is a structured signal: Ltac combinators such as try, repeat, first, and progress branch on success and failure, so a tactic script has a recovery path
✅ Fail asserts that a command is rejected: A development can test that a wrong proof fails, which keeps a tactic honest
✅ Qed runs the kernel check and Defined records the term: The sealing decision is explicit at the end of a proof
⚠️ Admitted and admit leave a gap the checker accepts: A development can be declared complete with an unproved lemma, so the guarantee holds only if the development contains none
⚠️ Axiom, Parameter, and Hypothesis add an assumption without a proof: The soundness of a result is relative to the axiom set it used



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ The logic core is sequential: A Gallina term is a pure value, so there is no shared mutable state in the language to race
✅ A development is checked file by file in parallel: coq_makefile -j and rocq makefile -j compile independent .v files in separate processes
✅ Asynchronous proofs run in a worker process: -async-proofs on delegates a proof to another process, so a document and the proof that fills it are decoupled
⚠️ The tactic monad threads one proof state: A tactic acts on the current goal, so the tactics in a script are ordered even though the resulting term is pure
⚠️ Parallel checking is a tool option, not a language guarantee: An interactive session with -async-proofs off is sequential, and the option is the user’s choice



1.1.6 Platform

❌ Rocq is not a general-purpose programming language: A term is written to be checked, and Gallina has no I/O, no foreign-function call, and no runtime of its own (P1)
❌ A deployed program exists only in the extraction target: Extraction emits OCaml, Haskell, or Scheme, so one development reaches three ecosystems but the verified artifact runs only as a program in another language (P1)
✅ The checker is an ordinary OCaml program: It builds and runs on the platforms OCaml supports, including Linux, macOS, and Windows
⚠️ The OCaml toolchain is required to build the checker: A plugin or a native_compute build depends on the OCaml environment, not only on Rocq itself



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Dependent types trade automation for certainty: The specification lives in the type, and every refinement obligation is discharged by a tactic or by hand
The ecosystem is small by scope: Rocq targets verification and mathematics, so a general-purpose library set is out of scope rather than missing
The academic audience is the intended one: The domain mark records a scope decision, not a defect of the language
Tactic scripts are a workflow choice: Ltac, Ltac2, and ssreflect are ways to construct a term, and a proof can also be written directly as a term
Prop erasure is a deliberate design: A proof in Prop is erased from the extracted program, so its cost is a checking cost rather than a runtime cost
Totality is required for a consistent logic: The termination obligation is the price of using one language for proofs and for programs




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The measured workload is proof checking: The kernel checks a term once, so the checking algorithm, not a program’s runtime, sets the cost
✅ Independent files are checked in parallel: -j and -async-proofs spread a build across the available cores
✅ A heavy reduction can run as compiled code: native_compute evaluates a term at the speed of compiled OCaml
✅ Extracted code runs at the target language’s speed: The deployed program’s performance is the target compiler’s concern
⚠️ Checking time grows with the proof: A large vm_compute, a deep induction, or a long auto search can take minutes, and the cost is paid on every rebuild



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is small and centred on academia: Outside the standard library, mathcomp, and the Rocq Platform, the set of maintained packages is thin (Ec3)
✅ opam installs Rocq, its libraries, and its plugins: The OCaml package manager is the distribution channel
✅ The Rocq Platform pins a compatible set: A Platform release fixes versions of libraries and plugins that are known to work together
✅ The landmark libraries are mature: mathcomp (Mathematical Components), stdpp, and CompCert are long-lived and actively maintained
⚠️ A plugin extends the checker from inside: An OCaml plugin reaches the engine directly, which is powerful and also couples the plugin to a Rocq version



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The rename from Coq to Rocq preserved compatibility: Rocq 9.0 continued to accept the Coq.* module paths and the coq* command names, so an existing development kept checking
✅ A release is versioned and pinned: opam records the Rocq version and the library versions a development was checked against
✅ Deprecation precedes removal: A renamed tactic or lemma warns before it stops working
✅ The changelog names each change: A release records the renamed lemmas and tactics with their replacements
⚠️ Library and tactic names do move between releases: A development that pins no version may need edits when it is checked under a later Rocq



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The domain is formal verification and mathematics: The language states and checks proofs, and it is not chosen for general software work (D1)
✅ It is a strong fit for the domain it targets: Machine-checked mathematics and verified software are what the system is built to do
✅ The CompCert verified C compiler is a landmark result: A realistic C compiler was proved correct in Coq, which is evidence that the domain fit works at scale
✅ Critical cryptography and kernel components have been verified in it: Rocq has been used to verify cryptographic primitives and operating-system kernel components
✅ Extraction bridges to an industrial artifact: A verified algorithm is extracted to OCaml or Haskell and then deployed
⚠️ A proof of a program is not the program: The extracted code is correct relative to the extracted semantics, and a declared axiom weakens the guarantee



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The learning curve is very steep: Dependent type theory, universes, and the calculus of inductive constructions must be understood before a nontrivial development can be written (L1)
❌ Tactic scripting is a second language: Ltac/Ltac2 and the ssreflect idioms are a distinct skill from writing a term
✅ A first proof is short to write: intros, reflexivity, and Qed complete a small example in the first session
✅ The reference material is thorough and maintained: The Rocq reference manual, the Software Foundations course, and the mathcomp book are stable resources
⚠️ An error message must be read against the goal state: The checker reports a goal and a term, and interpreting the report takes practice



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The core grammar is small: A term is an application, a fun, a match, or a let, and the proof language is a sequence of commands
✅ Notation and scopes localise a symbol: A notation applies only where its scope is open, so + can mean different things in different developments
✅ Inductive and record declarations read as their structure: Record point := { x : nat; y : nat } names the fields in one line
✅ Proof bullets give a proof a tree shape: -, +, *, and { ... } nest the goals, so the structure is visible
⚠️ Notation interaction is local knowledge: Two declarations for the same infix symbol, with associativity and precedence levels, can parse a term in a way the reader does not expect



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Checking is the test of the proved property: A development that compiles has been checked by the kernel, so the property needs no separate suite
✅ Qed seals a proof and runs the kernel check: The term is re-checked at sealing, independently of the tactics that built it
✅ Fail and Succeed test a command’s outcome: A regression test can require that a specific wrong proof is rejected
✅ Example gives an inline test: An anonymous lemma checks a claim at the point where it is stated
✅ coqdoc renders a checked example into the documentation: A documented example is the same checked term
⚠️ Only the stated property is checked: An Admitted lemma or an Axiom is accepted on trust, so the guarantee holds only over the proved fragment



1.2.8 Security

✅ The kernel check gives the strongest assurance available for the stated property: A Qed term is checked against the calculus, so the result holds as long as the kernel is trusted
✅ Gallina has no memory operation to misuse: There is no pointer arithmetic and no manual free in the logic core
✅ native_compute is opt-in: The compiled reduction is selected explicitly and is disabled by default, so the kernel’s own reduction remains the default path
⚠️ The trusted base includes the kernel, the extraction, and any axiom: A kernel defect, an extraction defect, or a declared axiom is outside the proof
⚠️ Extracted code inherits the target language’s safety: An OCaml or Scheme program is subject to that runtime’s own model




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No general foreign-function interface.
⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.

Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Rocq yields low core coupling for the narrow work it is built for: dependent types put the specification in the type, tactic scripts are separate from the terms they build, extraction decouples verification from the implementation language, and the logic core is pure and total. The core score loses only through P1, because the language does not function outside the domain of formal proof. The platform cost is the price of that focus — a small academic ecosystem, a domain lock-in to verification, and one of the steepest learning curves here. Main strengths: kernel-checked certainty, the CompCert landmark result, and extraction as the bridge to OCaml, Haskell, or Scheme; main weaknesses: the narrow domain, the thin ecosystem, and the depth of type theory and tactic knowledge required.

title: Prolog (SWI 9.4)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Prolog in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 55/100 · Ecosystem coupling 45/100 · Engineering readiness 53/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ There is no static type check (T1): A term’s type is its functor and its arity, known only at run time, so a type fault appears when the goal executes rather than when it is compiled
❌ There are no sum types (T4): An alternative is a separate clause or an atom such as ok and error(...), and nothing checks that the cases are exhaustive
❌ There are no generics (T5): Every predicate is polymorphic over any term by construction, so there is no declared type parameter that a definition could be reused over
❌ There is no namespace and no module boundary (T6, T11): The standard gives one global predicate space, so two files that define foo/2 collide, and the module system that SWI-Prolog provides is a non-standard extension
✅ Unification matches in any direction: append(X, Y, [1, 2, 3]) enumerates every split, so a relation is not fixed to one input and one output direction
✅ The clause head is the pattern match: len([], 0). states a case directly in the head, so matching and dispatch are the same mechanism



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Global mutable state is the default (C1): The clause database is one global store, and assertz/1, retract/1, and set_prolog_flag/2 change it from anywhere in the program
❌ There is no immutability by default (C2): A term is immutable once built, but the state the program reads — clauses, flags, and the global variables of b_setval/2 — is mutable without a declared owner
✅ A compound term is built by a functor and its arguments: point(1, 2) builds a term, and no constructor declaration must be kept in step with it
✅ A clause is a term and can be constructed at run time: assertz(Head :- Body) takes an ordinary term, so a program and its data share one form
⚠️ A clause added at run time depends on the database’s state: A program that asserts or retracts clauses couples its result to the clauses that are present and to the order they are in
⚠️ Global variables are not logical variables: b_setval/2 stores a value that survives backtracking, so a part of the state lives outside the logical model



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Backtracking reclaims automatically: When a goal fails, the bindings it made are undone and the space they held is reclaimed, so a search loop does not leak per-attempt state
✅ The system collects the heap and the stacks: garbage_collect/0 and the atom-space controls are system predicates, so a program never frees a term itself
❌ Collection is non-deterministic and stack-based (M2): Reclamation is the system’s decision, made through the trail, through stack unwinding, and through a garbage collection that the program cannot schedule
❌ There is no RAII (M3): There is no scope-bound destructor, so an open stream, a socket, or a temporary file is released by an explicit close/1, and an exception can skip it
❌ There is no ownership model (M4): No static lifetime or aliasing rule ties a term to an owner, so a shared structure is freed by the trail discipline rather than by a declaration
⚠️ Deep recursion grows the stacks: Recursion that is not a tail call consumes stack and heap, and the bound is a system limit rather than a language rule



1.1.4 Error

✅ throw/1 and catch/3 give a structured path: catch(Goal, Ball, Recovery) receives the thrown term and selects the recovery by matching it, so the handler is chosen by the error’s shape
✅ The standard error term is a structured value: error(existence_error(procedure, P), Context) and the type_error, domain_error, instantiation_error, and permission_error forms are declared in ISO/IEC 13211-1, so a handler matches a pattern and not a message string
✅ Failure stays distinct from an error: A goal that fails is not an error, and catch/3 does not intercept a failure, so the two outcomes remain separate
✅ A runaway goal can be bounded: call_with_depth_limit/3 and call_with_inference_limit/3 are SWI extensions rather than ISO predicates, so a non-terminating search can be bounded and reported
⚠️ A thrown ball of another shape is unchecked: A predicate may throw any term, and no declaration lists the throws it can make
⚠️ A catch-all handler hides the cause: catch(Goal, _, fail) turns every failure reason into a plain failure, so a bug looks like a false result



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ SWI-Prolog provides threads and message queues: thread_create/3, thread_send_message/2, and thread_get_message/1 pass terms between threads without shared memory
✅ An engine is an isolated computation: engine_create/3 and engine_next/2 (SWI) run a goal as an independent engine, so two computations interleave without sharing a stack
✅ Message passing is the idiomatic design: A worker thread that receives a goal on a queue and answers on another queue couples the two sides to a term shape rather than to a lock
✅ Constraint propagation needs no thread: library(clpfd) and library(clpz) propagate constraints inside one engine, so a constraint problem is solved by search rather than by parallelism
⚠️ The ISO standard defines no concurrency: The core standard has no thread or task, so every concurrency mechanism comes from one implementation
⚠️ Threads share the clause database: A mutation (assertz/1) or a global variable seen from two threads needs a lock such as with_mutex/2 or an explicit message protocol, and the system reports no race



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The ISO standard is the reference: ISO/IEC 13211-1 fixes the syntax and the built-ins, and parts 2 and 3 add modules and Definite Clause Grammars, so code written to the core runs on several systems
✅ Several independent implementations exist: SWI-Prolog, SICStus Prolog, GNU Prolog, YAP, Trealla, and Scryer Prolog implement the standard, and no single vendor owns the language
✅ The system embeds in a host program: libswipl and libsicstus expose Prolog as a library, so a host language can call a predicate directly
✅ The standard term syntax is a portable text form: write_canonical/1 and read/1 write and read a term in the standard syntax
⚠️ The standard covers the core, not the libraries: library(clpfd), library(lists), library(readutil), and the HTTP server are one system’s, so a program that uses them is bound to that system
⚠️ Behaviour outside the core differs: The ordering of assert and retract, tabling, and the exact error terms vary between systems, so portability means staying inside the core



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The declarative reading is the premise of the language: Writing what holds rather than how to find it is the design decision, and the loss of an explicit loop follows from it
The cut is a deliberate control tool: ! commits to the current clause, and the order-coupling it creates is the price of pruning the search rather than a forced property of every program
Clause order expresses a preference: Putting a base case first is a style that terminates a recursion, so order matters to the search and not to the specification
is/2 evaluates arithmetic eagerly: X is Y + 1 needs Y to be bound, which is a documented direction requirement rather than a coupling defect
Negation as failure is a semantics choice: \+ Goal succeeds when Goal fails, and the language documents the resulting restriction rather than hiding it
Prolog is not a general-purpose runtime: The assumption of a logic database and a search is a scope decision, not a coupling defect




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

❌ The core resolves goals over a clause database (R1): A call is a search over the clauses through the engine’s instruction set, so a tight arithmetic or string loop trails an ahead-of-time compiled language
✅ Indexing prunes the candidate clauses: First-argument indexing, and deep indexing in SWI-Prolog, selects the clauses that can match, so a well-keyed predicate does not scan the whole definition
✅ A last call runs in constant space: Tail-call optimisation executes a final goal in place, so an iterative predicate does not grow the stack
✅ Tabling avoids repeated subcomputations: :- table p/1 (XSB, SWI) memoises the answers of a relation, so a dynamic-programming problem is computed once
⚠️ The cost model is the search: Unification, backtracking, and choice points are the units of work, so performance depends on how the problem was written as a search
⚠️ A compiler is separate from the engine: compile/1 in SICStus and the JIT and optimised compiler in SWI change the measurement, so a benchmark states which mode and which system it used



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ There is no package manager across the systems (Ec1): The standard defines no distribution, and each system ships its own mechanism, so a dependency is shaped by the system that provides it
❌ The ecosystem is small (Ec3): The library set beyond the core, lists, apply, readutil, and the constraint libraries, is thin next to a mainstream language
✅ SWI-Prolog ships a large standard library: clpfd, clpq, assoc, sgml, http/http_open, prolog_pack, and pengines come with one installation, so common work needs no external package
✅ The systems are long-lived and maintained: SWI-Prolog has been developed since 1987, and SICStus, GNU Prolog, and YAP have decades of releases
✅ The main manual is thorough: The SWI-Prolog manual documents each built-in with its mode, its determinism, and its errors
⚠️ The community is small: Questions are answered, but by fewer people than in a mainstream language, so an unusual problem takes longer to resolve



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The ISO standard fixes the core: ISO/IEC 13211-1 (1995) pins the syntax and the built-ins, so core code does not move under a new release
✅ SWI-Prolog stays backward compatible: swipl runs old code, offers --traditional for a strict ISO mode, and adds features as extensions
✅ The established systems are stable: A program written for SICStus, GNU Prolog, or YAP years ago still runs on the current release
✅ A program can be confined to the standard: write_canonical/1, read/1, and the standard control constructs give a form that moves between systems
⚠️ The standard is not revised quickly: The core has seen no substantial revision since 1995, so a needed feature is added as an extension rather than to the standard
⚠️ Extensions do not move between systems: library(clpfd) and library(assoc) differ in name and in detail, so a program that uses them is fixed to one system



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The domain and the implementation are one choice (D1): The fit is logic programming over a clause database, and the system chosen fixes the flags, the library names, and the assert semantics
❌ It is a poor fit for general-purpose work (D2): File handling, text processing, and numeric computation read as additions to a search language, so a general application belongs in another language
✅ Excellent fit for a rule engine or an expert system: The facts and the rules are the program, and the inference engine is the language itself
✅ Constraint solving is a strength: library(clpfd) solves finite-domain constraints, so a scheduling or puzzle problem is a few clauses rather than an algorithm
✅ Natural-language processing is a traditional strength: A Definite Clause Grammar (-->) states a grammar production directly, and ISO/IEC 13211-3 standardises the form
⚠️ A service application needs a library on top: A web endpoint depends on library(http/http_server), which is one system’s addition to the core



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Declarative thinking is a different model (L1): A beginner must write relations instead of steps, and the change of mental model, not the syntax, is the hard part
❌ The search must be understood to debug a program: The order of the clauses, the trail, and the cut decide how a program behaves, and a wrong order is a common beginner fault
⚠️ Unification has its own rules: The treatment of the occurs check, the anonymous variable _, and the difference between = and == must be learned before a program can be read
✅ The core language is small: A program is facts, rules, and a query, and the constructs beyond :-, ,, ;, and ! are few
✅ The classic textbooks are excellent: The standard references, including Clocksin and Mellish, Sterling and Shapiro, and O’Keefe’s The Craft of Prolog, remain current



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Terms, clauses, and queries share one form: A fact and a rule differ only by the :- body, so a reader learns one shape
✅ A Definite Clause Grammar reads as a production: sentence --> noun_phrase, verb_phrase. states the rule directly
✅ The operator table can be extended: :- op(700, xfx, ===) declares a notation, so a domain can add an operator such as -->
✅ A clause ends with a full stop: The . terminates a clause and the term syntax is uniform across the file
⚠️ The comma has two roles: f(a, b) separates arguments and (a, b) conjoins goals, so the context decides the meaning of one character
⚠️ Operator precedence must be tracked: An expression such as a ; b, c parses by the precedence table, so a missing pair of brackets changes the meaning



1.2.7 Testing

❌ A type fault surfaces only at run time (G3): No static check rejects a goal, so a wrong argument, an unbound variable in an arithmetic goal, or a misspelled predicate fails during the run
✅ plunit ships with SWI-Prolog: :- begin_tests(...) and :- end_tests(...) declare tests, and run_tests/0 runs the suite
✅ Property-based testing is available: library(quickcheck) generates terms from a type skeleton and reports a minimal counterexample
✅ The tracer steps through the search: trace/0 and gtrace/0 show the call, exit, redo, and fail ports of every goal, so a search can be watched one step at a time
✅ A query is itself a test: A goal that must succeed and a goal that must fail are statements about the relation, so the test needs no fixture
⚠️ A left choice point is a fault a success hides: A predicate that should be deterministic can leave an alternative, so a test must assert det or semidet to catch it



1.2.8 Security

❌ Dynamic typing weakens a trust boundary (Q2): A term carries no declared type, so a value from an untrusted source is separated from a goal only by an explicit check, and the check is the programmer’s
✅ Unification binds symbols, not memory: There is no pointer arithmetic and no buffer in the language, so a buffer overflow cannot be written in Prolog source
✅ catch/3 isolates a failure: A goal that throws is caught at a known point, so a fault need not end the process
✅ The core has no text interpreter: ISO Prolog does not evaluate a string; a term is built from a functor and its arguments, so text becomes control only where the program asks for it
⚠️ call/1 on a term built from input is the injection pattern: call(term_to_atom(T, Input)) executes the goal that the input describes
⚠️ The atom space is finite: A program that makes an atom from every input, through atom_concat/3 or atom_length/2, can exhaust the atom space of the system

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.

⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.

Verdict: Prolog’s design yields a mixed profile: a moderate core coupling score (55/100) and a low platform and ecosystem score (45/100). One core mechanism is genuinely decoupling, because unification matches a pattern in any direction and so a relation is not fixed to one input and one output. Everything else is the price of the paradigm: there is no static type, no sum type, no generic, and no namespace or module boundary, the clause database is global mutable state, the search couples a result to clause order, collection follows the trail rather than the program, and the domain fit is narrow. The surrounding platform adds the rest, since the core resolves goals over a clause database, the standard has not moved since 1995, the ecosystem is small, and whichever system is chosen fixes the libraries.

title: Objective-C (2.0)
text: This assessment applies the coupling account — coupling as access to a shared resource, and the coupling floor [1], [2] — and the knowledge-embodiment theorem [3]; the language is assessed against its official reference [4].

title: Objective-C (2.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Objective-C in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 42/100 · Ecosystem coupling 65/100 · Engineering readiness 53/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Dispatch is resolved at run time (T3): A message send such as [obj doThing] compiles to objc_msgSend, and the selector is looked up as the message is delivered, so an object can receive a message its declared interface does not list and the fault appears as unrecognized selector sent to instance
❌ There is no namespace (T6): Every class and protocol shares one global name table, so code relies on prefixes such as NS, UI, and CG to keep names apart
❌ id erases the static type (T7): The generic object pointer carries no compile-time type, so a value held in id is checked only by -isKindOfClass: or -respondsToSelector: at run time
✅ Protocols separate specification from implementation: A @protocol declares a method set that any class can adopt with <NSCopying>, so conformance does not require inheritance and one class can adopt several protocols
✅ Categories extend a class without its source: @interface NSString (MyExtras) adds methods to an existing class, so a consumer extends behaviour without subclassing and without access to the original
⚠️ Static type information is optional and partly erased: Declared parameter and return types (NSString *, instancetype) are checked at compile time, but lightweight generics such as NSArray<NSString *> * and the nullability annotations nonnull and nullable are erased at run time



1.1.2 Construction

❌ There is no immutability by default (C2): NSString, NSArray, and NSDictionary each have a mutable counterpart, and a property declared strong without copy shares a mutable object with its setter; @property (copy) is the opt-in that protects it
✅ alloc and init separate allocation from initialisation: [[NSObject alloc] init] and a designated initialiser such as -initWithFrame: let one class route every construction path through one setup method
✅ @property synthesises the accessors: @property (nonatomic, copy) NSString *name; generates the getter, the setter, and the instance variable, so a consumer binds to the property name rather than to the ivar layout
✅ Blocks carry behaviour as a value: A ^-literal closure captures its environment and is passed as an argument, as in -[NSArray enumerateObjectsUsingBlock:], so a callback needs no delegate class
✅ Class clusters hide the concrete class: NSNumber and NSString return a private subclass from a factory method such as +numberWithInt:, so construction does not couple a caller to one implementation class
⚠️ +new and -init are conventions, not enforced rules: The runtime does not require an object to be initialised, so an uninitialised instance is possible and the class author must insist on the designated initialiser



1.1.3 Memory

✅ ARC removes manual retain and release: The compiler inserts objc_retain, objc_release, and the autorelease-pool calls at the right points, so the common case needs no memory-management call
✅ strong and weak state the ownership intent: @property (weak) id delegate; and __weak make the reference weak, and a weak reference zeroes itself when its referent is deallocated
⚠️ An autorelease pool defers the release: An autoreleased object lives until its enclosing @autoreleasepool drains, so a loop that builds many objects adds its own pool
❌ There is no RAII (M3): ARC is not block-scoped, so a resource that is not an object, such as a FILE *, a malloc block, or a Core Foundation handle, is released by an explicit call or a @try and @finally block
❌ There is no ownership model (M4): No static lifetime or aliasing rule bounds an object, so a strong reference cycle leaks until it is broken with weak
❌ Reclamation timing is not a language rule (M2): The language never states when an object is freed; the tracing collector that once shipped with the Apple runtime was deprecated and then removed, and ARC’s reference counting is a compiler convention rather than a language guarantee



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked (Er2): @throw, @try, @catch, and @finally carry an NSException that no signature declares, so a caller cannot see the failure set, and the convention reserves exceptions for programmer errors
✅ NSError ** reports a recoverable failure: A method such as -[NSString writeToFile:atomically:encoding:error:] writes the failure into an out-parameter, so a caller recovers without an exception
✅ @try, @catch, and @finally are structured: A @catch clause names the exception class, and @finally runs on both the normal and the exceptional path
⚠️ Two error conventions coexist: NSException marks a programming error and NSError marks a domain failure, so a caller must know which convention a given API follows
⚠️ A message to nil fails silently: [nil doThing] returns nil or 0 and raises nothing, so a missed wiring point produces no error
⚠️ NSAssert and NSParameterAssert are run-time checks: They abort in a debug build and are compiled out under NS_BLOCK_ASSERTIONS, so they do not enforce a contract in a release build



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Synchronisation is manual with no race detection (K3): @synchronized, NSLock, NSRecursiveLock, and dispatch_semaphore leave the reasoning to the programmer, and the compiler reports no data race
✅ Grand Central Dispatch separates work from threads: dispatch_async(dispatch_get_global_queue(0, 0), ^{ ... }) submits a block to a queue, so the code names a queue rather than a thread
✅ A completion block returns on a named queue: An asynchronous API takes a block and a queue, so a caller need not share mutable state with the worker
✅ NSOperationQueue declares dependencies: -[NSOperation addDependency:] orders operations in the queue, so sequencing is stated rather than hand-scheduled
✅ @synchronized gives a per-object mutex: @synchronized(self) { ... } serialises a critical section on one object without a separate lock object
⚠️ @property (atomic) does not make a compound operation atomic: The default attribute serialises each accessor call, so a check-then-set sequence over the same property can still interleave with another thread



1.1.6 Platform

❌ One vendor owns the mainstream platform (P2): The complete language, its reference compiler (Clang), and its flagship frameworks (Cocoa and Cocoa Touch) are Apple’s
✅ GNUstep provides a second implementation: The GNUstep runtime, Foundation, and AppKit reimplementations let much Objective-C code build off Apple’s platform
✅ The language is a strict superset of C: A .m file mixes C functions and structs with message sends, so any C library is callable directly
✅ Modules replace recursive header inclusion: @import Foundation; imports a clang module, so a build does not depend on #import order
⚠️ The frameworks differ by platform: AppKit on macOS and UIKit on iOS share Foundation but not the user-interface layer, so UI code does not move between them



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Message-passing syntax is a familiarity cost: [receiver selector:argument] differs from dot-syntax object languages, and the adjustment is a learning property rather than a forced dependency
Long method names are a deliberate style: -[NSString stringByReplacingOccurrencesOfString:withString:] is verbose but self-describing, which is a readability choice
Manual retain and release remains available: A project can leave ARC off and manage lifetimes itself, so the older memory model is a choice rather than a requirement
NSException for programmer errors is a policy: Treating an exception as a bug signal and NSError as a recovery signal is a convention the language permits but does not require
Prefixes mitigate the flat namespace: A class prefix is a convention that reduces collisions; it is a workaround for the missing namespace, not an additional coupling
A mixed Objective-C and Swift target is a migration decision: Both languages share the runtime and call each other, so how far to migrate is a project choice




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The language compiles to native code: Clang lowers Objective-C to machine code through LLVM, so a message send is a real call and a program needs no warm-up
✅ The runtime is thin and written in C: libobjc supplies the selector table, the class metadata, and the reference-counting helpers with little work beyond the message send
⚠️ objc_msgSend costs more than a static call: Every message send performs a selector lookup that is cached after the first use, so a tight loop of message sends is slower than the equivalent direct call
⚠️ Dynamic dispatch limits inlining and devirtualisation: Because the receiver’s class is known only at run time, the compiler cannot always inline a method body
⚠️ Key-value observing and method swizzling add indirection: Both change how a method runs after the fact, and the cost appears wherever they are installed



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The primary ecosystem is proprietary (Ec4): The reference documentation, the frameworks, and the IDE (Xcode) come from one vendor under its licence terms
✅ The toolchain is mature inside that ecosystem: Xcode supplies one editor, compiler, debugger (lldb), Interface Builder, and the Instruments profiler in one install
✅ CocoaPods, Carthage, and Swift Package Manager resolve dependencies: Several long-established package managers exist for Objective-C libraries
✅ GNUstep supplies a free Foundation: A portable implementation covers NSString, NSArray, and the rest of the Foundation API off Apple’s platform
⚠️ Current material is written for Swift first: The platform APIs and sample code are presented for Swift, so an Objective-C reader works from older or generated headers



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The language is frozen (V2): Objective-C 2.0 (2006) is effectively the last language revision, and platform-facing work has moved to Swift
✅ The compiler keeps supplying new features: ARC, blocks, object literals such as @[] and @{}, lightweight generics, and nullability annotations arrived as Clang features rather than as language revisions
✅ A mixed Objective-C and Swift target is supported: Both languages link against the same runtime and can call each other, so a project can migrate one file at a time
✅ Old source still compiles: OpenStep-era Foundation API and the 1990s NeXT runtime conventions are still supported by the current toolchain
⚠️ Documentation for new APIs follows the vendor’s current language: A header is the reliable reference for the Objective-C form of a new API



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The domain and the vendor are one decision (D1): The language is built for Apple’s platforms, so adopting it means shipping on macOS, iOS, iPadOS, watchOS, and tvOS
✅ Excellent fit for the Apple application model: The Cocoa delegate, target-action, and notification patterns and the main run loop are expressed directly in the language
✅ Foundation runs off Apple’s platform: Portable Foundation code from GNUstep works on Linux and other systems for command-line and server work
⚠️ Cross-platform work needs a second toolkit: GNUstep supplies Foundation but has no equivalent of a modern Apple user-interface layer
⚠️ Server and command-line use is marginal: The language is used for it, but the design centre is the application platform



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Message passing is a barrier for a newcomer (L1): [receiver selector:argument], the colon-bearing selector notation, and the @-keyword set differ from dot-syntax object languages
❌ The C substrate must be learned as well: Pointers, struct, C strings, manual C memory, and @encode sit underneath the object model, so the language is C plus message passing
⚠️ The runtime is a second topic: objc_msgSend, metaclasses, key-value coding and observing, and ARC semantics are separate from the source syntax
⚠️ Documentation quality follows the vendor: Apple’s guides and headers are thorough on the platform, and off-platform material is thinner
✅ The object model is conceptually small: Once the message send is understood, most of the rest follows from it, including classes, selectors, and protocols



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ A message send names every argument: [view addSubview:subview positioned:NSWindowBelow relativeTo:nil] labels each argument at the call site, so the call reads as a sentence
✅ Object literals are compact: @42, @[@"a", @"b"], and @{@"k": @1} build an NSNumber, an NSArray, and an NSDictionary in one form
✅ @property shortens an accessor pair: One declaration replaces a hand-written getter, setter, and instance variable
⚠️ The selector includes its colons: addSubview:positioned:relativeTo: is one name, so a missing or an extra colon changes the selector
⚠️ Dot syntax and brackets both reach an accessor: obj.prop and [obj prop] are interchangeable, so a reader must accept two spellings for the same call
⚠️ The preprocessor is part of the surface: #import, #define, and macro-based API patterns are load-bearing in existing code



1.2.7 Testing

✅ XCTest ships with the platform toolchain: XCTestCase, the XCTAssert family, and performance tests are part of the developer tools
✅ Instruments profiles a real run: The Time Profiler, Allocations, and Leaks instruments show where time and memory go, so a test can measure a change
✅ The debugger understands messages: lldb can break on a selector, inspect the arguments of a message send, and evaluate an expression in the running process
⚠️ The framework is tied to the toolchain: XCTest and the simulator come from one vendor, so an off-platform run needs GNUstep and a different harness
⚠️ A wrong selector passes the build: With dynamic dispatch a missing method or a wrong type is a run-time failure, so the tested paths matter more than the compiled ones



1.2.8 Security

✅ ARC removes a class of memory faults: The compiler owns retain and release, so a use-after-free from a missing release is rare in ARC code
✅ A weak reference does not dangle: weak and __weak zero the reference when its referent is deallocated, so a stale link becomes nil
✅ A message to nil is safe: [nil doThing] returns nil or 0 instead of trapping, which removes a class of null-dereference crash
⚠️ id permits type confusion: A value typed id accepts any object, and a wrong cast is caught only where the code checks the class
⚠️ C is still underneath: malloc, pointer arithmetic, and a file compiled with -fno-objc-arc bypass every object-model guarantee
⚠️ Method swizzling changes behaviour after the build: method_exchangeImplementations replaces an implementation at run time, which is powerful and easy to misuse




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

⚠️ One vendor decides the language’s direction.
⚠️ The specification is not public.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Objective-C’s design yields moderate language-imposed coupling, and its weakest core dimensions are the ones the language was built around. Dynamic dispatch, the flat global namespace, and the id pointer defer type and dispatch checks to run time (T3, T6, T7). Against that, protocols give multiple inheritance of specification without implementation, categories extend a class without its source, blocks carry a callback as a value, and ARC removes manual retain and release while weak makes a stale reference zero itself. Its main weaknesses lie underneath and around the object model: there is no ownership rule and no block-scoped release, exceptions are unchecked, and the entire platform is one vendor’s, so the domain, the evolution, and the ecosystem are all locked to the same decision.

1 Assessment
This page assesses Lean 4 in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 81/100 · Ecosystem coupling 65/100 · Engineering readiness 64/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Dependent types let a type name a value: Vector α n and Fin n carry the length in the type, so a length mismatch and an out-of-range index are rejected at elaboration
✅ Propositions are types, so a proof is a term: The Curry–Howard correspondence puts a theorem and a program in one system, and the same kernel checks both
✅ A structure type names its fields and their types: structure with typeclass fields gives a record whose construction is checked, and where supplies the values by name
✅ Typeclass resolution is checked instance search: An instance is found by the declared class at compile time, so a missing instance is an elaboration error rather than a run-time lookup
✅ Subtype couples a value to its proof: {x // p x} is a pair of a value and a proof that the predicate holds, so an invariant is carried by the term itself
✅ unsafe marks the one escape from the logic: A declaration that bypasses the kernel must be named unsafe, so the boundary is visible in the source



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Construction runs through the kernel, so an invariant cannot be skipped: A value of an inductive type is built by its constructors, and a term that does not fit the type fails elaboration
✅ where puts the field values beside the type: An instance of a structure is written with named fields, so a reader does not count an argument list
✅ macro and syntax extend the surface at the definition site: A notation for the domain is declared once and then used like a built-in
✅ deriving generates the mechanical instances: Repr, BEq, Hashable, and Inhabited are produced by the elaborator, so a type does not repeat boilerplate
✅ do notation builds the effectful value: Construction in IO, Option, or Except is written as a sequence of binds
⚠️ Termination is an obligation on every definition: A recursive def must be shown to terminate structurally or by a decreasing measure, so a natural formulation of an algorithm can need a proof before it compiles



1.1.3 Memory

✅ The compiler inserts the reference counting: Borrow inference decides which arguments are borrowed and which are owned, and emits the retain and release operations, so a pure definition never writes one
✅ There is no tracing collector: A value is reclaimed when its last reference goes away, so there is no collection pause to plan around
✅ A value of an inductive type is immutable: No term updates a field in place, so sharing is safe by construction
⚠️ A reference cycle is not collected: A mutable reference cell (IO.Ref) whose value points back to the cell keeps its storage alive, because reference counting has no cycle detector
⚠️ Allocation is not controllable from the source: The allocator is not a parameter and there is no placement control, so a program cannot choose where a value lives
⚠️ A deeply shared structure still pays a count per reference: A persistent structure that shares a subtree is counted at every edge, and the compiler removes many but not all of those operations



1.1.4 Error

✅ Option α and Except ε α are the error types: A partial function returns a value that states the failure, and do notation sequences the recovery path
✅ A total function cannot fail by definition: In the pure fragment the type states that the function returns, and partial is required to opt out of that guarantee
✅ Decidable turns a proposition into a branch that is total: if h : p then ... else ... computes from a proof of decidability, so the two branches cover the cases by construction
✅ There are no exceptions in the logic: An error is a value in the return type, so a computation that can fail carries the failure in its signature rather than raising out of it
⚠️ panic! and an IO failure leave the kernel’s guarantee: An abort at run time is not a term in the logic, and the type of the function does not mention it
⚠️ Error-freedom is a theorem, not an automatic result: To state that a function never fails, you prove it; the compiler does not derive the property



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ The pure fragment has no shared mutable state: A mathematical term is a value with no location, so two proofs cannot race by construction
✅ Task gives structured, joinable parallelism in IO: A task is a value that can be awaited, so a spawned computation is joined through its result
⚠️ There is no concurrency construct in the language: Parallelism lives in the IO monad through Task and the promise cell, so a concurrent program is an IO program like any other
⚠️ A promise carries a value between tasks and the program orders its use: Nothing in the type states when the value becomes available
✅ The runtime owns the thread pool: The scheduler and its thread count are runtime settings, so the language does not expose a thread object
⚠️ The kernel says nothing about a task’s behaviour: A theorem about a function does not constrain the parallel schedule that runs it



1.1.6 Platform

❌ Lean 4 is the only implementation: The language is defined by its own elaborator and kernel, so there is no second independent compiler to test the specification against (P1)
✅ The trusted kernel is small and portable: The elaborator is written in Lean and the kernel is a compact checker, so the language does not rest on a large run-time
✅ @[extern] and @[export] make the foreign boundary a declaration: A call out to C is written and recorded, so the escape from the language is visible in the source
✅ The output is C, so the target set is the C compiler’s: The compiler emits C and hands it to a C back end, so a Lean program runs where a C program runs
⚠️ A native build needs a C toolchain and the Lean runtime: The build environment is part of the platform, and a deployed binary carries the runtime
⚠️ The toolchain moves in nightly steps: A project pins its version in lean-toolchain, and a dependency may require a different one



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Proof work is a separate effort from programming: A def is not obliged to carry a proof, and requiring one is the author’s decision
The kernel is deliberately small and the tactics are not trusted: A tactic produces a term that the kernel rechecks, which is a decision about where trust sits
partial and unsafe are the intended escape hatches: A non-terminating or pointer-touching definition is expressible, at the cost of its guarantee
Typeclass search is a proof search with a cost: An instance can be ambiguous or expensive to find, and that is an elaboration property rather than a run-time coupling
The library is one large shared body: mathlib’s definitions belong to the community, so a development inherits its choices instead of buying a library
The audience is mathematics and verification: The adoption of the language follows from that, and it is a market fact rather than a mechanism of the language




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The compiler emits C, and a native optimiser then compiles it: The generated C passes through a mature C back end, so the run-time cost benefits from that pipeline
✅ Borrow inference removes most reference-count traffic: The compiler’s borrow analysis turns many retain and release pairs into nothing, so a pure functional definition stays close to imperative cost
✅ @[inline] and @[specialize] remove an abstraction at the seam: A monomorphic specialisation of a polymorphic definition is generated on request
✅ Compile-time evaluation removes run-time work: A proof discharged by decide or native_decide is computed while the project is built
⚠️ Elaboration dominates the build time: Typeclass search, tactic execution, and proof checking are spent at compile time, so a large development builds slowly even when its binary is small
⚠️ A count is not free on a shared structure: A persistent structure counted at each edge still pays for the sharing the compiler cannot prove away



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The package universe is small: Dependencies are resolved from git by lake, and the practical library set is mathlib, the core library, and a few support packages (Ec3)
✅ lake is a standard build tool and dependency resolver: lakefile.lean or lakefile.toml declares a package, lake build builds it, and lake-manifest.json records the resolved revisions
✅ The editor integration is first class: The Lean 4 server speaks LSP and the infoview shows the goal, the hypotheses, and the diagnostics beside the source
✅ mathlib is one of the largest libraries of formalised mathematics: It is developed in the open and its continuous integration checks every proof
⚠️ The community is academic and small: The centre of gravity is mathlib, the Zulip chat, and the university groups, and industrial use is rare
⚠️ A project’s revision set is tight against the toolchain: mathlib tracks recent Lean releases, so a project that pins an older toolchain cannot use the current mathlib



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ A project pins its toolchain and its dependency revisions: lean-toolchain names the version and lake-manifest.json names the commits, so a build is reproducible without a separate lock convention
✅ Lean 4 is the stable line and its minor releases are backward compatible: A project on a pinned version is not moved by a release it did not take
✅ The language and its libraries are open and publicly discussed: The request-for-comments archive and the community chat record why a feature changed
⚠️ Lean 4 replaced Lean 3 with a different language: A Lean 3 development is a porting project, and the mathematical libraries moved with the new language
⚠️ The ecosystem moves in nightly steps: A feature can land in a nightly build and reach a stable release later, so a dependency may require a version the project has not taken



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Proof engineering and formalised mathematics are the native domain: theorem, by, simp, and mathlib are built for that work
✅ Verified systems programming is supported: A verified algorithm compiles to C and ships as an ordinary binary, which is the growing use of the language
✅ It is a general-purpose functional language beside the proof assistant: A def with no proof obligation is ordinary functional code
❌ The domain lock-in is the point of the tool: The language expects a proof-carrying artifact, and a program that states no theorem gets little from the system (D1)
⚠️ mathlib is a shared global body rather than a set of packages: A mathematical development is expected to build on its definitions, so the notation and the lemma names belong to the community
⚠️ A formalisation is a research and maintenance commitment: A proof tracks the definitions it is about, so a change to one of them can invalidate a development



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The curve is very steep: Dependent types, the elimination rules, and the elaborator’s inference model are new to a working programmer (L1)
❌ Proof writing is a second skill on top of programming: Tactic scripts, the simp sets, and the explicit proof term are a subject of their own
❌ The elaboration is not visible in the source: Why a by simp succeeded, or why an instance was not found, must be read from the goal state and the options (L3)
✅ The infoview shows the goal and the hypotheses at the cursor: The state is displayed rather than inferred by the reader
✅ The libraries supply the lemmas: An algebra or order fact is used without being reproved
⚠️ The documentation trail is uneven: The reference manual is complete for the language, but much elaboration behaviour is documented in the source, and the community’s books are a growth area



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Term syntax reads like mathematics: ∀ x, P x → Q x, ∃, fun x => ..., and infix notation for the relations the library defines
✅ Notation is declared and hygienic: notation, infix, and macro add a form where it is defined, so the surface can match the domain
✅ do notation sequences effects as statements: let, if, and for inside do read like an imperative body over a monad
✅ Pattern matching is checked for exhaustiveness: A missing constructor is a compile-time error, so a case is not forgotten
⚠️ Layout is significant: do, by, and where blocks are delimited by indentation, so a re-indentation changes the parse
⚠️ A macro can change what a line means: macro and elab rewrite the surface, so the reader must know the notation the library installed



1.2.7 Testing

✅ #eval runs a term in the file: A definition can be evaluated and printed beside its proof, and #check reports its type
✅ example and by decide state a checked claim inline: A decidable proposition is proved by evaluation, and an example block is a test the elaborator runs
✅ lake test runs the project’s test executable: A test driver is declared in the package and run by the build tool
✅ #print axioms reports the assumptions behind a theorem: A proof that used sorry or an extra axiom shows the dependency, so an unchecked step is discoverable
⚠️ native_decide extends the trusted base: It closes a goal by evaluating compiled code, so the compiler and the runtime, not only the kernel, are relied on
⚠️ An IO program is outside the logic: The behaviour of a program that reads a file or a socket is tested as an ordinary program rather than proved



1.2.8 Security

✅ The kernel rechecks every proof term: A theorem that elaborates cannot be invalid, so a claimed property is a checked one
✅ sorry is visible and reportable: The placeholder closes any goal with a warning, and #print axioms shows that it was used, so an unfinished proof is discoverable rather than hidden
✅ unsafe names the escape from the logic: A declaration that bypasses the kernel is marked, so the boundary can be found in the source
✅ No pointer type exists in the language surface: A term written without unsafe cannot express an address, so the memory-safety class of bugs is outside the pure fragment
⚠️ The trusted base is wider than the kernel in a native binary: The runtime, the C compiler, and the runtime’s primitives are all in the path of a compiled program
⚠️ There is no capability model: IO gives a program the authority of the operating system, and the sandbox is the operating system’s




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Lean 4’s design produces the highest core score here, because its constructs are separating by construction. Dependent types let a type state a property of a value, propositions-as-types puts the specification and the program in one term, and the kernel rechecks every proof, so an invalid claim does not elaborate. Reference counting with borrow inference keeps the memory story deterministic and out of the source. Main strengths: an exact fit to mathematics and verification, a small trusted kernel, and a first-class editor and library. Main weaknesses: the language has a single implementation, the library universe beyond mathlib is small, the toolchain moves in nightly steps, and the curve is among the steepest.
