title: Delphi (12.3 Athens)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Delphi in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 43/100 · Ecosystem coupling 84/100 · Engineering readiness 38/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Unit interface sections separate the declaration from the implementation: A consumer compiles against the interface part of a unit and never sees its implementation part, so either part can change without the consumer being rewritten
✅ Class, record, and interface types are declared and checked at compile time: A method call, a field access, and an argument are resolved against the declared type, so no name lookup happens at run time
✅ Dotted unit names give a namespace: System.SysUtils, Vcl.Forms, and the project’s unit scope names qualify every entity, so two units may declare the same identifier without a collision
⚠️ A variant record is a sum type without a checked tag: A case part in a record lays alternatives over the same storage, but reading the field of the wrong alternative is not diagnosed, so the tag lives in the programmer’s discipline (T4)
⚠️ Generics exist but the constraint vocabulary is small: Generic classes and records (TList<T>, TDictionary<TKey, TValue>) have been in the language since Delphi 2009, but a type parameter can be constrained only by a class, a record, a constructor, or an interface, so older library code still passes TObject and TValue
⚠️ nil is a value of every class, interface, and pointer type: There is no non-nullable reference type, so a call through nil is a run-time fault rather than a compile-time error



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A property separates the name from the accessor: property Count: Integer read GetCount write SetCount lets a consumer use one name while the class moves between a field and a method without touching the consumer
✅ An event separates the publisher from the subscriber: property OnClick: TNotifyEvent and anonymous methods let the framework raise a notification without knowing which handler is attached, which is the observer pattern in the language
✅ A class helper extends an existing type from outside it: A helper adds a method to a class declared in another unit, so an extension does not require editing the type or inheriting it
✅ A constructor is an ordinary method named Create: Construction is a call rather than a special form, and Create may be virtual, so a factory returns the right subclass
✅ initialization and finalization give a unit a declared start and end: The start-up and shutdown code of a unit has a named place, so a unit-level resource is not acquired in a random procedure
❌ Mutability is the default: A field, a global variable, and an ordinary parameter are writable unless the declaration says const or constref, so the default reading of a variable promises nothing about it being unchanged (C2)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ Nothing ties a release to the end of a block: An object from Create is released by an explicit .Free, usually inside try/finally, and no destructor runs at scope exit, so cleanup is a written obligation (M1, M3)
❌ There is no ownership model: The compiler does not track which reference owns an instance, so a double .Free, a use after .Free, and a leak are neither diagnosed nor reported (M4)
⚠️ Managed types are reference-counted and the rule differs by compiler: string, dynamic arrays, and interface references release their storage when the last reference goes away, but an object is reference-counted only on the mobile compilers, so the lifetime rule depends on the target
⚠️ An interface reference cycle is never released: The reference count of a cycle never reaches zero and there is no tracing collector, so the cycle leaks unless a weak reference breaks it
✅ TComponent.Owner gives a declared lifetime to a component graph: A component frees the components it owns when it is freed, so the object graph of a form is released deterministically
✅ A managed record extends scope-tied release to a value type: Initialize, Finalize, AddRef, and RemoveRef operators let a record run code at the end of the block that holds it (Delphi 10.4 and later)



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked: raise needs no declaration in the signature and no caller is obliged to handle the exception type, so the failure set of a routine is not part of its interface (Er2)
✅ except with on E: T do binds the handler to a type: The handler names the exception class it catches and an unmatched exception propagates, so the recovery region is stated
✅ try/finally separates cleanup from recovery: A finally block runs on both the normal exit and the exceptional one, which is where a release belongs
✅ An exception object carries its own data: A class derived from Exception can carry context and raise propagates it unchanged, so a caller does not parse a message string
⚠️ A bare except swallows the cause: An except block without on catches everything, including an access violation, and the recovery code may not know which failure it is covering
⚠️ A memory fault arrives as an exception: A read through a dangling pointer raises EAccessViolation at the faulting instruction, so an unsafe pointer becomes a run-time error that the program may or may not handle



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Synchronisation is manual and unchecked: System.SyncObjs supplies TCriticalSection, TMutex, TSemaphore, TEvent, and TInterlocked, but the compiler does not check the locking discipline or diagnose a race (K3)
✅ System.Threading gives a task abstraction: TTask.Run, TParallel.For, and futures carry work across a thread pool, so a parallel loop is stated rather than hand-threaded
✅ TThread wraps a thread as an object with a lifetime: The execution and the termination of a thread belong to one object, and Synchronize and Queue marshal a call back to another thread
✅ A queued call separates a worker from the UI thread: TThread.Queue, TThread.ForceQueue, and PostMessage deliver work without a shared lock
⚠️ Shared mutable state is the default: An ordinary field or global variable is reachable from every thread, and the language does not mark which state is confined to one thread (K2)
⚠️ The VCL is single-threaded by contract: The GUI may be touched only from the main thread, and that rule is documented rather than enforced



1.1.6 Platform

✅ One source targets Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, and Linux: The Object Pascal front end and the RTL are shared, and only the GUI framework differs between the targets
✅ A second compiler implements the same language: Free Pascal and Lazarus compile Object Pascal in a Delphi-compatible mode ({$MODE DELPHI}), so a program is not bound to one vendor’s binary alone
✅ The RTL is usable without the GUI framework: A console or service program links the runtime alone, so a non-GUI program does not depend on a windowing framework
⚠️ FireMonkey is the cross-platform GUI path and it is second to the VCL: The component sets and the visual behaviour of the two frameworks differ, so a GUI program depends on the one it was written for
⚠️ A program that calls the Windows API is bound to Windows: The Windows unit, COM, and the registry are used beside the RTL, and that part of the program is not portable
⚠️ The compiler and the IDE are one vendor’s licensed product: The direction of the language follows that vendor, even though a compatible open compiler exists



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The VCL/FireMonkey choice is a GUI decision: A RAD component couples the program to the framework it was dropped onto, and the alternative is to build the user interface against the raw platform
Single inheritance is a deliberate simplification: The language gives interface types for the shared-behaviour case and keeps the class tree one level deep
The RAD model trades control for speed of construction: A designer-saved form and a live object graph are why the framework owns the lifetime of the components
nil is a convenience as much as a hazard: An unset reference has a natural empty value, and the discipline of an assigned check is the programmer’s
Pointer arithmetic is opt-in in practice: Pointer, GetMem, and System.Move exist for the low-level case, and ordinary code need not use them
The language is an Object Pascal dialect, not Pascal: The dialect follows from the RAD requirement, and the compatibility with Turbo Pascal is historical




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The compiler emits native machine code: dcc32 and dcc64 produce an executable directly, so no interpreter or JIT sits between the source and the CPU
✅ A desktop release does not scan the heap: With reference-counted strings, dynamic arrays, and interfaces, the runtime has no tracing collector, so there is no collection pause to plan around
✅ inline, const parameters, and record passing control cost at the declaration: The call convention is stated beside the routine rather than inferred from its use
⚠️ The classic optimiser is modest beside a modern back end: The vendor compiler does not apply the cross-module inlining and vectorisation that Clang or LLVM at -O2 applies, so a numerical kernel is usually delegated to a library
⚠️ An interface call is an indirect call: Dispatch through an interface adds an indirection the compiler cannot resolve across units



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The library pool is small and centered on the vendor’s own packages: A project draws on GetIt, the bundled RTL/VCL/FireMonkey, and a small third-party set, so a missing library is often written in-house (Ec3)
✅ The IDE is a complete tool: Editor, visual designer, debugger, profiler, and refactoring sit in one product, with no plugin assembly required
✅ GetIt and open source cover the common needs: The IDE’s package channel, and community projects such as DUnitX, Spring4D, and ORM and JSON libraries, supply the usual layer
✅ The vendor documentation is a reference work: The DocWiki holds an entry per type and per routine of the language, the RTL, and the VCL
⚠️ The platform is one vendor’s commercial product: The compiler, the IDE, and the frameworks are maintained by Embarcadero, so support and direction are commercial decisions
⚠️ Adoption is declining and the community is concentrated: The hiring pool and the library pool shrink with the Windows desktop market, and the active community is organized around a few sites



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Annual releases add features with a published changelog: Each 12.x release records its language and RTL additions in the release notes
✅ Backward compatibility is long-lived: Turbo Pascal-era source mostly still compiles with warnings, so a codebase is rarely rewritten for the toolchain alone
✅ A deprecation is reported with a replacement: The compiler warns on a deprecated routine and names its successor, so a migration is guided
⚠️ The roadmap is one vendor’s: A needed language feature waits for the vendor’s release decision, and the community cannot change the language
⚠️ A program that uses the VCL cannot leave Windows: The framework choice fixes the platform, and the cross-platform path is a separate framework
⚠️ A project is often pinned to an older IDE: The compiler version becomes part of the codebase, and an upgrade is a project of its own



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Windows desktop line-of-business software is the native target: A database front end, a form, and a grid are the idiom the framework is built for
✅ Rapid UI construction is a documented strength: The visual designer, the data-aware components (TDataSet, TDataSource), and live bindings make a screen quick to build
✅ A cross-platform client is supported through FireMonkey: One source produces a Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android client, although that path is secondary to the VCL
✅ Native Windows integration is direct: The Windows unit, COM, and the registry are reachable from the same code as the language
⚠️ The market the language fits best is now a legacy market: New Windows desktop development is a smaller share than web and service development
⚠️ The fit outside a GUI application is thin: A service, a web back end, or an embedded program is written against the RTL alone, with little framework support



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The curve is gentle for a Pascal or C-family developer: begin/end, a single-pass declaration order, and readable identifiers make the language quick to read
✅ The IDE teaches the framework interactively: Dropping a component and reading the generated code is the standard on-ramp
✅ A reader sees each name’s type at hand: var, const, and type sections and typed parameters put the declaration beside its use
⚠️ The framework is a second subject beyond the language: The VCL/FireMonkey object model, the streaming of a form (.dfm), and the RTTI layer are knowledge the language does not imply
⚠️ The Windows mental model is required for real work: The message loop, handles, threads, and COM are needed as soon as the program touches the system



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Keywords delimit blocks and the statements read as English: if ... then ... else, for ... do, while ... do, and begin/end
✅ Identifiers are case-insensitive and the layout is free: The compiler ignores case, and the IDE’s formatter keeps the source uniform across a team
⚠️ The language is verbose: Each declaration opens a var, const, or type section, and a unit needs an interface, an implementation, and a closing end. even for a few statements (S1)
⚠️ try and begin pairs nest into an end ladder: An ordinary routine with two try/finally blocks ends in a run of end; lines
⚠️ Attributes and compiler directives share the bracket notation: [Weak], {$IFDEF}, and {$WARN} mix the language and the compiler controls in the same text



1.2.7 Testing

✅ A test framework ships with the toolchain: DUnitX, and the older DUnit, provide fixtures, attributes, and assertions, and the IDE runs the suite
✅ The debugger steps through a test and shows the fault: The IDE debugger shows the call stack, the locals, and the thread state at the failure
✅ Assert is in the RTL: Assert(cond) raises EAssertionFailed when assertions are enabled, so a precondition is stated in the code
⚠️ The checks that would catch a fault are off by default: Range and overflow checking ({$R+}, {$Q+}) must be enabled per project, so an out-of-bounds index in a release build is undefined
⚠️ Assertions are compiled out of a release build: {$ASSERTIONS OFF} removes them, so their guarantee is a debug-time one
⚠️ Debugging is the vendor’s IDE’s: A command-line debug session is not the standard workflow, so a headless build server runs tests without the interactive state



1.2.8 Security

⚠️ Memory safety is not guaranteed: Pointer, GetMem/FreeMem, System.Move, and PChar arithmetic are available, nothing marks the part of a program that uses them, and in that part the type system is not in the path, so its safety is the author’s claim
✅ Managed types carry their length and are checked when range checking is on: {$R+} makes an out-of-range index raise ERangeError, and a string or a dynamic array knows its own length
✅ There is no dynamic evaluation of source text: The language has no eval that compiles a string, and reflection reaches only published members through the RTTI, so an injection path needs the program to build the call itself
⚠️ The language offers no sandbox and no capability model: A program runs with the authority of the process, and the mitigations (DEP, ASLR, control-flow guard) are linker and loader options




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

⚠️ No fast in-editor analysis.



1.3.5 Interop

⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

⚠️ One vendor decides the language’s direction.
⚠️ The specification is not public.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Delphi’s design yields a middling core score, because its separating constructs sit beside its coupling ones. The interface section of a unit, a property, an event, and an interface type each decouple a consumer from an implementation, while the single-inheritance tree is the one hierarchy the language imposes. Main strengths: native compilation, a gentle Pascal-derived syntax, and a mature IDE and framework for Windows desktop work. Main weaknesses: exceptions are unchecked, a release is written rather than tied to scope, references are nilable with no ownership check, and the platform is one vendor’s commercial product in a declining market.

text: This assessment applies the coupling account — coupling as access to a shared resource, and the coupling floor [1], [2] — and the knowledge-embodiment theorem [3]; the language is assessed against its official reference [4].

title: COBOL (ISO/IEC 1989:2023)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses COBOL in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 47/100 · Ecosystem coupling 54/100 · Engineering readiness 61/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Typing is weak and static: A PICTURE clause fixes an item’s shape, but a MOVE between items with different pictures converts the value silently, so the declared type does not protect it (T2)
✅ The Data Division declares the shape once: Level numbers and PICTURE state each item’s size and category, and the Procedure Division uses that declaration without repeating it
✅ Group items give a structured record: Level numbers nest elementary items inside groups, so a record layout is one declaration
✅ Fixed decimal arithmetic is exact: COMP-3 packed-decimal operations do not accumulate binary floating-point error, so the numeric representation matches monetary values
⚠️ USAGE decides the representation: COMP-3 (packed decimal), COMP (binary), and DISPLAY differ, and a move between them converts without a type error
⚠️ An alphanumeric item accepts any character string: An X(n) item holds any text, so a category mistake is caught only by the program’s own checks



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Every data item is visible to every paragraph: A WORKING-STORAGE item can be read and modified from any procedure, and before COBOL-85 the language offered no way to restrict access to it (C1)
✅ The four divisions separate concerns: Identification, Environment, Data, and Procedure give each declaration a fixed place, so data definition does not share a space with program logic
✅ CALL ... USING passes parameters to a subprogram: A called program receives its arguments explicitly, so a subprogram boundary is a declared interface
✅ LOCAL-STORAGE gives per-call state: It is allocated for each invocation, so a re-entrant call does not share the state held in WORKING-STORAGE
⚠️ PERFORM THRU names a range of paragraphs and passes nothing: The called region is a text span and the performed code communicates only through shared data items, with no parameter list and no call stack
⚠️ GO TO and ALTER break structured flow: The language permits control transfers that obscure which paragraph runs next



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Ordinary program data needs no allocator: WORKING-STORAGE and LOCAL-STORAGE come from a declared layout, so a program that uses only them calls no allocator and no free
✅ No garbage collector: Storage is fixed at compile time, so reclamation is deterministic and unobserved
✅ OCCURS declares fixed-size tables: The size of a table is known at compile time
⚠️ OCCURS DEPENDING ON varies a table’s length at run time: The logic then couples to the actual occurrence count
⚠️ ALLOCATE and FREE put deallocation back on the programmer: The 2002 standard added dynamic allocation for tables and objects, and release is an explicit statement



1.1.4 Error

❌ Error handling has no structured path: USE AFTER STANDARD ERROR and other declaratives are declared globally in the DECLARATIVES section, and control may or may not return to the failing statement (Er1)
✅ The declaratives section is separated from the main procedure: Recovery code is declared apart from the normal path
✅ FILE STATUS reports I/O results as data: A file’s FILE STATUS item holds a two-character code that the program can test after each I/O statement
✅ INVALID KEY and AT END put the failure case at the statement: READ ... INVALID KEY ... NOT INVALID KEY and AT END handle the result inside the operation itself
❌ An error need not terminate the program: A declarative can return control after a failure, so a caller cannot rely on termination
⚠️ No value carries the failure: There is no exception object and no result type, so detail travels only through shared items



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Concurrency belongs to the transaction monitor: EXEC CICS and IMS link a program to a transaction environment instead of a language thread model
✅ Batch steps are single-threaded by design: A batch program runs to completion without shared-memory concurrency
✅ The 2023 standard defines asynchronous messaging: ISO/IEC 1989:2023 adds asynchronous message handling and transaction processing, so a program need not hand-roll that loop
⚠️ The language has no threads or synchronisation primitives: Any parallel work couples the program to the monitor
⚠️ Shared WORKING-STORAGE across transactions needs external discipline: A pseudo-conversational program must reset its state between transactions



1.1.6 Platform

❌ A large share of production runs on IBM mainframes: Much COBOL executes on z/OS with IBM compilers, so practice is largely one vendor’s (P2)
✅ The language is an ISO standard: ISO/IEC 1989:2023 is the current edition, so the language is not owned by a single vendor
✅ GnuCOBOL is an independent compiler: It is an open-source project separate from GCC and translates COBOL to C
⚠️ Vendor extensions bind a program to a compiler: EXEC CICS, EXEC SQL, and vendor libraries do not compile unchanged elsewhere
⚠️ Newer standard features are unevenly implemented: The 2002 object-oriented features and the 2023 additions are not uniformly available across compilers



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The small standard library is a scope decision: The standard specifies 43 statements, 87 functions, and one class, and adds no general-purpose library beyond them
The fixed reference format comes from the punched card: Columns 1–6 hold a sequence number and column 7 an indicator, and free format is now permitted, so the old constraint is optional
Mainframe batch orientation is a scope decision: COBOL assumes file and transaction processing in a monitor, which suits high-volume work and excludes systems programming
The PICTURE-driven fixed record suits flat files: The declared layout matches a fixed-length record, which is a modelling choice for the domain
The installed base is a business constraint: Retaining legacy programs is an organisational decision, not a property of the language




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Compiled ahead of time to native code: IBM Enterprise COBOL and GnuCOBOL (through generated C) produce machine code, so no interpreter and no JIT warm-up sits on the path
✅ USAGE selects the representation per item: COMP-3 packs two digits per byte where compact storage matters
✅ A batch step amortises start-up over millions of records: One run processes the whole job
⚠️ Tuning is platform-specific: IBM’s optimiser and GnuCOBOL produce different code, so a tuned program does not transfer unchanged
⚠️ Exact decimal arithmetic is slower than binary: COMP-3 operations cost more than native binary arithmetic



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is legacy and vendor-fragmented: IBM, Micro Focus, and GnuCOBOL each supply their own compiler, runtime, and tooling (Ec3)
❌ The mainframe tooling is proprietary: The compilers, monitors, and debuggers are commercial products (Ec4)
✅ GnuCOBOL is open source and maintained: It gives the language a free compiler
✅ A long-lived body of documentation exists: The ISO standard and the vendor manuals are complete and stable over decades
✅ The deployed base is enormous: Gartner reported over 200 billion lines of COBOL in 1997, and the language remains among the most widely deployed
⚠️ The skills base is shrinking: Retirements reduce the pool of maintainers, a risk exposed by the COVID-era unemployment-systems crisis



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The standard is backward compatible across decades: COBOL-74, -85, 2002, 2014, and 2023 code coexist, and programs written decades ago still compile
✅ ISO/IEC 1989:2023 added modern features: Asynchronous messaging, transaction processing, and dynamic-capacity tables join the language
⚠️ Revisions are infrequent: A new standard edition arrives at intervals of a decade or more, so a needed feature waits a long time
⚠️ Adoption of a new feature is uneven: A compiler may not implement a standard feature for years after publication



1.2.4 Domain

❌ Strong lock-in to mainframe transaction and batch processing: The language assumes fixed records, files, and a monitor runtime, so code carries that shape outside its home domain (D1)
✅ Superb for high-volume batch and transaction processing: The fit to financial and administrative workloads is close
✅ Still runs the bulk of card-payment background processing: The source reports COBOL behind most credit and debit-card swipe processing
✅ Fixed-point decimal arithmetic fits money: The data model matches monetary computation without floating-point error
⚠️ Poor for nearly everything else: Interactive, systems, and scientific work have little COBOL tooling



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The learning curve is steep in practice: Verbosity and over 300 reserved words must be learned (L1)
✅ The syntax is English-like: MOVE A TO B, ADD ... GIVING, IF ... END-IF, and DISPLAY read close to prose
✅ The division structure is a fixed learning path: Four divisions in a defined order give a predictable place for each declaration
⚠️ The vocabulary is large: More than 300 reserved words, and each verb carries many optional clauses
⚠️ The tooling is not beginner-friendly: Mainframe editors, JCL, and compile procedures are learned separately from the language



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Verbose: Every statement names its verb and its operands, and paragraphs need explicit names (S1)
✅ English-like and self-describing: The verb names the operation, so a statement is readable without symbol decoding
✅ END-IF, END-PERFORM, and END-READ bound a scope: Explicit terminators remove the ambiguity of implicit scope
⚠️ Fixed-format column rules still shape style: Column 7 is an indicator and the code sits in columns 8–72 in the classic reference format, and free format is an option
⚠️ The four-division prologue is long: Even a minimal program declares Identification, Environment, Data, and Procedure



1.2.7 Testing

✅ FILE STATUS and INVALID KEY give checkable I/O outcomes: A test can assert on the status item after a file operation
✅ Compilers supply tracing and dump facilities: IBM Debug Tool and GnuCOBOL’s runtime tracing report execution, and COB_SET_TRACE enables a trace at run time
✅ GnuCOBOL runs on ordinary workstations: The open-source compiler executes test jobs locally
⚠️ No test framework is in the language or the standard: A harness is external, so a suite couples to the tooling
⚠️ A batch test needs representative data: The job needs real files and JCL, not just a unit of code



1.2.8 Security

✅ Fixed PICTURE sizes bound every item: An oversized source value is truncated or padded on assignment rather than overrunning a buffer
✅ No pointers in the classic language: A COBOL program cannot forge an address
✅ The transaction monitor authorises access: CICS and RACF check a transaction’s resource use
⚠️ Truncation is silent: A value that does not fit an item is truncated without an error, so data can be lost quietly
⚠️ Dynamic SQL is injectable unless host variables are used: EXEC SQL with host variables is parameterised, but a statement built from a string re-opens SQL injection

Verdict: COBOL’s two scores are deliberately even: its own constructs impose about as much coupling as its platform and ecosystem do. The four divisions and the PICTURE clause declare a record once, CALL ... Inside high-volume batch and transaction processing COBOL is excellent; outside that niche the fit is poor.

title: Ada (2022 / 2012)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Ada in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 77/100 · Ecosystem coupling 60/100 · Engineering readiness 57/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static typing rejects mismatched use at compile time: Every object, parameter, and function result carries a declared type, so an incompatible assignment or call is a compile error, not a run-time surprise
✅ Subtypes and range constraints narrow the value set: A subtype refines a base type with a range or index constraint, and a value outside it raises Constraint_Error at the boundary
✅ Variant records declare a sum type: A case part in a record declaration selects on a discriminant, so the alternatives are a closed, compiler-checked set
✅ Generic units decouple an algorithm from the types it operates on: A generic declaration names formal types and subprograms, and an instantiation binds them without editing the generic body
✅ Access values are checked: Dereferencing a null access value raises Constraint_Error, no pointer arithmetic is possible, and access designates a typed object
⚠️ Operator overloading makes a symbol mean whatever its package declares: Defining "+" or "=" for a private type is legal, so a reader must resolve an operator from the package that declares it (T8)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Package specification and body are separate units: package X is ... end X; declares the visible interface and package body X holds the implementation, so a client compiles against the declaration
✅ Private types hide the representation: private and limited private make the record fields invisible outside the package, so callers cannot couple to the layout
✅ Child units extend a parent without reopening it: package X.Y adds declarations in its own unit, so a subsystem grows without an edit to the parent body
✅ Constructors are ordinary functions: function Make (...) return T creates a value with no allocation and no special constructor syntax, so creation does not couple to a memory strategy
❌ Variables are mutable unless declared constant: There is no immutability by default, so a package body holds state that clients can reach and every call must re-establish (C2)
⚠️ Library-level variables share one elaboration order: A variable declared in a package body is initialised once, so a client’s behaviour depends on when that elaboration runs



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No garbage collector in the standard: The storage of a declared object is reclaimed at scope exit, so reclamation timing is not coupled to a collector’s pauses
✅ Controlled types give deterministic finalisation: A type derived from Ada.Finalization.Controlled runs Initialize, Adjust, and Finalize at defined points, giving RAII-style cleanup
✅ Storage pools decouple allocation from the type: Storage_Pool and Storage_Size are set per access type, so the allocator changes without a change to any client
✅ Representation clauses fix layout where needed: Size, Alignment, and Bit_Order state the representation explicitly, so memory layout is declared rather than inferred
⚠️ Unchecked_Deallocation is manual: An object created with new on the standard heap is released only by an explicit call to Ada.Unchecked_Deallocation, so lifetime is the programmer’s duty
⚠️ There is no ownership model: An access value can outlive its designated object after a deallocation, and the compiler does not prevent it



1.1.4 Error

✅ Exceptions are named and scoped: An exception section handles by exception identity with when E : Some_Error =>, so recovery does not depend on an error code
✅ Language-defined checks raise exceptions instead of corrupting memory: Range, index, discriminant, and access checks raise Constraint_Error or Program_Error at the point of violation
✅ Contracts raise Assertion_Error at the boundary: The Ada 2012 aspects Pre and Post and type invariants check a subprogram against its callers
✅ An exception carries diagnostic strings: Ada.Exceptions.Exception_Message and Exception_Information attach a message and a state snapshot to an occurrence
❌ No composable result type: A fallible operation reports through raise, so a caller cannot thread a success-or-failure value through an ordinary expression (Er4)
⚠️ pragma Suppress removes checks: Suppressing a check removes the exception with it, trading safety for speed



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Tasking is part of the language: task, task type, protected objects, and entries give concurrency without an external library
✅ Rendezvous decouples communication from shared memory: A caller and a task meet at an entry and exchange parameters directly, so the task’s data need not be globally visible
✅ Protected objects serialise access without hand-written locks: A protected body runs one action at a time, so the program does not write mutex code
✅ select states waiting and timeouts declaratively: select ... or accept, or delay, and else express the waiting alternatives in the construct
✅ Annex D states the real-time policy in code: pragma Priority, pragma Task_Dispatching_Policy (FIFO_Within_Priorities), and pragma Locking_Policy (Ceiling_Locking) declare priorities and locking
⚠️ Tasking couples a program to a run-time library: The GNAT run time and the chosen profile decide which tasking constructs exist



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The language is an international standard: ISO/IEC 8652 defines the language and ISO/IEC 18009 defines conformity, so no single vendor owns it
✅ Several independent compilers exist: GNAT (FSF and AdaCore) and other implementations compile the same standard
✅ Restricted profiles target bare hardware: pragma Profile (Ravenscar) and No_Tasking remove constructs a small target cannot support
✅ Hardware access is a language feature: pragma Import, pragma Export, and representation clauses reach registers and foreign code directly
⚠️ Certified toolchains are few: DO-178C qualification kits and ARINC 653 bindings come from a small set of vendors, among them AdaCore, DDC-I (SCORE-Ada on Deos), and Green Hills (AdaMULTI), so a certified build couples to one of them
⚠️ Outside the certified targets, porting is unusual: An untested platform gets few guarantees, because few ports are exercised



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Verbosity is a deliberate trade: begin/end pairs and spelled-out names make each construct readable at the cost of keystrokes; that is a style choice, not a dependency forced on a caller
Restricted profiles are a scope decision: pragma Profile (Ravenscar) removes dynamic task creation to make a program analysable, trading flexibility for a schedulability bound
No garbage collector is a scope decision: The standard leaves reclamation to the program, which suits real-time work and gives up the convenience of a collector
Ada is not a scripting language: Compilation and the Alire package manager assume a build step, which is a scope boundary rather than a defect
Certification effort is a process cost: DO-178C evidence follows from the domain’s safety obligation, not from a property of the language




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Ahead-of-time native compilation: GNAT emits machine code, so no interpreter and no JIT warm-up sits on the critical path
✅ No garbage collector: Reclamation is deterministic, so no collector pause enters a control loop
✅ Inlining and representation clauses give explicit control: pragma Inline, Size, and Address let a program fix code and layout where latency demands it
✅ The real-time policy is declared in code: Priority and locking pragmas state the scheduling behaviour the program assumes
⚠️ Checks cost run time unless suppressed: Range, index, and access checks are cheap but not free, and pragma Suppress trades them away
⚠️ The GNAT run time is large for small targets: A tasking-enabled build needs the run time, so bare-metal work uses the restricted profiles



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is small and niche: Alire and the available library set are a fraction of what mainstream languages offer (Ec3)
✅ GNAT is mature and production-quality: The same front end serves FSF GNAT and AdaCore’s GNAT Pro, and certified projects depend on it
✅ Alire provides a package manager: alr resolves dependencies and pins toolchains, so a project build is reproducible
✅ Reference material is complete and stable: The Ada Reference Manual (ISO/IEC 8652:2023), the Rationale, and the SPARK documentation are authoritative and long-lived
⚠️ The community is small: A developer usually meets Ada through an employer’s code base rather than through a public library ecosystem



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The standard moves slowly: Ada 2022 followed Ada 2012 by about a decade, so a needed feature waits for a revision (V4)
✅ Backward compatibility is strong: Ada 2012 and Ada 2022 add features and keep earlier conforming code compiling
✅ GNAT tracks the current standard: The compiler implements the latest revision and the certification profiles
⚠️ A new feature reaches users through GNAT: Adoption follows the compiler release cycle rather than the standard’s publication



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for safety-critical and real-time systems: Avionics, defense, rail, and space projects use Ada with DO-178C evidence
✅ Annex D and the Ravenscar profile cover hard real-time work: Priorities, ceiling locking, and static scheduling are language-level concerns
✅ Representation clauses reach embedded hardware: Registers and device layouts are declared, not accessed through undefined behaviour
❌ The fit outside its niche is poor: Web, data-science, and scripting work have little Ada support (D2)
⚠️ Certification artifacts are domain-specific: A DO-178C evidence set is not reusable in another regulated domain without rework



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The language is steep: Tasking, generics, representation clauses, contracts, and the Annexes present several distinct models (L1)
❌ The surface is large: The standard library, the Annexes, and the profiles add to the core language (L2)
✅ Reference material is comprehensive: The Reference Manual states every construct, and the SPARK documentation covers the proof subset
✅ A regular syntax helps after the first step: Statements end in ; and blocks are delimited by keywords, so there is no precedence puzzle
⚠️ Tasking is the hardest single topic: The rendezvous model and protected objects take practice to use well
⚠️ Mentors are scarce: The small community gives fewer examples and reviews than mainstream languages offer



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Verbose: begin/end pairs, full keywords, and repeated identifiers make even small programs long (S1)
✅ English-like and consistent: Ada.Text_IO.Put_Line ("x") reads as prose, and keywords are reserved words
✅ Block structure is explicit: Every construct closes with a keyword, so a reader never counts indentation
⚠️ Identifiers are Mixed_Case with underscores: The convention differs from camelCase and snake_case neighbours, though it is uniform
⚠️ Qualified names add verbosity: A fully qualified call such as Ada.Text_IO.New_Line is long where use clauses are avoided



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Contracts are executable: pragma Assert, the Pre and Post aspects, and pragma Assertion_Policy check invariants in the built program
✅ GNAT ships a test-generation tool: gnattest generates AUnit test skeletons from a package specification
✅ GNATprove proves the stated contracts on the SPARK subset: Sequential and concurrent SPARK code can be proved free of run-time errors
✅ GNATcoverage measures coverage: The tool reports statement and branch coverage for certification evidence
⚠️ No test framework is in the language: AUnit and gnattest are tools, so a suite couples to the GNAT toolchain



1.2.8 Security

✅ Typing and checks prevent memory misuse: Array, range, discriminant, and access checks catch violations before they become memory errors
✅ The standard defines the effect of constructs: Within the defined subsets there is no undefined behaviour, and SPARK removes the remaining cases
✅ No pointer arithmetic: An access value designates a typed object, so an address cannot be incremented into another object
✅ SPARK proves absence of run-time errors: The subset supports proof of freedom from run-time errors and of the stated contracts
⚠️ Unchecked_Conversion and System.Address re-open the unsafe surface: These features can defeat the type system where a program uses them




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

✅ A standards-qualified toolchain or an established safety standard covers this language.

title: Solidity (0.8.x)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Solidity in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 50/100 · Ecosystem coupling 61/100 · Engineering readiness 56/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Statically typed and compiler-checked: Every state variable, parameter, and return value has a declared type
✅ Value and reference types are distinguished: uint256, address, and bool are value types, while arrays, structs, and mappings are reference types
❌ No sum types: A choice between alternatives is an enum plus a struct, or a separate contract, and the compiler cannot check the union (T4)
✅ Contracts and interfaces declare the ABI: A function signature in an interface fixes the external call shape
✅ No null: A uint256 starts at 0 and an address starts at the zero address, so absence is a value convention
⚠️ The data location is stated at every use: memory, storage, and calldata must be written for a reference type, and a wrong location changes the meaning of an assignment



1.1.2 Construction

❌ A constructor is optional: A contract without an explicit constructor is deployed with default state, so deployment validation is optional (C4)
✅ Contracts are the unit of encapsulation: State and functions live in one contract, and external, public, internal, and private state the visibility
✅ Inheritance with C3 linearization gives a defined order: contract B is A orders the bases linearly, so super resolves predictably
✅ Mappings and structs are declared members: A mapping(address => uint256) and a struct state the storage shape
✅ Constructors and initializer functions validate deployment: constructor(...) and an initializer modifier set and check the initial state
⚠️ delegatecall couples two contracts to one storage layout: The callee runs against the caller’s storage, so the layouts must agree exactly



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No garbage collector and no collection pause: The EVM memory is a per-call byte array that is discarded when the frame returns
✅ The data location makes copying visible: memory copies a value into the call, and calldata reads it in place
✅ Values are freed when a call frame returns: The caller never frees memory
✅ constant and immutable remove a storage read: A value fixed at compile time or at construction is embedded in the bytecode
⚠️ Persistent storage is expensive and manual: A write to a fresh storage slot costs 20 000 gas, so layout and write count are economic decisions
⚠️ A storage pointer aliases contract state: A local storage reference points into state, so a write through it is persistent



1.1.4 Error

❌ Failure is checkable but not exhaustive: require and revert abort a call, and nothing forces a caller to handle the failure (Er3)
❌ An unchecked low-level call is silently ignored: (bool ok, ) = addr.call(...) compiles even when ok is discarded, so a failed external call can pass unnoticed
✅ require(cond, "reason") states a precondition: A failed precondition reverts with a message
✅ Custom errors carry structured data cheaply: error InsufficientBalance(uint256 available); and revert InsufficientBalance(a) return named fields
✅ try/catch handles an external call failure: Since 0.6 a failed external call can be caught
✅ Arithmetic is checked by default since 0.8: An overflow or underflow reverts, and unchecked { ... } is the explicit opt-out



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ The language has no concurrency: A transaction runs sequentially on a single EVM thread, so there is no concurrent primitive (K1)
❌ Execution is coupled to the gas limit: A call that runs out of gas reverts, so control flow depends on the gas the sender supplies
✅ A transaction is atomic: The state changes commit together or revert together, so no partial state remains
✅ External calls within one transaction are ordered deterministically: The sequence is fixed by the bytecode
⚠️ Reentrancy is an ordering hazard: An external call can re-enter the contract before it returns, so checks-effects-interactions or a reentrancy guard must be applied by hand
⚠️ Atomicity stops at the transaction boundary: Two contracts touched in one transaction succeed or fail together, and no further coordination exists



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The EVM is the only target: The compiler emits EVM bytecode, and there is no other runtime (P1)
❌ The chain context is injected into every contract: msg.sender, msg.value, block.timestamp, block.number, and tx.origin are globals, so logic is coupled to the caller, the block, and the chain
✅ EVM-compatible chains share the runtime: A contract deploys to Ethereum, an L2, or any other EVM chain
⚠️ The context globals differ in meaning per chain: On an L2 block.number may be the L1 height and the sequencer sets block.timestamp, so a timing assumption does not transfer
⚠️ An upgradeable contract separates logic from storage: A proxy delegates to an implementation, and the storage layout must stay compatible



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Gas metering is the execution model: A deliberate economic constraint, not a language defect
Turing completeness is an expressive-power choice: Decidable automated verification of arbitrary properties cannot follow from it
The domain is on-chain contracts: Outside that domain the language has no use, which is a scope decision
Inheritance is provided: The language includes single and multiple inheritance, and C3 linearization orders multiple bases
Static typing helps but does not remove domain risk: The type system checks types, not economic or adversarial behaviour
The 0.8 release line changes semantics: Checked arithmetic and removed implicit conversions are a deliberate tightening, not a defect




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The cost model is explicit in gas: Every operation has a known price, so cost is stated rather than measured
✅ The solc optimiser reduces the emitted bytecode: The compiler optimises the code it produces
✅ Execution is deterministic across nodes: Every node computes the same result, which consensus requires
⚠️ Performance is not measured in wall-clock time: Gas, not throughput, is the design constraint
⚠️ Storage reads and writes dominate cost: A warm storage read costs 100 gas and a write costs far more, so a layout decision sets the cost
⚠️ The EVM is slow in general-computing terms: A loop over state is expensive by construction



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Foundry, Hardhat, and Truffle provide build and test tooling: Compilation, testing, and deployment are covered
✅ OpenZeppelin Contracts gives audited base contracts: Standard tokens and access control arrive as reviewed libraries
✅ solc is a released, versioned compiler with a range pragma: A file states the compiler versions it accepts
❌ The ecosystem is niche, young, and chain-specific: Package reuse is limited to an EVM audience, and the tooling field is small (Ec3)
⚠️ Tooling churn is high: The build-tool field has shifted toward Foundry, and older tooling is losing support
⚠️ There is no language-level package manager: Dependency management comes from the build tool, such as npm or a git submodule



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The compiler is released on an active cadence: 0.8.x releases add features and fixes
✅ pragma solidity ^0.8.0 pins the compiler range per file: A source file states the versions it accepts
✅ Breaking changes are grouped into release lines: 0.8 turned on checked arithmetic and removed implicit conversions
✅ The release notes state every breaking change: A migration path is documented for each release
⚠️ The 0.x versioning carries no compatibility promise: Every minor release may break, so a compiler range is mandatory in practice
⚠️ A deployed contract cannot be changed: The bytecode on chain is fixed, so an upgrade needs a proxy pattern from the start



1.2.4 Domain

✅ The language is the right tool for EVM smart contracts: The ABI, the storage model, and the chain context match the problem
✅ The type-safe ABI supports standard interfaces: An ERC-20 or ERC-721 contract is expressed as an interface with typed functions
❌ Domain lock-in to on-chain contracts: Outside the EVM the language has no application (D1)
⚠️ Blockchain-specific concerns are only partly covered by constructs: Reentrancy, front-running, and key management have no dedicated language construct
⚠️ The gas model is part of the domain semantics: Every construct has an economic effect the programmer must consider



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The learning curve is steep: The blockchain model — accounts, gas, storage, reentrancy, and the ABI — must be learned on top of the language (L1)
✅ The syntax is familiar to JavaScript developers: The grammar is ECMAScript-like, with braces, semicolons, and dot access
✅ Modifiers give a readable access-control idiom: modifier onlyOwner states a precondition at the function
✅ The documentation and community resources are good: The Solidity documentation and the OpenZeppelin guides are maintained
⚠️ A mistake has a direct economic cost: A vulnerability in a deployed contract can be exploited immediately, so experience is expensive to acquire



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ ECMAScript-style syntax: Braces, semicolons, and the . member operator match JavaScript
✅ Modifiers are a declarative precondition: A modifier wraps the function body and names the condition at the signature
✅ Data locations are stated in the signature: function f(uint[] calldata xs) shows where the argument lives
✅ Contract and interface declarations read as a module: The contract is the top-level unit and names its own scope
⚠️ Inline assembly { ... } uses the lower-level Yul syntax: A low-level block changes the language inside the braces
⚠️ A modifier hides the code it wraps: The reader sees the modifier name, not the rewritten body



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Foundry runs tests written in Solidity: forge test executes contracts as tests
✅ Hardhat runs a TypeScript test suite against a local chain: Accounts, deployment, and assertions are scripted
✅ Fork testing reproduces mainnet state: forge test --fork-url runs against a pinned block
✅ Fuzzing and invariant testing are built into Foundry: A property is checked over generated inputs
✅ Coverage and gas reporting are available: forge coverage and forge snapshot report coverage and cost
⚠️ The compiler does not catch reentrancy or access-control faults: Those faults pass every type check



1.2.8 Security

❌ The domain has canonical vulnerability classes: Reentrancy, front-running, and access-control faults are the field’s recurring failures, and Solidity was partly blamed for The DAO hack in 2016 (Q3)
⚠️ Reentrancy needs an explicit ordering discipline: Checks-effects-interactions or a reentrancy guard must be applied by hand
✅ Arithmetic is checked by default since 0.8: An overflow or underflow reverts rather than wrapping silently
✅ require and custom errors make a failure explicit: A failed precondition reverts with a reason
⚠️ delegatecall and low-level calls bypass type checking: The callee and the target are chosen at run time
✅ Static typing and the ABI prevent type confusion at the boundary: An external call is encoded against a declared signature




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No general foreign-function interface.
⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [5]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [6].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [7].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Solidity’s design yields high language-imposed coupling, most of it imposed by its domain. The type system is static and the data locations are explicit, but the EVM injects the chain context into every contract, execution is single-threaded and gas-metered, and the language runs nowhere else. Main strengths: a type-safe ABI, checked arithmetic since 0.8, custom errors, and mature test tooling in Foundry and Hardhat. Main weaknesses: no sum types, an optional constructor, a failure path a caller may ignore, no concurrency, platform lock-in to the EVM, and a security model in which reentrancy and access-control faults are the domain’s canonical failures.

title: Erlang (OTP 29)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Erlang in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 69/100 · Ecosystem coupling 76/100 · Engineering readiness 72/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Dynamic typing: A value carries its type at run time, so a type fault appears when the expression executes (T1)
❌ No declared parameter or return types: -spec is optional metadata, and the language has no generic type parameters (T5)
❌ No sum types: A tagged tuple such as {ok, Value} or {error, Reason} is a convention, and no type checks the union (T4)
❌ Dispatch is checked at run time: Mod:Fun(Args) resolves when called, so a missing function fails there rather than at compile time (T3)
✅ -spec and Dialyzer give optional static analysis: A success-typing pass over the compiled BEAM files detects inconsistent calls
✅ Atoms serve as named constants: An atom such as ok, error, or undefined is a distinct value, so the language needs no null



1.1.2 Construction

✅ All data is immutable: A term cannot be changed after it is built
✅ A pattern in the clause head selects the construction path: The arguments decide which clause runs
✅ Records and maps declare named structure: -record(user, {name, age}) gives compile-time named fields over a tuple
✅ State is a value threaded through recursion: An OTP behaviour receives its state and returns the new state, so no object owns it
✅ A process is the unit of mutable state: A gen_server owns its state and exposes it by message
⚠️ A record is a tuple: Field access is positional at run time, so the record definition must be shared by every module that uses it



1.1.3 Memory

❌ Collection is per-process and non-deterministic: A process collects its own heap on its own schedule (M2)
✅ A private heap confines a pause: A collection affects one process, and there is no global stop-the-world pause
✅ No manual deallocation: The VM reclaims memory, and a program never frees a term
✅ Off-heap binaries are reference counted: A binary above the heap threshold is shared between processes rather than copied
⚠️ A large live set costs more per collection: A process that accumulates state pays a higher collection cost
⚠️ An ETS table lives outside the collector: The table persists until its owner deletes it or dies



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked: throw, error, and exit are not declared, so a caller cannot see the failure set from a signature (Er2)
✅ “Let it crash” makes failure a supervision event: A supervisor restarts a failed process, and the normal path carries no recovery code
✅ Links and monitors define propagation: link/1 couples the fates of two processes, and monitor/2 reports a failure without dying
✅ A pattern-match failure raises a defined error: An unmatched value raises badmatch, and an unmatched clause raises function_clause
✅ try/catch/after is available when recovery is local: A catch clause separates throw, error, and exit
⚠️ A restart resets process state: Supervision restores the process, not the data it held, so state must be recoverable



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ The actor model is the core of the language: Processes share no memory and communicate by message
✅ spawn, link, and monitor are primitives: Starting and observing a process needs no library
✅ The BEAM schedules preemptively by reductions: A process cannot hold a scheduler indefinitely
✅ Messages are immutable values: A message is copied or shared by reference count, never aliased mutably
✅ Distribution is built into the VM: net_kernel and epmd let a process send to a node as if it were local
⚠️ Distribution is designed, not automatic: Node failure, network partition, and message loss must be handled by the application



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The BEAM is portable and open source: The Erlang runtime runs on Linux, macOS, Windows, and BSD
✅ Hot code loading is a runtime feature: code:load_file/1 replaces a module while the system runs
✅ A release bundles the runtime and the application: release_handler and reltool produce a deployable node
✅ Distribution across nodes is a platform feature: Nodes discover each other and pass messages without an external broker
⚠️ The runtime must be present: An Erlang program runs on the VM, so the artefact is not a native binary on its own



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The syntax is Prolog-derived: The form is unfamiliar to most developers; this is a learning property, not a coupling
Distribution is a design task: The language supplies the transport, and the application decides the failure semantics
Weak CPU-bound performance is a domain fit note: The VM is built for I/O concurrency, not for numeric loops
Hot upgrade constrains state handling: The running system can change module code, so the application must supply a code_change/3 callback to migrate state
Atoms are named constants in place of null: Absence is carried by an atom convention such as undefined
Records are tuples by design: The representation is a deliberate choice made for compactness and speed




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The BEAM handles very many concurrent I/O processes: A process is cheap and needs no thread
✅ BeamAsm compiles hot code: The JIT added in OTP 24 means bytecode is not always interpreted
✅ Per-process collection avoids a global pause: A collection affects one process
✅ Reduction scheduling bounds latency: A process yields after a fixed number of reductions
⚠️ CPU-bound computation is weak relative to native code: A tight numeric loop trails C or Rust
⚠️ A NIF runs on a scheduler thread: A native function that runs long blocks other processes on that scheduler



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Hex.pm and rebar3 cover packages and builds: A registry, dependency resolution, and release builds are all present
✅ OTP ships with the language: Supervision, gen_server, application, and release handling are part of the distribution
✅ Elixir libraries are reachable through interop: The two languages run on one VM and call each other directly
✅ The flagship projects are long-lived and battle-tested: RabbitMQ, CouchDB, Riak, and WhatsApp’s messaging stack are Erlang systems
✅ OTP is documented as a first-class topic: The OTP design principles document the behaviours
⚠️ The library count is smaller than the mainstream: Fewer general-purpose packages exist outside messaging and telecom



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The language has kept backward compatibility for decades: Code written against an old OTP release continues to run
✅ Hot code loading decouples deployment from runtime: A module is replaced while the system runs
✅ code_change/3 migrates state across a version change: An OTP behaviour converts old state to the new shape
✅ OTP release handling gives a controlled upgrade path: release_handler applies a version change to a running node
⚠️ A hot upgrade must be designed: State migration and dependency order are the application’s responsibility



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for distributed, fault-tolerant systems: Supervision, distribution, and the actor model match the problem directly
✅ Proven in telecom and messaging: WhatsApp, RabbitMQ, and Discord’s infrastructure run on the BEAM
✅ Binary parsing is a strength: The bit syntax <<A:8, B:16/little>> matches a protocol frame directly
❌ Poor fit for CPU-bound numerical work: The VM is not built for dense numeric computation, so that work belongs in another language (D2)
⚠️ Distribution across nodes requires explicit design effort: The application must decide how to handle a lost node



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The learning curve is steep: A developer learns functional programming, the actor model, and OTP at once (L1)
❌ The Prolog-derived syntax is unfamiliar: The ., ,, and ; delimiters and the term syntax differ from the mainstream (L1)
⚠️ The surface is large: The language, the OTP behaviours, and the VM’s semantics are separate bodies of knowledge (L2)
✅ The official documentation is thorough: The Erlang reference manual and the OTP design principles are authoritative
✅ The community is established: Decades of accumulated material and answered questions exist



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The term syntax is uniform: Every construct is a term, and a module is a sequence of forms ending in a period
✅ The delimiter roles are consistent: A comma separates expressions, a semicolon separates clauses, and a period ends a form
✅ Bit syntax is compact for protocols: A binary pattern states field widths and endianness in one expression
✅ Pattern matching is part of the function-head syntax: A clause states its cases directly
⚠️ The comma, semicolon, and period distinction is easy to get wrong: One misplaced delimiter changes the meaning of a form
⚠️ Atoms and variables differ only by case: ok is an atom and Ok is a variable



1.2.7 Testing

✅ EUnit and Common Test ship with OTP: Unit tests and system tests are part of the standard distribution
✅ Property-based testing is available: PropEr and QuickCheck generate inputs from a property
✅ Tracing and observer inspect a running system: dbg, recon, and the observer tool expose processes, messages, and scheduler load
✅ Common Test runs a distributed suite: A test can start several nodes and drive them together
❌ Errors surface at run time: Dynamic typing defers a type fault to the executed path (G3)
⚠️ Dialyzer catches some faults and not all: Success typing proves the absence of some inconsistencies, not the presence of correctness



1.2.8 Security

✅ Process isolation contains a fault: A crashed process does not corrupt another process’s memory
✅ Messages are immutable values: No shared mutable state exists to race on
✅ The supervision tree bounds a failure: A restarted process returns the system to a known state
⚠️ The atom table has a fixed limit: list_to_atom/1 or binary_to_atom/2 on untrusted input can exhaust the table, whose default ceiling is about one million atoms
⚠️ binary_to_term/1 on untrusted input is dangerous: Decoding an external term can allocate a large structure unless the safe option is used
⚠️ A NIF and a Port reach unsafe code: Native code can break the VM’s guarantees

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

Verdict: Erlang’s design yields moderate language-imposed coupling in the domain it was built for. The actor model removes shared memory from concurrency, immutability removes in-place mutation, and “let it crash” with OTP supervision moves recovery out of the business logic.
