title: Dart (3.12)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Dart in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 54/100 · Ecosystem coupling 84/100 · Engineering readiness 72/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Sound null safety: String and String? are distinct types, and Dart 2.12 and later check the difference at compile time
✅ Static typing with inference: var, final, and const infer a type, and that type is checked everywhere the value is used
✅ Sealed classes give exhaustive matching: A sealed class hierarchy lets the analyser check a switch expression for exhaustiveness
✅ Records give structural data: (int, String) is a value type with no class declaration, and its fields are named or positional
✅ Pattern matching decouples destructuring from accessors: An object, list, or record pattern pulls values apart without getter calls
✅ Extension methods add behaviour outside the type: An extension on String adds methods without subclassing or changing the class



1.1.2 Construction

✅ late decouples initialisation from construction: A late final field is initialised on first access, so the constructor need not compute it
✅ Factory constructors decouple construction from allocation: A factory constructor can return a cached instance, a subtype, or a constant instead of a fresh object
✅ const constructors build compile-time constants: A const value is canonicalised, so equal constants share one instance
✅ State lives in the object: The language forces no global mutable state, and an instance is the natural unit of state
✅ Named and optional parameters state the construction contract: Point({required int x, int y = 0}) names each argument at the call site
⚠️ A library-level var is global mutable state: Mutable top-level variables are permitted, so global coupling needs discipline rather than the compiler



1.1.3 Memory

❌ The VM collects garbage: Allocation and reclamation are automatic, and the program cannot choose when a pause happens (M2)
❌ No RAII: The language has no scope-exit destructor, so an opened File or socket must be closed by hand or in a try/finally (M3)
❌ No ownership or borrow model: Aliasing is unrestricted, so two references can hold the same mutable object and the VM alone tracks its lifetime (M4)
✅ No manual deallocation: Ordinary Dart never frees memory, so a double free or a use after free cannot occur in managed code
✅ Each isolate owns a separate heap: An isolate collects its own garbage, so a pause is confined to one isolate
⚠️ Finalizer and weak references are best effort: Finalisation runs when the collector decides, not at a moment the program chooses



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked: throw accepts any object and no signature declares what a function can throw, so a caller cannot read the failure set from the type (Er2)
⚠️ try/on/catch/finally gives a structured path: The recovery path is separate from the normal path, but the caught type is matched at run time
⚠️ Error and Exception are a convention: Error marks a programming fault and Exception a recoverable condition, and nothing enforces the split
✅ finally separates cleanup from recovery: The block runs whether the body succeeds, throws, or returns
✅ Future failures stay inside the chain: async/await routes a thrown object to the awaiting caller, and catchError handles it beside the value
✅ assert states a precondition in development mode: An assertion runs in development and JIT mode, so a violated invariant fails early



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Isolates share no memory: Each isolate has its own heap and communicates only by message, so a data race between isolates cannot occur
✅ Future and async/await suspend without blocking: An await yields the event loop instead of holding a thread
✅ Stream composes asynchronous sequences: await for and stream transformers chain events without callback nesting
❌ No race detection inside an isolate: The event loop runs each callback to completion, and the language provides no lock or race checker for shared mutable state (K3)
✅ Isolate.run and ports marshal by copy: A message is copied or transferred, so a value cannot be shared accidentally
✅ One event loop per isolate removes most synchronisation: Application code on a single isolate needs no lock



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Ahead-of-time compilation to native code: dart compile exe and the Flutter release build produce native ARM and x64 binaries with no interpreter
✅ Web targets are first class: dart compile js and dart2wasm emit JavaScript and WebAssembly for browsers
✅ The development VM supports hot reload: The kernel VM and the JIT path give an edit-and-reload cycle without a rebuild
✅ No vendor runtime lock-in: One source runs on the Dart VM, as native code, and in a browser
⚠️ Flutter is the dominant consumer: Server use through Shelf and Dart Frog is real but far smaller



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The ecosystem outside Flutter is small: Most packages target Flutter, so a non-UI project has fewer libraries; this is a community outcome, not a language mechanism
Null-safety migration of old packages is unfinished: An unmigrated package carries an unsound boundary, and opting out with a // @dart=2.x comment is a legacy choice
JIT in development and AOT in production is a tooling split: Hot reload needs the JIT, and a release build needs the AOT compiler
Familiar syntax is a familiarity choice: The C-style grammar is close to Java and TypeScript, which lowers the barrier but is not a coupling property
dart:ffi reaches native code: FFI is an explicit escape hatch, so the memory-safety guarantees of managed code do not extend across it
Dart is a general-purpose language with a UI-heavy reputation: The reputation follows Flutter, not a scope limit in the language




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Production code is compiled ahead of time: The Flutter release toolchain and dart compile emit native machine code, so the hot path holds no interpreter
✅ Startup is fast: An AOT binary starts without a warm-up phase, which matters for a mobile cold start
✅ The JIT optimises development runs: The development VM profiles and recompiles hot functions, so hot reload keeps speed
❌ The collector pauses the mutator: The generational garbage collector stops execution during a collection, which appears as a frame-time spike (R2)
⚠️ Throughput is good but not hand-tuned C: AOT output is close to a native compiler’s, but a numeric kernel has no SIMD or arena control in the language



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ dart pub and pub.dev are mature: Version constraints, a lockfile, and a central registry are part of the SDK
✅ The SDK ships the toolchain: dart analyze, dart format, dart test, and dart fix need no extra install
✅ Google backs the language: Funding and staff come from one large vendor, which keeps the toolchain coherent
❌ The package ecosystem is small outside Flutter: The great majority of packages are Flutter plugins, so a server or CLI project finds fewer libraries (Ec3)
⚠️ Null-safety migration is still in progress for old packages: An unmigrated dependency weakens the soundness guarantee at the boundary
⚠️ A single vendor holds the roadmap: The language specification and the Flutter release train come from one company



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Dart 3 unified the language at 100% null safety: One soundness model now applies to all migrated code
✅ Language versions are declared per library: A // @dart=3.0 comment pins a library to a language version, so a migration can be staged
✅ dart fix --apply automates migrations: Mechanical rewrites for deprecations ship with the SDK
✅ The language changes on a predictable cadence: Releases follow the Flutter stable train, so a team can plan an upgrade
⚠️ Older packages may lag the current release: A dependency that targets an older language version keeps its old semantics



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for cross-platform UI: Flutter renders one widget tree on iOS, Android, web, and desktop from one source
✅ Server-side use is supported: Shelf and Dart Frog provide HTTP servers and routing on the same runtime
✅ Browser output works through JavaScript and WebAssembly: dart compile js and dart2wasm cover the web target
✅ Command-line tools are a supported target: dart compile exe produces a standalone binary
⚠️ Non-Flutter use is uncommon: Examples, packages, and hiring lean toward UI development



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The syntax is familiar: The C-style grammar and the type annotations resemble Java, C#, and TypeScript
✅ Inference keeps annotations light: var, final, and collection literals let a beginner write working code early
✅ The official documentation is thorough: dart.dev carries a language tour, codelabs, and the effective-Dart guides
✅ Null safety gives a clear first rule: The compiler’s null-safety errors teach the distinction between T and T? quickly
⚠️ Dart 3 features are recent: Records, patterns, and sealed classes postdate many tutorials, so older material omits them



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Familiar C-style syntax: Braces, semicolons, and the . member operator match the mainstream
✅ Expression-oriented switch: A Dart 3 switch expression returns a value and reads as a mapping from case to result
✅ String interpolation is built in: "value: $x" embeds an expression without a concatenation call
✅ Named arguments make call sites self-documenting: theme: dark, dense: true states the intent at the call
⚠️ Asynchronous code colours functions: An async function returns Future<T>, so a caller must be asynchronous to await it
⚠️ Null-aware operators add punctuation: ?., !, and ?? are concise but stack up in dense expressions



1.2.7 Testing

✅ package:test is the standard runner: dart test discovers files under test/ and reports structured failures
✅ flutter_test covers widget tests: WidgetTester pumps frames and finds widgets by key or text
✅ The analyser catches errors before the test run: dart analyze reports type and null-safety faults without executing code
✅ Asynchronous and golden tests are supported: expectLater and matchers handle Future and Stream results
⚠️ There is no single mocking standard: mockito with code generation and mocktail without it are both common



1.2.8 Security

✅ Sound null safety removes null dereference: A String? cannot be used as a String without a check or an explicit !
✅ Static typing rejects type confusion at compile time: The analyser rejects an assignment the type system forbids
✅ Bounds checking is always on: An index outside a list’s range throws RangeError rather than reading adjacent memory
✅ No eval and no dynamic code execution: The language has no construct that turns a string into code
⚠️ Web output inherits browser risks: A compiled script still runs inside the browser’s security model




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [5]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [6].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [7].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

title: Assembly (x86-64, System V AMD64 ABI)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Assembly in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 10/100 · Ecosystem coupling 58/100 · Engineering readiness 68/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ There is no type system: An operand is a register or a memory address of a fixed width, and the assembler does not check that an integer, a pointer, and an address are used consistently (T1)
❌ No sum types: An alternative must be encoded by hand in a register or in a memory layout the programmer invents (T4)
❌ No generics: A macro can repeat a sequence, but there is no type parameter through which a repeated sequence can be checked (T5)
❌ No namespaces: Every global symbol shares one flat namespace in the object file, so a collision is resolved by naming convention (T6)
❌ No null safety: A null pointer is a zero register value, and a load from it is an ordinary instruction (T10)
❌ No module boundary: Separate translation units share the same global symbol space and ABI, and the only encapsulation is the assembler’s local label (T11)



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Registers are global mutable state: Every instruction reads and writes the same fixed register file, so the meaning of a register depends on the whole instruction stream (C1)
❌ Mutability is the only mode: Nothing is immutable unless a section is marked read-only, and that is enforced by the loader rather than by a type (C2)
❌ Construction is allocation: Creating a value means writing a register or a memory cell that must already have been reserved (C3)
❌ No constructor or validation: A value is legal only because the programmer kept it legal, and nothing checks it (C4)
✅ Macros decouple a repeated sequence: .macro in GAS and %macro in NASM let a reusable instruction sequence be named and expanded, so a repeated pattern is written once
✅ Sections separate data from code: .text, .data, .rodata, and .bss place each kind of content in its own segment of the object file



1.1.3 Memory

❌ Every allocation and deallocation is manual: The stack frame, the malloc call, and the free call are the programmer’s responsibility (M1)
❌ No release tied to scope: There is no RAII; nothing runs at the end of a block (M3)
❌ No ownership model: A pointer may alias, dangle, or be freed twice, and the assembler does not see pointers as a type (M4)
✅ The stack is a structured allocation: push/pop and the rsp/rbp frame give a scoped allocation with a defined lifetime for the duration of a call
⚠️ The layout is the ABI’s, not the program’s: The System V AMD64 ABI fixes which registers are caller-saved and how the stack frame is formed, so the layout choices are constrained



1.1.4 Error

❌ There is no structured error path: No exception, no error type, and no return-result convention; a failed call is signalled by a flag or a register the caller must test (Er1)
❌ An error can be ignored by design: A non-zero value in rax or a set carry flag does nothing unless the code branches on it (Er3)
❌ No composable result type: An error cannot be returned as a value the caller’s code carries in a checked way (Er4)
✅ Flags give a structured condition test: cmp and test set ZF, CF, SF, and OF, and a conditional jump branches on a named condition
⚠️ The recovery path is a jump target: Recovery is a branch to a label, so its structure exists only in the programmer’s discipline



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Shared mutable state is the default: Registers and memory are equally visible to every core, and there is no notion of private state (K2)
❌ Synchronisation is manual with no race detection: A lock is a lock prefix on one instruction or a call into a library, and nothing analyses the program for a race (K3)
❌ No structured concurrency: A thread is a clone or pthread_create call, and nothing scopes or joins its lifetime (K4)
✅ Atomic operations are instruction-level: lock cmpxchg, lock xadd, and mfence express a defined atomic primitive directly
✅ The lock prefix gives a defined ordering: It serialises the decorated instruction across the cores of the machine
⚠️ The memory ordering is reasoned about by hand: The x86-64 model is comparatively strong, but nothing in the language states or checks the ordering the algorithm needs



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The program is bound to one instruction set: x86-64 opcodes do not run on AArch64 or RISC-V, so the source is not portable across architectures (P1)
❌ The calling convention is one ABI: A call must agree with the System V AMD64 register and stack rules, so the function interface is fit for one platform’s convention
✅ The object format is documented and stable: An ELF object file is linked with the platform linker through a published format
✅ The assembler is a choice within the target: GAS and NASM produce code for the same instruction set
⚠️ Windows uses a different x86-64 convention: The Microsoft x64 ABI differs from System V in its argument registers and its shadow space, so the source is bound to one operating-system convention as well
⚠️ Extension instructions need runtime dispatch: AVX-512 and the other vector extensions require a CPU feature check before they are used



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Full machine control is the point: The absence of an abstraction layer is a deliberate removal, not a defect
Assembly is a last resort by design: It is used where a higher-level language cannot express the operation
A hand-written kernel can repay the discipline cost: The performance-critical kernel and the cryptographic primitive are the cases where it does
Reverse engineering is a use, not an application: Disassembly is read, not maintained as a product
The dialect choice is a surface choice: The Intel and AT&T notations name the same instruction set
Inline assembly inside a host language is a scoping decision: What remains is a coupling to the compiler’s asm syntax




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The program is the machine code: There is no interpreter, JIT, or runtime between the source and the CPU, so the cost of an instruction is the instruction
✅ Instruction selection is under program control: lea, fused operations, and vector instructions can be chosen for each site
✅ There is no runtime start-up cost: A static executable needs no runtime initialisation beyond the loader
⚠️ The CPU optimises beyond the instruction stream: Out-of-order execution, branch prediction, and the micro-operation cache mean the source-order cost is not the measured cost
⚠️ A hand-written routine can lose to a compiler: Without the optimiser’s cross-block analysis, hand-scheduled and hand-allocated code can be slower than -O2 output



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ There is no package manager: A dependency is an object file or a linked library, resolved by the linker and the build script (Ec1)
✅ The assemblers are standard and maintained: GAS, NASM, and the LLVM assembler are widely available
✅ The code interoperates with C at the ABI: An assembly routine can be called from C and can call C
⚠️ The reusable corpus is small: Most assembly source is written for one program and its ABI, so few libraries exist as assembly source



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The instruction set is specified and backward compatible: x86-64 adds encodings and keeps the earlier ones
✅ New extensions are opt-in: SSE, AVX, and AVX-512 code is gated by CPU feature detection rather than by the instruction set as a whole
✅ The manuals are public and maintained: The Intel SDM and the AMD APM document each instruction
⚠️ Assembler syntax is not standardised across tools: GAS and NASM disagree on directives, operand order, and macro syntax
⚠️ A microarchitecture change invalidates tuning: Code hand-scheduled for one CPU generation can be mistuned on the next



1.2.4 Domain

✅ The kernel-level operations are the native domain: Hardware access, interrupt entry, context switch, and boot code
✅ Some instructions are reachable only here: The special registers, cpuid, rdtsc, and the privileged instructions have no higher-level equivalent
✅ Vector kernels benefit: A hand-tuned SIMD routine writes exactly the instruction the target supports
❌ It is a poor fit above the machine: With no types, no data abstraction, and no error handling, ordinary application logic is expensive to write and to change (D2)
⚠️ Even kernel work is mostly C with small assembly islands: The fit is real but narrow



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The curve is extremely steep: The programmer must hold the register file, the instruction set, and the target ABI in mind at once
❌ There is no abstraction to learn instead of the machine: Nothing is hidden and nothing is named above the instruction level
✅ The reference material is complete and public: Intel and AMD document every instruction and every flag
✅ The machine gives immediate feedback: A debugger shows the registers and the memory directly
⚠️ Three bodies of knowledge are separate subjects: The instruction set, the ABI, and the toolchain must each be learned on its own



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ The Intel and AT&T dialects differ in the same instruction set: Operand order reverses and the register and constant prefixes differ, so the notation is a toolchain choice
⚠️ The directive syntax differs by assembler: GAS uses .globl and .section, NASM uses global and section
⚠️ Every operand form is spelled out: %rax, $42, and 8(%rbp) write the addressing mode at each site
✅ The mnemonics are short and uniform: mov, add, and jmp each name one operation
⚠️ A label is a fixed position in the code: A label names a location for a jump, a call, or a data symbol, so a transfer target is coupled to that position in the listing



1.2.7 Testing

❌ There is no test framework in the language: A test is a program that runs and compares, and the harness lives outside the assembler (G1)
❌ Debugging is low-level: The debugger exposes registers and raw memory, so a fault is found in machine state rather than in a named abstraction (G2)
✅ A single-step debugger is exact: gdb and lldb can run one instruction and show every register and flag
✅ Repetition is deterministic: With no scheduler and no collector, the same input produces the same instruction sequence
⚠️ The usual check is a test in a higher-level language: The assembly routine is called from C and compared there



1.2.8 Security

❌ Every memory-safety class is open: A buffer overflow, a use-after-free, a double free, and an out-of-bounds write are all possible and nothing prevents them (Q1)
❌ Return-oriented programming is possible: The stack holds return addresses that are writable, so a memory write can redirect control flow
❌ There is no bounds checking and no guard page by default: An array index is an address calculation
⚠️ Stack canaries, ASLR, and CET are external mitigations: They come from the toolchain flags, the loader, and the operating system, and the source must cooperate with them
✅ Non-executable and write-or-execute pages are available: The operating system can mark the stack non-executable and enforce W^X, which removes some code injection
✅ The sandbox is the operating system’s: A program runs with the privileges the loader grants it, not with a language-level capability model




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

⚠️ The specification is not public.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

Verdict: Assembly’s design produces the lowest core score in this comparison, because it removes every separating construct rather than misplacing one. There is no type system, no release tied to scope, no structured error path, and no concurrency construct; the register file is global mutable state, and the machine is the only abstraction. What the language does give is exact control: the programmer chooses the instruction, the register, and the schedule, and the flags give a defined condition test. Main strengths: no runtime overhead, direct access to the privileged instructions, and a fully public specification. Main weaknesses: the source is bound to one instruction set and one ABI, every memory-safety class is open, and the work is expensive to learn, to test, and to maintain.

This assessment applies the coupling account — coupling as access to a shared resource, and the coupling floor [1], [2] — and the knowledge-embodiment theorem [3]; the language is assessed against its official reference [4].
Analysis against Ruby 4.0 (December 2025). YJIT is production-ready since Ruby 3.2+.

title: Ruby (4.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Ruby in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 28/100 · Ecosystem coupling 58/100 · Engineering readiness 88/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Duck typing: No compile-time type checking, coupling invisible
❌ Pattern matching (3.0+) is not exhaustive: A case/in with no else raises NoMatchingPatternError at run time rather than reporting a missing case
✅ Mixins: Include modules for behavior without inheritance
⚠️ Open classes: Can modify any class, creates action-at-a-distance coupling
⚠️ RBS type signatures: External type system (.rbs files) — static checking via Steep/Sorbet, not built into runtime
✅ Blocks/Procs/Lambdas: First-class functions decouple behavior
❌ Method_missing: Dynamic dispatch hides coupling, runtime failures



1.1.2 Construction

✅ initialize separate from new: Construction logic decoupled
✅ Data.define (3.2+): Immutable value objects like records/kotlin data classes
⚠️ Class methods for factories: Common pattern but not enforced
❌ No validation enforcement: Constructor invariants not checked
❌ Monkey patching: Can modify any class anywhere, global coupling
❌ Global variables: $global creates pervasive coupling
❌ Class variables: @@var shared across all instances, couples classes



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Garbage collection: Automatic, no manual management
⚠️ GC pauses: Non-deterministic, couples performance to runtime (improved by YJIT’s reduced allocation rate)
✅ No manual deallocation: Can’t have use-after-free
✅ YJIT reduces GC pressure: Faster execution means fewer long-lived allocations



1.1.4 Error

❌ Unchecked exceptions: raise doesn’t appear in signatures
❌ Broad rescue: rescue without type catches everything
✅ Pattern matching with => operator (3.0+): Can destructure error objects structurally
❌ Silent failures: Methods often return nil instead of raising



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Global VM Lock (GVL): Like Python’s GIL, couples threads to single core
✅ Fibers + Fiber Scheduler (3.0+): Cooperative concurrency with io_uring support for async I/O
✅ M:N thread scheduler (3.3+, experimental → progressing): Lightweight userspace threads
⚠️ Ractors: Actor-like concurrency (3.0+), still evolving
❌ Shared mutable state: No protection, race conditions easy



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No company owns the language: Ruby is developed by the ruby-core community under the Ruby Licence, dual-licensed with the two-clause BSD licence
✅ Several implementations exist: MRI (Matz’s Ruby Interpreter) is the reference implementation, alongside JRuby on the JVM, TruffleRuby on GraalVM, and mruby for embedded use
✅ The runtime is portable: MRI builds on Linux, macOS, Windows through RubyInstaller, and the BSDs
✅ The JVM is an available target: JRuby runs the same language on the Java platform, so Ruby code is not confined to one runtime
✅ Packaging is vendor-neutral: RubyGems and Bundler fetch gems from any repository, not from one vendor’s service



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Programmer happiness is the design goal: Ruby favours expressive code over enforcement, a deliberate trade of static guarantees for code that reads like prose
Parentheses are optional: The grammar treats a method call and a local variable alike, a readability choice whose cost is ambiguity in dense expressions
Everything is an object: Numbers, strings, and classes all respond to methods, a uniform model that removes special-case rules and adds method lookup to every value
Visibility is cooperative: private and protected can be bypassed with send, so encapsulation is a convention the language does not enforce — a deliberate openness rather than a dependency




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ YJIT (production-ready since 3.2): 3-5x speedup in many benchmarks; reduced GC pressure
❌ GVL: Couples multithreading to single core (still present in Ruby 4.0)
⚠️ The JIT is opt-in: YJIT must be enabled with --yjit or RUBY_YJIT_ENABLE=1, so a default run stays interpreted
⚠️ High memory: Object overhead significant (partially offset by YJIT)
⚠️ Optimization hard: Dynamic nature limits static optimization



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ RubyGems: Massive ecosystem
⚠️ Rails dominates the ecosystem: Most Ruby applications are Rails applications, so the framework’s conventions and release cycle set the pace for the rest
✅ Bundler: Dependency management works well
✅ IDE support: RubyMine, VSCode good
✅ Rich ecosystem: Mature, well-established



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Backward compatible: Ruby 2→3→4 mostly smooth
✅ Regular releases: Annual release cycle
✅ YJIT: Major performance investment
⚠️ RBS/Sorbet: Type signatures external, not core language
⚠️ GVL: Still present, no removal timeline



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for web: Rails is industry standard
✅ Good for scripting: Clean syntax for automation
⚠️ Improved for performance-sensitive: YJIT closes gap but still slower than compiled languages
❌ Not for systems: GC, interpreted, GVL
⚠️ DevOps tools: Chef, Puppet use Ruby



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Very gentle: Readable, intuitive
✅ Principle of least surprise: Design philosophy
✅ Excellent resources: Why’s Poignant Guide, Rails tutorials
✅ Quick productivity: Can build apps immediately



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Beautiful syntax: Minimal noise, readable
✅ Flexible: Multiple ways to express intent
✅ Blocks: Elegant for DSLs and callbacks
✅ Optional parentheses: Clean, natural language-like



1.2.7 Testing

✅ RSpec, Minitest: Excellent testing frameworks
✅ Pry: Interactive debugger, REPL
✅ Test culture: TDD/BDD strong in Ruby community
⚠️ Runtime errors: No compile-time checks



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents memory bugs
❌ Type confusion: Dynamic typing allows anything
❌ Monkey patching: Can introduce vulnerabilities
⚠️ Rails security: Framework helps, but language-level gaps




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.

title: PHP (8.5)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses PHP in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 28/100 · Ecosystem coupling 69/100 · Engineering readiness 84/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

⚠️ Type declarations (PHP 7+): Gradual typing, improving
✅ Interfaces decouple: Can program to interfaces
❌ Weak typing historically: Type juggling couples
⚠️ Traits: Multiple inheritance-like, can couple
❌ Inconsistent stdlib: strpos vs str_replace couples to memorization
✅ Namespaces scope every name: A namespace declaration qualifies a class, function, or constant, so two libraries can define the same short name
⚠️ Magic methods can hide coupling: __get, __call obscure behavior



1.1.2 Construction

⚠️ Constructors can have side effects: No enforcement
❌ No immutability by default: Everything mutable
⚠️ Dependency injection available: Frameworks support it
❌ Global state tempting: $_GET, $_POST, $_SESSION couple



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Reference counting: Immediate deallocation when references drop to zero
✅ Cycle collector: Detects and breaks circular references
✅ Request-scoped by default: Each request has isolated memory, cleared after request
❌ Long-running processes leak: Traditional PHP has no long-lived processes, but Swoole/ReactPHP do
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free in pure PHP
⚠️ Extensions can leak: C extensions may have memory issues



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions unchecked: No type tracking
⚠️ Error vs Exception confusion: Two error mechanisms couple
❌ @ operator suppresses errors: Hides coupling
⚠️ Modern frameworks handle better: Laravel/Symfony impose discipline



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Shared-nothing by default: Each request is separate process
✅ Fibers (PHP 8.1): Built-in cooperative concurrency — enables async I/O without external extensions
⚠️ No built-in async event loop: Fibers need a framework (ReactPHP, Swoole) for full async; however Revolt/Amp provide fiber-based event loops
❌ Global state couples across requests: Sessions, databases



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No company owns the language: PHP is maintained by The PHP Group and released under the PHP Licence, a permissive BSD-style licence
✅ The reference implementation is free software: The Zend Engine is developed in the open and shipped by every Linux distribution
✅ The interpreter is portable: PHP runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows, under Apache, nginx through PHP-FPM, and IIS
✅ Commodity hosting provides it: Most shared hosts include a PHP runtime, so deployment needs no platform purchase
✅ No single distribution is required: Distribution packages, official builds, and vendor bundles run the same language



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The language began as a page preprocessor: PHP grew from a templating tool, so markup and logic still share one file — a design origin whose cost is mixed presentation and behaviour
Every variable carries a $: The sigil marks a variable at a glance and cannot be omitted, a notation decision rather than a type-system one
The core library assumes one short request: Functions such as header() and session_start() act on the current request, an assumption that costs when the same code must run in a long-lived worker
Frameworks define the architecture: PSR interfaces and the Laravel or Symfony conventions shape practice more than the language does — an ecosystem convention, not a dependency the language forces
Feature growth is version-gated: Enums, readonly classes, and property hooks arrive release by release, so the style a codebase may use follows its minimum supported version — an evolution cost, not a coupling




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Interpreted: Slower than compiled languages
✅ PHP 8+ JIT: Significant improvements for CPU-bound workloads
⚠️ Shared-nothing: Each request starts fresh (couples to memory)
✅ Fibers: Cooperative concurrency without process overhead
⚠️ OPcache helps: But couples deployment to caching



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Composer: Good package manager
✅ Large ecosystem: Packagist has many packages
✅ Laravel, Symfony: Mature frameworks
✅ IDE support: PHPStorm excellent, VSCode good
⚠️ Quality varies: Many low-quality packages



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Improving rapidly: PHP 8.1-8.5 added enums, fibers, readonly, property hooks, asymmetric visibility, clone with, pipe operator
✅ Regular releases: Yearly cadence
⚠️ Legacy burden: Must support old code (PHP 5.x still in the wild)
❌ Inconsistent stdlib: function_name vs functionName — PHP 8.x is standardizing but still inconsistent



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for traditional web: WordPress, Drupal, Laravel
⚠️ Backend only: Can’t do frontend (obviously)
✅ Fibers enable async: Modern PHP can do async I/O natively
⚠️ CLI possible: But uncommon relative to Python/Ruby
❌ No systems programming: Not suitable



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Very gentle: Easy to start
✅ Lots of resources: Tutorials, documentation
⚠️ Bad habits easy: Superglobals, $ prefix confusion
✅ Quick productivity: Deploy immediately



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ C-like syntax: Familiar but verbose
✅ Property hooks (8.4): Eliminates getter/setter boilerplate
✅ Asymmetric visibility (8.4): Clean access control
❌ Superglobals: $_GET, $_POST everywhere
❌ Inconsistent stdlib: Hard to remember function names



1.2.7 Testing

✅ PHPUnit: Industry standard
⚠️ Xdebug: Works but setup needed
✅ Property hooks + readonly: Easier to test (less setup)
⚠️ Error reporting: Improving with strict types



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents memory bugs
❌ SQL injection: Easy to do wrong (prepared statements help but not enforced)
❌ XSS: Template systems help but not enforced
❌ Superglobals: Injection attack surface
⚠️ Modern frameworks help: But not language-level




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.6 Governance

Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

❌ Interpreted by default: the slowest class in the energy and time benchmarks [5]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [6].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [7], [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

title: JavaScript (ES2025)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses JavaScript in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 28/100 · Ecosystem coupling 73/100 · Engineering readiness 96/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ No static types: All coupling deferred to runtime
✅ Prototypes decouple: Can modify behavior without inheritance
⚠️ Duck typing: Structural at runtime, but no safety
❌ Type coercion couples: Implicit conversions hide intent
❌ Undefined/null confusion: Two absence types couple



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Object literals: Simple construction without classes
⚠️ Prototypes flexible: Can change after construction
❌ new keyword confusing: this binding couples to call context
⚠️ Factory functions decouple: Can avoid new entirely
❌ Global scope couples: window, globalThis everywhere
❌ Module side effects: Import order matters
❌ Prototype pollution: Can modify built-in prototypes globally



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Garbage collection decouples memory: Generational GC (implementation dependent)
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: V8, SpiderMonkey, etc. have different characteristics
❌ Closure captures create leaks: Easy to accidentally hold references
❌ Event listener leaks common: Forgotten listeners prevent collection
✅ Reference cycles are collected: A mark-and-sweep collector reclaims objects that point at each other, so a cycle alone is not a leak
⚠️ WeakMap/WeakRef help: Can create weak references, but not automatic



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions unchecked: No type tracking
❌ Promise rejection unchecked: .catch() optional
⚠️ Result types possible: Libraries exist but uncommon
❌ Callbacks couple error/success: (err, result) mixes concerns



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Single-threaded event loop: A long task blocks every other callback, so no second core is available for CPU-bound work
✅ Async/await separates: Explicit async functions
❌ Promise errors untracked: Rejection type unknown
⚠️ Web Workers separate: Explicit message passing, but manual



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No vendor owns the language: ECMAScript is standardized by Ecma International as ECMA-262 and evolves through the public TC39 proposal process
✅ Independent engines implement it: V8, SpiderMonkey, and JavaScriptCore are separate implementations, so a program is not bound to one vendor’s runtime
✅ A runtime exists on every platform: Every web browser ships an engine, and Node.js, Deno, and Bun run the language outside the browser
✅ The source is portable between hosts: The same script runs in a browser and in Node.js; only the host API differs, not the language



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Dynamic Typing vs. Predictability: All coupling deferred to runtime, no compile-time detection
Flexibility vs. Correctness: Can modify anything at runtime, couples correctness to discipline
Type Coercion: Implicit conversions couple values to contexts ("5" + 3 === "53", "5" - 3 === 2)
This Binding: Function context couples to call site (.call(), .apply(), .bind() required)
Callback Hell vs. Promises vs. Async/Await: Three async paradigms couple code to era written
Module Systems: CommonJS vs. ES6 modules couples code to environment (Node vs. browser)
Prototype Chain: Inheritance couples objects to prototype chain modifications




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ JIT optimization: V8, SpiderMonkey fast
⚠️ Unpredictable: Performance depends on JIT behavior
⚠️ GC pauses: Non-deterministic
✅ Event loop: Efficient for I/O
❌ Single-threaded: Couples CPU-bound work to event loop



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Massive ecosystem: Npm largest package ecosystem
✅ Excellent tooling: Webpack, Vite, ESBuild, Babel
✅ Great IDE support: VSCode, WebStorm
⚠️ Dependency hell: node_modules coupling
✅ Browser DevTools: Best-in-class debugging



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ TC39 process: Predictable evolution
✅ Backward compatible: Old code keeps working
✅ Transpilation: Babel enables future features
⚠️ ES6 adoption: Took years to become standard



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for frontend: Only native browser language
✅ Great for full-stack: Node.js backend
✅ Strong for scripting: Quick prototypes
❌ Poor for systems: No control, GC
⚠️ CPU-bound: Single-threaded limits



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Gentle start: Easy to begin
⚠️ Weird parts: this, prototypes, coercion
✅ Massive resources: Tutorials everywhere
❌ Mastery hard: Closure, async, event loop



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Concise: Arrow functions, destructuring
✅ Flexible: Multiple paradigms
⚠️ Inconsistent: Many ways to do things
❌ Coercion surprises: [] + {} !== {} + []



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Jest, Mocha, Vitest: Mature frameworks
✅ Excellent debuggers: Chrome DevTools
✅ Source maps: Debug original code
⚠️ Async debugging: Promises/async can be tricky



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents memory bugs
❌ Prototype pollution: Object mutation vulnerabilities
❌ XSS: DOM manipulation couples to security
⚠️ npm vulnerabilities: Dependency attack surface

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.

Verdict: JavaScript’s dynamic nature defers all coupling detection to runtime. Prototypes and object literals provide flexibility but no guarantees. Global scope and unchecked errors create pervasive coupling. Main strength: object literals and prototypes are simple. Main weakness: no type system means coupling invisible until runtime.

title: D (2.112)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses D in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 57/100 · Ecosystem coupling 84/100 · Engineering readiness 65/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static typing with inference: auto, template argument deduction, and typeof infer most declarations, so the type is fixed at compile time without being written at every site
✅ Templates avoid the angle-bracket problem: Instantiation uses the ! syntax (foo!int, foo!(int, string)) with if (isInputRange!R) constraints, so generic code carries none of C++’s nested <> noise
✅ Modules are the compilation boundary: A module is declared with module in one source file and consumed with import, so there are no headers and no include guards tying a declaration to a textual include order
✅ UFCS decouples call syntax from the definition site: x.f(y) is rewritten to f(x, y), so a free function composes into a method-call chain without being a member of the type
✅ immutable and const are transitive: A qualifier reaches through pointers and members, so a read-only view is stated once rather than per access
⚠️ Operator overloading is not visible in cost: opBinary, opCmp, opIndex, and opAssign let a type redefine +, <, [], and =, so a dense expression can hide work the call site does not show (T8)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Structs are constructed in place: struct is a value type, so a local, a field, or an array element is constructed where it is declared without a heap allocation
✅ Contract programming separates the specification from the body: in, out, and invariant blocks state preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants as separate declarations, so a check is not buried in the implementation
✅ scope guards attach cleanup to the construction site: scope(exit), scope(success), and scope(failure) run at block exit beside the code that acquired the resource
✅ @disable this() forbids an illegal construction: A type can delete a constructor, so an object cannot be built by calling new
⚠️ Mutability is the default: A variable is mutable unless it is declared immutable or const, so immutability is opt-in rather than the default reading of a declaration (C2)



1.1.3 Memory

❌ Garbage collection pauses are non-deterministic: The default new path allocates on the collector’s heap, and a collection runs on the collector’s schedule rather than the program’s (M2)
⚠️ RAII is partial: Struct destructors (~this) and scope(exit) release a value type deterministically, but a class instance is collected, so its destructor has no defined run time (M3)
❌ No ownership or lifetime checking: The compiler does not track which reference owns an allocation, so a dangling pointer or a double release in @system code is not diagnosed (M4)
✅ @nogc removes the collector from a call tree: A @nogc function may not allocate through the GC, so its pauses are excluded at compile time
✅ -betterC excludes the runtime entirely: The program links without druntime or the collector, which is what the embedded and no-GC case needs
✅ destroy releases a value at a chosen point: destroy(x) runs the destructor and resets the value, giving an explicit release where the collector would otherwise decide



1.1.4 Error

❌ Unchecked exceptions are the only error channel: throw needs no declaration in the signature and the compiler does not check that a handler exists; nothrow is an opt-in promise (Er2)
✅ nothrow names the functions that cannot fail: A nothrow function may not throw, so the property is checked at the declaration
✅ scope(failure) separates the recovery path from the normal path: Cleanup written there runs only when the block leaves by an exception
✅ try/catch/finally is the standard shape: A catch clause names the type it handles, and finally runs on every exit
⚠️ Contracts and assertions disappear under -release: in, out, and assert are compiled out in a release build, so their guarantee is a debug-time one



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ The shared qualifier makes cross-thread state visible: Data declared shared cannot be read or written through an ordinary reference, so the cast that crosses a thread boundary is the place the synchronisation is declared
✅ std.concurrency gives message passing: spawn starts a thread with its own message queue, and send/receive pass values between threads without a shared lock
✅ std.parallelism gives structured parallel loops: parallel and taskPool map a loop body over a range, so the common data-parallel case is stated rather than hand-threaded
✅ Atomic primitives are in the standard library: core.atomic provides atomicOp, cas, and atomicLoad, so a lock-free update has a named primitive
❌ Synchronisation is manual and unchecked: synchronized, Mutex, and core.atomic are the only tools, and the compiler does not prove the locking discipline or detect a race (K3)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Three independent compilers target the same language: dmd uses its own Digital Mars backend, ldc uses LLVM, and gdc uses the GCC backend, so a program is not bound to one vendor’s toolchain
✅ Native code is produced for many targets: Linux, Windows, macOS, and the BSDs on x86, x86-64, ARM, and AArch64 are supported targets
✅ C and C++ interoperability is a language feature: extern(C), extern(C++), and the importC compiler feature let a D module call existing C and C++ binaries without a binding generator
✅ -betterC removes the runtime dependency: A BetterC program links like a C program, without druntime or a GC
✅ The C preprocessor is not part of the language: There is no textual include and no macro layer above the module system
⚠️ The three compilers advance at different rates: ldc and gdc follow dmd’s front end with a lag, so a version-specific feature may not be available on every compiler at once



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Better C++ is a target, not a guarantee: Porting C++ to D is a rewrite with its own cost, and the two languages interoperate at the ABI rather than at the source
GC or manual memory is a per-program choice: -betterC and @nogc buy determinism at the cost of the collector’s convenience
Compile-time execution is a deliberate shift of work: CTFE, static if, and string mixins move computation to the build, so it is not a runtime mechanism at all
Multiple paradigms widen the surface: Imperative, object-oriented, functional, and metaprogramming styles are all supported, and the choice is the programmer’s
Niche adoption is a market fact, not a language defect: The smaller library pool follows from adoption, not from a construction of the language




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Native compilation with no interpreter: dmd, ldc, and gdc emit machine code, so there is no bytecode dispatch or JIT warm-up between the source and the CPU
✅ ldc and gdc reuse mature optimisers: The LLVM and GCC backends apply the optimisation pipeline that compiles C and C++
✅ CTFE moves work to compile time: static if, mixin, and template instantiation are evaluated by the compiler, so the runtime pays nothing for them
✅ @nogc bounds the runtime cost of a call tree: A function that cannot allocate has no collector interaction at all
⚠️ The collector remains a latency risk: Throughput is good, but a collection can still lengthen a pause in code that allocates, so a latency-sensitive path needs @nogc (R2)



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The library pool is small: dub’s package registry is far smaller than crates.io, npm, or Maven, so a project is more likely to write a library than to find one (Ec3)
✅ dub is a standard package manager and build tool: dub.json or dub.sdl declares dependencies and targets, and dub build, dub run, and dub test cover the ordinary workflow
✅ The C and C++ ecosystems are reachable: extern(C), extern(C++), and importC reduce the need for a D-specific binding
✅ vibe.d supports web services: An asynchronous I/O framework covers HTTP and socket work on the D runtime
⚠️ Corporate backing is weak: The language is carried by its contributors rather than by a large vendor, so long-term support is the community’s



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ A deprecation cycle precedes a removal: A feature is deprecated for a release series before it is removed, and the changelog records both steps
✅ -preview flags gate changes to the front end: A new language behaviour ships behind a flag first, so a change can be tested before it becomes the default
✅ The DIP process documents proposals publicly: The D Improvement Proposal repository holds the rationale for a language change
⚠️ Removals do happen: The changelog records deprecated features that were later dropped, so older source can need an edit at a major front-end step
⚠️ Front-end versions differ across the three compilers: A change fixed in dmd reaches ldc and gdc later, so a project can be pinned to one compiler for a period



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Systems and performance work is the design target: Native code, value types, and direct C interop are the native idiom
✅ Game development is a stated fit: The GC can be excluded, structs stay in place, and templates specialise per case, which is what a game loop needs
✅ Embedded and no-runtime work is supported by -betterC: The program links without druntime, so it fits a bare-metal or constrained target
✅ Web services are supported by vibe.d: The framework covers asynchronous HTTP on the same runtime
⚠️ The collector is the wrong model for hard real-time: A latency bound requires @nogc or BetterC throughout the allocating path
⚠️ D is rarely the default choice in any of these domains: The fits are real, but the surrounding library and hiring pool is smaller



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Moderate for an experienced C++ developer: Templates, RAII-style cleanup, and value types have direct C++ analogues
✅ Templates are easier to read than C++ templates: The ! instantiation syntax and if constraints remove the ambiguity of nested angle brackets
✅ Contract programming is a small notation: in, out, and invariant are a few keywords over the ordinary function body
⚠️ The metaprogramming surface is large: Templates, static if, CTFE, traits, and string mixins each have their own rules
⚠️ The memory model is two models at once: A developer must know which allocations are collected and which are not, and @nogc makes the distinction a compile-time obligation
⚠️ Four paradigms are available at once: Imperative, object-oriented, functional, and metaprogramming styles widen the surface a newcomer must choose from



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Cleaner than C++ for similar expressive power: A module is one file, there is no header text, and there is no preprocessor
✅ ! makes template instantiation unambiguous: foo!int cannot be confused with a comparison, which is C++’s parsing problem
✅ auto removes a declaration without hiding the type: The type is inferred and still checked at compile time
✅ scope(exit) is a compact cleanup notation: One line states the release that other languages spell as a try/finally
⚠️ Attributes accumulate on a signature: @safe @nogc @property nothrow pure and their variants stack up, and the combination is part of the contract
⚠️ String mixins hide the generated code: mixin("...") inserts source the reader cannot see in the file’s order



1.2.7 Testing

✅ unittest blocks are part of the language: A unittest { ... } block sits beside the code it tests, and it is compiled in when the -unittest flag is passed
✅ dub test runs the blocks: The package manager builds and runs the test configuration
✅ Contracts are executable invariants: in, out, and invariant checks fail with a trace when a precondition is broken
✅ Coverage is built in: dmd -cov writes a per-line coverage report from a normal run
⚠️ Tests are compiled only with -unittest: A release build carries no test code, so the test set is a build configuration rather than a language guarantee
⚠️ The test library is third-party: Fixture, mocking, and property-test helpers come from packages such as unit-threaded rather than from the standard library



1.2.8 Security

✅ @safe is checked by the compiler: @safe code may not do pointer arithmetic, lose a type through a cast, or call @system code, so the unsafe operations are the ones that were declared
✅ Bounds checking is kept where it is required: An array or a slice carries its length, and @safe code retains the index check
✅ Variables are initialised by default: A variable starts at its .init value, so the uninitialised-read class of bug does not arise as it does in C
⚠️ @trusted and cast are the escape hatch: A @trusted function or a pointer cast re-opens the unsafe surface, and its correctness is the author’s claim
⚠️ The collector and the runtime are part of the attack surface: A bug in druntime or the collector is reachable from a @safe program
⚠️ -release removes the contract checks: Assertions and contracts are compiled out, so a release build relies on the checks that @safe keeps




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: D’s design yields moderate language-imposed coupling for a language of its reach. The module system replaces headers, UFCS separates call syntax from definition, and contract blocks separate the specification from the body. Predicates such as @safe, @nogc, and nothrow turn several memory and error properties into declared and checked facts. Main strengths: compile-time execution removes metaprogramming from the runtime, three independent compilers keep the toolchain from locking in, and -betterC reaches the embedded case. Main weaknesses: unchecked exceptions are the only error channel, the collector’s pauses are not deterministic, no ownership model detects aliasing, and the ecosystem stays niche with weak corporate backing.

title: Transact-SQL (SQL Server)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Transact-SQL in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 58/100 · Ecosystem coupling 69/100 · Engineering readiness 61/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static typing over SQL data types: Every variable, parameter, and column has a declared type, and a block that violates it fails at parse or bind time
✅ Table variables and table-valued parameters carry a declared row type: DECLARE @t TABLE (...) and a user-defined table type pass a typed row set between units
✅ A procedure parameter declares its type and direction: @p int OUTPUT fixes the type and the direction, so a caller binds to a signature
⚠️ DECLARE @name defaults to NULL (T10): A declared variable starts as NULL, so an unassigned variable is valid and propagates NULL into the expression
⚠️ NULL comparison needs three-valued logic: With ANSI_NULLS ON (the default, and the only supported setting since SQL Server 2017), @x = NULL is unknown, so a check needs IS NULL
⚠️ There is no type beyond a SQL data type: No user-defined sum type or generic exists, so a variant is modelled with nullable columns or a discriminator



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A stored procedure provides modularity with a declared interface: CREATE PROCEDURE names the unit, its parameters, and its result, and can return a status value and OUTPUT parameters
✅ A view or an inline table-valued function separates consumers from the query: The exposed relation is stable while its defining query can change
✅ A table-valued parameter passes a row set without a shared temporary table: A user-defined table type plus a TVP parameter removes the need for a global temporary table
✅ Set-based statements compose without a cursor: INSERT ... SELECT, UPDATE ... FROM, and MERGE express the whole transformation in one statement
⚠️ Triggers fire implicitly: An AFTER or INSTEAD OF trigger runs in response to a data change, so the writer of a statement cannot see from the statement which code will run
⚠️ Session SET options change the meaning of a statement: ANSI_NULLS and QUOTED_IDENTIFIER are captured when a stored procedure is created, while DATEFORMAT applies when the statement runs, so the same text can parse or convert differently elsewhere



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No manual memory management: The SQL Server buffer pool and the query workspace own the memory, and a batch never names an address
✅ The server grants memory to a query: The query’s memory grant comes from the server’s calculator or the Resource Governor, so the batch does not request bytes
✅ Buffer pool and tempdb behaviour are server configuration: max server memory, the tempdb files, and a Resource Governor pool are settings, not batch properties
⚠️ A sort or hash can spill to tempdb: An operation whose grant is too small writes to tempdb, which costs I/O even though the language hides allocation
⚠️ A cursor allocates per fetch: A row-by-row cursor uses workspace per fetch, so the memory pattern follows the loop



1.1.4 Error

✅ TRY ... CATCH gives a structured path: The CATCH block runs on error and exposes ERROR_NUMBER, ERROR_MESSAGE, ERROR_SEVERITY, and ERROR_LINE
✅ THROW and RAISERROR raise with a number and a message: THROW 50001, 'msg', 1 carries a number, so a handler can branch on it
✅ XACT_STATE() and @@TRANCOUNT tell the handler whether the transaction is committable: A doomed transaction is detectable inside CATCH
⚠️ Errors ignored or non-exhaustive (Er3): A CATCH block that swallows the error, or a skipped @@ERROR check, lets the batch continue past the failure
⚠️ Errors do not abort the batch by default: Without SET XACT_ABORT ON, a statement error rolls back that statement and the batch continues
⚠️ Severity decides whether the caller sees the error: A low-severity error is informational, so the same statement text can pass a caller by



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Transactions group statements atomically: BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK make a unit of work commit or abort as one
✅ Isolation levels are selectable and versioned: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED (default), REPEATABLE READ, SNAPSHOT, and SERIALIZABLE, while the database options READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT and ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION switch READ COMMITTED to row versioning and enable SNAPSHOT
✅ Snapshot isolation removes reader–writer blocking: With READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON, a reader uses row versions and does not block a writer
✅ Set-based statements reduce explicit locking: One UPDATE moves many rows without a row-by-row lock protocol in application code
❌ Shared mutable state by default (K2): SET options, CONTEXT_INFO, and a global temporary table ##t are visible to code the caller did not write
⚠️ A locking hint couples the query to the engine’s concurrency model: WITH (NOLOCK), UPDLOCK, and READPAST are engine-shaped and must agree with the application’s lock ordering



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Client interfaces are standard: ODBC, JDBC, OLE DB, and ADO.NET reach the engine, so a client is not bound to one binary protocol
✅ Bulk interfaces are documented: bcp and BULK INSERT use a documented format, so data exchange is not tied to an application API
⚠️ Two implementations exist under separate vendors: Microsoft SQL Server and SAP ASE share a lineage and a core syntax, but the two diverge, and Microsoft and SAP document them separately
⚠️ Azure SQL is the same vendor with a different deployment: The managed service changes availability, administration, and some features, so code targets a specific surface
❌ Cannot function outside one vendor (P1): The language needs SQL Server, Azure SQL, or SAP ASE
❌ The T-SQL surface is engine-specific: TOP, IDENTITY, GO, the sys catalog views, and the sp_ procedures are SQL Server features, so a port to another engine is a rewrite



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Logic beside the data is deliberate: Keeping a rule in the database guarantees it for every writer
A cursor is a deliberate trade for row-by-row work: It makes a per-row algorithm expressible, at the cost of the set-based model
Dynamic SQL is deliberate for DDL and for a flexible query: sp_executesql and EXEC reach constructs a static statement cannot name
NOLOCK trades consistency for concurrency: A reader that accepts dirty reads avoids blocking
The engine is proprietary by design: The licence buys one integrated stack of engine, tooling, and support
T-SQL is not a general-purpose language: The assumption of a SQL Server database is a scope decision




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ A cost-based optimiser with a plan cache executes a statement: A procedure’s plan can be reused, so the caller does not choose an access path
✅ A columnstore index and batch mode scan analytically: CREATE COLUMNSTORE INDEX plus batch mode processes a large scan in vectorised batches
✅ Query Store records plans and regressions: An operator can see a plan change and force a previous plan
✅ In-memory OLTP tables are lock-free and memory-optimised: MEMORY_OPTIMIZED = ON tables and natively compiled procedures remove latch contention
⚠️ Parameter sniffing can choose a plan for the wrong input: A cached plan built for one parameter value can be poor for another
⚠️ A plan can regress without a query change: New statistics, a version upgrade, or a changed data volume can select a worse plan



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Tooling is mature and first-party: SQL Server Management Studio, Azure Data Studio, and sqlcmd cover administration and query work
✅ The market and the hiring pool are large: SQL Server is widely deployed in Microsoft environments, so documentation, training, and consultants are abundant
✅ Cloud deployment is a first-party service: Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance run the same engine with a managed administration model
❌ Proprietary (Ec4): The engine, the tooling, and the support come from Microsoft (and, for ASE, from SAP) under licence
⚠️ The ASE toolchain is separate from the SQL Server toolchain: SAP maintains its own documentation, tools, and support, so knowledge does not transfer freely



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The release cadence is regular and active: SQL Server ships a major release periodically, and Azure SQL receives continuous updates
✅ A compatibility level keeps old behaviour: A database at an older compatibility level keeps the older optimiser and syntax behaviour while the engine is upgraded
✅ The engine leads the standard: TRY ... CATCH, MERGE, window functions, and JSON support arrived as engine features, so users get them without waiting for the standard
⚠️ A deprecated feature is warned and then removed: The documentation lists deprecated features, and an upgrade can require edits
⚠️ Feature availability differs by edition and deployment: An Enterprise feature or an Azure-only feature may not exist on a local Standard edition



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for transactional and analytical logic in the database: A stored procedure runs beside the data with a plan and a transaction
✅ One language spans OLTP and analytics: Set-based DML, window functions, and a columnstore scan all live in the same language
✅ The surrounding pipeline is first-party: Integration Services, the Agent scheduler, and Reporting Services cover the rest of a data workflow
❌ Domain and vendor lock-in (D1): The language exists inside SQL Server or SAP ASE, so both the domain and the vendor are fixed
⚠️ Procedural row logic reads poorly: A row-by-row algorithm in a cursor is verbose and slow beside its set-based equivalent
⚠️ It is not a runtime for arbitrary programs: The language assumes a SQL Server database and a set-based workload



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Gentle for a SQL developer: A procedure with BEGIN ... END, TRY ... CATCH, and SELECT ... INTO is readable to anyone who knows SQL
✅ Documentation and examples are complete: The Microsoft T-SQL reference documents every statement with examples
⚠️ The procedural and the set-based model coexist: A developer must choose between a cursor and a set-based statement, and the wrong choice shows up as a performance problem
⚠️ NULL handling must be learned: With ANSI_NULLS ON, = NULL never matches, and a comparison with NULL yields unknown
⚠️ Plan and locking behaviour is a separate body of knowledge: Performance work means reading plans and lock waits rather than syntax
⚠️ The SAP ASE dialect diverges in details: Differences in GO, IDENTITY, and built-in functions mean knowledge transfers only in part



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Keyword-based and readable: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE and BEGIN ... END read close to English
✅ A procedure is a readable unit: The parameter list, the body, and the RETURN value are declared in one CREATE PROCEDURE statement
✅ GO marks a batch boundary in a script: The client tool sends the batch, so the boundary is visible in the source
⚠️ SET options prefix every script: SET NOCOUNT ON, ANSI_NULLS ON, and QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON are usually written at the top, so the boilerplate grows
⚠️ @ and @@ distinguish kinds of variable by convention: A local variable, a parameter, and a global function share the sigil, so a reader distinguishes them by spelling
⚠️ Identifier quoting depends on a setting: [name] and "name" both quote an identifier, and the second form needs QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON



1.2.7 Testing

✅ tSQLt is the established framework: An open-source unit-test framework runs test classes with mocked tables and assertions
✅ TRY ... CATCH makes a unit test expressible in the language: A test procedure asserts and THROWs on a mismatch
✅ A transaction wraps a test and rolls it back: The database is unchanged after the test
✅ Error metadata supports an assertion on a failure path: ERROR_NUMBER and ERROR_MESSAGE inside CATCH let a test check the rejection
⚠️ The base product ships no test framework: tSQLt is a third-party install, so a suite depends on deployment and permissions
⚠️ A server-side suite needs a server: The harness needs a SQL Server instance, so the tests couple to infrastructure



1.2.8 Security

✅ sp_executesql with parameters removes the injection surface: EXEC sp_executesql N'SELECT ... WHERE x = @p', N'@p int', @p = 1 passes the value out of band
✅ GRANT, DENY, and REVOKE with roles express least privilege: Access is declared per object, per schema, and per role
✅ Row-level security limits what a statement can see: A SECURITY POLICY with a predicate function filters rows by the caller’s identity
✅ EXECUTE AS makes the effective identity explicit: A procedure can run as its owner or as a named user
❌ Known vulnerability/injection (Q3): A statement built with EXEC (@sql) from concatenated input lets the input become code
⚠️ Dynamic SQL and owner-rights execution re-open the risk: EXEC on a built string, sp_OA* procedures, and xp_cmdshell where enabled defeat parameterisation




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

⚠️ One vendor decides the language’s direction.
⚠️ The specification is not public.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs inside a database engine: energy and time are the engine’s, not the program’s.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [5].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Transact-SQL’s coupling follows its host engine. Stored procedures, views, and table-valued parameters give real modularity, TRY ... CATCH gives a structured failure path, and the optimiser, Query Store, columnstore, and in-memory OLTP carry performance work. Main strengths: a mature first-party toolchain, a regular release cadence, and standard client interfaces. Main weaknesses: the language only runs on SQL Server or SAP ASE, the useful surface is engine-specific, NULL starts in every declared variable, an unhandled CATCH continues the batch, cursor code paths are slow, and a string-built statement is a standing injection hazard.
