title: SAS (9.4 / Viya)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses SAS in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 51/100 · Ecosystem coupling 54/100 · Engineering readiness 34/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Dynamic typing with no static check (T1): A variable takes its type when the DATA step first builds the row, so a mismatch appears at run time
⚠️ Two types exist and a character length is fixed at first use: A variable is numeric or character, and a later longer value is truncated to the length already set
⚠️ The dataset carries the schema, not a declaration: A variable list comes from the dataset descriptor, so a variable’s type is read from data rather than from source
✅ LENGTH and ATTRIB declare a variable explicitly: A length, a type, and a format can be fixed before the data arrives, which decouples the variable from the value that first creates it
✅ FORMAT and INFORMAT separate presentation from storage: A date is a number with a DATE9. format, so a reader sees a date and the value stays numeric
❌ There is no type beyond a column in a dataset: SAS has no user-defined type, generic, or interface, so a richer value is encoded in columns



1.1.2 Construction

✅ The DATA step separates data handling from analysis: A DATA step reads, merges, filters, and derives; a PROC step analyses and reports, so the two are distinct statement kinds
✅ A PROC step names its analysis and takes a dataset: PROC MEANS data=work.sales; performs one analysis on one input, so the analysis is not tangled with retrieval
✅ SET, MERGE, and BY compose datasets declaratively: A join is declared with a BY key, so the key is the join condition rather than a hand-coded loop
❌ No immutability by default (C2): A DATA step can overwrite the dataset it reads (data work.x; set work.x;), and every variable is reassignable
❌ A macro is the only module mechanism: %MACRO is text substitution, so an expansion depends on the macro symbol table and on the place of the invocation
⚠️ The DATA step’s implicit loop carries state across rows: RETAIN and the automatic _N_ follow the row stream, so row order becomes part of the result



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No manual memory management: The SAS supervisor allocates and frees the buffers of a step, and the program never names an address
✅ The program-data vector bounds per-row state: A step holds one row’s variables in a fixed vector, so the program does not size buffers
✅ The resource envelope is a configuration choice: SORTSIZE, MEMSIZE (on the hosts that provide it), and the Viya CAS memory settings are set outside the program
⚠️ A large sort spills to the work library: A sort or a hash join that exceeds its memory writes to the utility library, so the temporary footprint follows the data volume
⚠️ A macro variable persists for the whole session: A %LET value stays until it is reassigned, so it is shared state that outlives the step that set it



1.1.4 Error

✅ OPTIONS ERRORABEND stops the session on an error: An error ends the run instead of continuing, which turns a silent failure into a visible one
✅ A macro-level guard can abort the run: %IF &SYSERR %THEN %ABORT reads the error status and stops the batch
❌ No structured error path (Er1): SAS has no exception construct, so a DATA step records an error, writes a note to the log, and by default continues to the next observation
⚠️ An error is reported in the log, not to the caller: A step sets &SYSERR and the automatic _ERROR_ flag, so detection is by log inspection or a macro check
⚠️ Error checking is opt-in per step: The default continues on many data errors, so a batch run can finish with a wrong dataset



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Procedures can use several threads: OPTIONS THREADS lets PROC SORT, PROC MEANS, and PROC SQL use more than one processor
✅ SAS/CONNECT and MP Connect distribute work across sessions: A job can be split over several SAS sessions on one host or across hosts
✅ A dataset is locked per member: Two writers do not share a row buffer, so member-level locking prevents a concurrent overwrite in one library
⚠️ The language offers no lock or atomic primitive: Coordination is the platform’s library locking and the scheduler’s, not a construct in the DATA step
⚠️ The macro symbol table is shared session state: One step’s %LET or CALL SYMPUT is visible to every later step in the session



1.1.6 Platform

❌ Cannot function outside one vendor (P1): The language needs a SAS installation, and a program’s unit of deployment is a SAS library on a SAS host
❌ SAS datasets are the interchange unit: The persistence format is a proprietary member of a SAS library
⚠️ Viya is a second runtime under the same vendor: Viya runs the language on the CAS engine with cloud deployment, but it is the same vendor’s platform, not an independent implementation
✅ A dataset can be written to the documented XPORT transport form: The XPORT engine with PROC COPY produces the openly documented transport format that the FDA requires for electronic submissions, and other tools can read it
⚠️ Open-source interop exists from inside the platform: PROC PYTHON and PROC R call R and Python, so part of a workflow can use an open tool



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The DATA-step/PROC-step split is a deliberate separation of concerns: Retrieval and analysis are distinct statement kinds by design
The dataset is the only data abstraction: One table shape for all data keeps the language uniform, at the cost of encoding a richer value in columns
A macro is a text-substitution preprocessor: It keeps a repeated block in one place, at the cost of visibility at expansion time
Point-and-click Enterprise Guide serves a non-programmer task: Hiding the language suits a code-free workflow, so the GUI’s coupling to the engine is the product’s purpose
A proprietary platform is traded for a regulated-industry toolchain: One vendor with documented releases and validation packages suits a regulated deliverable
Viya chose coexistence over replacement: Modernising the architecture while keeping SAS 9.4 running is a compatibility decision




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The DATA step and the procedures run compiled code: A step is compiled to a program-data-vector loop executed by the supervisor
✅ Multithreading and the CAS engine parallelise heavy work: Threaded procedures and distributed in-memory execution in Viya carry the large jobs
✅ An index or the SPD engine avoids a full scan: A lookup by an indexed key or by the multi-threaded SPD engine reads fewer pages than a sequential pass
⚠️ A sort can dominate a job’s time and space: A sort that exceeds memory spills to the work library, so a job of a given size needs a matching utility allocation
⚠️ A BY-group analysis requires sorted input: Many procedures need the data sorted by the BY key, which makes a sort a precondition of the analysis



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ The library is large and mature inside its industry: SAS ships statistical, econometric, clinical, and operations-research modules with long support windows
✅ Regulated statistical practice has decades of SAS convention: Clinical and regulated reporting follows CDISC standards and platform validation practice
✅ Viya adds open-source tooling: Jupyter, Python, R, and REST interfaces connect to a Viya deployment
❌ Proprietary (Ec4): The product is licensed by subscription, and its modules are licensed separately
❌ Small, niche, and increasingly legacy (Ec3): The language’s own market has shrunk against R and Python, so new analysts and new packages arrive more slowly
⚠️ The ecosystem is closed: A shared contribution is an in-house macro or user-defined format, not a package drawn from an open index



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Long-term stability is a stated commitment: A program written for an earlier release of the same generation still runs on a later one
✅ The vendor carries validated code forward: Existing 9.4 language support continues in Viya, so a submission program is not stranded
⚠️ The language has evolved slowly: SAS 9.4 has been the reference release since 2013, and the DATA-step and PROC syntax is largely unchanged
⚠️ The modern architecture is a second platform: Viya changes deployment, engines, and administration, so a move to it is a platform migration rather than a language upgrade
⚠️ Evolution follows the vendor’s roadmap: A new feature appears at the vendor’s next release, not at a date the community fixes



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for regulated statistical reporting: A DATA step plus a PROC produce a documented, reproducible table
✅ Clinical and financial workflows have a fixed vocabulary: PROC LIFETEST, PROC PHREG, PROC FREQ, and PROC LOGISTIC name the standard analyses directly
❌ Domain and vendor lock-in (D1): The language is built for statistical analysis on a SAS platform, so both the domain and the vendor are fixed
⚠️ The regulatory transport requirement has narrowed: The FDA still requires the open SAS V5 XPORT transport format for datasets, but CDISC standards define their content and other tools can write the format, so the language’s old regulatory moat has shrunk
⚠️ General-purpose programming sits outside the design centre: Text processing, user interfaces, and systems work are not the intended use
⚠️ Analysts increasingly use R and Python beside it: An open-source language is cheaper per seat and easier to hire for



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The DATA-step/PROC-step division is teachable: A beginner learns retrieval in a DATA step and analysis in a PROC, and the two do not mix
✅ Documentation and training are complete and vendor-provided: SAS documentation, courses, and certification cover every module
⚠️ Steep (L1): The DATA step’s implicit loop, the program-data vector, and the two-match step of MERGE are unlike any other language’s execution model
⚠️ DATA-step syntax is idiosyncratic: Statements are KEYWORD variable=value; lines whose effect depends on their order in the step
⚠️ Macro programming is a second language on top: %MACRO, &var, %eval, and the quoting functions (%str, %bquote) have their own rules



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Statements are keyword-led and read as English: PROC SORT data=a; by x; run; states the operation and the key
✅ A PROC block is small per analysis: An analysis reads as PROC name data=...; plus a few statements
❌ Verbose (S1): A typical step is a list of KEYWORD option; lines, and necessary statements such as LENGTH, FORMAT, and LABEL add lines before any data is touched
⚠️ Every step must be closed by RUN or QUIT: A missing RUN; means the step does not execute, and a missing QUIT leaves a procedure open
⚠️ The semicolon and the % sigil each carry meaning: A missing semicolon changes the statement, and a macro reference without % or & is treated as text
⚠️ Formats and informats add a name to every value: date9., $char20., and best12. decorate a declaration, so a reader learns a second vocabulary



1.2.7 Testing

✅ PROC COMPARE reports differences by variable and observation: A regression test is a dataset comparison with a named result
✅ A check step can assert its own expectation: A step can read the result and %ABORT on a wrong value, and OPTIONS ERRORABEND turns a data error into a stop
✅ The log is the primary diagnostic instrument: With MPRINT and MLOGIC it names the step and the macro line that failed
⚠️ No test framework ships with the language: A test is a SAS program, so the harness is a script or a scheduler around it
⚠️ Errors are runtime-only: A wrong type or a missing file appears when the step runs, not before
⚠️ A passing run can still contain errors: The default continues after many errors, so a clean exit code does not imply a clean run



1.2.8 Security

✅ No pointers and no manual memory access: The language offers no address arithmetic, so the memory-corruption class does not apply
✅ Access control is a platform feature: Library and table permissions, metadata-server roles, and Viya identities control who reads a dataset
✅ Viya records an audit trail: A deployment logs who ran which action against which resource
⚠️ A macro variable can build a statement: &SYSFUNC and a resolved macro variable are expanded into syntax, so a value that carries user input can become code
⚠️ Encryption and transport security are configuration choices: A library can be encrypted and a connection secured, but the default is the site’s decision
⚠️ A dataset member is a binary file with no per-row rule: A leaked member is a full data dump, so row-level restriction must be built above the format




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

⚠️ No fast in-editor analysis.



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No general foreign-function interface.
⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

⚠️ One vendor decides the language’s direction.
⚠️ The specification is not public.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

⚠️ Runs inside a database engine: energy and time are the engine’s, not the program’s.

title: PL/SQL (Oracle)
text: This assessment applies the coupling account — coupling as access to a shared resource, and the coupling floor [1], [2] — and the knowledge-embodiment theorem [3]; the language is assessed against its official reference [4].

title: PL/SQL (Oracle)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses PL/SQL in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 39/100 · Ecosystem coupling 61/100 · Engineering readiness 46/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static typing over SQL data types: Every variable, constant, parameter, and function return declares a type, and a mismatch is a compilation error
✅ %TYPE and %ROWTYPE anchor a declaration to the schema: emp%ROWTYPE follows the table’s column list, so a column change does not require editing the declaration
✅ Subtypes declare a constrained domain once: SUBTYPE and a constrained type such as NUMBER(7,2) state a range or a shape and reuse it
❌ NULL is not type-safe absence (T10): An unassigned variable and an unused column are NULL, and NULL propagates through expressions, so IF x = 5 is not true when x is NULL
✅ A REF CURSOR carries a row set without fixing its row type: SYS_REFCURSOR passes a result between program units, so the producer and the consumer need not share a record type
⚠️ Implicit conversion is allowed: Oracle converts between numeric and character types on its own, so a mismatch can pass compilation and fail at run time



1.1.2 Construction

✅ The package separates specification from body: The spec declares the public interface — types, variables, constants, exceptions, cursors, and subprograms — and the body holds the implementation, so a consumer binds to the spec
✅ Subprogram overloading is available in a package: Two subprograms with one name differ by parameter list, so a family of operations shares one name
✅ A cursor FOR ... LOOP iterates the query result directly: Iteration ends at the result’s last row, so the code does not track a row count
❌ Global mutable state by default (C1): A package variable is declared once and lives for the whole session, so every caller that touches the package sees and changes the same value
⚠️ Package initialisation runs on first use: An initialisation block in the body runs when the package is first touched in the session, so setup timing follows call order
⚠️ Triggers fire implicitly: A trigger runs in response to an insert, update, or delete, so the writer of a statement cannot see from the statement which code will run



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No manual memory management: The Oracle server owns SGA and PGA memory, and a block never names an address or frees a byte
✅ The server sizes the work areas: Automatic PGA management gives a sort or a hash operation its memory from PGA_AGGREGATE_TARGET, so the block does not reserve it
⚠️ A session-scoped collection holds its memory: An associative array or nested table kept in a package variable stays for the session, so retained state is a standing cost
⚠️ A bulk fetch needs a deliberate size limit: BULK COLLECT ... LIMIT bounds a fetch, and its absence can materialise a whole result set in PGA
✅ A cursor is released by CLOSE: The server reclaims the cursor’s memory, so the program does not track bytes



1.1.4 Error

✅ The block separates the normal path from the recovery path: DECLARE ... BEGIN ... EXCEPTION ... END; gives a named handler section
✅ Exceptions are matched by name: A predefined exception (NO_DATA_FOUND, TOO_MANY_ROWS, ZERO_DIVIDE) and a user-declared EXCEPTION are caught by name, and WHEN OTHERS catches the remainder
✅ RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR sets a code and a message: A custom failure carries a number in the application range −20000 to −20999, so a caller can branch on it
⚠️ WHEN OTHERS hides the class of the failure (Er3): A handler that catches everything without logging SQLCODE and SQLERRM, or that does not re-raise, lets the enclosing block see a normal return where the inner block failed
⚠️ No composable result type (Er4): A failure cannot be returned as a value the caller must inspect, so error information does not compose through a call chain



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Transactions are the unit of concurrency: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT make a unit of work atomic, so a block does not coordinate with other sessions statement by statement
✅ An autonomous transaction decouples a log write: PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION commits on its own, so the entry survives the caller’s rollback
✅ SELECT ... FOR UPDATE names the rows to lock: The lock is declared by the cursor text rather than by a separate call
❌ Shared mutable state by default (K2): A package variable is shared with every program unit that runs in the session, and nothing in the declaration marks it private
⚠️ No language-level synchronisation and no race detection: PL/SQL has no mutex or atomic primitive, so serialisation rests on Oracle’s row locks and on the application’s lock ordering
✅ DBMS_LOCK provides an explicit lock service: A named user lock serialises a critical section across sessions



1.1.6 Platform

✅ It implements the ISO SQL/PSM stored-module standard: Persistent stored modules are specified in ISO/IEC 9075 Part 4, so the package and block model is standard in concept
⚠️ It is implemented outside Oracle Database: TimesTen and IBM Db2 support PL/SQL, so there is more than one implementation, though the dialects are not fully interchangeable
❌ Cannot function outside one vendor (P1): A PL/SQL program needs an Oracle-family database, so the unit of deployment is an Oracle schema
❌ The useful surface is Oracle-specific: DBMS_* server packages, ROWNUM, sequences, and SQL%ROWCOUNT are Oracle features, so the code cannot move to another engine unedited
⚠️ A port to Transact-SQL is a rewrite, not a translation: Feature differences and different concurrency and locking models separate the two dialects



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

A session-scoped package variable is a deliberate cache: Keeping a value for the session trades hidden shared state for a repeated read
Implicit conversion is convenient in short blocks: Letting numeric and character types mix keeps ad-hoc code short, at a cost that appears in code that must be reliable
A trigger is a data-integrity mechanism: A rule kept in the database is enforced for every writer, where the same rule in the application would be visible at each call site
Logic beside the data is the purpose of the language: A procedure that runs in the database avoids shipping rows to a client
PL/SQL is not a general-purpose language: The assumption of an Oracle database is a scope decision
Dynamic SQL buys flexibility: EXECUTE IMMEDIATE runs DDL and changes object names in a statement, which static SQL cannot do




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Compilation happens at deployment: A package or procedure is compiled once and the stored form is reused, so a call does not re-parse the source
✅ Native compilation is selectable: PLSQL_CODE_TYPE = NATIVE compiles to machine code, so a hot subprogram does not pay the interpreter
✅ Bulk processing amortises the SQL boundary: FORALL and BULK COLLECT move many rows per round trip, so per-row context switches do not dominate
✅ The optimiser and the SGA serve the data path: Plan selection and buffer caching are the server’s job, not the block’s
⚠️ Cost follows the plan and the retained state: A poorly chosen plan, or a package variable holding a large collection, is a cost the unit cannot see



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is proprietary (Ec4): The engine, the tooling, and the support come from Oracle under licence
✅ Tooling is mature and long-established: SQL*Plus, SQL Developer, and third-party IDEs have existed for decades
✅ Published practice is extensive: The PL/SQL language reference, the database manuals, and decades of books and courses document the language in detail
⚠️ Capability follows the licence: Tooling, support, and advanced features are licensed per seat or per processor, so a team reaches only what it has bought
⚠️ Enterprise code bases are long-lived and heavy: A schema commonly spans many versions, so a change has to keep the oldest callers working



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Backward compatibility is strong: A program written for an early Oracle release generally still compiles and runs in the current one
✅ Edition-based redefinition supports an online change: EDITIONABLE objects let a new version of a package be deployed and switched over without downtime
✅ Deprecation is announced before removal: Oracle documents deprecated features, so an upgrade is planned rather than discovered
⚠️ A language feature arrives with a database release: Adoption timing therefore follows the customer’s upgrade cycle, not a separate language release
⚠️ A new feature is unavailable on a pinned older database: Code that must run on an old release cannot use a recent construct



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for data-centric business logic: A procedure operates on tables with SQL directly, so a rule runs where the data is
✅ The language is a full procedural language inside SQL: Loops, records, collections, and subprograms live in the same unit as the queries
✅ Server packages reach outside the schema: UTL_FILE, UTL_HTTP, and DBMS_SCHEDULER give file, network, and job facilities from inside the database
❌ Domain and vendor lock-in (D1): The language exists to run inside an Oracle database, so the Oracle data tier is the only domain
⚠️ A trigger can hide a domain rule: An invariant implemented in a trigger is enforced for every writer, but a reader of the application source cannot see it
⚠️ The language is not a general-purpose runtime: A user interface, a heavy text workload, or a high-rate service belongs in another language beside PL/SQL



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Moderate for a SQL-plus-Pascal background: The block structure follows Ada and Pascal, so a developer from those languages reads it quickly
⚠️ The SQL-to-PL/SQL boundary needs practice: A SELECT inside a block must return exactly one row, so NO_DATA_FOUND and TOO_MANY_ROWS are everyday cases
⚠️ Package semantics take time: Spec versus body, per-session package state, and initialisation timing are not visible in the syntax
⚠️ Exception semantics reward careful reading: An exception in a nested block propagates to the enclosing handler unless it is handled there
✅ The reference documentation is complete: The Oracle Database PL/SQL Language Reference documents every construct with examples



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Readable and keyword-led: Statements read as verbs — INSERT INTO, FETCH, RAISE — so intent is visible
✅ Blocks nest visibly: An inner BEGIN ... END holds its own declarations and handler, so scope follows the indentation
❌ Verbose (S1): Even a small unit needs a declaration section, a BEGIN ... END, and an exception section, so the block structure adds lines to every subprogram
⚠️ END closes several constructs: END IF;, END LOOP;, and a package END must each be matched, so a long body is read against its terminators
⚠️ A large package body is one long file: The spec and the body are a unit boundary, not a file-per-subprogram rule



1.2.7 Testing

✅ utPLSQL is the established framework: An open-source test framework runs suites with assertions and reporting, so tests need not be hand-rolled
✅ Transaction control isolates a test: A test can run and ROLLBACK, leaving the database unchanged
✅ The toolchain traces execution: DBMS_PROFILER, DBMS_TRACE, and the hierarchical profiler report call counts and coverage
⚠️ The base product ships no unit-test framework: SQL Developer offers a unit-testing feature, but the language itself has no test construct
⚠️ A suite depends on grants and deployment: The framework is installed in the database it tests, so permissions and schema state are preconditions



1.2.8 Security

✅ Bind variables remove the injection surface: EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'SELECT ... WHERE x = :1' USING v passes the value out of band, so it cannot change the parse
✅ DBMS_ASSERT validates an identifier before interpolation: SIMPLE_SQL_NAME, QUALIFIED_SQL_NAME, and ENQUOTE_NAME check the string
✅ The rights model is explicit: AUTHID DEFINER and AUTHID CURRENT_USER select whether a unit runs with its owner’s privileges or the caller’s
✅ Privileges are granted per object: GRANT EXECUTE ON pkg TO role scopes access, and the package specification is the grantable interface
❌ Known vulnerability/injection (Q3): EXECUTE IMMEDIATE and DBMS_SQL build a statement as text, so concatenated input can become code
⚠️ Definer’s-rights code can escalate: A unit that runs with its definer’s rights reaches more than the caller, so it needs an audit




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

⚠️ One vendor decides the language’s direction.
⚠️ The specification is not public.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs inside a database engine: energy and time are the engine’s, not the program’s.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [5].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
Under a single partitioning rule, a module can deviate in exactly two ways: it can hold elements that do not belong, or it can be missing elements that do. These defects are independent — a module can have either, both, or neither — and they demand opposite repairs. That structure forces the answer to a natural question: how many numbers must a cohesion metric report?
This page proves that the answer is two. One axis cannot distinguish the two failure modes; two axes can; and no third axis adds anything for this purpose. The pair — purity and completeness — is the minimal adequate output for a rule.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
1 One rule, two opposite defects
Fix a partitioning rule PP [1] and assess a module MM against the class CC it should realize.

Impurity. MM contains an element outside CC. The remedy is to remove it — to split.
Incompleteness. Some element of CC lies outside MM. The remedy is to add it — to merge.

Write the two axes as
purity(M)=|M∩C||M|,completeness(M)=|M∩C||C|.
\text{purity}(M) = \frac{|M \cap C|}{|M|},
\qquad
\text{completeness}(M) = \frac{|M \cap C|}{|C|}.

Both lie in [0,1][0,1]. The two defects are independent in the strict sense: all four combinations occur.

The two failure modes point in opposite directions. Merely knowing that “cohesion is low” is therefore of no help: the correct action could be to split or to merge, and the two actions are opposites.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
2 One axis is not enough

Proposition (dimensional necessity). Let s(M)=g(purity(M),completeness(M))s(M) = g(\text{purity}(M), \text{completeness}(M)) be any scalar that factors through the pair. (a) If gg is symmetric, there are two modules of opposite defect whose scores are exactly equal. (b) If gg is continuous and strictly increasing in each argument, the two defect classes are indistinguishable to any finite precision, and no threshold on the score separates them.

Proof. Fix a rule with a class CC of size 44, and four foreign elements x1,…,x4x_1,\dots,x_4 from another class.

M1=C∪{x1,…,x4}M_1 = C \cup \{x_1,\dots,x_4\} has purity=4/8=1/2\text{purity} = 4/8 = 1/2 and completeness=4/4=1\text{completeness} = 4/4 = 1: impure but complete.
M2={a,b}M_2 = \{a,b\} for a,b∈Ca,b \in C has purity=2/2=1\text{purity} = 2/2 = 1 and completeness=2/4=1/2\text{completeness} = 2/4 = 1/2: pure but incomplete.

Both are realizable in one system.
(a) A symmetric gg gives s(M1)=g(1/2,1)=g(1,1/2)=s(M2)s(M_1) = g(1/2, 1) = g(1, 1/2) = s(M_2) — exactly equal scores for opposite defects. The geometric mean pc\sqrt{pc} scores both at 1/21/\sqrt{2}; so does the arithmetic mean, and every other symmetric aggregate.
(b) The impure-but-complete modules trace the curve B1={(p,1):0<p<1}B_1 = \{(p,1) : 0<p<1\}; the pure-but-incomplete modules trace B2={(1,c):0<c<1}B_2 = \{(1,c) : 0<c<1\}. Strict monotonicity makes g(1,1)g(1,1) the supremum of gg on both curves; continuity makes each image g(B1)g(B_1), g(B2)g(B_2) an interval with that same supremum. Two intervals with a common supremum overlap, so some (p*,1)∈B1(p^*,1) \in B_1 and some (1,c*)∈B2(1,c^*) \in B_2 satisfy g(p*,1)=g(1,c*)g(p^*,1) = g(1,c^*). An impure-complete module and a pure-incomplete module therefore share the same score, and their images approach one another without limit as either defect shrinks. No threshold on the score line can separate “split” from “merge.” ◼\blacksquare
This is why “low cohesion” as a single graded quantity cannot guide a repair. The score is monotonically related to both faults, but it cannot tell the designer which of the two is present — the one thing the designer needs to act.
A caveat keeps the claim honest. The impossibility is for scalars that behave as measurements — symmetric, or continuous and monotone in the two axes. A pathologically discontinuous injection could in principle pack the pair into one real number, but such a function is not a score: it carries no magnitude or ordering that corresponds to defect severity, and it does not arise from the purity/completeness semantics. Every actual cohesion score — a product, a mean, a weighted sum, a distance from the ideal — is continuous and monotone, and every one of them falls to the proposition.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
3 Two axes are enough
The pair not only fails to lose information — it loses none that matters. It determines the failure mode exactly.

Proposition (sufficiency). The pair (purity(M),completeness(M))(\text{purity}(M), \text{completeness}(M)) determines which of the four states a module is in.

Proof. Two equivalences, immediate from the definitions.

purity(M)=1⇔|M∩C|=|M|⇔M⊆C\text{purity}(M) = 1 \iff |M \cap C| = |M| \iff M \subseteq C: no element of MM lies outside its class, i.e. MM is pure.
completeness(M)=1⇔|M∩C|=|C|⇔C⊆M\text{completeness}(M) = 1 \iff |M \cap C| = |C| \iff C \subseteq M: no member of the class lies outside MM, i.e. MM is complete.

So the pair (p,c)(p,c) reports, coordinate by coordinate, whether the module is impure (p<1p<1) and whether it is incomplete (c<1c<1) — the two booleans the remedy depends on. The four cases of the table are read off directly, and with them the correct action. ◼\blacksquare
Together the two propositions give the result: one axis is insufficient; two axes are sufficient. For a single rule, two metrics are necessary and enough.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
4 Why exactly two — not three
Two axes are the minimum, and they are also the maximum needed for the failure-mode question, because a partition admits exactly two failure modes.
The reasoning is a counting one. Relative to the class CC, each element of the module is either inside CC or outside it, and each member of CC is either inside MM or outside it. Two independent questions therefore arise — does MM hold foreign elements? and is MM missing class members? — and they are independent because all four combinations are achievable (the table above exhibits each). To determine the failure mode is to answer both booleans; two coordinates answer two independent booleans minimally. A third coordinate could describe the module more finely (which elements are foreign, how the class is scattered), but it would carry no additional information about which failure mode applies — the axis count the schema requires.
This is why a pairwise, two-axis reading is the correct working form, not a convenience: it is exactly the dimension at which the failure mode becomes visible and no further.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
5 Many rules, many pairs
A system is often assessed under several partitioning rules at once — logical structure, deployment, security, platform. Each rule is its own partition of the same element set, and each admits the same two failure modes, so each contributes its own (purity, completeness) pair. For kk rules the cohesion profile is the 2k2k-tuple of pairs [1].
The necessity argument applies rule by rule: one number cannot serve a single rule, so one number certainly cannot serve the joint requirement. And the pairs are genuinely irreducible across rules. When two rules cross-cut — neither refines the other — placement under one carries no information about placement under the other. The same physical placement can be correct under one rule and wrong under another, and a repair that improves one pair can degrade another. Each rule must be read on its own terms.
When one rule refines another, the pairs are still both needed: the coarse rule frames the fine one, and a clean finer-rule pair does not vouch for the coarser placement that contains it. The coarse pair is load-bearing and must be read first.
The general form, then: two axes per rule; 2k2k axes for kk rules. Collapsing across rules to a single scalar repeats, one level up, the error the proposition already rules out within a rule — it discards the distinction between defects that call for opposite actions.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
6 Where this comes from
The two-axis structure is Condition 4 (adequate dimensionality) of the cohesion metric conditions, and the 2k2k-tuple is the cohesion profile, both developed in On the Nature of Cohesion [1]. The companion page Why cohesion has no scalar metric extends the same obstruction from diagnosis to the placement verdict: a scalar cannot decide whether an element is misplaced, and any scalar that appears to is the rule in disguise.


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

On the Nature of Cohesion: Cohesion as Correctness Relative to a Partitioning Rule — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21703193

title: Cohesion Metrics: What Each One Actually Measures
text:
The cohesion survey [1] reviews every metric in the literature that carries a “cohesion” label: 24 metrics, from LCOM1 (1994) to MOGA (2010). Its finding is stark: every one of them measures a structural property of the code — shared fields, call connections, dependency edges, execution traces — and none measures cohesion itself. The proliferation is itself a symptom: the field has never agreed on what cohesion is, so each metric chose a different structural graph to stand in for the concept.
This page summarizes what each metric actually measures. For the series’ positive account — cohesion as correctness relative to a partitioning rule — see core conclusions.

title: Cohesion Metrics: What Each One Actually Measures
text:
1 Measuring cohesion by its absence
The best-known family is literally named for a lack: LCOM stands for Lack of Cohesion in Methods. Higher LCOM means less cohesion. This is not a polarity quirk that a sign change would fix. An LCOM variant counts something structural — method pairs that do not share fields, connected components that are absent — and negating the score yields only the negation of the proxy, not cohesion.
There is a deeper confusion beneath the naming. Every LCOM variant operates on the method–attribute access graph: the raw input is a coupling relation. LCOM counts pairs for which that coupling does not hold and reports the count as cohesion. By its own data, the LCOM family is a family of coupling metrics that have been called cohesion metrics since their origin.

text:

title: Cohesion Metrics: What Each One Actually Measures
text:
3 Why this matters
The metrics differ in which coupling relation they extract, which transformation they apply, and which normalisation they prefer. They do not differ in what they measure: all measure coupling and report it as cohesion.
This has three practical consequences, developed in the survey:

The cohesion–coupling tradeoff is an artifact of measurement convention. Cohesion metrics count internal edges and coupling metrics count cross-boundary edges of the same graph. Designers balancing the two are balancing one dependency relation against itself under two labels.
A high score can mask a mess. When elements that belong apart happen to share many fields or call each other, LCOM, TCC, and LCC all report high cohesion. Structurally cohesive modules receive a quality signal the metric cannot support.
LCOM-triggered refactoring can reward the wrong direction. Standard heuristics treat LCOM thresholds as extract-class triggers. But LCOM detects structural clustering, not principled misgrouping.

None of this makes the metrics useless. Correlation with fault-proneness and maintenance effort has been reported across multiple studies, so structural scores work as screening heuristics and change predictors. The limitation is interpretative: the score measures coupling density, and domain knowledge about grouping conditions is needed to say more.

title: Cohesion Metrics: What Each One Actually Measures
section: 4 Where the series goes from here
text:
4 Where the series goes from here
The survey establishes the negative result: no structural metric measures principled cohesion. Later papers in the cohesion series give cohesion a positive definition — correctness relative to a partitioning rule — and derive a metric from the reason elements change rather than from the footprint of their co-location. See core conclusions and knowledge embodiment.

title: Cohesion
text: The cohesion series reworks one of the oldest concepts in software design. Its core conclusions are developed across this set of pages.

title: Cohesion
text:
1 Where cohesion sits
Cohesion and coupling are the two classical “quality” measures of modular structure. The cohesion series gives cohesion a principled definition: correctness relative to a partitioning rule [1]. The coupling page does the same for coupling — and shows that within any single dimension, coupling is a consequence of cohesion, not an independent objective.
Cohesion is distinct from IVP, though the two are related. IVP groups elements by change-driver assignment. Cohesion is the more general measure of correctness relative to any partitioning rule. The change-driver rule is one instance of that general idea — the instance IVP is built on.

title: The Right Axis Is Not Style: A Response to Fritzsche and Amariles
text:
Two recent posts disagree about Clean Architecture, and the disagreement is instructive: it is an argument about the wrong axis.
Rico Fritzsche’s “Why Are We Still Talking About Clean Architecture?” argues to retire the layered family in favor of a Functional Core / Imperative Shell split. David Román Amariles replies that the two are not mutually exclusive: separating business rules from side effects and controlling the direction of dependencies address different concerns, and a system can have both.
Both arguments hold within their scope, and the scope is what neither argument states. The tool that supplies it is the change-driver structure of the domain. Once it is on the table, the question stops being which style wins and becomes which case the domain is in.

title: The Right Axis Is Not Style: A Response to Fritzsche and Amariles
text:
1 The formal apparatus, briefly
The Independent Variation Principle (IVP) governs one thing: where elements belong. Given the element set EE and the change-driver assignment Γ(e)\Gamma(e) — the set of change drivers whose state changes create a modification requirement for element ee — the principle is the conjunction of four conditions [1]:

Admissibility — every element has at least one change driver: ∀e∈E,|Γ(e)|≥1\forall e \in E,\ |\Gamma(e)| \geq 1.
Element Form — every element is either pure (|Γ(e)|=1|\Gamma(e)| = 1) or irreducibly composite: no proper subset of its driver set can achieve its purpose, and no decomposition into sub-elements with strictly smaller driver sets jointly preserves that purpose.
Separation — elements assigned different sets of change drivers reside in different modules: Γ(e1)≠Γ(e2)⇒M(e1)≠M(e2)\Gamma(e_1) \neq \Gamma(e_2) \Rightarrow M(e_1) \neq M(e_2).
Unification — elements assigned the same set of change drivers reside in the same module: Γ(e1)=Γ(e2)⇒M(e1)=M(e2)\Gamma(e_1) = \Gamma(e_2) \Rightarrow M(e_1) = M(e_2).

The modules of a compliant system are the Γ\Gamma-equivalence classes of EE. Separation and Unification are the partition content: failing Separation is contamination (elements driven by different conditions co-reside), and failing Unification is scatter (elements that change together are split across modules).
A change driver is an exogenous forcing condition whose change creates a requirement for governed elements to change — a condition anchored in a regulation, a contract, an interface specification, or another domain artifact whose authority is external to the system. Drivers are discovered, not chosen.
Note what the four conditions leave out: purity of functions, ports, adapters, or dependency direction. Those are shapes the partition takes in particular domains. They are not the principle.

title: The Right Axis Is Not Style: A Response to Fritzsche and Amariles
section: 2 Where Amariles’ argument holds: the two concerns are independent

title: The Right Axis Is Not Style: A Response to Fritzsche and Amariles
section: 3 Where Fritzsche’s argument holds: the port does not remove the dependency
text:
3 Where Fritzsche’s argument holds: the port does not remove the dependency
His point is narrower than a rejection of abstraction. It is that inverting a dependency changes its direction in the source and does nothing else:

Dependency inversion makes it possible to reverse source code dependencies… However, the functional dependencies remain.

That is the placement result. A change driver is external and fixed by the domain. No design move adds, removes, or transmutes one. The service still needs the reservation data before it can apply its rules — whether the call passes through a database driver, an adapter, or an interface.
Amariles’ own examples show the same placement at work. The PS5 port in his game example does not eliminate the need to persist progress. It moves that need behind a boundary, and the gameplay code stops naming the mechanism. That is a real and practical benefit, and it is a benefit of placement: the correct implementation of the persistence obligation now sits somewhere the gameplay code need not know about. The obligation itself has not moved.
His .NET example shows the same thing. EvaluateBooking.Execute is pure; the repository call is not. The function is pure because the external call was moved out of it, not because the architecture made it so.

title: The Right Axis Is Not Style: A Response to Fritzsche and Amariles
text:
4 The axis nobody is using
Here is where the argument stalls, and it is the same stall on both sides.
Fritzsche’s case against dependency inversion is an observation: “how often have I seen someone come up with the idea of replacing the database technology in an existing application? Exactly zero times!”
Amariles answers with a counterexample: the game that must run where its SQLite binary is unavailable.
Both moves are about how often substitution happens. The observation that database substitution is rare is domain-bound, and the game is a fair counterexample to it. But substituting one frequency claim for another does not settle the question, because frequency is not the criterion. Whether an element’s correctness conditions require knowledge of the infrastructure it depends on is a structural fact about the domain’s governing artifacts, and it holds whether or not the substitution ever occurs [2].
The structural fact is a condition. Write H for Knowledge Independence: no domain change-driver has correctness conditions that require knowledge of an infrastructure system. Write H0 for Behavioural Self-Containment: the module computes every required change from its own inputs, with no dependence on external state at all. H0 implies H, and not conversely — a module can read external domain state, such as a customer’s recorded credit history, while remaining entirely ignorant of infrastructure. Two conditions that can fail independently give three cases:








Case
Condition
What the core can be




(a)
H0 holds
A pure functional core — no repository, port, or adapter


(b)
H holds, H0 fails
A core behind a port expressed in domain vocabulary


(c)
H fails
No infra-ignorant core; the knowledge must live somewhere



Both posts reason inside case (a), where a pure functional core is available. Fritzsche’s pure function is case (a) exactly. Amariles’ port is the correct answer in case (b), and his objection that the two coexist is the observation that one system can contain modules in different cases. Neither post reaches case (c), where the question is not which style to use but whether the knowledge can be excluded at all.

4.1 What case (c) looks like
H fails in two ways, and neither is a modelling mistake.
Direct. A governing artifact states a correctness condition in terms of infrastructure behaviour. “A patient record must be retrievable within 500 ms under peak load” is a change driver anchored in a medical-device regulation. Its correctness condition is a statement about storage and indexing performance. No implementation ignorant of storage semantics satisfies it.
Indirect. A domain rule’s correctness depends on the outcome of an infrastructure process. A credit rule says: “approve an order only if the customer’s outstanding balance, including committed but not yet settled orders, stays within the credit limit.” “Committed but not yet settled” refers to persistence state under concurrent write. Two storage architectures with different isolation levels produce different answer sets for the same underlying events, and therefore different approval outcomes. The domain rule’s correctness is functionally determined by the storage layer’s guarantee.
Fritzsche’s own observation points at the indirect case. He writes: “Query capabilities, transaction behaviour, and consistency guarantees are largely determined by the database used.” When a domain rule’s correctness condition depends on those guarantees, the database is not a detail. It is part of the domain’s causal structure.
When H fails, no reformulation of the domain removes the required knowledge while preserving correctness. The infra-ignorant core is not hard to reach. It is impossible. Enforcing it produces either an incorrect implementation or an abstraction that quietly models a different, simpler domain.

title: The Right Axis Is Not Style: A Response to Fritzsche and Amariles
section: 5 The stability ordering: what sets the direction
text:
5 The stability ordering: what sets the direction
“Clean Architecture is fundamentally concerned with the direction of dependencies” is the style’s own account, and it is worth reading closely, because the direction is not arbitrary — it is fixed by a stability ordering.
Clean Architecture’s Dependency Rule points dependencies toward more stable elements. Martin measures stability with two structural metrics: instability I=Ce/(Ca+Ce)I = C_e/(C_a + C_e), the ratio of efferent to total coupling, and abstractness AA, the fraction of abstract types. The Main Sequence A+I=1A + I = 1 is the claimed optimal locus [3].
Neither metric references a change driver. II counts packages in the import graph; AA counts abstract type declarations. They measure structural self-containment — an element is “stable” because nothing imports force it to change — not change-driver identity. The stability ordering is therefore a proxy for the change-driver structure, not a measurement of it.
The proxy is useful where it tracks the domain’s actual ordering, and the theory has a name for the ordering it tracks. A driver stability ordering is a partial order on change drivers, where γ1≻γ2\gamma_1 \succ \gamma_2 holds when γ1\gamma_1 activates less often and γ2\gamma_2’s requirements are chosen to satisfy decisions γ1\gamma_1 governs. Read on this ordering, dependency inversion says that elements governed by the volatile driver depend on elements governed by the stable one, rather than the reverse.
That is the strongest defensible reading of Amariles’ position, and on this ordering it is a real result rather than a proxy — provided the ordering holds. It holds for tax law and a payment gateway. It fails where a domain rule’s correctness depends on what the storage layer guarantees; there, the stable element is the infrastructure behaviour, because the domain rule’s correctness now depends on its outcome. The dependency should then point the other way, and the style’s blanket inward rule asserts a direction the domain does not have.
Two constraints guard this reading, and both bear on the exchange. First, the ordering is a property of the domain’s causal structure, not a rank intrinsic to a driver: stability is one of the two relations in the pair, and it never licenses calling any driver “primary,” “dominant,” or “main.” Second, it informs the direction decision only — it does not change which elements belong in which module, which is the partition’s job. Direction and partition are separate questions, and the two get conflated when the exchange is read as a disagreement about styles rather than about which question is being asked.

title: The Right Axis Is Not Style: A Response to Fritzsche and Amariles
section: 6 What the theory confirms in each
text:
6 What the theory confirms in each
Read against the three cases, the exchange resolves into scope conditions rather than verdicts.
The two approaches operate on different questions. Purity is a property of an element’s driver set (case (a)); a port is the shape a module takes when it needs external domain state (case (b)); dependency direction is a separate decision, governed by the stability ordering where that ordering holds. Nothing in the theory requires choosing one, which is the substance of Amariles’ argument.
The port relocates a need; it does not delete one. “The functional dependencies remain” holds in every case. It is decisive only in case (c). In cases (a) and (b) the family’s prescriptions match what the domain calls for, and a pure functional core is a restatement of case (a). The scope of the conclusion is narrower than the argument’s reach.
Both arguments rest on frequency. Fritzsche observes that database substitutions are rare; Amariles answers that other domains differ. Both observations may be accurate. Neither is the criterion. The criterion is whether the domain’s governing artifacts place infrastructure knowledge in a module’s correctness conditions — a fact about the domain, not about substitution rates.
Case (c) appears in neither. Which is where the discussion has real consequences. A conclusion that the style is wrong understates the domain’s latitude; a conclusion that the styles coexist leaves the reader without the case where no style applies.

title: The Right Axis Is Not Style: A Response to Fritzsche and Amariles
text:
7 What to do instead
The question “Clean Architecture or Functional Core / Imperative Shell?” sets the axis on style. The right axis is the domain’s change-driver structure, which the style does not select.
It is, for each module, two questions answered from the domain’s governing artifacts:

Does any correctness condition require knowledge of an infrastructure system? (This decides H.)
Does the module depend on any external state at all? (This decides H0.)

Then:

Case (a), H0. A pure functional core. No repository, port, or adapter. Adding one is unnecessary indirection. This is what Functional Core / Imperative Shell describes.
Case (b), H holds. A port or repository expressed in domain vocabulary. The module needs external state, but the state is domain-governed, so the contract is expressible in domain terms. This is the case the hexagonal prescription was designed for.
Case (c), H fails. Accommodate the infrastructure knowledge. Either keep it in the domain module, or move it to an explicitly domain-scoped adapter whose change-driver assignment is stated and whose behaviour is independently testable against the domain change-driver. What is not sound is enforcing infra-ignorance and accepting an incorrect or unverifiable model as the cost of structural conformance.

The style does not choose the case. The domain does.

title: The Right Axis Is Not Style: A Response to Fritzsche and Amariles
text:
8 Wrapping up
The theory confirms both observations under their scope. Dependency inversion moves a dependency without removing the driver behind it. Direction and separation are independent concerns that a system can satisfy at once.
The qualification worth adding is one of scope. The infra-ignorant core exists if and only if H holds, and H is discovered from the domain’s governing artifacts, not assumed. When H fails, every style in the family — Clean, Hexagonal, Onion, and Functional Core / Imperative Shell alike — arrives at the same fork: embody the required knowledge, or ship a model that cannot satisfy its obligations.
The two posts are not in conflict. They are answering different halves of a question that has three answers, and neither half needs the other retired.

The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

The Independent Variation Principle: Deriving Optimal Module Boundaries from the Element–Change-Driver Graph — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.20794332
On the Nature of Coupling: All Coupling as Shared Resource Access — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21925122

The conditional analysis of the infra-ignorant core is developed in The Domain–Infrastructure Boundary as a Structural Property of the Driver Set.

title: The Cohesion Series and IVP — Five Papers Published
text:
The cohesion paper series is now published in full — five papers that build a chain from the concept of cohesion to the Independent Variation Principle (IVP).
The chain:
Additional paper: the historical survey of 24 cohesion metrics — DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21703227.

title: The Cohesion Series and IVP — Five Papers Published
text:
1 Two derivations
Last month’s preprint — Deriving Optimal Module Boundaries from the Element–Change-Driver Graph — proved that the Γ\Gamma-equality partition is the unique cost-minimizing modularization through a self-contained graph-theoretic counting argument: two lemmas on the element–change-driver incidence graph show that scattering same-driver elements or mixing different-driver elements strictly increases cost.
The cohesion series derives the same conclusion through a different route: define cohesion as a schema parameterized by partitioning rules, instantiate a metric, prove optimality under change-isolation, and justify that objective against a richer maintenance-cost model. Different apparatus, same endpoint.

title: The Cohesion Series and IVP — Five Papers Published
section: 2 How the series builds a cohesion schema
text:
2 How the series builds a cohesion schema
The cohesion-2 paper argues that cohesion is correctness relative to a partitioning rule — an equivalence relation on elements anchored in domain artifacts (regulations, contracts, protocols). Under kk rules, it is a 2k2k-tuple — kk (purity, completeness) pairs, one per rule — because each coupling concern, modeled by its governing change driver, resolves into a partitioning rule over the one element set. Cohesion-4 fills one slot with a concrete metric. Cohesion-5 proves which partition is optimal. Cohesion-6 justifies the cost objective. Cohesion-7 states the principle and examines its assumptions.

All papers free on Zenodo. Also referenced: the graph proof (June 2026).

title: On the Nature of Cohesion
text:
I’ve published a new paper: On the Nature of Cohesion: Cohesion as a Two-Axis Schema.
Cohesion is one of the oldest concepts in software design — introduced by Stevens, Myers, and Constantine in 1974, taught in every curriculum, invoked in every code review. For fifty years, the field has struggled to define it formally. Every published definition is a characterization, not an operational criterion. Every published metric measures a structural proxy.
The paper surveys the major cohesion metrics from the literature, formalizes what cohesion is under any admissible modularization principle, develops the necessary conditions a principled cohesion metric must satisfy, and diagnoses why existing approaches fall short.
If you teach cohesion, apply it in code reviews, or work on software metrics — this paper directly concerns the concept you’re using.
Yannick Loth. On the Nature of Cohesion: Cohesion as a Two-Axis Schema. June 2026.
DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20492913 — free on Zenodo.

title: SRP Is Wrong: The Cardinality Error in the Single Responsibility Principle
text:
I’ve published a new paper: Why SRP Is Wrong: The Cardinality Error in the Single Responsibility Principle.
SRP — “a class should have only one reason to change” — is wrong. Not vague or misunderstood. Wrong.
The adapter pattern is a counterexample. A Stripe payment adapter has two reasons to change: the internal PaymentProcessor interface changes, or Stripe’s API changes. Under Martin’s own interpretation of his terms, that’s two — not one.
SRP’s prescribed remedy is to split the module. But splitting an adapter destroys its function — mediation requires both domains’ knowledge in the same reasoning step. Three salvage attempts (DTO intermediate, mapping table, delegation) all fail. The adapter is irreducibly composite.
The class of counterexamples is not marginal. Every façade, bridge, API gateway, protocol translator, and anti-corruption layer that mediates between independent domains is equally a counterexample. Most complex systems contain them.
The paper formalizes the refutation in the change-driver apparatus with complete theorems and proofs. The formal apparatus is not needed to follow the argument — the counterexample stands alone — but is provided for readers who want the argument in precise, verifiable form.
Paper: Why SRP Is Wrong: The Cardinality Error in the Single Responsibility Principle., May 2026.
If you teach SRP or apply it in code reviews: does this refutation change how you think about the principle?

title: Where Do Interfaces Live? IVP Answers What SOLID Cannot
text:
If you know a software architect, a professor who teaches SOLID, or anyone who takes design principles seriously — I’d appreciate you sharing this with them.
Two companion papers established the structural biconditional between ISP and per-client DIP (paper 1) and proved that Martin’s packaging principles are jointly unsatisfiable for the resulting configuration — specifically, CCP and REP cannot both be satisfied (paper 2).
This third paper applies the Independent Variation Principle (IVP) to the same five-element setup and obtains two results from a single application.

title: Where Do Interfaces Live? IVP Answers What SOLID Cannot
section: 1 Result 1: DIP → ISP, formalized in IVP terms
text:
1 Result 1: DIP → ISP, formalized in IVP terms
The first companion paper proved the structural biconditional: ISP ↔︎ per-client DIP. This paper formalizes the forward direction (DIP implies ISP) in IVP terms. Each interface slice shares its client’s change-driver assignment. The IVP biconditional (elements co-reside iff they share driver assignments) closes the proof: the slices are disjoint because the clients belong to different modules. IVP adds formalism to one direction of a valid structural biconditional; it is useful here but not indispensable.

title: Where Do Interfaces Live? IVP Answers What SOLID Cannot
text:
2 Result 2: A unique modularization
This is where IVP is essential.
Five elements: provider A, clients B and C, interface slices I_B and I_C. Three distinct driver assignments: {γ_ord} for B and I_B, {γ_rep} for C and I_C, {γ_ord, γ_rep, γ_impl} for A.
IVP-3 (elements with different driver assignments cannot co-reside) and IVP-4 (elements with identical driver assignments must co-reside) together admit exactly one partition:

Module B: B and I_B (both driven by γ_ord)
Module C: C and I_C (both driven by γ_rep)
Module A: A alone (composite: γ_ord, γ_rep, γ_impl)

Each interface slice lives with its client — not as a design preference, but as a consequence of the axioms applied to the causal structure of change.

title: Where Do Interfaces Live? IVP Answers What SOLID Cannot
text:
3 What this settles
The packaging paper showed that eight principles — DIP, ISP, and six packaging principles (REP, CCP, CRP, ADP, SDP, SAP) — give three incompatible answers (with client, with provider, own module) and no meta-criterion for choosing. IVP eliminates two of the three by deriving the answer from Γ.
If two engineers disagree about where I_B belongs, the disagreement traces to a disagreement about Γ — about what can cause I_B to require modification. That is an epistemic question about the system, not a design preference. IVP converts a judgment call into a falsifiable claim.

title: Where Do Interfaces Live? IVP Answers What SOLID Cannot
text:
4 What IVP’s placement produces
The paper verifies that the unique IVP partition delivers:

Change isolation: a change to γ_ord modifies Module B (containing B and I_B) and nothing else. Module C is untouched.
No shotgun surgery: the pathology that scattered interface placement creates is eliminated by construction.
Acyclic dependencies in the provider–client subgraph: A depends on Module B and Module C (for the interface specifications it implements). Neither client module depends on A. No cycle exists in this subgraph.
Independent deployability: each module can be released independently.

title: Where Do Interfaces Live? IVP Answers What SOLID Cannot
text:
5 The paper
“The Interface Segregation Principle Is a Corollary of the Dependency Inversion Principle — A Formal Proof via the Independent Variation Principle”

Paper: https://zenodo.org/records/19641242

The first paper showed ISP and DIP produce the same structure. The second showed SOLID’s principles can’t agree on where to put it. This one shows IVP can.
If you think the unique partition is wrong — that I_B belongs somewhere other than with B — I’d like to hear the argument. What change driver does I_B respond to, if not B’s?

title: SOLID: ISP Is Just DIP Applied Twice
text:
If you know someone who teaches or researches software design principles, I’d appreciate you sharing this — the argument needs to be challenged by people who take SOLID seriously.

The Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) is widely taught as the fourth independent letter in SOLID. I’ve written a short paper showing it isn’t independent at all: it is a special case of DIP’s ownership clause applied once per client–provider edge.
Once both principles are stated precisely enough to reason about formally, the argument is straightforward. DIP’s ownership clause says the client defines the interface it depends upon. Apply that to one client: you get one client-specific interface. Apply it to a second client of the same provider: you get a second, different interface. The provider now implements both, each client sees only its own slice, and no client depends on methods it doesn’t use — which is exactly what ISP prescribes. At the class level, the two principles produce the identical structure: the same classes, the same interfaces, the same dependency and implementation relationships.
The converse also holds: any ISP-compliant segregation is structurally indistinguishable from the result of applying DIP’s ownership clause per client.
I’m not saying that naming ISP is useless — naming the corollary directs attention to the per-client application of DIP, which textbooks consistently underemphasize. The claim is narrower: ISP prescribes no design action that per-client DIP doesn’t already prescribe.
The paper also examines why this connection went unnoticed for nearly thirty years. The most fundamental reason is that both principles were stated as informal design directives illustrated by examples, making logical derivation impossible until they are stated precisely. Other factors include DIP’s single-client framing, ISP’s status as the least-scrutinized SOLID principle, and the strong prior created by the five-letter acronym.
Building on observations by Henney, Oldwood, Kaminski, and North that SOLID’s principles overlap, I traced a specific derivation that, to my knowledge, has not been identified before: DIP’s ownership clause applied per client is ISP.
The full structural proof (at the class level), worked example, and historical analysis are freely available:
“The Interface Segregation Principle Is a Corollary of the Dependency Inversion Principle: A Structural Proof”

Paper: https://zenodo.org/records/19633560
DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19633560


At the class level, is there a case where ISP prescribes a different structure than per-client DIP? If you think ISP adds something at other levels (packages, APIs, services), I’d be interested in that too — the paper’s scope is class-level, and extensions are future work.

title: Which Java Construct Should You Use? Let Change Drivers Decide
text:
A change driver is anything that, when it changes, forces an element of a system to change. The Independent Variation Principle (IVP) constrains how modules and their elements relate to these drivers: elements sharing a module must have the same driver assignment, and elements with different driver assignments must live in different modules.
Applied to Java constructs, the lens separates essential coupling — the drivers the situation actually requires — from accidental coupling — the drivers the chosen construct drags in for reasons that have nothing to do with the situation. Picking the right construct is picking the one whose realization carries only the essential drivers. Throughout the article, “before” constructs carry accidental coupling (typically an implicit outer-instance reference, a synthetic class file, or a mutation channel the situation does not need); “after” constructs remove the accidental artifacts and keep only what the situation requires.
