title: File Locking (and the JVM)
text:
I originally posted this on 2010/07/23 on my personal blog.

File locks control access to a file or a range of bytes within a file. This is necessary in situations where multiple simultaneously executing programs need to modify the same file.
File locking functionalities are provided within the NIO API, or more specifically in the java.nio.channels package.
The two most important classes for file locking are java.nio.channels.FileChannel and java.nio.channels.FileLock.
Several methods provide file locking:
FileLock FileChannel.lock()
FileLock FileChannel.lock(long position, long size, boolean shared)
FileLock FileChannel.tryLock()
FileLock FileChannel.tryLock(long position, long size, boolean shared)
lock() acquires an exclusive lock on the entire file, and blocks until the lock is acquired, tryLock() is identical but returns null if the lock cannot be acquired. The methods with parameters lock only regions of a file, the shared parameter is true for a shared lock and false for an exclusive lock.
A shared lock prevents other concurrently-running programs from acquiring an overlapping exclusive lock, but does allow them to acquire overlapping shared locks. An exclusive lock prevents other programs from acquiring an overlapping lock of either type.
Once you don’t need the lock anymore, release it with FileLock.release().
That seems to be a great solution, but there are limitations, related to the operating system the JVM runs on:

Some systems only provide advisory file locking: applications that don’t acquire locks may still write the file.
Some systems make it impossible to lock a file and map it into memory. On those, you won’t be able to use a MappedByteBuffer to access file.
File locks are held by the Java Virtual Machine, not by individual programs. Two programs in the same JVM won’t be able to simultaneously acquire a lock on the same file.
Opening multiple channels on the same locked file should be avoided, as on some systems, closing a channel on a file releases all locks on the file held by the same JVM.
On networked file systems, file locking should be avoided – or at least, relying on file locking mechanisms should be avoided, as it’s dependent on the networked file system implementation.

title: IVP
text:
The Independent Variation Principle applied to software architecture: elements assigned to the same change driver belong in the same module; elements assigned to different drivers belong in different modules [1].
This section covers the formal theory of IVP for software — the system tuple, change drivers, the Γ-equivalence partition, unit purity and completeness, and the axioms.

title: IVP
text:
1 Core theory
The theory is developed in detail in the core theory pages:

The software system tuple — the model the principle is stated over.
Change drivers and assignment — what a change driver is and how elements are assigned to them.
The structural formulation of IVP — the statement of the principle and its four conditions.
The Γ-equivalence partition — the object the principle produces.
The partition theorem — the unique compliant module structure.
Scope and validity conditions — the premises, preconditions, and applicability gates the results depend on.
Consequences and application — what follows, and the six-step procedure.

title: IVP
text:
2 Consequences

How to apply IVP — the six-step process and a fully worked example.
Software clustering — how IVP dissolves the modularisation optimization problem.

The knowledge-embodiment theorem, which connects maximal cohesion to the embodiment of domain knowledge, is a result of the cohesion theory rather than of IVP itself. It is covered under cohesion.


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

The Independent Variation Principle — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.20794332

All published papers

title: The Structural Formulation of IVP
text: This is the statement of the Independent Variation Principle itself. Everything else in the core theory — the partition, purity and completeness, the partition theorem — is either an ingredient the principle needs or a consequence it produces. This page states the principle.

title: The Structural Formulation of IVP
text:
1 The principle in one sentence
For a software system S=(F,κF,E,Coupling,C,Γ)S = (F, \kappa_F, E, \text{Coupling}, C, \Gamma), IVP prescribes the partition of the element set EE induced by the equivalence relation
e1∼Γe2⇔Γ(e1)=Γ(e2). e_1 \sim_\Gamma e_2 \iff \Gamma(e_1) = \Gamma(e_2). 
The modules of an IVP-compliant system are the Γ-equivalence classes of the element set: elements assigned the same set of change drivers belong in the same module, and elements assigned different sets belong in different modules.
That single sentence is the whole principle. The four conditions below are not additional rules — they are that sentence stated as four obligations a module structure must satisfy.

title: The Structural Formulation of IVP
text:
2 The four conditions

IVP-1 — Element Admissibility. Every element has at least one change driver: |Γ(e)|≥1|\Gamma(e)| \geq 1. No element floats free of the change structure.
IVP-2 — Change-Driver Assignment / Element Form. Every element is pure (|Γ(e)|=1|\Gamma(e)| = 1) or irreducibly composite. The model admits only elements whose driver set is exactly what the domain requires.
IVP-3 — Unit Purity / Separation. Elements with different driver assignments reside in different modules: Γ(e1)≠Γ(e2)⇒M(e1)≠M(e2)\Gamma(e_1) \neq \Gamma(e_2) \Rightarrow M(e_1) \neq M(e_2).
IVP-4 — Unit Completeness / Unification. Elements with the same driver assignment reside in the same module: Γ(e1)=Γ(e2)⇒M(e1)=M(e2)\Gamma(e_1) = \Gamma(e_2) \Rightarrow M(e_1) = M(e_2).

Separation (IVP-3) is the “do not mix” half: elements that answer to different change drivers must not co-reside. Unification (IVP-4) is the “do not split” half: elements that answer to the same change drivers must co-reside. Together they force exactly one module structure — the Γ-equivalence partition.

title: The Structural Formulation of IVP
text:
3 Why the two halves matter
Each half corrects one classic failure.
A module that violates separation mixes elements that change for different reasons. When one change driver activates, the module must change in part, dragging unrelated elements into the blast radius.
A module that violates unification splits elements that change for the same reason. When that change driver activates, the change must be made in several places, and keeping them consistent is coordination cost.
Both are placement errors. Both are named by a condition, which makes them diagnosable.

title: The Structural Formulation of IVP
section: 4 Admissibility and element form set the model
text:
4 Admissibility and element form set the model
The first two conditions govern what counts as an element at all. IVP-1 says every element belongs to the change structure. IVP-2 says every element’s driver set is exactly what the domain requires — an element is single-driver, or multi-driver in a way that is irreducible, never accidentally bloated.
These two prepare the element set EE for the grouping that IVP-3 and IVP-4 then prescribe.

title: The Structural Formulation of IVP
section: 5 The principle is a criterion, not a recipe
text:
5 The principle is a criterion, not a recipe
IVP is stated over a system tuple that is read off the domain. Once Γ\Gamma is fixed, the principle determines the structure. This is what makes IVP a criterion: it does not suggest a structure, it names the structure the change drivers require.

title: The Structural Formulation of IVP
section: 6 How the rest of the core theory follows
text:
6 How the rest of the core theory follows

The Γ-equivalence partition is the object the principle produces.
Purity and completeness are the two properties a module gets from the partition.
The partition theorem says the compliant structure is uniquely this partition.

The statement above is the foundation; the other core-theory pages develop what it implies.

title: The Structural Formulation of IVP
text:
7 Where the derivation lives
The derivation that this is the unique cost-optimal structure under the change-management hypothesis is proved in the published paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1], and the proof that the four conditions — Admissibility, Element Form, Separation, Unification — are necessary and jointly exhaustive is developed in the paper on cohesion and change propagation [2]. The purity and completeness properties the conditions produce are defined formally in the paper on the nature of cohesion [3].


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

The Independent Variation Principle — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.20794332
Cohesion and Change Propagation: Four Necessary Conditions for Optimal Modularization — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21362420
On the Nature of Cohesion: Cohesion as Correctness Relative to a Partitioning Rule — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21703193

All published papers

title: The Partition Theorem
text: The four conditions of IVP do more than describe what a compliant module looks like. They determine the module structure uniquely.

title: The Partition Theorem
text:
1 The claim
A modularization that satisfies all four IVP conditions must be the Γ-equivalence partition — unique up to coarsening ties.
Two elements with the same change-driver assignment must co-reside (Unification), and two elements with different assignments must not co-reside (Separation). These two constraints together fix which elements belong together: exactly the Γ-equivalence classes, and nothing else.
There is no latitude in a compliant structure. Once you have read the change-driver assignment Γ\Gamma off the domain, the partition is determined.

title: The Partition Theorem
section: 2 Why this is not a design choice
text:
2 Why this is not a design choice
This is the force of the result. Classical modularization advice often treats “how to cut modules” as a judgement call, one of many defensible choices. The partition theorem says that under the change-management criterion, it is not a choice. If your goal is to contain change — to make the module that must change together and nothing else — then the Γ-equivalence partition is the answer, and it is the only answer.
This is what makes IVP diagnostic rather than suggestive. Given the domain, it reads off the structure the domain requires.

title: The Partition Theorem
text:
3 Up to coarsening ties
The phrase “up to coarsening ties” records one genuine freedom. Within a single Γ-equivalence class, all elements are identical with respect to change: they answer to the same drivers. You may therefore subdivide a class into smaller modules, or keep it as one, without violating any condition. The subdivision is free for readability, team structure, or packaging — it does not change the change-containment behaviour.
What is not free is merging across classes or splitting within a class so that elements respond to different drivers are mixed. The partition’s boundaries between classes are forced; its internal subdivision is not.

title: The Partition Theorem
text:
4 Where the proof lives
The derivation that the Γ-equivalence partition is the unique cost-optimal structure is proved in the published paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1], which gives a counting argument on the element–change-driver incidence graph showing that grouping elements by their change-driver sets minimizes change propagation cost. The cost-minimisation of the partition is further developed in the paper on cohesion and change propagation [2] and the paper on minimizing change propagation and maintenance cost [3].


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

The Independent Variation Principle — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.20794332
Cohesion and Change Propagation: Four Necessary Conditions for Optimal Modularization — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21362420
Why Minimizing Change Propagation Minimizes Maintenance Cost — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21362542

All published papers

title: The Γ-Equivalence Partition
text:
IVP prescribes one module structure: the Γ-equivalence partition. This page explains that object — what the equivalence relation is, what properties its classes have, and how multi-driver elements fit.
The principle itself — its one-sentence statement and the four conditions — is stated on the structural formulation page. Here we work with the object the principle produces.

title: The Γ-Equivalence Partition
text:
1 The equivalence relation
Define the relation Γ̃\tilde{\Gamma} on the element set EE by:
e1∼Γe2⇔Γ(e1)=Γ(e2) e_1 \sim_\Gamma e_2 \iff \Gamma(e_1) = \Gamma(e_2) 
Two elements are change-driver-equivalent when they are assigned the same set of change drivers. This relation is an equivalence relation: it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Therefore it partitions the element set into equivalence classes.
The Γ-equivalence partition 𝒫Γ=E/Γ̃\mathcal{P}_\Gamma = E / \tilde{\Gamma} is the set of these classes. Each class collects exactly the elements that respond to the same change drivers.

title: The Γ-Equivalence Partition
text:
2 Purity and completeness
A module drawn from this partition has two properties.

Purity. The module contains no element from outside its Γ-equivalence class. Every element in the module is Γ-equivalent to every other. When a change driver activates, every element affected lives in this module — and nothing unrelated lives here.
Completeness. The module contains every element of its Γ-equivalence class. Nothing that should be here has been placed elsewhere. When a change driver activates, no element that must change is scattered across other modules.

Purity is the module-level form of Separation (IVP-3): no foreign elements. Completeness is the module-level form of Unification (IVP-4): no missing elements. A module that is both pure and complete is maximally cohesive with respect to the change-driver rule. It is the unit that contains exactly the elements a change driver forces to change together, and nothing else. The formal account of purity and completeness as correctness relative to a partitioning rule is given in the published paper on the nature of cohesion [1], and the change-driver-assignment instantiation of the schema is developed in the paper on causal cohesion [2].

title: The Γ-Equivalence Partition
text:
3 Multi-driver elements
Not every element is pure. An adapter that must satisfy both the domain’s rule and a foreign interface has |Γ(e)|>1|\Gamma(e)| > 1. Its driver set is irreducible: it genuinely needs all of its drivers.
An element is single-driver or multi-driver. The word “impure” applies to a module, not an element: a module is impure when it groups elements that are not Γ-equivalent. A module containing a multi-driver element is necessarily impure, because that element answers to drivers its pure neighbours do not. The adapter is well-designed; the impurity it forces on its module is necessary, not a mistake.

title: The Γ-Equivalence Partition
section: 4 The partition is what IVP produces
text:
4 The partition is what IVP produces
Because IVP prescribes exactly this partition, the partition theorem is the result that the compliant structure is unique — the structure is determined once Γ\Gamma is read off the domain.


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

On the Nature of Cohesion: Cohesion as Correctness Relative to a Partitioning Rule — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21703193
Causal Cohesion — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21703156

All published papers

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
text: Change drivers are the engine of the whole theory. Everything the Independent Variation Principle prescribes follows from the set of change drivers and the way elements are assigned to them.

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
text:
1 What a change driver is
A change driver is a discrete, identifiable source of variation that can cause elements to require modification. It is an external condition in the operating domain: when it activates, part of the system must change.
The tax legislation is a change driver. When it changes, every element that embodies tax knowledge must change. A payment-routing standard is a change driver. The target platform is a change driver. A security classification is a change driver.
At the leaf level, a change driver is identical to a coupling dimension: both name a dimension along which elements vary together.

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
section: 2 Change drivers are discovered, not chosen
text:
2 Change drivers are discovered, not chosen
This is the load-bearing fact about change drivers. The set CC is a fact about the domain, not a design choice. The analyst discovers which external conditions force the system to change; the designer does not invent them.
Change drivers are external and fixed by the domain. No design move adds, removes, or transmutes a driver. A change driver exists because the domain’s causal structure produces it, not because a designer decides it should exist.
This is why the theory is a diagnostic instrument rather than a recipe: it tells you to read the change structure off the domain, not to impose it.

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
text:
3 The assignment function
The change-driver assignment Γ:E→𝒫(C)\Gamma : E \to \mathcal{P}(C) maps each element to the set of change drivers that force it to change.

An element with |Γ(e)|=1|\Gamma(e)| = 1 responds to exactly one change driver. Such an element is pure.
An element with |Γ(e)|>1|\Gamma(e)| > 1 responds to several. It is composite.
A composite element is irreducibly composite when no proper subset of its driver set can achieve its purpose — it genuinely needs all of them. Adapters and translators are typical examples: a module that must both follow the domain’s rule and satisfy a foreign interface is irreducibly multi-driver.

The assignment is read from the domain’s causal structure. Whether an element is pure or composite is not a label the designer attaches; it follows from which external conditions actually force the element to change.

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
text:
4 Driver independence
Two change drivers are independent when their knowledge slices do not overlap and activating one does not logically force the other. Driver independence is a well-formedness condition on the driver set, not a hypothesis the theory requires. If two drivers are mutually coupled — each activation forces the other — they do not individuate two distinct sources of change and are correctly treated as one.

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
text:
5 Driver omission and refinement
The granularity at which you read the driver set is a modelling choice. You may split one change driver into finer ones, or merge several into one coarser driver. The structural results of the theory are invariant under this refinement: a finer grain yields a richer CC with no loss of structural validity.
Omitting a driver — failing to record a genuine source of change — is a different matter. It coarsens the optimal partition and leaves that change uncontained. Driver omission is the failure mode the theory warns against: if a real change driver is missing from CC, the modules built from the incomplete set will not contain the changes that driver produces.
The taxonomy of change drivers and the discovery tests used here are developed in the published paper on the change-driver taxonomy [1], and the question of what counts as the source of a change driver is examined in the paper on whether a change driver is an actor or a document [2]. The formal account of the assignment function and of driver independence is part of the Independent Variation Principle paper [3].


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

The Change-Driver Taxonomy — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21669704
Change Driver: Actor or Document? — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21669958
The Independent Variation Principle — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.20794332

All published papers

title: Independent Variation Principle
text:
The Independent Variation Principle (IVP) is a theory of how structured systems are organized around the sources of change that act upon them.
A system’s structure should separate the elements that vary independently — elements driven by different sources of change belong in different modules — and unify the elements that vary dependently — elements driven by the same source of change belong in a single module.
The principle and the proof that this module structure is the cost-minimising one are published in the paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1].
This site is the working home for that theory and its applications.

title: How to Apply IVP
text:
Applying the Independent Variation Principle is an iterative design activity, not a mechanical algorithm. It follows a six-step cycle; you revisit earlier steps as understanding deepens. The depth of analysis should be proportionate to the system’s expected lifetime and how often it changes.
This page first lays out the six steps, then works through them on a complete example, following the principle as stated in the published paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1].

title: How to Apply IVP
text:
1 The six-step process

Identify the elements. Choose the grain of artifact the analysis operates on — functions, classes, methods, data structures, modules. Every element is something that can change in response to a change driver.
Identify the change drivers. Read the external conditions whose activation forces the system to change. This is discovery, not invention. Apply the “who asks for this change?” and “independent clock” tests: a change driver is a source of variation that can change without forcing the others to change.
Map drivers to elements. Assign each element the set of change drivers that force it to change — build the assignment Γ\Gamma. Record whether each element is pure (one driver) or composite (several).
Assess the current modularization. Compare the existing module structure to the Γ-equivalence partition. Name the violations: which modules are impure (IVP-3), which are incomplete (IVP-4).
Refactor toward compliance. Move elements so the structure converges to the partition. Merge modules that scatter one driver’s elements; split modules that mix different drivers.
Verify and iterate. Re-check the assignment and the partition as understanding deepens and as the domain changes.

title: How to Apply IVP
section: 2 A worked example: a notification system
text:
2 A worked example: a notification system
To make the process concrete, consider a notification system of the kind found in any SaaS application. It is small enough to fit one page yet rich enough to exhibit both a Unit Purity and a Unit Completeness violation.

2.1 The starting point
The system sends notifications to users when events occur — account creation, order placed, payment failed, subscription expiring. It supports three delivery channels (email, SMS, push) and enforces business rules such as user preferences and rate limits.
A developer has implemented all of this in a single class, NotificationService, containing these nine methods:







Element
Responsibility




e1e_1: resolveTemplate
Selects the message template for a given event type


e2e_2: renderContent
Populates the template with event-specific data and policy-driven personalization


e3e_3: deliverEmail
Sends the notification via SMTP


e4e_4: deliverSMS
Sends the notification via SMS gateway API


e5e_5: deliverPush
Sends the notification via push notification service


e6e_6: checkPreferences
Evaluates which channels the user has enabled


e7e_7: enforceRateLimit
Throttles notifications per channel (max NN per hour per user)


e8e_8: logDelivery
Records each delivery attempt for audit compliance and channel metrics


e9e_9: formatForChannel
Adapts the rendered message to each channel’s constraints (e.g. SMS length, push truncation)



All nine elements live in one module: Mnotify={e1,…,e9}M_\text{notify} = \{e_1, \dots, e_9\}. As in a real system, the elements differ in how many change drivers force them to change: some are pure (assigned to one driver), others are composite (assigned to several).


2.2 Step 1: System description
The element inventory is the table above; at this granularity, each method is an element. The system’s purpose FF: deliver event-triggered notifications to users through their preferred channels, subject to business rules.


2.3 Step 2: Change driver identification
Apply the “who asks for this change?” and “independent clock” tests.

Message content changes when the marketing team redesigns templates, when the UX team changes wording, or when a new event type is added. None of these affect delivery or channel preferences.
Delivery infrastructure changes when operations switches SMTP providers, when the SMS gateway publishes a new API version, or when a new channel (e.g. WhatsApp) is added. These do not affect message content or business rules.
Business policy changes when the product team modifies rate limits, when legal requires changes to audit logging, or when new preference options are introduced. These are independent of formatting and delivery.

Analysis reveals three change drivers:
C={γcontent,γchannel,γpolicy} C = \{\gamma_\text{content},\ \gamma_\text{channel},\ \gamma_\text{policy}\} 
The “independent clock” test confirms their independence: a template redesign (γcontent\gamma_\text{content}) can happen without changing the SMS gateway (γchannel\gamma_\text{channel}) or the rate-limiting rules (γpolicy\gamma_\text{policy}), and vice versa.

Five elements are pure (|Γ(e)|=1|\Gamma(e)| = 1); four are composite (|Γ(e)|=2|\Gamma(e)| = 2). Each composite element is irreducibly so — both of its drivers genuinely force it to change:

e2e_2 renderContent changes when the message content changes and when policy-driven personalization (language, consent) changes.
e7e_7 enforceRateLimit changes when the policy sets a new limit and when a channel’s capacity changes.
e8e_8 logDelivery changes when audit policy changes and when the channel’s reporting format changes.
e9e_9 formatForChannel changes when content changes and when a channel’s constraints change.

None of these can be split into sub-elements with strictly smaller driver sets, so each is an irreducible composite — the realistic norm, not a special case.


2.5 Step 4: Compliance assessment
Evaluate the monolithic modularization {Mnotify}\{M_\text{notify}\}:

Element Admissibility (IVP-1). Every element has a non-empty Γ(e)\Gamma(e). ✓
Change-Driver Assignment (IVP-2). Every element is pure or irreducibly composite. ✓ (the four composite elements are all irreducible.)
Unit Purity (IVP-3). Γ(Mnotify)\Gamma(M_\text{notify}) contains γcontent,γchannel,γpolicy\gamma_\text{content}, \gamma_\text{channel}, \gamma_\text{policy} and elements with six distinct driver-assignment sets coexist in one module. Violated.
Unit Completeness (IVP-4). With only one module, all elements responding to each driver are trivially together. ✓ (trivially)

The diagnosis: MnotifyM_\text{notify} is a mixed module. Any activation of a change driver touches the whole module, even though only a subset of its elements actually varies. This is the god-module pattern.


2.6 A naive first attempt
A common first instinct is to decompose by technical layer: one module for content handling, one for transport, one for business logic, one for logging.
ModuleSet1={Mcontent,Mtransport,Mlogic,Mlogging} \text{ModuleSet}_1 = \{M_\text{content},\ M_\text{transport},\ M_\text{logic},\ M_\text{logging}\}

By technical category, the modules look clean — each holds the elements that “feel like” they belong to that layer. But the driver assignments tell a different story:

Unit Purity (IVP-3). Three of the four modules are mixed — they group elements that answer to different drivers. McontentM_\text{content} mixes content and policy (because e2e_2 is composite), MtransportM_\text{transport} mixes channel and content (because e9e_9 is composite), and MlogicM_\text{logic} mixes policy and channel (because e7e_7 is composite). Violated.
Unit Completeness (IVP-4). Elements answering to γpolicy\gamma_\text{policy} are scattered across McontentM_\text{content}, MlogicM_\text{logic}, and MloggingM_\text{logging}; elements answering to γchannel\gamma_\text{channel} across MtransportM_\text{transport}, MlogicM_\text{logic}, and MloggingM_\text{logging}. Violated.

The technical-layer decomposition fails on both directives. A change in business policy touches three modules; a change in a channel’s infrastructure touches three modules. This is shotgun surgery spread wide, plus hidden coupling: the composite elements land in whichever layer their technical category suggests, silently wiring together drivers that should be separated.
Why this mistake is common. Decomposing by technical layer (presentation, logic, data) is a deeply ingrained habit. Technical layers sometimes conform to change drivers, but not always — and the more composite elements a system has, the more the two diverge. The test is not “what kind of thing is this element?” but “what causes this element to change?” A composite element belongs with the elements it shares drivers with, not with the layer its name suggests.


2.7 Step 5: The IVP-compliant decomposition
The fix is to group elements by their exact driver-assignment set. Each distinct set forms one equivalence class — one module. The nine elements fall into six classes:

2.8 Step 6: Reflecting on the result
The three modularizations differ in how far a change propagates. The measure that matters is not how many modules are touched, but how many elements must be inspected or modified when a change driver activates — and how many of those were touched unnecessarily.
When a driver activates, the elements that must change are fixed by the domain: γcontent\gamma_\text{content} forces e1,e2,e9e_1, e_2, e_9; γchannel\gamma_\text{channel} forces e3,e4,e5,e7,e8,e9e_3, e_4, e_5, e_7, e_8, e_9; γpolicy\gamma_\text{policy} forces e2,e6,e7,e8e_2, e_6, e_7, e_8. The monolithic design places all nine elements in one module, so every driver activation touches all nine elements, even though only a fraction of them actually vary — up to six unnecessary touches per change. The IVP-compliant design touches exactly the elements that must change and nothing else — zero unnecessary touches, because every module holds only the elements of its driver. This is what IVP’s partition theorem guarantees: the IVP-compliant modularization minimizes change propagation — the scope that must be read and modified when a change driver activates.
The composite elements make the per-driver footprint larger than in a pure system — γchannel\gamma_\text{channel} alone forces six elements across three modules — but this is the domain’s cost, not a defect: each of those elements genuinely must change when the channel changes. IVP cannot reduce the required set; it only ensures that nothing outside it is touched.


2.9 What about dependencies between modules?
The modules in ModuleSet2\text{ModuleSet}_2 will have structural dependencies between them: the orchestration that calls resolveTemplate, then checkPreferences, then deliverEmail introduces inter-module coupling.
IVP does not eliminate dependencies — it organizes them. Dependencies between modules conforming to different change drivers are expected and manageable. Dependencies within a mixed module are the hidden ones that cause maintenance surprises. The composite modules sit between the pure ones by necessity: e9e_9 bridges content and channel, e2e_2 bridges content and policy, e7e_7 and e8e_8 bridge policy and channel. Each is an explicit bridge the domain requires — better a few named bridges than a hidden tangle inside a monolithic module.

title: Software Clustering
text:
Software clustering is the problem of recovering or prescribing the modular structure of a software system. For three decades it was studied as an optimization problem over a dependency graph. IVP reframes it: the difficulty of the problem is not an intrinsic feature of modularisation, but a consequence of doing it without a semantic criterion.
This page explains what IVP concludes about software clustering — why the traditional problem is hard, how IVP dissolves that hardness, and what the shift costs.

title: Software Clustering
text:
1 The traditional problem is NP-complete
Classical software clustering treats modularisation as an optimization problem: given a dependency graph, find the partition of elements that maximises cohesion and minimises coupling.
Mitchell and Mancoridis established in 2006 that this problem is NP-complete [1]. The field responded with metaheuristic search — hill-climbing, genetic algorithms, weighted graph partitioning — each searching for structurally good partitions that, in the worst case, cannot be found exactly in polynomial time.
The hardness is real, but it characterises the difficulty of partitioning without a semantic criterion, not an inherent difficulty of modularisation itself. Without knowing why elements change together, the optimiser cannot distinguish a well-motivated partition from a coincidental one. It must search exponentially many groupings, with no basis for preferring one structurally plausible partition over another.

title: Software Clustering
text:
2 What “cohesion” means in clustering
Classical clustering does not define cohesion by intent. It defines it operationally, as the internal connectivity of a cluster.
Given the dependency graph and a candidate partition, count for each module the edges inside it (cohesion) and the edges that cross its boundary (coupling). Every objective in the field is built on those two counts:

Modularisation quality (MQ). The cluster factor CF(M) = μ / (μ + ½·ε) combines the counts, and MQ averages it over the modules. TurboMQ weights edges by shared source file for multi-file systems. [2]
Modularity. The Newman–Girvan objective replaces the raw internal count with the excess of internal edge mass over a degree-preserving null model. [3] Optimising it is strongly NP-complete. [4]
Pattern-based clustering. ACDC recognises a subsystem as a body that dominates a cluster, then adopts orphans by connectivity — no scalar, but the same criterion of internal connectivity. [5]
Association-matrix clustering. Similarity is computed from shared data or calls, and cohesion is the sum of intra-cluster similarities. [6] [7]
Within-cluster compactness. Tools that borrow a data-clustering objective use the within-cluster sum of squares directly.

Cohesion and coupling therefore read the same graph. They differ only in which edges they count. A survey of the cohesion-metrics literature reaches the same conclusion from the metric side: cohesion metrics and coupling metrics examine the same graph and differ only in which partition of the edge set they report. [8]

title: Software Clustering
text:
3 IVP supplies the missing criterion
IVP provides the semantic criterion the traditional problem lacks.
Every element is governed by one or more change drivers: external conditions that, when they change, require the element to be modified. The change-driver assignment Γ:E→𝒫(C)\Gamma : E \to \mathcal{P}(C) maps each element to its set of governing drivers. The IVP partition 𝒫Γ=E/Γ̃\mathcal{P}_\Gamma = E / \tilde{\Gamma} — grouping elements with identical driver assignments — is the modularisation that minimises both module-touch count per driver activation and within-module contamination cost.

title: Software Clustering
text:
4 Given Γ, clustering is polynomial
Once Γ\Gamma is in hand, no search is needed. Each element already carries its own module membership in Γ(e)\Gamma(e): two elements belong to the same module precisely when they share the same driver-assignment set. The bound O(n⋅dmaxlog⁡dmax)O(n \cdot d_{\max} \log d_{\max}) falls out of the mechanics of that grouping, not from any deep theorem — you can count the operations yourself.
Deriving the cost, step by step, using the six-step application procedure:

Identify the elements (step 1). The analysis has n=|E|n = |E| elements to place. Every element appears once in the pass.
Map drivers to elements (step 3). Each element ee carries its assignment set Γ(e)\Gamma(e), of size |Γ(e)|≤dmax|\Gamma(e)| \le d_{\max}. Set equality does not depend on the order of its members, so each element needs a canonical form before it can serve as a grouping key.
Canonicalise each element’s key (step 5, preparation). Sorting the drivers inside each set makes every element’s key unambiguous: {a,b}\{a, b\} becomes the same key as {b,a}\{b, a\}. Sorting one set of size at most dmaxd_{\max} costs at most dmaxlog⁡dmaxd_{\max} \log d_{\max} operations. Across all nn elements this is O(n⋅dmaxlog⁡dmax)O(n \cdot d_{\max} \log d_{\max}).
Group by identical key (step 5, main pass). Elements that share a driver-assignment set produce the same canonical key and therefore hash to the same bucket. Inserting one element costs O(dmax)O(d_{\max}) — hashing the set and comparing it against the keys of existing buckets. Across all nn elements this is O(n⋅dmax)O(n \cdot d_{\max}).
Read off the modules. Each bucket is one equivalence class — one module. The number of modules is the number of distinct keys, never more than nn. Emitting them costs O(n)O(n).

Step 3 dominates the total: hashing (step 4) is O(n⋅dmax)O(n \cdot d_{\max}) and read-out (step 5) is O(n)O(n), while sorting is the only step carrying a log⁡dmax\log d_{\max} factor, so it sets the rate. So the whole pass is
O(n⋅dmaxlog⁡dmax) O(n \cdot d_{\max} \log d_{\max}) 
When dmaxd_{\max} is bounded by a constant — the practical case, where no element answers to more than a handful of drivers — each element’s work is one small sort and one hash, so step 3 costs O(n)O(n) and the whole pass simplifies to O(n)O(n).
The result is deterministic. Every module in the IVP partition satisfies maximal causal cohesion Hcausal(M)=(1,1)H_\text{causal}(M) = (1, 1), and no other partition achieves (1,1)(1, 1) for all modules.
The same problem is strongly NP-complete over the dependency graph alone and polynomial when the driver assignment is supplied. The complexity class tracks the availability of the semantic criterion.

title: Software Clustering
text:
5 Clustering is not IVP
The output of clustering and the output of IVP share a shape: both partition the elements into modules. The relation that defines the partition differs, and the relation is the content.

Clustering partitions by graph connectivity (or by co-change similarity). Elements go together when they connect.
IVP partitions by Γ-equality. Elements go together when they share the same change drivers.

When dependencies track drivers, the two relations induce the same partition, and clustering acts as a search for the IVP partition. When they diverge, they diverge in both directions. An element that responds to two drivers is adjacent to both driver groups; a connectivity objective keeps it with one of them, while IVP isolates it. Two renderers for the same format that never call each other carry no edge between them; a connectivity objective separates them, while IVP joins them. Neither error is visible from the dependency graph, because both are defined relative to a Γ the graph does not carry.
This is why IVP does not derive from clustering, and does not replace it as a search method. IVP supplies the criterion the clustering objective lacks; clustering supplies a heuristic that approximates it when the criterion is not yet known. The clustering objective scores a partition by the same quantity it optimises — internal edge density — so it cannot say whether the partition is right. IVP is the independent criterion that the cohesion survey found missing from the literature. [8]
One clustering signal samples a different relation and is worth distinguishing, though it is not a better-measured one. Co-change groups elements that historical commits modified together. [9] A call edge records a standing interaction that a change may never exercise; a co-change records an actual modification, so co-change bears on the same question a change driver answers — what varies together — where connectivity does not. That is an alignment of modality, not of accuracy. Co-change fires both when a shared condition forces two elements to change and when a change to one element propagates to a dependent element, and it also fires on commit batching and on refactoring churn. Its error runs in both directions, and its size is not measurable from the co-change data alone. Co-change is a different proxy, not an established better one.
The confound has a direction. Shared-driver pairs co-change symmetrically; change propagation is one-directional, from the element depended upon to the element that depends on it. The directed conditional frequencies therefore carry more than a symmetric co-change count — but only as a filter that rules pairs out. Symmetry is necessary for driver-equivalence, not sufficient (mutual dependencies and commit batching produce it for the wrong reason), and asymmetry alone cannot separate genuine propagation from one element carrying every driver of the other.

title: Software Clustering
text:
6 The cohesion-coupling tension dissolves
The classical imperative — “maximise cohesion, minimise coupling” — treats the two as a trade-off to be balanced with weights. Under IVP, the trade-off was an artifact of optimising without a criterion.
Once every module achieves maximal causal cohesion, the coupling that modularisation can eliminate is eliminated by the same construction that maximises cohesion. The normative decomposition simultaneously maximises cohesion and minimises avoidable coupling — one optimum, not two. The weights encoded a problem that a principled criterion removes rather than solves.

title: Software Clustering
section: 7 The hard part shifts to driver identification
text:
7 The hard part shifts to driver identification
The polynomial result is conditional on Γ\Gamma being known. The complexity of the modularisation problem depends on what information is available:

Γ\Gamma fully known — polynomial: O(n⋅dmaxlog⁡dmax)O(n \cdot d_{\max} \log d_{\max}).
Γ\Gamma partially known — a mix: polynomial for the assigned elements, the traditional hard case for the rest.
Γ\Gamma entirely unknown — the NP-complete traditional case.

The polynomial advantage is therefore proportional to the completeness of the driver analysis. The hard part shifts from combinatorial search to driver identification — an epistemic problem that domain analysis must address.
The shift is an improvement, not a cost-shifting trick. Driver identification yields reusable knowledge about the domain. Partition search yields a configuration that is discarded on every requirements change.

title: Software Clustering
section: 8 Structural clustering returns as a hypothesis generator
text:
8 Structural clustering returns as a hypothesis generator
When change drivers resist identification, structural clustering does not vanish — it changes role. It is demoted from design criterion to hypothesis generator.
Two reasons drive identification difficulty:

Epistemic. The change drivers exist and are well-defined, but the analyst cannot see them — missing domain expertise, absent artifacts, an inherited system with no design records. The drivers are there to be found.
Structural. The domain itself resists a clean decomposition — dense driver overlap, single-authority greenfield systems, rapidly changing driver sets. No sharp partition exists to recover.

Structural clustering helps with the first and not the second. In the epistemic case, dependency density and co-change history carry indirect evidence about the hidden driver structure and can be mined for it. A cluster the algorithm produces is a question worth asking: these elements are structurally close — is there an external condition whose activation would require all of them to change together? In the structural case, the underdetermination is real: no method recovers a sharp partition, because none exists.

title: Software Clustering
text:
9 Scope and limitations
The polynomial result holds when Γ\Gamma is known. The IVP advantage narrows in three cases:

Single-authority greenfield systems — all elements governed by a single driver; the partition is one module, and the analysis is trivial.
Systems with dense driver overlap — many elements with large, overlapping driver sets; the module count is genuinely large because the domain’s change structure is entangled.
Systems in rapid-change domains — driver assignments change frequently; the partition must be recomputed, and while each update is polynomial, the cumulative cost may be non-trivial.

Driver-equivalence does not put every element in its own module. Two elements share a module precisely when they share a driver assignment, and in any real system many elements do. The number of modules is the number of distinct driver-assignment sets, not the number of elements.

title: Software Clustering
text:
10 Where the proofs live
The claim that the Γ-equivalence partition is the unique partition achieving maximal causal cohesion for all modules, and that the cohesion-coupling tension dissolves, follows from the partition result proved in the published paper on the Independent Variation Principle [10], with the causal cohesion metric developed in the paper on causal cohesion [11] and the cost-minimum of the partition in the paper on change propagation and maintenance cost [12].

title: Consequences and Application
text: The core theory — system tuple, change drivers, Γ-equivalence partition, and the partition theorem — has direct consequences for how software is structured, and it yields a concrete procedure for applying it.

title: Consequences and Application
text:
1 Consequences
Several practical consequences follow from the core theory.
Change is contained. A module built as a Γ-equivalence class contains exactly the elements a change driver forces to change together, and nothing else. When a driver activates, the developer opens one module, changes what is inside, and nothing unrelated is disturbed.
Coupling is explained, not traded off. The partition removes the coupling that comes from misplacement: no element that changes together is split across modules, so no accidental cross-boundary dependency remains. The coupling that survives is the coupling the domain itself imposes between distinct driver classes — necessary coupling, not accidental.
Cohesion is a consequence of the partition. A module that is one Γ-equivalence class is pure (no foreign elements) and complete (no missing elements). That is maximal cohesion under the change-driver rule. Cohesion is not a separate knob to tune; it follows from grouping by the correct criterion.
Structure is read from the domain. The partition theorem says the compliant structure is determined once Γ\Gamma is known. Architecture becomes a reading of the domain’s change structure rather than a stylistic choice.
Wrong groupings are diagnosable. A module that mixes elements answering to different drivers, or that scatters one driver’s elements across several modules, violates a named condition. The theory names the violation and points at the fix: reunite the Γ-equivalence class.

title: Consequences and Application
text:
2 The six-step application process
Applying IVP is an iterative design activity, not a mechanical algorithm. It follows a six-step cycle; you may revisit earlier steps as understanding deepens. The depth of analysis should be proportionate to the system’s expected lifetime and how often it changes.

Identify the elements. Choose the grain of artifact the analysis operates on — functions, classes, data structures, modules.
Identify the change drivers. Read the external conditions whose activation forces the system to change. This is discovery, not invention.
Map drivers to elements. Assign each element the set of change drivers that force it to change: build Γ\Gamma.
Assess the current modularization. Compare the existing module structure to the Γ-equivalence partition. Name the violations: which modules are impure, which are incomplete.
Refactor toward compliance. Move elements so the structure converges to the partition.
Verify and iterate. Re-check the assignment and the partition as understanding deepens and as the domain changes.

title: Consequences and Application
section: 3 What IVP does and does not tell you
text:
3 What IVP does and does not tell you
IVP is a theory of where to place elements so that change is contained. It is precise about that and silent about several other things.
It does not tell you how to implement an element, only where it sits. It does not decide whether a system is correct — placement is not correctness. It does not optimize performance, security, or other quality attributes directly, though those can enter the analysis as change drivers. It is one criterion applied to one decision: where does each element belong.
Those limits are the subject of the theory’s formal treatment, not hidden in the small print. The premises and preconditions the theory assumes, and the gates that decide whether it applies to a system, are collected on the scope and validity conditions page.

title: Consequences and Application
text:
4 Where the proofs live
The theorems — the partition theorem, the uniqueness result, the consequences derived from the axioms — are proved in the published papers: the partition and its cost-optimality in the paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1], the four conditions in the paper on cohesion and change propagation [2], the maintenance-cost minimum of the partition in the paper on change propagation and maintenance cost [3], and the purity and completeness properties in the paper on the nature of cohesion [4].

title: IVP Core Theory
text:
This is the formal heart of the Independent Variation Principle as applied to software. Here we explain the model the theory works on, the principle itself, and what follows from it.
The principle is stated and proved in the published paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1].
The core theory has seven parts.

The software system tuple. The model of a software system the principle is stated over: purpose, domain knowledge, elements, coupling, change drivers, and the change-driver assignment.
Change drivers and assignment. What a change driver is, how elements are assigned to them, and how the assignment is discovered from the domain.
The structural formulation of IVP. The statement of the principle itself — the one-sentence Γ-equivalence rule and the four conditions.
The Γ-equivalence partition. The object the principle produces, and what purity and completeness mean.
The partition theorem. The result that the compliant module structure is uniquely the Γ-equivalence partition.
Scope and validity conditions. The premises, preconditions, and applicability gates the results depend on.
Consequences and application. What the theory implies for structuring software and the six-step procedure for applying it.

The knowledge-embodiment theorem — which links maximal cohesion to the embodiment of domain knowledge — is a result of the cohesion theory, not of IVP itself. It is treated on the cohesion page, because it states a property of cohesion, and cohesion is a design principle distinct from IVP.

title: Scope and Validity Conditions
text:
The partition theorem is a conditional result. It holds for systems that meet a set of premises and preconditions, and it returns a stronger conclusion when two further premises hold. This page states all of them in one place: the assumptions the derivation rests on, the preconditions that must hold for the result to apply, and the gates that decide whether IVP is the right tool for a given system.
The principle itself is stated on the structural formulation page, and the object it produces is described on the Γ-equivalence partition and partition theorem pages. This page records the conditions those results assume.

title: Scope and Validity Conditions
text:
1 The three unconditional premises
Three premises are required for the derivation to apply at all.

The change-driver hypothesis. Elements change because external conditions change. Each element’s driver assignment Γ(e)\Gamma(e) captures that causal structure: γ∈Γ(e)\gamma \in \Gamma(e) exactly when activating γ\gamma creates a requirement to modify ee, established by the counterfactual test against the domain artifact that anchors γ\gamma.
A causal domain model. The system has a functional purpose FF and relevant causal domain knowledge κF\kappa_F, and every element embodies some part of κF\kappa_F.
Change-propagation minimisation as the objective. Cost is measured as access cost plus interference, so the target is the modularisation that minimises the scope read and modified when a change driver activates. The change-management hypothesis supplies this objective — minimise the lifetime cost of change — and change-propagation minimisation is how the derivation measures it.

Premises 1 and 2 together support Admissibility and Element Form. Premises 1 and 3 support Separation and Unification.

title: Scope and Validity Conditions
text:
2 The two conditional premises
Two further premises are required only for the stronger forms of the result.

The contamination premise — strict Separation and uniqueness. A γ\gamma-irrelevant co-resident in a touched module imposes non-zero verification overhead. Under this premise, Separation is strictly forced between classes with disjoint driver sets, and the optimal partition is unique. Without it, Separation is a propagation-neutral tie, and the Γ-equivalence partition is one propagation-minimal modularisation but not the only one.
The coefficient condition (⋆)(\star) — total-maintenance-cost optimality. For every irreducibly composite element e*e^{*} and every pure element ee whose driver set is a proper subset of Γ(e*)\Gamma(e^{*}), write S=Γ(e)S = \Gamma(e) for the shared drivers and U=Γ(e*)\Γ(e)U = \Gamma(e^{*}) \setminus \Gamma(e) for the unshared drivers. The condition is
(⋆)α∑γ∈Uλ(γ)+2ωc≥∑γ∈Sλ(γ), (\star)\quad \alpha \sum_{\gamma \in U} \lambda(\gamma) + 2\omega_c \;\ge\; \sum_{\gamma \in S} \lambda(\gamma), 
where λ(γ)\lambda(\gamma) is a change driver’s activation frequency, α\alpha is the interference coefficient (reading plus disturbance penalty per irrelevant co-resident), and ωc\omega_c is the cognitive cost per co-located pair. When (⋆)(\star) holds, the propagation minimum also minimises total maintenance cost. When it fails at some composite/sharer pair, a coarsening of the Γ-equivalence partition achieves lower total cost, and that pair needs a direct cost comparison.

title: Scope and Validity Conditions
text:
3 Precondition: driver independence
The companion results assume that distinct change drivers are independent: their knowledge slices are disjoint, and their activation events are logically independent. The load-bearing requirement is weaker. The partition prescription stays valid whenever no pair of drivers has both overlapping knowledge slices and mutual activation-coupling.
If two drivers always activate together in both directions, they are not two drivers: no element can be governed by one without the other. Merge them into a single driver, and the partition is correct for the merged driver. A pair with overlapping slices but no mutual coupling is harmless: an element that carries both drivers becomes an irreducible composite in its equivalence class, and the overlap is orthogonal to partition correctness.
Driver independence is therefore not an external stipulation. It is a well-formedness condition on the driver set CC.

title: Scope and Validity Conditions
text:
4 Precondition: decisional autonomy
The organisational unit that owns a module must be able to modify, test, and deploy within its scope without cross-unit coordination. If every change needs external sign-off, even a pure and complete module carries coordination overhead that the cost model does not capture.
Decisional autonomy is an organisational property, not a property of the code or the causal structure. The theory derives the module boundaries that minimise change propagation; it does not guarantee that those boundaries align with decision-making authority. When autonomy fails, real cost is change-propagation cost plus coordination overhead, and the partition that minimises the first may not minimise the sum. Two remedies are available: align team boundaries to the Γ-equivalence classes (reverse Conway’s Law), or add the organisational objective to the analysis and accept a composite optimum.

title: Scope and Validity Conditions
section: 5 Does IVP apply to your system?
text:
5 Does IVP apply to your system?
Two gates decide applicability: is the system maintenance-dominated, and is its causal structure known?

Within the yes/yes cell, the preconditions and conditional premises above further qualify the result. When the driver set contains mutually activation-coupled overlapping pairs, merge them. When decisional autonomy fails, extend the objective or restructure the teams. When (⋆)(\star) fails at a composite/sharer pair, use a direct cost comparison over candidate coarsenings for that pair.

title: Scope and Validity Conditions
section: 6 What the derivation does not supply
text:
6 What the derivation does not supply

Driver identification. The assignment Γ\Gamma is assumed available; the derivation does not perform domain analysis for any specific system. Driver identification is domain analysis, grounded in the counterfactual test against domain artifacts.
Irreducibility determination. Reducibility judgments assume that the element’s purpose specification is available; the derivation does not decide reducibility from code alone.
Driver coverage. A system whose causal structure has not been documented is not a system that defies IVP — it is a system awaiting domain analysis. Whether every such system yields to driver analysis is an empirical question the theory does not settle.

title: Scope and Validity Conditions
text:
7 Where the analysis lives
The three unconditional premises, the two conditional premises, and the two preconditions are examined in the paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1]. The four conditions as necessary and jointly exhaustive, and the contamination premise for strict Separation, are developed in the paper on cohesion and change propagation [2]. The coefficient condition (⋆)(\star) and the total-maintenance-cost result are developed in the paper on minimising change propagation and maintenance cost [3].
What IVP does not address at all — runtime behaviour, performance, security, teams, process, and tooling — is recorded on the consequences and application page.


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

title: The Software System Tuple
text:
The Independent Variation Principle is stated over a model of a software system. This model names every object the theory needs to reason about change. It is called the software system tuple.
The tuple is written S=(F,κF,E,Coupling,C,Γ)S = (F, \kappa_F, E, \text{Coupling}, C, \Gamma). Each entry is one ingredient of the model.
The first five ingredients are inputs. They describe the system and its environment as the analysis finds them. The sixth, Γ\Gamma, is the pivot: it is the map the whole principle operates on.

title: The Software System Tuple
text:
1 What the tuple is for
The tuple gives the theory a fixed vocabulary. When the site says “a change driver,” “an element,” or “the coupling relation,” it means exactly the object named in the tuple. The tuple does not describe a new kind of system. It describes any software system in terms that make its structure under change visible.
The tuple is defined and discussed in the formal papers. Here we explain what each entry means and why the tuple is built this way. The software system tuple S=(F,κF,E,Coupling,C,Γ)S = (F, \kappa_F, E, \text{Coupling}, C, \Gamma) is the model the Independent Variation Principle is stated over, as defined in the published paper on the principle [1]. The role of the causal domain knowledge κF\kappa_F in the model is developed in the paper on the nature of cohesion [2].

title: The Software System Tuple
text:
2 Elements respond to change drivers
The central modelling move is Γ\Gamma: every element is assigned the set of change drivers whose activation would force it to be modified. A computeTax() function is assigned the tax-legislation driver, because when the tax rate changes, the function must change. A sanitizeInput() function is assigned the sanitization-policy driver.
The assignment is not arbitrary. It is read from the domain: which external conditions, if they activate, force this element to change. Whether an element responds to one driver or several is a property of the domain’s causal structure, not a choice the designer makes.

title: The Software System Tuple
text:
3 Two sets must be distinguished
Γ(e)\Gamma(e) is the set of change drivers that force element ee to change. The module driver set Γ(M)\Gamma(M) of a module M⊆EM \subseteq E is the union of the driver sets of its elements.
These are different objects. Γ(e)\Gamma(e) is a set of drivers for a single element. Γ(M)\Gamma(M) is a set of drivers for a group of elements. Keeping them separate matters when the theory reasons about how elements group into modules.


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

The Independent Variation Principle — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.20794332
On the Nature of Cohesion: Cohesion as Correctness Relative to a Partitioning Rule — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21703193
