title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Almost every design pattern/principle can be used as a completeness-check on domain knowledge.
When you’re reaching for a pattern, ask “does the domain knowledge mandate the coupling this pattern would add or remove?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, the knowledge prescribes the structure directly — the pattern adds nothing the domain hadn’t already decided.
Each family of patterns sharpens that question in its own way. Where a family frames it differently, its framing opens above that family’s posts.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Abstract Factory Pattern

GoF Intent: “Provide an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The set of concrete types that must vary together (the “product family”) is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “when you’re in context X, you use implementations A₁, B₁, C₁; in context Y, you use A₂, B₂, C₂” — and that these groupings are cohesive units in the domain (e.g., a regulatory regime, a hardware platform, a deployment tier) — then an Abstract Factory is just embodying that knowledge. The factory interface is the domain’s own abstraction; the concrete factories are its real partitions.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates product-family coherence but the language offers no native construct to express “these N types co-vary.” The Abstract Factory is a technical artifact that closes the gap — it prevents each client from individually selecting concrete types, which would scatter the family-binding knowledge across the system and create accidental coupling (every client must know which concrete A goes with which concrete B).








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The domain has no notion of product families. The concrete types vary independently. Forcing them into an Abstract Factory imposes a grouping the domain doesn’t recognize — it bundles change-drivers that are actually independent, creating a single point of modification for unrelated changes. That’s the cohesion-reducing move.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain recognize the concrete-type groupings as a thing?

If yes → applicable. The Abstract Factory is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s the code inventing knowledge the domain doesn’t have.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#GoF #EIP #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #Domain #Knowledge #DesignPrinciples #Java #C# #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #FP



References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Strategy Pattern

GoF Intent: “Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable. Strategy lets the algorithm vary independently from clients that use it.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The existence of multiple algorithms for the same operation is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “this operation admits variants A, B, C, and there is a domain rule that selects among them,” then Strategy is just embodying that knowledge. The strategy interface is the domain’s own abstraction (the what); the concrete strategies are its real alternatives (the how).






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates algorithmic substitutability — it recognizes that the operation meaningfully differs across contexts, and a domain rule dictates which variant applies. The Strategy pattern closes the gap: it prevents each caller from embedding variant-selection logic inline, which would scatter the selection rule across the system and create accidental coupling (every caller must re-encode which variant to use under which conditions). The pattern collects each variant behind a shared interface; the selection rule lives wherever the strategy reference is assigned.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The domain has no notion of multiple algorithms for this operation. The “variants” are a decomposition artifact, not a domain partition — the developer split one algorithm into pieces for readability or reuse and wrapped them in a strategy interface as organizational glue. This imposes a grouping the domain doesn’t recognize: it bundles what the domain treats as one thing into an interface-plus-implementations structure, adding ceremony that signals a richness of variation that isn’t there. If the variants also pull in different data dependencies, Strategy scatters data-acquisition logic across implementations that must each independently discover their inputs.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain recognize multiple algorithms for this operation as a real thing?

If yes → applicable. Strategy is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s the code inventing variation the domain doesn’t have.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.





References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Observer Pattern

GoF Intent: “Define a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that “a change in A constitutes a domain event that B, C, and D must know about” is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that certain state transitions are meaningful events to other entities — that the event is a first-class domain concept — then Observer is just embodying that knowledge. The subject interface is the domain’s own event source; the observer interface is the domain’s own event consumer.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that certain state changes constitute events with multiple consumers, and the set of consumers is open-ended. Observer closes the gap — it prevents the event source from encoding the full list of consumers and their reaction logic inline, which would bundle every downstream concern into a single class and couple the event source to each consumer’s change-drivers.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “event” is not a domain event — nothing in the domain recognizes the state transition as meaningful in itself. B must recompute when A changes not because the domain treats A’s transition as an event, but because the developer chose to cache or denormalize. Observer used for technical consistency (UI model-view synchronization, the GoF’s canonical example) is valid engineering. The cohesion risk is when notification cascades for technical reasons (cache invalidation, denormalization-update chains) are presented as domain event propagation, inventing event semantics the domain model never had.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would the domain model this state transition as an event even if the system weren’t software?

If yes → applicable. Observer is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s the code manufacturing events the domain doesn’t have.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#GoF #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #FP #CodingPatterns #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Dispose Pattern

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a resource has a bounded lifetime — that acquiring it and releasing it are two ends of a single domain transaction — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “this resource must be acquired before use and released after, and the interval between acquisition and release is a meaningful domain scope (a session, a connection, a lock window),” then Dispose is just embodying that knowledge. The disposal interface is the domain’s own “bounded lifetime” contract; the using block is the domain’s own scoping rule made mechanical.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that a resource has a deterministic end-of-life tied to a domain scope. Dispose closes the gap — it prevents each caller from manually pairing acquire and release calls, which would scatter the lifetime knowledge across the system. Every call site would need to know both the acquisition protocol and the release protocol, coupling unrelated code to resource lifecycle details it shouldn’t own.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “resource” is not a domain resource — it’s a memory-management artifact. The developer wraps a plain object in IDisposable because the GC won’t finalize it soon enough, not because the domain mandates a bounded lifetime. Dispose here addresses a runtime behavior, not domain knowledge. Infrastructure resources — file handles, database connections, network sockets — have bounded lifetimes by OS nature, and Dispose is correct for them even when the domain is silent. The inapplicable case: domain objects with no resource semantics beyond memory, where disposal introduces lifecycle coupling the domain never defined.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would the domain model this resource as having a defined end-of-life — or is the resource inherently finite by the nature of the computing environment?

If yes → applicable. Dispose catches up to domain knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. But the resource is infrastructure (files, sockets, connections) or the domain is resource-constrained (embedded/real-time), it remains valid — the bounded lifetime comes from the environment. If purely a GC workaround, the pattern adds lifecycle coupling the domain didn’t require.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DotNet #CSharp #IDisposable #DisposePattern #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #OOP

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Adapter Pattern

GoF Intent: “Convert the interface of a class into another interface clients expect. Adapter lets classes work together that couldn’t otherwise because of incompatible interfaces.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that two entities must talk to each other but speak incompatible languages is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “system A understands protocol α, system B understands protocol β, and there is a domain rule requiring A and B to interoperate,” then Adapter is just embodying that knowledge. The adapter is the domain’s own translation rule; the adapted interface is the domain’s own target vocabulary.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates interoperability across a boundary the domain itself recognizes — a third-party service, a legacy subsystem, an external standard, a different bounded context. The adapter closes the gap: it isolates the translation logic in one place rather than forcing every caller of B to speak B’s protocol directly. Without it, each caller would embed translation logic inline, coupling unrelated code to B’s vocabulary and scattering the adaptation rule across the system.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “incompatibility” is not a domain boundary — it’s a pair of self-owned interfaces that encode the same concepts differently. Wrapping one in an adapter to match the other adds a permanent translation layer between abstractions that should be unified. Sometimes this is transitional — two teams built different interfaces that need reconciliation. But when the adapter becomes permanent without a unification plan, it institutionalizes an interface mismatch the domain never imposed. The distinguishing test is whether both sides have independent change-driver authorities: an adapter between domain port and infrastructure adapter (Hexagonal/Ports-and-Adapters) embodies a domain-imposed boundary, not duplication disguised as adaptation.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain recognize the two sides of the adapter as genuinely separate things that must interoperate?

If yes → applicable. The adapter is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s indirection the domain didn’t impose — which may still be legitimate if the sides have distinct authorities (e.g., domain port vs. infrastructure), but warrants unification if the same team owns both.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#GoF #AdapterPattern #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #FP #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Builder Pattern

GoF Intent: “Separate the construction of a complex object from its representation so that the same construction process can create different representations.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that constructing an object is a multi-step process whose steps are domain-significant — not just parameter-passing — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “creating an X requires collecting parts A, B, C from different sources, in an order that matters, with validation between steps,” then Builder is just embodying that knowledge. The builder is the domain’s own construction protocol; each step is a domain operation.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that construction is a process, not a one-shot operation. The object cannot be created atomically because its parts come from different domain sources or require intermediate domain validation — and a partially-built object is a meaningful domain state (a draft, an incomplete form, a staged assembly). Builder closes the gap: it isolates the construction logic so the object doesn’t expose setters allowing mutation after construction, and so callers don’t each re-encode the construction sequence.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The domain has no notion of incremental construction. All parts are available at once, and a partially-built object has no domain meaning. Builder is often reached for here to emulate named parameters — e.g., Pizza.builder().size(12).crust("thin").sauce("marinara") reads better than positional new Pizza(12, "thin", "marinara"…). But this ergonomics problem exposes a deeper gap: the constructor arguments are weakly typed. crust isn’t a String, it’s a Crust. Once the domain is properly typed — Pizza(Size, Crust, Sauce, Set<Topping>) — the constructor is self-documenting and Builder adds nothing. Builder here isn’t fixing a language limitation, it’s masking underspecified types.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain treat “in the process of being built” as a real state?

If yes → applicable. Builder is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. Check first whether weak typing or some other issue is the real gap. When the domain is properly typed and construction is still painful, the language genuinely lacks expressive constructors — but this is rare and worth distinguishing from a type-design gap.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#GoF #BuilderPattern #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #FP #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Command Pattern

GoF Intent: “Encapsulate a request as an object, thereby letting you parameterize clients with different requests, queue or log requests, and support undoable operations.” [1, p. 233]

The pattern decouples invoker from receiver — the invoker must NOT know which concrete receiver handles the request. This is structural: the invoker dispatches to a Command interface and stays receiver-agnostic. (Queuing, logging, and undo follow from the encapsulation.)

The knowledge gap it signals
Command needs the invoker to be receiver-agnostic. The question is not “would the domain break if the invoker knew?” — the pattern exists because the invoker must NOT know. The gap: does your architecture need receiver-agnostic dispatch?






ImportantWhen it’s needed



The invoker must dispatch to different receivers without knowing which at compile time: a menu dispatches to dialogs, a scheduler to job handlers, a transaction manager to rollback actions, an event bus to subscribers. The invoker cannot name the receiver — requests are queued, parameterized, or submitted by unknown clients. Command closes the gap: the interface abstracts over receivers the invoker was never meant to know.








WarningWhen it’s not needed



The invoker always calls the same concrete receiver. Wrapping every service-method invocation in a Command interface because “we might need undo later” adds indirection where the invoker already knows its target. The interface adds maintenance and dispatch overhead to a call that should be direct. Command here guesses at flexibility no requirement demands.








TipThe faithfulness test — a 3-step decision procedure




Does the invoker need to dispatch without knowing the concrete receiver?
Is there more than one receiver, or will the receiver be determined at runtime?
Decide. If yes → applicable (Command provides the receiver-agnostic dispatch your architecture needs). If no → inapplicable (call directly). If you can’t answer → unclear — you haven’t found the pattern wrong, you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.



CQS/CQRS “Command” is a different concept — a message that mutates state (contrast: Query) — and is not covered here.

#GoF #CommandPattern #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling



References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Composite Pattern

GoF Intent: “Compose objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. Composite lets clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly.” [1]

The GoF Composite pattern composes objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. It lets clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly through a shared Component interface.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The domain recognizes a part-whole hierarchy where the whole and its parts answer the same questions. A department and its sub-departments both have budgets. A file and a directory both have sizes. When you find yourself reaching for Composite, the gap is: does the domain actually treat wholes and parts uniformly, or are you imposing a tree structure on something the domain views as flat or differently?






ImportantWhen the pattern follows domain knowledge



The domain has genuine part-whole recursion where the same operations apply at every level. Making “a department contains sub-departments, and both compute a budget” explicit in the domain model is the work. Composite’s uniform interface then prevents callers from branching on “is this a single thing or a group?” before every operation — the hierarchy delegates recursively, and callers operate on the abstract type.








WarningWhen the pattern overreaches



The domain has no part-whole recursion. The hierarchy is a tree-shaped data structure for navigation convenience, not a domain fact. UI component trees are the GoF’s canonical Composite example and are valid — they address the domain of UI toolkit design, where the part-whole relationship IS the problem space. A file-system directory tree is domain recursion; an internal cache organized as a tree for lookup efficiency is not. When the hierarchy is artificial, leaf types implement operations that make no sense for them — a structural mismatch the domain did not create.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain say “an X is either a single thing or a group of things, and both answer the same questions”?

If yes → applicable. The pattern codifies what the domain already dictates.
If no → inapplicable. The tree structure may still be valid — valid in infrastructure domains (UI toolkits, scene graphs, ASTs) where the part-whole relationship IS the problem space — but misplaced where the domain has no recursion.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#GoF #CompositePattern #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Decorator Pattern

GoF Intent: “Attach additional responsibilities to an object dynamically. Decorators provide a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
A decorator adds behavior without changing the interface or what the object is. Domain intuition: a paper invoice through administration. One office stamps “PAID” — still an invoice, now endorsed. Another stamps “CONFIDENTIAL” — still an invoice, now classified. Each endorsement decorates without changing identity; for clients it is still the same object. The gap: what is intrinsic to the entity vs. an optional endorsement. An unpaid invoice is still an invoice — “paid” is an endorsement, not part of what makes it an invoice. Baking payment status into the invoice class reveals the gap.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



A responsibility is optional — some objects need it, others don’t. Without Decorator, independent endorsements must be enumerated by subclass, conditional-branch, or enum state. For fully independent endorsements factoring into 2ⁿ combinations, that is an explosion the domain never created. Each decorator stays a single endorsement.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The wrapping transforms the object’s semantics instead of endorsing it. Tax calculation that changes the invoice total is Pipes and Filters: sequential transformations producing a semantically different result, not a stamp. Decorator preserves contract meaning — the invoice is still an invoice after every endorsement. If wrapping changes what the thing is, you are not decorating.
Also inapplicable when the added behavior is independent of the causal domain — pure orthogonal wrapping (logging, caching, auth, retry): a business-agnostic interceptor, not a domain endorsement. The GoF’s examples (scrollbars, borders, buffered streams) are infrastructure. The pattern’s domain value emerges when the business operates through endorsements on stable documents: approvals, certifications, status stamps.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can each responsibility be attached or removed without changing what the object is?
A “PAID” stamp doesn’t make an invoice something else → applicable (Decorator). Tax wrapper changes the total → inapplicable (Pipes and Filters, not Decorator). If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.



#GoF #DecoratorPattern #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #FP #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: State Pattern

GoF Intent: “Allow an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes. The object will appear to change its class.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
That an entity’s behavior depends on which state it’s in — and that the set of states and the transitions between them are domain rules — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes a state machine — “an order starts as Pending, can transition to Confirmed or Cancelled, and in each state different operations are allowed” — then State is just embodying that knowledge: each state is a domain state; each transition is a domain rule.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain recognizes a state machine: a finite set of states, well-defined transitions, and behavior that varies per state. Each state is a real domain notion the domain expert can name, say what operations it permits, and say what can follow it. State preserves the domain’s own boundaries: one module per domain state, keeping each state’s rules with its state.
Lifecycle vs interchangeable choice is the discriminator. State is right only when switching behavior is the object moving through stages of a lifecycle — each stage follows from and leads to others. If the switches pick between interchangeable alternatives with no ordered progression, the domain describes a Strategy, not a State machine.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “states” are not domain states — they’re status flags with no behavioral variation. An entity carries several independent flags, each its own domain notion: active, verified, and premium are each judged on their own. Collecting these into one lifecycle and treating each combination as a state only works if the domain recognizes a lifecycle over those combinations — but it doesn’t. The domain expert sees three separate facts, not stages that follow one another.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can the domain expert draw the state-transition diagram from memory?

If yes → applicable. State is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s boolean flags encoded as a state machine — the domain doesn’t define a lifecycle over these combinations.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

A second check: does the object appear to change its class when it changes state — does its whole behavior repertoire shift? Real states do. Flags merely flip a bit; the behavior was never different.



#GoF #StatePattern #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #FP #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Template Method Pattern

GoF Intent: “Define the skeleton of an algorithm in an operation, deferring some steps to subclasses. Template Method lets subclasses redefine certain steps of an algorithm without changing the algorithm’s structure.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that operations share an invariant skeleton with variant steps can be domain knowledge — but only when the skeleton itself is a domain rule. If your domain model already crystallizes that “the regulatory review process has the same framework (notify, review, approve) regardless of jurisdiction; only the steps within each phase differ,” then Template Method is just embodying that knowledge. The base class is the domain’s own procedural framework; the hook methods are the domain’s own variation points. In most applications, however, the “skeleton” is code similarity mistaken for domain structure — the domain expert sees one coherent algorithm, not a template with extension points.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain recognizes the skeleton as a domain-invariant process: a regulatory framework, a certification pipeline, a protocol with mandated phases. Template Method closes the gap: it prevents each implementation from re-encoding the invariant sequence, which would scatter the procedural knowledge across the system and risk divergence. The base class is the domain’s own “these steps always happen in this order” rule; the concrete subclasses fill in the domain’s own variation points.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The skeleton is code similarity, not domain structure. “ReportGenerator has a generate() method that calls openFile(), writeData(), closeFile() — and CSV and PDF differ only in writeData().” The domain doesn’t recognize openFile/writeData/closeFile as a legitimate decomposition — it sees “generate a report.” Template Method here encodes a technical sequence (file open/write/close) as if it were a domain invariant, coupling all report types to a file-based implementation. When a report type arrives that doesn’t use files, the template breaks.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you state the invariant skeleton as a domain rule without mentioning implementation details?

If yes → applicable. Template Method is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s code similarity mistaken for domain invariance.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Facade Pattern

GoF Intent: “Provide a unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem. Facade defines a higher-level interface that makes the subsystem easier to use.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a subsystem presents a single entry point — that “to interact with this part of the system, you go through here” — is domain knowledge if the boundary is a domain boundary. If your domain model already crystallizes that “ordering involves inventory, payment, and shipping, but from the customer’s perspective it’s one operation,” then Facade is just embodying that knowledge. The facade is the domain’s own simplified interface; the subsystem behind it is the domain’s own internal complexity.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain recognizes a bounded context: a cluster of related operations that outsiders should consume through a single, simplified interface. Facade closes the gap: it prevents every external caller from knowing the internal structure of the subsystem and orchestrating calls to its components directly. Without it, each caller would couple to the subsystem’s internal topology, making every internal refactor a cross-system ripple. The facade is the domain’s own “this is the interface” contract.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “subsystem” is not a domain boundary — it’s a package the developer created for code organization. A facade over “DataAccessLayer” or “UtilPackage” isn’t expressing a domain simplification; it’s expressing an organizational boundary the domain model doesn’t define. The risk is that over time, every cross-cutting concern lands in the facade, coupling unrelated domain rules under a single class. The distinction matters: a Repository (facade over data access in DDD) IS domain-meaningful; a general-purpose “Utils” facade is not.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain recognize this boundary as a meaningful simplification — “you deal with X, not with the machinery behind X”?

If yes → applicable. Facade is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s an organizational boundary the domain doesn’t recognize — valid for technical subsystems (the GoF’s compiler example), but structurally different from a domain-simplification facade.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Singleton Pattern

GoF Intent: “Ensure a class only has one instance, and provide a global point of access to it.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that there is exactly one of something — and that “exactly one” is a domain rule, not a coincidence — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “there is one and only one tax authority, one central bank, one system clock,” then Singleton is just embodying that knowledge. The singleton instance is the domain’s own uniqueness constraint; the global access point is the domain’s own “ask the one X.”






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates uniqueness: the concept itself implies singleness, and having two would be a domain error. Singleton closes the gap: it prevents the system from accidentally creating duplicate instances of something that the domain says cannot be duplicated. Without enforcement, every caller becomes a potential duplication point — the uniqueness knowledge is scattered across the system as a convention (“don’t create two”) rather than a constraint.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “uniqueness” is not a domain constraint — it’s a convenience. The developer makes it a singleton because “we only need one right now” or “it holds configuration we want globally accessible.” The domain doesn’t forbid a second instance; it just doesn’t happen to need one yet. Singleton here conflates “currently one” with “necessarily one,” encoding a temporary deployment fact as a permanent structural constraint. When the system later needs a second instance — per-tenant configuration, per-region cache — the singleton becomes the bottleneck that must be unwound.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would having two instances violate a rule the domain expert would immediately recognize as wrong?

If yes → applicable. Singleton is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a global access point for convenience — valid when a single instance is structurally required (configuration, application-scoped state), but avoid encoding “currently one” as “necessarily one” when it blocks future multiplicity.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Bridge Pattern

GoF Intent: “Decouple an abstraction from its implementation so that the two can vary independently.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that an abstraction and its implementation vary independently is domain knowledge — but the two axes need not both be domain-recognized. The GoF’s own Window/WindowImp example separates domain abstraction from platform-specific implementation; one axis is technical. If your domain model crystallizes that “a Payment can be Credit, Debit, or BankTransfer, and it can be processed via Stripe, PayPal, or DirectBank — and these two axes are independent concerns,” then Bridge is just embodying that knowledge. The abstraction hierarchy is the domain’s own “what” axis; the implementation hierarchy may be domain (payment processors) or technical (rendering engines, database backends). Both are valid; the true test is independent variation, not domain recognition of both axes.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain recognizes two independent axes of variation: the concept and its operational mechanism vary for different reasons. Bridge closes the gap: it prevents the combinatorial subclass explosion (CreditStripePayment, CreditPayPalPayment, DebitStripePayment…) that would couple the two axes artificially. Each axis stays in its own hierarchy, matching the domain’s own separation of concerns.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The two “axes” don’t vary independently — they always change together. A Bridge where both hierarchies are expanded in lockstep adds indirection with no separation benefit. The GoF designed Bridge for decoupling abstraction from implementation; the decoupling must be genuine. When the “implementation” dimension is purely technical (rendering engine, database backend), Bridge is still structurally valid — it separates domain from infrastructure, matching the GoF’s canonical use case. The inapplicable case is when the separation is artificial: both axes change for the same reason, making the indirection pure overhead.








TipThe faithfulness test



Do the two axes vary independently — would a change to one necessitate a change to the other?

If yes → applicable. Bridge is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The two axes don’t genuinely vary independently — the separation adds structure without benefit.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Proxy Pattern

GoF Intent: “Provide a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that access to an entity must be mediated — that “you don’t talk to X directly; you go through a surrogate that controls, delays, or logs the interaction” — is domain knowledge when the mediation is a domain rule. If your domain model already crystallizes that “access to the ledger requires authorization checks and an audit trail,” then Proxy is just embodying that knowledge. The proxy is the domain’s own access-control rule; the real subject is the domain’s own protected resource.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that interaction with an entity carries cross-cutting concerns that are themselves domain rules: access control, audit logging, lazy resolution of a heavyweight resource whose loading is a domain event. Proxy closes the gap: it isolates the mediation logic so that neither the caller nor the subject needs to embed it. Without the proxy, every caller would need to perform the access check, or the subject would need to know about authorization — both coupling the entity wrongly.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The mediation is not a domain rule — it’s infrastructure. Caching proxies, network-transparency proxies, and lazy-loading proxies are the GoF’s own canonical Proxy variants — structurally valid and correct. The faithfulness test identifies a distinction within valid Proxy usage: domain-driven mediation (access control, audit) carries domain semantics; infrastructure-driven mediation (latency, remoting, memory) serves technical concerns. Both are legitimate; the risk is using a Proxy where the indirection adds no control, or where it violates transparency — introducing timing/failure semantics that differ from the real subject in ways that break callers.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the mediation itself a domain rule — would a domain expert describe the access control, the audit requirement, the lazy resolution as part of how the system should work?

If yes → applicable. Proxy is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s infrastructure mediation — valid and canonical GoF usage, but serving technical rather than domain semantics.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Iterator Pattern

GoF Intent: “Provide a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a collection should be traversed without exposing its structure — and that the traversal itself is a domain-meaningful act — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “you can walk through the orders, one by one, in submission order, and the fact that they’re stored in a B-tree is irrelevant to the walker,” then Iterator is just embodying that knowledge. The iterator is the domain’s own traversal protocol; the aggregate is the domain’s own collection.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain recognizes sequential traversal as a first-class operation on collections, and the internal structure of the collection is not something external callers should depend on. Iterator closes the gap: it prevents every caller from indexing into the collection directly, which would couple callers to the collection’s storage structure. When the underlying structure changes — from array to tree to stream — the callers are unaffected.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The traversal is doing work the language already does, and no domain boundary is being protected. In languages where iterators are built into the standard library and every collection exposes them, writing a custom Iterator reimplements language-native traversal — not domain knowledge. The domain doesn’t distinguish “iterate with a cursor object” from “iterate with a loop” — both are “go through the items.” Custom Iterator here adds a class hierarchy and a stateful traversal object for something for-each already handles, adding architectural weight where the domain has none. When traversal ORDER is domain-significant (topological sort, priority-based, spatial), a custom iterator DOES encode a domain rule and is applicable.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the traversal protocol protect a domain boundary — would exposing the internal structure violate a domain rule?

If yes → applicable. Iterator is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It reimplements language-native traversal — legitimate when the language lacks built-in iteration, but adding a class hierarchy for something for-each already handles.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Factory Method Pattern

GoF Intent: “Define an interface for creating an object, but let subclasses decide which class to instantiate. Factory Method lets a class defer instantiation to subclasses.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the choice of which concrete type to create is a domain decision — and that the decision belongs to a specific domain context — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “when processing a domestic order, create a DomesticTaxCalculator; when processing an international order, create an InternationalTaxCalculator — and the order type determines the calculator type,” then Factory Method is just embodying that knowledge. The factory method is the domain’s own “decide which implementation” rule.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that the concrete-type decision is a domain rule embedded in a specific context. The factory method closes the gap: it prevents the decision from being made at every call site, which would scatter the domain rule across the system. Instead, each context owns its creation decision, and callers get the right object without knowing how the choice was made. The domain rule lives in one place — the factory method — matching the domain’s own delegation.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “choice” is not a domain rule — it’s a configuration switch. The factory method returns ImplementationA or ImplementationB based on an environment variable, a feature flag, or a dependency-injection binding. The domain doesn’t recognize “the class to use depends on the deployment environment” as a domain rule — the domain expert doesn’t know or care which class is instantiated in staging vs. production. Factory Method here wraps a DI binding in domain-shaped ceremony, adding an inheritance hook for a decision that a config file could make.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the decision of which concrete type to create governed by a domain rule that a domain expert could articulate?

If yes → applicable. Factory Method is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a dependency-injection binding expressed as a subclass hook — structurally valid for framework extensibility, but not a domain-driven creation rule.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Prototype Pattern

GoF Intent: “Specify the kinds of objects to create using a prototypical instance, and create new objects by copying this prototype.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that creating an object by copying an existing one is the domain-correct way to instantiate it — not just a performance optimization — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “a new insurance policy starts as a copy of the template policy; a new document inherits the template’s clauses and only overrides what differs,” then Prototype is just embodying that knowledge. The prototype instance is the domain’s own exemplar; the clone operation is the domain’s own “create from template” rule.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain recognizes prototypical instances: “standard policy,” “default configuration,” “base contract.” Creating from a prototype closes the gap: it prevents the “default” knowledge from being a static initializer or a constructor with dozens of default arguments, which would scatter the exemplar knowledge across parameter lists. The prototype centralizes the exemplar — change the template, and all new instances inherit the change.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “prototype” is not a domain exemplar — it’s a runtime clone to avoid the cost of calling new. The developer uses clone() because construction is expensive or the object graph is complex, not because the domain recognizes template-based creation. Prototype here substitutes object copying for proper instantiation, coupling the system to clone semantics (shallow vs. deep, mutable field hazards) that the domain never asked for. The domain expert would say “you don’t photocopy a policy to create a new one — you issue a new policy.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain have a concept of a “template” or “standard” instance that new instances are based on?

If yes → applicable. Prototype is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s clone() as a substitute for proper construction.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Flyweight Pattern

GoF Intent: “Use sharing to support large numbers of fine-grained objects efficiently.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that many objects share the same intrinsic state — and that this shared state is domain-significant, not an accident of design — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “every character rendered in this document shares a font, size, and style; the only thing that varies per character is its position,” then Flyweight is just embodying that knowledge. The flyweight object is the domain’s own “shared properties” bundle; the extrinsic state is the domain’s own “per-instance” data.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain recognizes a large population of entities whose commonality is a domain category: all instances of type X share intrinsic properties Y, and those properties define the category. Flyweight closes the gap: it prevents each instance from carrying a copy of the intrinsic state, which would scatter the category definition across thousands of objects. The shared flyweight is the single point of truth for “what it means to be a character in 12pt Times,” matching the domain’s own category abstraction.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “shared state” does not correspond to a domain category — it’s data that happens to repeat. The developer extracts repeated fields into a flyweight because the profiler showed memory pressure, not because the domain recognizes a shared category. Flyweight is the GoF’s canonical performance pattern — memory efficiency IS its stated intent. The faithfulness test is supplementary: if the intrinsic state ALSO maps to a domain category (tile type, material definition), the pattern survives domain evolution; if purely memory-driven, it remains valid GoF engineering but may need revision when memory pressure shifts. In domains like game dev (tile types) and frontend (CSS classes), the performance and domain motivations coincide — Flyweight is doubly justified.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain have a name for the category defined by the shared intrinsic state?

If yes → applicable. Flyweight is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s legitimate memory optimization — valid GoF usage, but the pattern should be reconsidered when memory pressure shifts rather than when the domain evolves.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Chain of Responsibility Pattern
text:
Case study: Chain of Responsibility Pattern

GoF Intent: “Avoid coupling the sender of a request to its receiver by giving more than one object a chance to handle the request. Chain the receiving objects and pass the request along the chain until an object handles it.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a request should be passed along a chain of handlers until one handles it — and that the order of handlers is a domain rule — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “an expense report goes to the manager; if within their limit, approved; otherwise, passes to the director; if within their limit, approved; otherwise, passes to the VP,” then Chain of Responsibility is just embodying that knowledge. Each handler is a domain role; the chain order is the domain’s own escalation path.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates an ordered escalation or filtering chain: a request walks a domain-defined sequence of reviewers, each with authority to handle or pass. Chain of Responsibility closes the gap: it prevents the caller from knowing the entire chain structure, coupling it to the organizational hierarchy. The chain can be reconfigured — new approval levels added — without changing the caller. The chain is the domain’s own delegation rule, not a technical convenience.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The chain order is not a domain rule — it’s a fallback heuristic. “Try handler A; if it returns null, try B; if that returns null, try C.” The GoF’s canonical help-system example (GUI containment hierarchy) IS a sequential delegation chain with meaningful order — valid GoF usage. The inapplicable case is specifically when the order is arbitrary or meaningless, and what you actually want is a handler registry or map lookup. The risk is using a sequential search where the order is neither domain-mandated (escalation) nor structurally meaningful (containment hierarchy) — making behavior depend silently on registration order, which the domain never specified.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would the domain expert describe this as an escalation or delegation path — and can they name the order without looking at the code?

If yes → applicable. Chain of Responsibility is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a sequential search with no domain grounding — valid for containment hierarchies (the GoF’s help system) but fragile when order is arbitrary.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Mediator Pattern

GoF Intent: “Define an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact. Mediator promotes loose coupling by keeping objects from referring to each other explicitly, and it lets you vary their interaction independently.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a set of entities should communicate only through a central coordinator — and that the coordination logic is itself a domain concept — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “when a flight lands, the gate must be updated, baggage handling must be notified, and the arrival board must refresh — and no one talks to anyone else directly; the control tower coordinates everything,” then Mediator is just embodying that knowledge. The mediator is the domain’s own coordination hub; the colleagues are the domain’s own independent actors.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that a set of entities interact through a central coordinator whose logic is a domain rule, not a technical convenience. Mediator closes the gap: it prevents each colleague from knowing about every other colleague, which would create an N² coupling mesh where every entity’s change-drivers are coupled to every other entity’s. The mediator owns the interaction rules, matching the domain’s own hub-and-spoke structure.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “coordinator” is not a domain hub — it’s a god object that accumulated orchestration logic because each colleague was shielded from every other colleague’s interface. The mediator collects every cross-entity interaction into one class not because the domain has a central coordinator, but because direct dependencies were to be avoided at any cost. The result is a single point of coupling for every entity interaction — a class that changes whenever any two colleagues need a new interaction, bundling unrelated domain rules under one roof. The GoF’s dialog-box mediator (widgets coordinating through a central controller) is valid when the coordination rules are coherent; the anti-pattern is when the mediator has no single coordination logic and becomes a catch-all.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain have a name for the coordinator that a domain expert would recognize as doing this job?

If yes → applicable. Mediator is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a collection of indirect dependencies — the coupling is only hidden, not reduced.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#GoF #MediatorPattern #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #FP #Coupling #Cohesion

[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Memento Pattern

GoF Intent: “Without violating encapsulation, capture and externalize an object’s internal state so that the object can be restored to this state later.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that an entity’s state can be captured and restored — and that this is a domain operation, not a debugging aid — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “a document has versions; an order can be rolled back to a previous state; a workflow checkpoint can be saved and resumed,” then Memento is just embodying that knowledge. The memento is the domain’s own snapshot; the originator is the domain’s own versioned entity; the caretaker is the version keeper.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates state capture and restoration as domain operations: undo (the GoF’s canonical motivation, valid for interactive applications where undo is a user-facing operation), version history, checkpoint/restore, game save/load, workflow rollback. Memento closes the gap: it prevents the originator from exposing its internal state to the caretaker, which would couple the caretaker to the entity’s private structure. The memento is an opaque snapshot — the caretaker holds it without knowing what’s inside — matching “the archive stores versions; it doesn’t parse them.”








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “snapshot” is not a domain operation — it’s an internal save-point for maintenance purposes. The GoF’s canonical Memento motivation is undo — and undo IS a domain operation in interactive applications, so a Memento for Ctrl+Z is domain-valid. The inapplicable case is Memento for purely internal needs — a serialization hook for debugging, a temporary checkpoint for an optimization pass, a save-point tied to implementation rather than to a domain concept like “version” or “checkpoint.” When the caretaker accesses the memento’s internal state (defeating encapsulation), or a simple data copy would suffice, the three-class protocol adds overhead the domain didn’t ask for.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain recognize “save state” and “restore state” as operations a domain expert would perform — versioning, checkpointing, rolling back?

If yes → applicable. Memento catches up to domain knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s infrastructure snapshotting — valid GoF usage, but the pattern’s structural weight only pays off when the domain treats versioned state as a first-class concept.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#GoF #MementoPattern #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #OOP #FP



References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Visitor Pattern

GoF Intent: “Represent an operation to be performed on the elements of an object structure. Visitor lets you define a new operation without changing the classes of the elements on which it operates.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that an operation must be defined over a fixed set of element types — and that new operations are added more often than new element types — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “a tax rule must be applied to every kind of financial instrument (stock, bond, derivative), and new tax rules appear more frequently than new instrument types,” then Visitor is just embodying that knowledge. The element hierarchy is the domain’s own stable taxonomy; each visitor is a domain operation that must handle every case.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain has a stable type hierarchy and a family of operations that must be exhaustive over it. Visitor closes the gap: it prevents each operation from being scattered across the element classes as a method, which would couple the element hierarchy to every operation’s change-drivers. Adding a new operation means adding one visitor class, not modifying every element.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The distinction depends on hierarchy stability, exactly the GoF’s design trade-off. AST visitors over syntax trees, the GoF’s canonical example, are valid: compiler construction IS a domain, and AST traversal IS a domain operation. The inapplicable case is when the hierarchy genuinely IS unstable — new element types arrive frequently, requiring modification of every visitor. The GoF explicitly warn against Visitor in this scenario. In languages with pattern matching over sum types (modern Java, Scala, Rust), Visitor’s double-dispatch machinery is largely redundant — but without it, Visitor remains the standard encoding. The faithfulness test separates genuinely stable taxonomies (financial instruments, document types) from those that change next sprint.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain have a stable taxonomy of element types, and do operations over that taxonomy arrive more frequently than new element types?

If yes → applicable. Visitor is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The hierarchy is unstable — or your language already has pattern matching over sum types, making Visitor’s double-dispatch unnecessary.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Interpreter Pattern

GoF Intent: “Given a language, define a representation for its grammar along with an interpreter that uses the representation to interpret sentences in the language.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the domain has its own language — a grammar, a syntax, and rules for evaluating sentences in that language — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “a trading system has a domain-specific language for defining trading strategies; a rule engine evaluates expressions like ‘if risk > threshold and exposure > limit, then reject’,” then Interpreter is just embodying that knowledge. The grammar is the domain’s own syntax; each expression type is a domain concept.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain has a well-defined grammar that domain experts use to express rules, queries, or configurations — and the grammar is stable enough to justify encoding it as a class hierarchy. Interpreter closes the gap: it gives each grammar rule its own class, so a new expression type adds one class rather than modifying a monolithic parser. The parse tree is the domain’s own sentence structure; the interpret() method is the domain’s own evaluation rule.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “language” is not a domain language — it’s a configuration format, a query syntax, or a wire protocol the developer designed. The developer defines a grammar, creates a class per production, and builds an interpreter — but the domain expert would never write a sentence in this language; they’d fill out a form or click a button. Interpreter here adds a class hierarchy for every grammar rule, coupling the grammar to the implementation so that changing the syntax means changing the class structure. A parser generator or a simple recursive-descent parser would handle the same task without institutionalizing the grammar as a class hierarchy.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would the language’s vocabulary serve a recurring need where the grammar is stable enough to justify encoding as a class hierarchy — and would domain experts recognize the language’s expressions as things they reason about?

If yes → applicable. Interpreter is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a parser for a technical language — valid when the grammar is stable and the language serves a real need, but not a domain language the domain expert would recognize.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Content-Based Router Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do we handle a situation where the implementation of a single logical function (e.g., inventory check) is spread across multiple physical systems?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that messages carry content that determines their destination is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “an order from region R goes to warehouse W, a payment above threshold T goes to fraud-check,” then Content-Based Router embodies that knowledge. The routing table is the domain’s own dispatch logic; each destination is a domain actor that receives specific kinds of work.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that which component receives a message depends on the message’s content — and the classification rule is a domain rule, not a technical convenience. When a claims-processing domain says “auto claims under $5,000 go to fast-track; auto claims over $5,000 go to full review; all property claims go to property adjustment,” the router encodes domain knowledge that would otherwise be buried in each receiving component’s guard clause. Without the router, every receiver must independently re-implement content-based filtering, scattering the routing rule across the system and creating accidental coupling — each receiver must know about every message type it could receive.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “routing” is not a domain rule — it’s a technical partition masquerading as a content decision. “Based on the message XML namespace, route to parser version 1 or version 2.” Or “route to the service instance with the lowest current load.” The domain doesn’t recognize XML namespaces, parser versions, or load distribution as input variables — it sees “process this order.” Content-Based Router here becomes a technology-level dispatcher that hides the real domain concern (what happens to the order?) behind a mechanical classification the domain expert would never produce. When the routing criteria are implementation details, every domain change that affects content may invisibly re-route without the domain expert knowing.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can a domain expert produce the routing table from their own knowledge, without asking an engineer what’s “technically easier”?

If yes → applicable. Content-Based Router is the code catching up.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a technical switchyard disguised as domain routing.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Publish-Subscribe Channel Pattern

EIP Intent: “How can the sender broadcast an event to all interested receivers?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that multiple parties independently care about the same occurrence is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “when an order is fulfilled, the warehouse needs to restock, the customer needs a notification, the loyalty program needs to update points, and the finance system needs to recognize revenue,” then Publish-Subscribe is just embodying that knowledge. The topic is the domain event; the subscribers are domain actors who, by the rules of the domain, must react when that event occurs.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that one occurrence triggers multiple independent responses — and the publisher has no domain reason to know about the subscribers. A publisher should not know who consumes its events; the event itself is the coupling point, and the downstream reactions are separate domain responsibilities. Publish-Subscribe closes the gap: it prevents the publisher from growing a list of explicit callbacks for each new consumer, which would couple the publisher to downstream concerns it has no domain interest in. Each subscriber declares its interest in the event independently; the publisher emits once and the domain network reacts.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “subscribers” are not domain-independent — they are implementation partitions of a single domain concern. Splitting a single logical operation into multiple subscribers bound by a publish-subscribe channel creates an invisible coupling: the subscribers depend on each other’s execution to complete the operation, but neither the channel nor the subscribers encode this dependency. The domain says “one procedure does X, then Y, then Z” — but Publish-Subscribe scatters X, Y, Z into independent endpoints whose ordering is implicit. A domain expert would say “no, X and Y and Z are the same thing.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you name the event and every subscriber using only domain vocabulary, with no implementation words?

If yes → applicable. Publish-Subscribe is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. You’re broadcasting for technical convenience, not because the domain broadcasts.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Dead Letter Channel Pattern
text:
Case study: Dead Letter Channel Pattern

EIP Intent: “What will the messaging system do with a message it cannot deliver?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that some messages cannot be delivered and that the domain has rules for what happens then is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “an insurance claim missing a policy number is undeliverable and goes to manual triage; a payment with a mismatched currency code goes to the reconciliation desk; and anything else unrouteable gets queued for the operations team,” then Dead Letter Channel is just embodying that knowledge. The dead-letter queue is the domain’s own undeliverable-work queue; the dead-letter consumer is the domain’s own exception-handling actor.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain recognizes that messages can legitimately fail to reach a destination, and the domain itself distinguishes categories of failure with different remediation paths. Dead Letter Channel closes the gap: it prevents each sender from embedding fallback logic for the failure it caused, which would scatter undeliverable-work handling across every component and create accidental coupling — each sender would need to know about manual triage, reconciliation desks, and operations queues. The dead-letter queue consolidates exception routing into one place, reflecting the domain’s own classification of failure modes.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The dead-letter channel is a catch-all for anything the developer didn’t handle — “put failed messages here and we’ll figure it out later.” The domain has no classification of failure modes, no notion of undeliverable work as a distinct domain state, and no remediation process. The dead-letter queue becomes silent data loss: messages accumulate in a queue no one monitors, and the domain event they represented is simply dropped. A domain expert would say “what do you mean the order disappeared — did it ship or not?”








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain have a named process, role, or procedure for handling work that cannot reach its destination?

If yes → applicable. Dead Letter Channel is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a black hole with a tidy name.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#EIP #DeadLetterChannel #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Message Filter Pattern

EIP Intent: “How can a component avoid receiving uninteresting messages?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a component should only receive a subset of the messages flowing through the system is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “the premium-customer system cares only about orders from customers at loyalty tier 3 or above; the standard-order pipeline should never see test-mode orders,” then Message Filter embodies that knowledge. The filter predicate is the domain’s own membership condition.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain assigns different message subsets to different domain actors — and the subset condition is a domain rule, not a performance optimization. Message Filter closes the gap: prevents each receiver from re-implementing the filter in a guard clause at the entry point, which would couple the receiver to message types it should have no knowledge of. A receiver that filters out orders below $1,000 at its own entry point must still know that such orders exist — spreading knowledge of the full message universe into every receiver. The filter externalizes the membership rule so each receiver sees only its domain-relevant messages.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The filter is adopted without a constraint that selects which messages to drop — “drop messages when queue depth exceeds 500” or “route every other message when CPU is > 80%.” Queue depth and CPU load tell you that you need to shed load — not which messages to shed. The filter predicate (drop oldest? drop lowest-priority? drop at random?) is undetermined by the constraint. When selection is arbitrary, the filter couples message survival to infrastructure state without a defensible rule.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you state the filter predicate as a domain rule — a sentence that starts with “The system is only interested in messages where…” and mentions no implementation concepts?

If yes → applicable. Message Filter is the code catching up — a constraint external to the code (membership condition, regulatory boundary, domain scope rule) selects which messages pass.
If no → inapplicable. You’re dropping messages without a constraint that identifies which ones.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#EIP #MessageFilter #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Recipient List Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do we route a message to a list of dynamically specified recipients?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a message has a domain-determined list of recipients — where the list itself is a domain artifact, not a configuration file — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “a customs declaration must go to the importing country’s customs authority, the exporting country’s customs authority, the carrier, and the importer of record; a trade confirmation goes to both counterparties’ settlement desks,” then Recipient List is just embodying that knowledge. The list of recipients is the domain’s own distribution rule.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that a single message be delivered to a specific, domain-determined set of recipients — and those recipients are each domain actors, not technical mirroring targets. Recipient List closes the gap: it isolates the distribution logic so the sender doesn’t embed a hardcoded list of downstream systems, which would couple the sender to the topology of the integration landscape. Without it, adding a new regulatory recipient means modifying the sender’s code — making the sender change with the regulatory environment even though its domain logic (produce the trade confirmation) hasn’t changed.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The recipient list is an availability tactic — send to primary and backup instances, or fan-out to multiple replicas. The domain doesn’t recognize “instance 1” and “instance 2” as distinct recipients; it recognizes one recipient (the order-processing system) — the fact that it runs on two machines is an implementation detail. Recipient List here masks infrastructure redundancy as domain distribution, creating coupling between the sender and deployment topology. A domain expert would say “just send it to order-processing — how many machines that runs on is not my concern.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert, given only knowledge of the business process, produce the same list of recipients without knowing how the system is deployed?

If yes → applicable. Recipient List is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s deployment topology leaking into domain logic.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.
