Every deviation is a place where the real business knowledge escaped the model — often a rule that was never articulated, an exception handled by habit. Mining is the only indicator here that cannot be argued with: it reports what happened, not what was believed.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the log match the model — and if it does not, which one does the business intend to be true?

If they match → the model is knowledge.
If they diverge → the deviation is the gap; resolve it with the experts, in one direction or the other.
If you can’t answer → you have found the gap without even needing a question.




#ProcessMining #ConformanceChecking #BusinessProcess #ProcessModeling #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Choreography vs. Orchestration

Peltz: Orchestration centralizes control in a single coordinator; choreography distributes it across cooperating peers. [23]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Who sees and who coordinates the process is organizational knowledge. Orchestration puts one party in charge of the whole flow; choreography describes each participant’s behaviour and lets no one own the whole. “We drive the process with our suppliers” versus “each party acts on the messages the others send” is a real, and often disputed, business distinction.






ImportantWhen the model is faithful



The domain has a genuine coordinator — a platform, a lead party, a clearing house — and orchestration records that authority accurately. Or the domain is genuinely peer-to-peer, and the choreography correctly denies any one party full visibility. Either way, the model’s visibility boundary is one the business recognises.








WarningWhen the model misrepresents



Orchestration is chosen because the tool makes it easy, and the model asserts a central authority the business never granted — the coordinator now holds knowledge that was never theirs to hold. The reverse is just as common: a choreography is drawn over what is in fact one party driving everything, hiding the dependency and the accountability. The model claims a distribution of control that does not exist.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does one party genuinely have the whole picture and drive the flow, or does each participant know only its own part?

If one driver → orchestration is the domain’s own authority.
If peers → choreography.
If you can’t answer → the gap is ownership of the process, which nobody has assigned.




#Choreography #Orchestration #BusinessProcess #ProcessModeling #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: State Machines for Business Entities
text:
Case study: State Machines for Business Entities

Harel: Statecharts model the permitted states and transitions of a system. [24]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a thing may change only in ways the business allows is domain knowledge. “An order cannot go from shipped back to draft”; “a claim cannot be approved before it is assessed.” A state machine is that fact made executable: named states and permitted transitions, so the entity’s allowed changes are stated once and enforced everywhere.






ImportantWhen the model is faithful



The business names the states and the moves between them, and experts recognise a forbidden transition as a real error (“you can’t un-ship an order”). The state machine is the domain’s own rule about how things may change, and every code path that touches the entity obeys it.








WarningWhen the model misrepresents



A status field is written freely by whichever code path runs, and the “states” are whatever strings appear. Then the model claims transitions the business forbids — a refunded invoice that is later marked paid, an approved claim that was never assessed. The absence of a state machine is not neutral: it asserts that any change is possible, which is a claim the domain denies.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can an expert list the states and say which moves are forbidden — and would a forbidden move be a business error?

If yes → the state machine is the domain’s own transition rule.
If no → free-form status is faithful; a machine would invent states.
If you can’t answer → the gap is the lifecycle: nobody has said what this thing’s allowed changes are.




#StateMachine #BusinessProcess #Lifecycle #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #DomainDrivenDesign #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: EPC — Event/Function Alternation

Scheer: An event-driven process chain alternates events and functions to describe a process. [25]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
EPC’s structural claim is that events and functions alternate: every action is triggered by a state, and produces one. That is a domain distinction — an event is a fact the business observes (“what happened”), a function is an act the business chose (“what we did”). These are different kinds, and EPC forces the difference where BPMN does not.






ImportantWhen the model is faithful



The business genuinely distinguishes the state that licenses an action from the action itself, and the alternating chain captures it: nothing is done without a condition that made it permissible. This is also why an EPC compiles almost as-is to event handlers — events are named states, functions are transitions, and the diagram hands you the transition table, not just a flowchart.








WarningWhen the model misrepresents



A fact is recorded as an act, or an act as a fact: “shipped” modelled as a step, “verify” modelled as an observation. Then the alternating chain collapses and the model no longer says what licensed what. Or the domain never draws the distinction: the business sees one move, not a fact that licenses an act. The alternation then forces an event and a function apart where the domain saw a single step, and the model asserts a difference the business never made.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is this element something we observed or something we did — and does every action have a state that licensed it?

If the distinction holds → EPC’s alternation is the domain’s own grammar.
If not → the chain has lost the knowledge, or the domain never drew the distinction.
If you can’t answer → the gap is the triggering condition, which is where domain knowledge is usually thinnest.




#EPC #EventDrivenProcessChains #BusinessProcess #ProcessModeling #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: SLA / Escalation

Dumas et al.: A process commitment with a time bound and an escalation path taken when it is missed. [26]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the business has promised a time in which something will happen — and a defined response when it does not — is domain knowledge. “Claims are acknowledged within two days”; “if the approval is not given by Friday, it goes to the manager.” Deadlines, escalation, and delegation are that fact made executable: the promise, the clock, and the authority to escalate.






ImportantWhen the model is faithful



The domain states the promise, the clock, and who acts when it lapses. The model records the domain’s own obligation (“we owe this within X”) and its own escalation path (“then this role decides”). The timer looks technical; the bound itself is a domain decision — the promise’s clock.








WarningWhen the model misrepresents



A timeout is added for resilience — “give up after 30 seconds.” Even this is a domain decision: someone chose the bound. If the domain has not named the promise and the response, the timeout asserts a rule nobody decided. Or a real SLA is invisible: the model contains no clock for a promise the business makes to customers, so lateness is discovered by complaint. Both claims are about time: one asserts an unstated bound, the other hides a stated one. The escalations the business actually uses — four-eyes rules, delegation, standing authority — are left out of the model entirely.








TipThe faithfulness test



Has the business promised a time here, and named who acts when it passes?

If yes → the clock and the escalation are the domain’s own promise.
If no → the timeout still encodes a chosen bound; the gap is that the domain has not stated the promise. Calling it an SLA asserts an obligation nobody made.
If you can’t answer → the gap is the promise: nobody has said how long is acceptable or what happens if it lapses.




#SLA #Escalation #BusinessProcess #ProcessModeling #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Encapsulation

Parnas: Modules should hide a design decision behind an interface so that the decision can change without affecting clients. [27]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
An encapsulation boundary splits a type into what callers may depend on and what they never see. The real claim is not “something is hidden here” but “this interface is exactly what callers need.” That claim has content only if the team knows the callers’ needs — which parts the domain assigns to this thing, and which are one way of fulfilling them. The gap shows when the split is drawn by habit: the interface carries choices no caller asked about, or withholds something needed. Where the domain fixes a concrete detail, that detail belongs in the interface; an abstraction above it asserts a concept nobody decided.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The team can point at each exposed operation and name the need it serves: “converting a payment uses the current rate” is a domain-assigned responsibility, and how the rate is stored is one way of fulfilling it. Callers depend on the responsibility, not the fulfillment, so reworking the internals touches no one.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Encapsulation as a default virtue. Private fields with public getters and setters: the representation becomes part of the commitment, so an internal choice and the callers’ needs are fused — reworking the internals means renegotiating with every caller. Interfaces wrapped around things no caller needs: commitments with nobody to commit to. Where the domain mandates the concrete detail, the abstraction asserts a concept nobody decided; the concept is unwritten, and callers couple to the invention. The mirror failure: withholding what callers need produces workarounds — reflection, duplicated internals, paths that bypass the boundary. The mechanism runs without the knowledge.








TipThe faithfulness test



For each thing this type exposes: which need does it serve? For each thing it withholds: why may no caller reach it?

If you can answer both → applicable. The boundary is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If the answer is “private by default” → inapplicable. The mechanism runs without the principle.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You found incomplete domain knowledge, not a wrong pattern.




#Encapsulation #InformationHiding #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Inheritance / Subtyping

Liskov and Wing: A subtype must be usable in place of its supertype without altering the correctness of the program. [28]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Every extends freezes a classification into the code: the child is declared a kind of the parent, for all time. That claim has content only if the domain draws the distinction — if a domain expert would state the classification as a fact of the business, and if substitution holds under every change the domain can force. The gap shows when the hierarchy answers a question nobody asked the business: the taxonomy reflects how the code happens to be organised, not how the domain classifies. The square–rectangle trap is the textbook case; the everyday version is a parent class that exists only because two classes shared three methods.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The classification is a domain fact with a forcing condition. Banking regulation distinguishes account types, and a savings account IS a bank account in the regulator’s own language — substitution is a legal truth, not a programming nicety. When the business itself reasons through the subtype (“any account may be frozen; savings accounts additionally accrue interest”), the hierarchy is the code catching up to the knowledge.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Inheritance used to reuse implementation. Two classes share code, someone extracts a base class, and the child is coupled to every future change of the parent — while the code asserts a classification the domain has not stated; that knowledge is unwritten. The parent’s change reasons and the child’s diverge, but the hierarchy forces them to travel together: a change the domain aims at one concept lands on both. The taxonomy hat hides the actual structure, which was coincidence of code, not identity of concept.








TipThe faithfulness test



For a given extends: would a domain expert state this classification as a fact of the business — and does the subtype remain substitutable under every change the domain can force on the parent?

If yes to both → applicable. The hierarchy is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If the honest answer is “we wanted to share the code” → inapplicable. Reuse wearing a taxonomy hat.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#Inheritance #Subtyping #LSP #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Composition over Inheritance

Gamma et al.: Favour object composition over class inheritance. [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Choosing inheritance freezes a relationship as permanent taxonomy; choosing composition says the relationship is a role — attached, detachable, reassignment-capable. An employee is a person who plays the employee role; a discount policy is attached to an order, not what an order is. The gap shows when the structural choice was made for reuse or convenience without asking which reading the domain supports — the choice still encodes a claim about the business, and that claim is unwritten until the domain states it. Only one reading is true.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



Composition wins when the domain itself reassigns roles: a contractor becomes an employee; a customer is also a supplier; a policy attaches to this order today and that one tomorrow. Roles vary independently of the carrier’s identity, and composition encodes exactly that independence — a change in the role’s rules arrives without touching the thing that plays it. Inheritance stays honest in the opposite case (#136): the domain holds the classification fixed, and a changed relationship would mean a different thing entirely.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Composition adopted as a blanket slogan. The relationship is a stable domain classification, but the code models it as an attachable role “for flexibility” — flexibility against a change no domain mechanism can force. The price is real: indirection, identity workarounds (the composed parts re-deriving what “the same thing” means), and a structure that invites the domain-illegal move — swapping a component the business considers constitutive.








TipThe faithfulness test



For a given relationship: can the domain change it without changing the thing’s identity?

If yes — the business reassigns, swaps, stacks roles → composition. The domain treats it as played, not inherited.
If the domain would say “it would then be a different thing” → the classification is stable; inheritance may be the honest encoding.
If you can’t answer → unclear. The structure is a guess about permanence the business never confirmed.




#CompositionOverInheritance #Inheritance #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself)

Hunt and Thomas: Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous representation within a system. [29]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
DRY is about knowledge, not text — but the only instrument the programmer has operates on text. Two fragments look alike, someone extracts the common code, and the extraction itself is a claim: “these are one rule, and a change to it must reach both.” That claim has content only if the domain agrees. The gap shows when the team merged by similarity without asking whether one domain decision stands behind both fragments — the merge couples two change drivers, and when one rule moves and the other must not, the shared abstraction breaks in production.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



Both fragments encode the same domain decision: the same VAT rule, the same rounding policy, the same eligibility criterion. The domain itself guarantees they change together — when the rule is revised, every place that applies it must move in lockstep, and a single representation is what makes that guarantee structural rather than hopeful. The deduplication is the code catching up to the knowledge.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Merging by text similarity. Two price calculations that coincide today because the numbers happen to align; two validation blocks that share a shape but answer to different authorities. The duplication was the faithful structure — two rules, two drivers, two futures — and the merge planted a coupling no rule behind the fragments mandates; if each fragment answers to a different authority, each rule is unwritten and the merge hides both. Every later change now starts with an archaeology dig: which of the callers may follow this edit, and which must be peeled off first?








TipThe faithfulness test



For a candidate merge: if the domain rule behind fragment A changes, must fragment B change with it — always, by the domain’s own logic?

If yes → one knowledge, one representation. Merge.
If no → the duplication is faithful. Extracting couples two drivers.
If you can’t answer → unclear. The similarity is visible; whether it is one rule is exactly the knowledge you’re missing.




#DRY #DontRepeatYourself #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Law of Demeter

Lieberherr and Holland: A method should talk only to its immediate collaborators, not to their collaborators. [30]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Every reach-through chain asserts that the caller’s business genuinely depends on the far object along this route — that the path is a stable domain relationship, not an accident of object layout. Sometimes it is: an order’s customer’s billing address is a path the business itself reasons about. Sometimes it is digging: the caller exploits an implementation trail, following a route that exists only in the object graph. The gap shows when nobody can say which of the two a given chain is — the coupling exists, its legitimacy unexamined.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The law earns its keep where the chain is NOT a domain path. Rewriting a.b().c() into a direct ask keeps the caller coupled only to the object whose job the operation is — so when the intermediate structure changes for its own reasons, the caller doesn’t move. The caller now depends on what the domain mandates (the outcome) and not on what it doesn’t (the route). Note the asymmetry: the law is a heuristic about structure; its violations are the signal worth auditing, one chain at a time.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Mechanically eliminating every chain. Where the chain is a domain relationship the business itself reasons about, the rewrite replaces a recognised route with a direct ask nobody decided; where it was an implementation route, wrapper methods tunnel the same dependency and only move the coupling out of sight. The caller’s real dependence on the far object is hidden, not removed.








TipThe faithfulness test



For a given chain: is this path a relationship the domain itself recognises, or a traversal of an object graph that exists only as implementation?

If the domain recognises it → the coupling is mandated; keep it visible and direct.
If not → the path exists only as an implementation route; the chain couples the caller to structure the domain never mandated.
If you can’t answer → unclear. The navigation compiled, but nobody checked it against the map.




#LawOfDemeter #TellDontAsk #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: YAGNI

Fowler: Build only what the requirements demand now; do not add speculative generality. [31]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Every “we’ll need this to be flexible” asserts that the domain can force a variation here — a forcing condition exists, and the structure stands ready for it. The gap is anticipating variation no domain mechanism can force: a plugin point for providers the market does not contain, a config switch for a rule the business holds fixed, an abstraction layer against a change nobody can cause. The reverse gap is costlier: “you aren’t gonna need it” said about a variation the business has already announced — the seam was domain knowledge, and YAGNI was invoked to unsee it.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



No forcing condition exists for the anticipated change, and the team can say so honestly — not “we didn’t ask,” but “we asked, and the domain holds this fixed.” Deleting the speculative structure removes a coupling to a phantom driver: the code now covers exactly the variations the domain can produce, and nothing pays rent for the rest. YAGNI here is knowledge applied, not effort avoided.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Two failure modes, same root. YAGNI invoked against a variation the domain demonstrably forces — a regulator who can change the rule, a market that adds channels, a pricing policy with a history of revision — because “we’ll add it when we need it,” as if adding structure under deadline pressure were free. The refusal asserts that no forcing condition exists; the domain has one, so the seam’s absence is a structure nobody decided. And the mirror: building for a forcing condition nobody can name. Both share one gap: the future change was decided without consulting the domain that owns it.








TipThe faithfulness test



For a given piece of flexibility (or a refused one): name the forcing condition that would make you use it.

If you can name the domain mechanism → the structure is knowledge, whether you build it now or deliberately defer it.
If the answer is “someday, maybe” → the structure is a guess; YAGNI applies.
If you can’t answer either way → unclear. The decision to build or not build is currently a coin flip dressed as engineering judgment.




#YAGNI #DesignPrinciples #ExtremeProgramming #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Information Hiding (Parnas)

Parnas: Decompose a system by hiding the design decisions most likely to change behind stable interfaces. [27]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Parnas’s rule works at the system level: derive module structure from the inventory of decisions, grouped by what could force them to change. One module may hide several decisions — when the same conditions force them to change together — and one decision may not be split. The likelihood reading asks for a forecast that can never be checked when it is made. The recoverable reading lists decisions whose forcing conditions are demonstrable today — a regulator who has revised the rule. The gap shows as a break in the correspondence: co-changing decisions split across modules, or change-apart decisions hidden behind one wall.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The correspondence holds both ways. Every module hides a cluster of decisions that share their forcing conditions, so one change event has one address; every decision with a demonstrable forcing condition lives in one such module. The structure is a complete map of the domain’s known forcing conditions.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Two failures, same root. Decomposition by likelihood guess: boundaries drawn around decisions someone felt were change-prone, with no forcing condition anyone can name — speculation wearing Parnas’s hat. And decomposition by data shape or technical layer: all DTOs here, all controllers there, all “utilities” in a third drawer. Such a module hides no domain decision; its secret is a formatting convention. Meanwhile the genuinely volatile decisions — pricing policy, eligibility rules, regulatory thresholds — leak across five modules each, and the inventory of real forcing conditions is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Compare the modules with the decisions whose forcing conditions are demonstrable today. Are decisions grouped by shared forcing conditions?

If the correspondence holds both ways → applicable. The decomposition is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If co-changing decisions are split, or change-apart decisions share a wall → the correspondence breaks; that break is the gap.
If a module hides no decision → it is a drawer, not a module.




#InformationHiding #Parnas #Encapsulation #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Tell, Don’t Ask

Hunt and Thomas: Tell an object what to do rather than asking it for its state and acting on it yourself. [29]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
if (account.balance > amount) account.withdraw(...) looks harmless — but the overdraft rule just lived in the caller. Every “ask then decide” asserts that the decision belongs outside the object whose state feeds it; every “tell” asserts it belongs inside. Both are placement claims about domain knowledge, and both can be wrong. The gap shows when the placement was never reasoned about: rules drift into whichever file was open, and the object that owns the state no longer owns the rule that governs it — so a change to the rule hunts through every caller.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The decision is a function of one object’s own state and constitutes one domain rule: overdraft policy on the account, eligibility on the application, validity on the certificate. Telling places the behavior where its change driver points — when the policy is revised, exactly one module moves, and no caller needs to know that anything changed. The placement is the code catching up to where the knowledge already lives in the business.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Dogmatic “never return data.” Objects swallow decisions that belong to collaborators, growing into gods of their own state; or tell-methods sprout callback and lambda parameters so the caller can smuggle its decision back in through the tell — the knowledge moved syntactically while the dependency stayed exactly where it was. The deeper miss: a decision that consults several objects’ state is a collaboration, and no amount of telling removes that coupling — it only hides which object is actually deciding.








TipThe faithfulness test



For a given decision: which object’s state does the domain rule consult?

If one object’s → tell it. The rule lives where its data lives.
If several objects’ → the decision is a collaboration; place it explicitly (a policy, a service) instead of tunnelling it through a tell.
If you can’t say whose state the rule reads → unclear. The behavior is placed, but nobody knows by what knowledge.




#TellDontAsk #LawOfDemeter #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Extension Points

The domain knowledge gap it signals
Every extension point — a plugin interface, a strategy slot, a template method — claims “the domain varies here, and not there.” No slogan tells you which point to build or when; a module can be extensible somewhere, never everywhere, so every seam is a bet about the location of change. The gap is the bet placed without the knowledge that settles it. Two failure signatures follow: seams on axes the domain holds fixed, and hardcoding on the axis it varies — the pricing formula’s shape changes while the seam sat at the rates.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



Current domain knowledge selects the seam — not clairvoyance, but a forcing condition the business can point to now: tax rules the jurisdiction already revises on a schedule, payment methods the market keeps adding, report formats a regulator has already changed twice. Build the seam where change has already shown itself. The next variation arrives as a new implementation plugged into the same seam, and the code already written stays untouched.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Speculative extension points: abstractions for a second backend never funded, hooks for customizations never requested, strategies for jurisdictions never entered. Each wrong seam is worse than dead code — it looks deliberate and nothing flags it for removal, so the coupling accumulates as the codebase ages. And the inverse failure: the axis of demonstrated volatility was hardcoded, so every real change edits the code that was supposed to stay fixed.








TipThe faithfulness test



For a given extension point: which change has the domain already shown it can force along this axis — and is everything outside the seam safe from the changes shown elsewhere?

If you can point to demonstrated volatility → applicable. The knowledge selected the seam.
If the justification is “we might need it” → inapplicable. Speculation wearing a principle’s hat (#140 applies).
If you can’t answer → unclear. The structure bets on a change map nobody has drawn — that map is the missing knowledge.




#ExtensionPoints #YAGNI #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Immutable Value Objects

Evans: Value objects should be immutable: rather than modifying one, you create a new one in its place. [15]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Post #85 covered the identity question: a value object claims that identity doesn’t matter, that equality by content is the domain’s own notion of sameness. What remains for this folder is the mutation question. Making a class immutable asserts: “when this fact changes, the domain replaces it — the old one stops being true.” An address correction is a new address, not a mutated one; a price revision supersedes the old price. Where it goes wrong: immutability chosen for technical convenience — thread safety, cacheability — applied to facts the domain revises. Thread safety is a real requirement, but it does not decide whether a fact is replaced or mutated; the domain does. If the domain revises the fact, immutability asserts a replacement nobody decided — the rule is unwritten — and builders and copy-methods must emulate updates the business performs. And the inverse gap: mutable value-shaped objects whose shared aliasing silently couples changes that should be independent.






TipThe faithfulness test



For a value-shaped class: when this fact “changes” in the business language, does the old one stop being true — or does the same thing acquire a new state?

If the old one stops being true → replace, and immutability is the code catching up.
If the same thing acquires new state → this was never a value question; the identity question from #85 (and #86) decides the structure.
If the domain language has no answer yet → unclear. The keyword is written; the knowledge it encodes is not.




#ValueObjects #Immutability #DDD #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Static Fields and Methods
text:
Case study: Static Fields and Methods

The domain knowledge gap it signals
Every static is a placement claim: this fact or behavior exists independent of any particular thing — it holds for the type itself. That claim has content only if the domain speaks that way: a conversion constant the physics fixes, a rule that governs the concept rather than its instances, construction logic that is merely named creation (#91). The gap shows when static was chosen so the code could reach something without knowing which thing owns it — the knowledge lives nowhere, so it lives everywhere.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The fact is genuinely instance-independent in the domain: a mathematical constant, a classification rule that holds for the type as such, a factory method that names a construction the business names (“Money.euros(amount)”). No instance could carry the knowledge, because no instance is what the knowledge is about.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Two classic traps, same root. Static mutable state — the cache, the counter, the registry — asserts “the whole universe of discourse shares one of these.” Sharing scope is a domain decision. If the domain has not named it, the assertion is a claim nobody decided — the mandate is unwritten, not absent — and the result is a hidden global that couples every caller to one change driver. And the static utility class: behavior that acts on instances, parked at the type level — the class asserts a type-level fact the domain never stated. Even static final deserves suspicion: TAX_RATE = 0.21 hardcodes a domain decision with a forcing condition — the value is fixed so far, the speculative seam’s mirror image (#140, #143).








TipThe faithfulness test



For a given static member: does the domain state this fact without referring to any particular instance — or did the code lose track of which thing owns it?

If the domain speaks instance-free → applicable. The keyword encodes the knowledge’s true level.
If the knowledge consults one thing’s state → inapplicable. Place the behavior with the thing.
If it’s shared mutable state nobody justified → unclear at best. The coupling is real; the mandate for it was never checked.




#Static #GlobalState #DesignPrinciples #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Command Pattern

GoF: Encapsulate a request as an object, thereby letting you parameterize clients with different requests, queue or log requests, and support undoable operations. [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that an action is a first-class thing — not just a method call — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “an operation must be recorded, queued, undone, or scheduled — the action itself is a domain entity with identity and lifecycle,” then Command is just embodying that knowledge.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain treats actions as entities: they can be stored, replayed, reversed, and audited. An order-fulfillment system where “ShipOrder,” “CancelOrder,” and “RefundOrder” are domain commands — with undo semantics, execution timestamps, and audit trails — is the domain speaking. Command closes the gap: it prevents the action logic from being a method buried on some service class, which would make the action invisible to the domain model. Instead, each command is a domain object with its own data, validation, and undo path.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “commands” are not domain commands — they’re method-call wrappers. Wrapping every service-method invocation in a Command object because the framework expects it doesn’t reify a domain concept; it wraps function calls in infrastructure ceremony. Command here adds object-allocation and indirection costs to what should be a direct call, signaling entity-richness where the domain has none. Event-sourcing architectures are a valid exception — commands as persisted entities with identity serve a persistence/routing infrastructure that IS the architecture.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain expert talk about this operation as a thing that exists — “the shipment,” “the refund,” “the approval request”?

If yes → applicable: Command is the code catching up to the knowledge. If no → inapplicable: it’s function-call packaging. If you can’t answer → unclear: you haven’t found the pattern wrong, you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#GoF #CommandPattern #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #FP #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Dependency Injection

Fowler: A form of Inversion of Control in which a component is given its dependencies rather than creating them itself. [32]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
With dependency injection, a service declares: I need these dependencies — but I do not need to know where to get them, or how to build them; give them to me. A faithful declaration carries domain knowledge: an order service needs persistence and messaging. Even which database, which queue, and how they are built is a domain decision: someone chose them. The interface states the need; the composition root supplies the answer. The gap it signals is whether the need is real and whether the supply can vary.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The need is real and the supply can vary. The order service always needs persistence; which database serves it can change. The interface declares the need once; the composition root supplies the answer.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The need is invented, or the need is real but the supply cannot vary. Either way the injection point asserts a boundary the domain never decided: the external seam is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the need real, and can the supply vary?

If the need is real and the supply can vary → applicable. Dependency injection is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If the need is invented → inapplicable; nothing to abstract. If the supply cannot vary → inapplicable; no variation justifies it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: DI is not the composition root
text:
DI is not the composition root
DI is a technique: how a service declares its dependencies and receives them from outside.
The composition root is a place: where the application assembles its object graph, at the entry point. Only applications should have one — composition belongs to the application. A DI container belongs only there.
DI does not specify where the object graph is assembled; the composition root answers that.
Two failures hide when the names are conflated: - Scattered wiring: composition at each use site, with no root. A deployment change touches many files. - A frozen choice: a root that bakes a per-operation choice in at startup.

#DependencyInjection #CompositionRoot #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Composition Root

Seemann: A single, logical location in an application where modules are composed together. [33]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The assembly looks purely technical, but it is still a domain decision: the same modularization rule decides where the composition root goes, what each service receives, what belongs inside each service, and whether each dependency is fixed for the object’s lifetime. The root decides those choices once, for the whole graph. The rule is derived from domain knowledge: it follows from which choices the domain owns and which it leaves open. The service’s content is fixed by the rule, not by the wiring that supplies it. The gap is the rule: if you cannot say which choices the domain owns, you cannot say where the composition root goes or what the services contain.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The modularization rule is clear, so the composition root sits where it belongs, and each service receives what the rule assigns. A change to one choice touches one place.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The rule is unstated. A choice the domain owns is supplied at the composition root, so the domain can no longer vary it — every such change now edits the composition root. Or the composition root sits in a library or framework, so it carries choices that belong to its caller.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you state the rule that places the composition root and assigns what each service receives?

If yes → applicable. Composition Root is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The composition root is placed by guesswork.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#CompositionRoot #DependencyInjection #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Modularization #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Installing Archlinux with software raid1, encrypted filesystem and LVM2
text:
I wrote that article for my personal blog 2010-08-01, so it may be a bit outdated, yet the info might still be useful, so here it is.
I have not tested this setup with a recently, so please be aware that the described steps may not work with an up-to-date ArchLinux version.
On the web, you’ll find how to setup ArchLinux with LVM, or with RAID, or with encryption, but not with the combination of these three technologies. This article explains the different steps I took to setup these three technologies with ArchLinux.

title: Installing Archlinux with software raid1, encrypted filesystem and LVM2
text:
1 Required skills
Sound understanding of Linux (ArchLinux specifics may be useful…) and RAID, LVM2, partitioning, encryption.

title: Installing Archlinux with software raid1, encrypted filesystem and LVM2
text:
2 The story
During the last days I reinstalled my server (AMD x86_64), which runs several VirtualBox VMs, with ArchLinux.
It’s a simple PC with 3 hard drives: one for the OS and two 500GB drives which hold my data and VMs.
Here’s the detail of my hard disk setup:

The OS hard drive: This one is encrypted using LUKS and then runs LVM for the partitioning. There are 2 primary partitions: one for /boot, not encrypted, and one which contains the encrypted LVM partitions. Thus, the root partition is encrypted and on LVM, which needs specific setup in Grub.
The 2 data hard drives: These are raid-1 (simple duplication), the raid array is encrypted, and the partitioning is done using LVM. The array only contains 1 single primary partition, spanning the whole space and containing the LVM partitions.

I never dared install ArchLinux on top of this setup before (so I ran my server using openSUSE, and recently Fedora 13), because of the not so user friendly ArchLinux install software. I added encryption to my setup when I installed Fedora 13, using the Fedora installer Anaconda. But some days ago, as I encountered several issues using Fedora 13, I decided to give ArchLinux a try. Please note that I was really surprised by the Fedora 13 release (it’s quite slick and very stable), but ArchLinux (the control I have over it and the gargantuous software collection it provides) is better suited to my advanced needs. More precisely, in Fedora 13, I’ve found nothing as easy as netcfg to setup my network interfaces like I wanted (quite complicated, not explained here). So here are the steps:

title: Installing Archlinux with software raid1, encrypted filesystem and LVM2
text:
3 Hard drive setup
Setup the hard drives (partitioning, RAID-1 and LVM2) with the Fedora 13 installer Anaconda. Simply put in the Fedora 13 install disk and make a simple install with the correct disk setup you need. The installed OS will be of no use, the purpose here is to setup the disks, not the OS. The Fedora 13 install software is very easy to use, as the hard drive setup is visual. openSUSE may be OK as well, as Yast is visual and easy to use as well.

title: Installing Archlinux with software raid1, encrypted filesystem and LVM2
text:
4 ArchLinux installation
Boot using the ArchLinux Install CD. Choose the correct keymap for your PC:
km
Load the encryption, raid1 and LVM modules:
modprobe dm-crypt
modprobe dm-mod
modprobe raid1
Assemble the raid (as it was created with the Fedora 13 installer, there is no need to create it):
mdadm -A /dev/md0 /dev/sdc1 /dev/sdb1
Setup encryption on the OS hard drive and the data array (again, as the encrypted drives already exist, there is no need to create them, simply open them with your passphrases):
cryptsetup luksOpen /dev/sda2 system
cryptsetup luksOpen /dev/md0 data
Scan for LVM volume groups and keep them in memory:
vgscan
vgchange -ay
Then run the ArchLinux install software:
/arch/setup
Configure your installation (use the existing partitions!) until when packages were installed. Immediately after package installation, change to another terminal with the key combination CTRL-ALT-F2, and login as root. Now, replace the mdadm.conf file by the one corresponding to your setup (this step is needed, as this file is used to generate the initrd image with mkinitcpio):
rm /mnt/etc/mdadm.conf
mdadm --examine --scan >> /mnt/etc/mdadm.conf
Come back to the install software with the key combination CTRL-ALT-F1. Now, in the install software, edit your configuration files:

4.1 rc.conf
USELVM=yes
KEYMAP=be-latin1
You may replace be-latin1 with your keymap.


4.2 mkinitcpio.conf
MODULES=(... dm-mod dm-crypt aes_x86_64 raid1 ...)
HOOKS=(... mdadm keymap encrypt lvm2 filesystems...)
The order in the HOOKS array is very important:

keymap permits to set the keymap before the encryption password for the drives is required.
encrypt is necessary to decrypt the drives, which allows content access to lvm2
lvm2 provides partitions, which are needed to mount the filesystems

I think the mdadm hook is not needed, as the root partition is not on top of a raid. But if it was, it would be required! Based on your setup (lvm2 over encryption over raid, encryption of single lvm2 drives,…), the order may change, so your understanding of how these technologies are set up on your drives really is relevant.


4.3 locale.gen
Remove the leading dashes (#) in front of your locale.


4.4 pacman.conf
Strictly speaking, this is not needed at all for this setup, but I can’t imagine using ArchLinux without this repository, so I always enable it:
[archlinuxfr]
Server = http://repo.archlinux.fr/x86_64
Now validate your config files. The system launches mkinitcpio, which generates initrd images. Now edit your menu.lst file. Add cryptdevice=/dev/sda2:vg_system to the kernel line (adapt it to your config, replace sda2 by your encrypted partition and vg_system by your LVM2 volume group’s name). Following are my configurations:
# (0) Arch Linux
title  Arch Linux
root   (hd0,0)
kernel /vmlinuz26 root=/dev/mapper/vg_system-root cryptdevice=/dev/sda2:vg_system ro
initrd /kernel26.img

# (1) Arch Linux
title  Arch Linux Fallback
root   (hd0,0)
kernel /vmlinuz26 root=/dev/mapper/vg_system-root cryptdevice=/dev/sda2:vg_system ro
initrd /kernel26-fallback.img
Save the file, install grub to your MBR. Now, to automatically mount the encrypted data partitions (those on the raid1), the system must know your passphrase. That’s the purpose of the /etc/crypttab file.
nano /mnt/etc/crypttab
Add the line:
data /dev/md0 PASSPHRASE
The device `/dev/md0` should be the same as the one in `/etc/mdadm.conf`.
Replace `PASSPHRASE` with the one you chose for your system.
Make sure `/etc/crypttab` is only readable by root, or maybe someone else may read your passphrase!
The use of /etc/crypttab conveniently avoids asking the user for two passphrases, one for the OS encrypted drive and one for the data encrypted drive. At boot, you enter your OS-encrypted-partition passphrase, and then the system reads /etc/crypttab to decrypt the data-encrypted-partition.

title: Installing Archlinux with software raid1, encrypted filesystem and LVM2
text:
5 Enjoy!
Now, if everything went fine, you may reboot and enjoy using your fresh ArchLinux system.
Should there be some steps you don’t understand or with errors, feel free to leave a comment, I’ll do the corrections.

title: Understanding Certificates in the Digital World
text:
0.1 TL;DR
Digital certificates are the digital counterpart to physical ID cards or passports.
Their trustworthiness and validity stems from the reliability and credibility of the issuing entity (the CA, respectively the government).


0.2 Intro
In our increasingly digital world, ensuring security and authenticity online is more crucial than ever. Whether you’re shopping online, accessing your bank account, or simply browsing the web, the need for secure communication and trust in the entities you interact with cannot be overstated. This is where digital certificates come into play. Much like an ID card verifies your identity in the physical world, a digital certificate verifies identities and secures communications in the digital realm.
Let’s dive into what digital certificates are and how they function similarly to ID cards.


0.3 What is a Digital Certificate?
A digital certificate is a digital document used to authenticate the identity of an entity and establish secure communications. Entities can include websites, individuals, devices, or software. Think of it as a virtual passport that confirms the legitimacy of the entity and contributes to ensure that any data transmitted between you and the entity is secure (the certificate alone is not enough, the communication protocol is important as well).


0.4 Contents of a Digital Certificate

Entity Information:

Subject: The entity the certificate is issued to. For example, in an SSL/TLS certificate for a website, the subject is typically the domain name of the website.
Issuer: The entity that issued the certificate. This is usually a Certificate Authority (CA).
Serial Number: A unique identifier assigned by the issuer to the certificate.
Validity Period: The period during which the certificate is considered valid, including a start date and an expiration date.

Public Key:

The public key of the entity, used for encryption, digital signatures, or both. This key is mathematically linked to a private key held by the entity.

Digital Signature:

A digital signature created by the issuer using its private key. It ensures the integrity and authenticity of the certificate. If the signature can be verified using the issuer’s public key, the certificate is considered valid.

Certificate Extensions:

Key Usage: Specifies the cryptographic operations that the public key can be used for, such as encryption, digital signatures, or both.
Subject Alternative Name (SAN): Additional identities for which the certificate is valid, such as alternative domain names for a website.
Basic Constraints: Specifies whether the certificate can be used as a Certificate Authority to issue other certificates.
Extended Key Usage: Further specifies the purposes for which the public key can be used, such as client authentication, server authentication, or code signing.



Notes 1. A certificate is meant to be shared with other entities, which is why… 2. The private key is not part of the certificate. 3. The CA itself may be authenticated by another CA, which might as well be authenticated by another one and so on, until the root CA is attained: this is the CA trust chain.



0.5 How Does an ID Card Work?

Issuance of ID Card:

An individual provides personal information and undergoes identity verification by a relevant authority, such as a government agency or employer, to obtain an ID card.
The authority verifies the identity of the requester and issues the ID card containing their personal details and photograph.

Authentication and Identity Verification:

When presenting the ID card, the information on the card is compared with the individual presenting it to verify their identity.
This authentication process ensures that the person holding the ID card is indeed the legitimate cardholder and is authorised to access the services or privileges associated with the card.

Access to Privileges and Services:

ID cards grant access to various privileges and services based on the authority associated with the card. For example, a driver’s license grants the holder the privilege to operate a motor vehicle.
By presenting the ID card, individuals can access these privileges and services, ensuring that only authorised individuals benefit from them.




0.6 How Does a Digital Certificate Work?

Certificate Issuance: An entity generates a public-private key pair and submits a certificate signing request (CSR) to a Certificate Authority (CA). The CA verifies the identity of the requester and issues a digital certificate containing the public key.
Authentication and Secure Communication:

Websites: Your browser requests the site’s digital certificate and verifies it, ensuring you are communicating with the legitimate site.
Emails: Email clients can use certificates to encrypt and sign emails, ensuring confidentiality and authenticity.
Software: Developers sign their software with certificates to prove that it has not been tampered with.
Individuals: Digital certificates can authenticate individuals for access to secure systems or documents.




0.7 Types of Digital Certificates
There are different times of digital certificates which serve different purposes:

SSL/TLS Certificates: Secure communications between browsers and websites.
Client Certificates: Authenticate users or devices to a server.
Code Signing Certificates: Verify the identity of the software publisher and ensure the integrity of the software.
Email Certificates (S/MIME Certificates): Secure email communications by encrypting and signing emails.
Document Signing Certificates: Digitally sign documents to ensure their authenticity and integrity.
Root and Intermediate Certificates: Form the foundation of trust in the PKI hierarchy, used by Certificate Authorities to issue end-entity certificates.


Types of government-issued IDs Governments typically issue various types of identification documents to their citizens, residents, and other individuals. These IDs serve different purposes and may vary depending on the country and its regulations. Here are some common types of IDs issued by governments: 1. National Identity Cards (NIC): - National identity cards are government-issued documents that serve as official proof of identity for citizens or residents. They typically include the individual’s name, photograph, date of birth, and sometimes other identifying information such as address or identification number. 2. Passports: - Passports are travel documents issued by governments to their citizens for international travel. They contain personal information about the passport holder, including their photograph, nationality, date of birth, and passport number. 3. Driver’s Licenses: - Driver’s licenses are issued by government agencies to individuals who have passed the required tests to operate motor vehicles legally. In addition to serving as proof of identity, driver’s licenses also indicate the holder’s authorisation to drive specific types of vehicles. 4. Social Security Cards: - Social Security cards are issued in some countries to individuals who have registered for government social security programs. They typically contain a unique identification number assigned to the individual for tracking purposes. 5. Residence Permits: - Residence permits are issued to non-citizen residents by governments to legally reside in a country for a specified period. These documents typically include the individual’s name, photograph, and information about their immigration status. 6. Voter ID Cards: - Voter ID cards are issued to eligible voters by election authorities to facilitate voting in elections. They serve as proof of identity and eligibility to vote. 7. Military IDs: - Military identification cards are issued to members of the armed forces and their dependent. They serve as proof of military affiliation and may grant access to military facilities and services. 8. Government Employee IDs: - Government employee IDs are issued to individuals employed by government agencies. They serve as proof of employment and may grant access to government facilities and services.
These are just a few examples of the types of IDs that governments commonly issue. The > specific types and requirements for obtaining them vary by country and jurisdiction.



0.8 Digital Certificates vs. ID Cards: The Similarities
Usually, the government trusts local authorities (municipality) to authenticate a person and to make the ID request. The government then creates the ID, which is then handed to the person by the requesting local authority. The role of the government is similar to the role of a CA.
People and organisations usually trust the government-delivered ID: sometimes, this is even mandated by law. This trust in the government is what makes this system robust - whether one likes the government or not.

Identity Verification:

ID Card: Confirms your identity with personal details and a photograph, typically issued by a government or other trusted entity.
Digital Certificate: Confirms the identity of an entity, typically issued by a trusted CA after verifying the entity’s credentials.

Trust:

ID Card: We trust ID cards because they are issued by recognised authorities like governments.
Digital Certificate: We trust digital certificates because they are issued by recognised CAs, which follow rigorous verification processes.

Authentication:

ID Card: Used to prove your identity when accessing restricted areas, conducting transactions, or during identification checks.
Digital Certificate: Used to prove the identity of an entity, ensuring secure and authenticated communications.

Security Features:

ID Card: Contains physical security features like holograms, watermarks, and micro-printing to prevent forgery.
Digital Certificate: Contains cryptographic elements like public keys and digital signatures to prevent tampering and ensure authenticity.

Validity period:

ID Card: Has an expiration date.
Digital Certificate: Has a limited validity period which specifies the time frame during which it is considered valid and trustworthy. After the expiration date, the certificate is no longer considered valid, and relying parties should not trust it for secure communications.

Renewal Process:

ID Card: Must be renewed before it expires. Renewal typically involves obtaining a new ID from the issuing government and only using the new one (in some countries, authorities may even require that old IDs are given back to the government).
Digital Certificate: Must be renew by their holders before they expire to ensure uninterrupted secure communication. Renewal typically involves obtaining a new certificate from the issuing Certificate Authority (CA) and replacing the old certificate with the new one.

Types:

ID Card: Various types of IDs are issued by governments and are used for different purposes.
Digital Certificate: Various types of digital certificates are used for different purposes.




0.9 Practical Examples of Digital Certificates in Use

Secure Web Browsing: When you visit a website starting with https://, the communication protocol and the site’s digital certificate ensure that your communication with the site is encrypted and secure, protecting sensitive information like passwords and credit card numbers.
Email Security: Digital certificates can secure email communications by encrypting emails and enabling digital signatures, ensuring that your emails are confidential and authenticated.
Software Integrity: Developers use digital certificates to sign software, ensuring users that the software has not been tampered with and is from a legitimate source.
Individual Authentication: Organisations issue digital certificates to employees, enabling secure access to corporate systems and data. These certificates ensure that only authorised individuals can access sensitive information.
Document Signing: Digital certificates are used to sign electronic documents, providing a digital equivalent of a handwritten signature and ensuring the document’s integrity and authenticity.



0.10 Conclusion
Digital certificates play a vital role in maintaining trust and security in the digital world, much like ID cards do in the physical world. They verify the identities of entities, establish secure communications, and ensure data integrity. By understanding how digital certificates function and their similarities to ID cards, we can better appreciate the underlying mechanisms that keep our online interactions safe and trustworthy. So next time you encounter a digital certificate, you’ll know that it is hard at work, verifying identities and securing your digital environment.

title: An exercise in semantics - Method vs Function
text:
In the programming terminology, we often encounter the terms method and function. Let’s engage in an exercise in semantics, broadening our understanding to consider the contextual nuances that shape both terms.
In many programming languages, such as JavaScript or Python, modules or namespaces provide a structural framework for organising code and enforcing encapsulation. Within these constructs, functions can be grouped together, forming cohesive units of functionality within a specific context. It is within this context that we propose a reevaluation of terminology. ## TL;DR In OOP, a method is a function that is associated with an object.
In a more general form: In programming, a method is a function that is related to a context and whose visibility/accessibility is restricted by that context, where context, relation to the context and visibility/accessibility restriction all depend on the specific programming language considered.

title: An exercise in semantics - Method vs Function
text:
1 Introduction
The terms method and function are often used interchangeably, but there are key differences between them, especially in object-oriented programming (OOP). The following sections provide a detailed comparison.

title: An exercise in semantics - Method vs Function
text:
2 Function

Definition: A function is a block of code designed to perform a specific task. It is defined independently and can be called with parameters to execute its task.
Context: Functions are not inherently associated with any object. They can be standalone or part of a module.
Usage: Functions are used to encapsulate reusable code and can be called from anywhere in the program if they are in scope.
Syntax Example (in Python):
def add(param1, param2):
    # function body
    return param1 + param2

title: An exercise in semantics - Method vs Function
text:
3 Method

Definition: A method is a function that is associated with an object. In OOP, methods define the behaviours of an object and can operate on data contained within the object (its attributes).
Context: Methods are defined within a class and must be called on an instance of that class (or the class itself for class methods).
Usage: Methods are used to manipulate the data of an object and to perform operations related to that object. They can access and modify the object’s state.
Syntax Example (in Python):
class MyClass:
    def add(self, param1, param2):
        # method body
        return param1 + param2

# Creating an instance of MyClass
obj = MyClass()
# Calling the add method on the object
result = obj.add(1, 2)

title: An exercise in semantics - Method vs Function
text:
4 Key Differences

Association:

Function: Independent, not tied to any object.
Method: Bound to an object (instance method) or a class (class method/static method).

Self Parameter (Python Specific):

Function: No implicit parameter.
Method: The first parameter is typically self for instance methods, which refers to the instance of the class.

Calling:

Function: Called directly by its name (if in scope) or via module reference.
Method: Called on an instance or class.

Scope:

Function: Can be globally scoped or limited to a specific module.
Method: Scoped within the class definition and often interacts with the instance’s attributes and other methods. ## The case of static methods in Java


Given the definition of a method provided supra, one may wonder why static methods in Java should be called method instead of function: static methods are indeed not linked to an object.
In Java, static methods are linked to a class rather than an instance of the class, but they are still considered methods for several reasons rooted in object-oriented programming principles and terminology:

4.1 1. Context and Namespace

Class Context: Static methods belong to the class’s namespace and are defined within the class body. Even though they do not operate on an instance of the class, their definition within the class ties them to the class’s scope.
Encapsulation: By being part of the class, static methods help encapsulate functionality that is logically related to the class but does not require access to instance-specific data.



4.2 2. Access and Usage

Access: Static methods are called using the class name, reflecting their association with the class. This usage pattern reinforces their identity as methods within the class. Private static methods may be called from non-static methods of the same class, reinforcing the conceptual link between a static method and instances of its containing class.
Functionality: Static methods can access other static methods and static variables of the class. This capability aligns with the class-level context and differentiates them from standalone functions.



4.3 3. Terminological Consistency

Method: In OOP, the term method is used to describe functions that are defined within a class, regardless of whether they operate on instances or not. This convention maintains consistency in terminology.
Class Methods: Similarly, class methods are also considered methods because they are associated with the class and can access class-level data and methods. Static methods fit this conceptual framework.



4.4 Example to Illustrate the Concept
Here’s a Python example to illustrate how static methods fit within a class:
class MathUtility:
    # A static method
    @staticmethod
    def add(a, b):
        return a + b

    # Another static method
    @staticmethod
    def subtract(a, b):
        return a - b

# Calling static methods using the class name
result1 = MathUtility.add(5, 3)
result2 = MathUtility.subtract(10, 4)

print(result1)  # Output: 8
print(result2)  # Output: 6
Thus, even though static methods do not operate on instances, their definition within a class and their role in encapsulating class-related functionality justify their classification as methods rather than standalone functions.

title: An exercise in semantics - Method vs Function
text:
5 My opinion
I would argue that the link to an object or a class may be a bit too restrictive, when using the term method.
Consider expanding the context beyond objects and classes to include modules or namespaces. In many languages, modules or namespaces provide a way to group related functions and restrict their visibility from outside contexts. This grouping can enforce encapsulation and modularity in a manner similar to classes.
The key is understanding that what distinguishes a method from any other kind of function is the relation to some context as well as a visibility/accessibility specific to that context.
Note that I do not further define what the kind of the relation should be, given that it may differ with many languages, and given that any further specification may not be general enough to be compatible with the constructs of all existing or future languages.
For instance, in JavaScript or Python, functions defined within a module or namespace can be considered methods of that module if they are meant to operate within its context. These functions might not belong to a specific object or class, but they are still tied to the module’s scope and restricted in their visibility and access.
Therefore, it might be appropriate to use the term method instead of function in such contexts. The essential characteristics that differentiate methods from functions—namely, the contextual association and restricted visibility—are present, but at the level of a module or namespace rather than an individual object or class.
By broadening our perspective, we can recognise that methods do not need to be limited to the traditional object-oriented paradigm. Instead, they can exist within any structured context that enforces scope and encapsulation, whether it be a class, module, or namespace.

title: An exercise in semantics - Method vs Function
text:
6 Summary
While, by definition, as methods are a special kind of function, both functions and methods perform similar roles by encapsulating code for reuse, methods are functions that live inside objects and are meant to operate on the data contained within those objects. Functions are more general-purpose and not tied to any particular data structure.

title: Cohesion Is About Knowledge: Why High Cohesion Makes Code Easier to Understand
text:
We’ve all heard that “high cohesion” is good. But what does cohesion actually mean?
Most definitions focus on the mechanics: “elements that belong together should be grouped together.” But this raises the question: how do we know what “belongs together”?
The answer lies in understanding cohesion as a knowledge organization principle.

title: Cohesion Is About Knowledge: Why High Cohesion Makes Code Easier to Understand
text:
1 The Knowledge Perspective
Here’s a more fundamental way to think about cohesion:

Cohesion is about grouping knowledge that changes for the same reason

Knowledge that varies together should be grouped together. Knowledge that varies independently should be separated.
When you have high cohesion, all the knowledge in a unit changes for one reason—driven by one change driver. When you have low cohesion, the knowledge in a unit changes for multiple independent reasons—driven by different, unrelated change drivers.
Let me show you what this means in practice.

title: Cohesion Is About Knowledge: Why High Cohesion Makes Code Easier to Understand
Cohesion Is About Knowledge: Why High Cohesion Makes Code Easier to Understand
text:
3 What Knowledge Do You Need?
To understand the Order class, you need to know about:

Order domain logic (items, totals, discounts)
PDF generation (libraries, templates, formatting)
Email systems (SMTP, templates, recipients)
Inventory management (stock levels, reservations)
Analytics systems (tracking, event formats)

That’s five different areas of knowledge—and they change for completely different reasons:

Order logic changes when business rules change
Invoice generation changes when document requirements change
Email changes when notification preferences change
Inventory changes when warehouse systems change
Analytics changes when tracking requirements change

A developer working on discount logic shouldn’t need to understand PDF generation. A developer fixing email issues shouldn’t need to understand inventory systems.
This is low cohesion. The knowledge is scattered across unrelated concerns.

title: Cohesion Is About Knowledge: Why High Cohesion Makes Code Easier to Understand
text:
4 The Independent Variation Principle
The Independent Variation Principle (IVP) states four directives:

IVP-1 (Element Admissibility): every element must be governed by at least one change driver.
IVP-2 (Change Driver Assignment): assign each element every change driver whose knowledge it embodies; a multi-driver element must be irreducible.
IVP-3 (Unit Purity — Separation): elements governed by different change drivers belong in distinct units.
IVP-4 (Unit Completeness — Unification): elements governed by the same change driver belong in a single unit.

IVP provides a precise way to identify low cohesion:

When a module contains knowledge that varies for independent reasons, cohesion is low


4.1 What Is a Change Driver?
A change driver is a reason why code needs to change. The same concept appears in other design principles (Single Responsibility Principle, Common Closure Principle) under different names: “reason to change”, “actor”, “source of change”.
These terms are used interchangeably—they all refer to the same underlying concept.
Change drivers have these characteristics: - Independent triggers: They activate for different reasons at different times - Different stakeholders: Different people or teams decide when and how each driver triggers - Distinct knowledge domains: Each driver requires understanding different areas of expertise
For example: - Business rule changes are driven by product managers adjusting pricing, discounts, or validation rules - Infrastructure changes are driven by platform engineers optimizing databases or APIs - UI changes are driven by designers and frontend teams improving user experience
When multiple independent change drivers affect the same module, that module has low cohesion.
Let’s identify the independent change drivers in our Order class:


4.2 1. Business Rules

Discount calculations
Order validation
Tax calculations
Pricing logic

Stakeholder: Product managers, business analysts


4.3 2. Document Generation

PDF formatting
Invoice templates
Receipt layouts

Stakeholder: Design team, legal/compliance


4.4 3. Communication

Email templates
Notification timing
Delivery channels (email, SMS, push)

Stakeholder: Marketing, customer service


4.5 4. Warehouse Operations

Inventory tracking
Stock reservations
Fulfillment systems

Stakeholder: Logistics team


4.6 5. Data & Analytics

Event tracking
Metrics collection
Reporting

Stakeholder: Data science team
These are five independent sources of change—different stakeholders, different reasons to change, different timelines.
When they’re all mixed in one class, every change forces you to understand all five concerns, even if you’re only modifying one.

title: Cohesion Is About Knowledge: Why High Cohesion Makes Code Easier to Understand
section: 5 High Cohesion: Grouping Knowledge by Change Driver

title: Cohesion Is About Knowledge: Why High Cohesion Makes Code Easier to Understand
text:
6 The Benefits of High Cohesion

6.1 Reduced Cognitive Load
When you need to understand discount logic, you only need to understand the Order class. You don’t need to know anything about PDFs, emails, or analytics.
When you need to change email templates, you only need to understand OrderNotifier. You don’t need to understand order pricing or inventory management.
Each unit requires understanding only one area of knowledge.


6.2 Localized Changes
Each change driver affects exactly one module: - Business rules → Order - Document requirements → InvoiceGenerator - Communication needs → OrderNotifier - Warehouse operations → InventoryManager - Analytics tracking → OrderAnalytics
Changes are localized to the relevant knowledge area.


6.3 Independent Evolution
The PDF library can be upgraded without touching order logic. The analytics system can be replaced without touching email code. Order validation can be enhanced without touching inventory management.
Each knowledge area evolves independently.

title: Cohesion Is About Knowledge: Why High Cohesion Makes Code Easier to Understand
section: 7 The Relationship Between Cohesion, Knowledge, and Change Drivers
text:
7 The Relationship Between Cohesion, Knowledge, and Change Drivers
Here’s the key insight:
High cohesion = Knowledge driven by one change driver is grouped together
Low cohesion = Knowledge driven by different change drivers is mixed together
Or more precisely:

Cohesion measures how well a module’s knowledge aligns with a single change driver

This explains why high cohesion improves maintainability:

Easier to understand: You only need to understand knowledge relevant to one change driver
Easier to change: When a change driver triggers, you modify exactly one module
Easier to test: Each module tests knowledge for one change driver in isolation
Easier to parallelize work: Different teams own different change drivers and their corresponding modules

title: Cohesion Is About Knowledge: Why High Cohesion Makes Code Easier to Understand
text:
8 How to Identify Low Cohesion
The key is identifying change drivers. Ask these questions about your classes/modules:

8.1 1. What are the change drivers?
What are the different reasons this unit might change? - Business rule changes? - Technology/infrastructure changes? - Performance optimizations? - UI/UX changes? - Compliance/regulatory changes?
If there are multiple independent reasons to change, you have multiple change drivers → low cohesion.


8.2 2. Who owns each change driver?
For each potential change, who decides when and how it happens? - Product managers (business rules)? - Platform team (infrastructure)? - Frontend team (UI/UX)? - DevOps (performance)? - Data team (analytics)?
Multiple stakeholders = multiple change drivers = low cohesion.


8.3 3. What knowledge does each change driver require?
For each change driver, what do you need to understand to make that change? - When business rules change, do you need to understand PDF generation? - When document templates change, do you need to understand order validation? - When analytics requirements change, do you need to understand email delivery?
If one change driver forces you to understand knowledge from other change drivers, they’re inappropriately coupled → low cohesion.


8.4 4. Do change drivers vary independently?

Can business rules change without affecting document generation?
Can analytics requirements change without affecting inventory management?
Can notification preferences change without affecting order validation?

If these vary independently but are in the same module → low cohesion.

title: Cohesion Is About Knowledge: Why High Cohesion Makes Code Easier to Understand
text:
9 The Decision Framework
When designing or refactoring code:

Identify change drivers: What are the independent reasons this code might change?
