SRP
“The system calculates pay, formats statements, and emails them”
Three separate statements, each with its own governing authority
Three pure elements, each {γ_i}
IVP-2 decomposes reducible composites; IVP-3 separates. Wrong in general: SRP also demands splitting irreducible composites (adapters) that IVP-2 correctly permits.


OCP
“The system sends notifications by email”
“Notification is governed by notification requirements. Each channel — email, SMS, push — has its own governing infrastructure.”
{γ_notification} for service and interface; {γ_notification, γ_email}, {γ_notification, γ_sms}, {γ_notification, γ_push} for channels (irreducible composites)
IVP-3 separates per channel; IVP-2 permits the irreducible composite; IVP-4 unifies service with its interface


LSP
“Rectangle and Square are shapes with width and height”
“Rectangle has independent width and height. Square has a single side length with the constraint width = height.”
{γ_rect} for Rectangle, {γ_square} for Square
IVP-3 separates; the subtype relationship was forced onto two types with different invariants. Hybrid: when Γ is correct but contract is broken, Bertrand Meyer’s Design by Contract is needed.


ISP
“The system has a reporting interface serving accounting, analytics, and management”
Three separate client contracts, each governed by its own driver
Interface-client pairs share Γ
IVP-4 unifies each pair; IVP-3 separates across clients


DIP
“OrderProcessor persists orders to MySQL”
“Order processing and persistence technology vary independently”
{γ_order} for processor and interface, {γ_persistence} for implementations
IVP-3 separates abstraction from implementation



The pattern is uniform for SRP, OCP, ISP, and DIP. Each identifies a particular way domain knowledge is incomplete or incorrectly expressed. The prescription is always the same: decompose the compound or incomplete knowledge statement into irreducible sub-statements with distinct driver assignments; let the code structure emerge from correct Γ.
SRP is additionally wrong in general: it demands purity (|Γ(e)| = 1) for every element, failing to recognize legitimate irreducible composites such as adapters, facades, and protocol translators. IVP-2’s irreducibility test is the correct criterion — it decomposes the reducible (PayCalculator) and permits the irreducible (payment-to-FX adapter). SRP lacks this distinction.
LSP is a hybrid. When the structural placement is wrong — types with different invariants forced into a hierarchy — the violation resolves like the others: correct Γ, IVP separates, the problem disappears. When the structural placement is correct but the behavioral contract is broken, Bertrand Meyer’s Design by Contract is needed. The other four heuristics are purely knowledge diagnostics; LSP spans both domains.

title: SOLID Heuristics Reveal Incomplete Domain Knowledge — Nothing More
text:
8 What This Means
Were domain knowledge always causally complete and correctly documented, the four IVP directives would produce the correct design automatically. Γ would capture every element’s causal dependencies. IVP-2 would flag every reducible composite. IVP-3 and IVP-4 would produce the unique module partition. There would be nothing for SRP, OCP, ISP, or DIP to do.
The heuristics exist only because, in practice, domain knowledge is incomplete or incorrectly expressed. When a designer applies SRP to a class with multiple reasons to change, they are correcting a knowledge defect — the statement “the system calculates pay, formats statements, and emails them” should be three statements. When a designer applies DIP to a concrete dependency, they are correcting a knowledge defect — the statement “OrderProcessor persists to MySQL” bundled abstract capability with implementation detail.
SOLID heuristics are reports of incomplete knowledge. They do not produce correct structure from correct inputs — they diagnose incorrect inputs. IVP is the general law that would be sufficient if knowledge were complete.
The fact that the IVP-derived structures are identical to what each heuristic prescribes — same class decomposition, same abstraction boundaries, same interface segregation — is not a coincidence. Three independent discovery paths converge on the same structural conclusions: mathematical derivation from cost axioms, empirical debugging experience encoded in SOLID, and epistemic insight that software design is knowledge work. When a heuristic’s prescription matches what IVP derives from correct Γ, the heuristic identifies a genuine structural condition; IVP explains why that condition holds. When a heuristic diverges — SRP demanding splits of irreducible composites — IVP identifies the error and supplies the correct criterion.
This framing has practical consequences. A designer who understands IVP has no need for SRP, OCP, ISP, or DIP as separate rules. IVP provides a strictly stronger and more precise criterion — one that avoids the errors those heuristics introduce outside their narrow conditions. SRP demands splitting legitimate multi-driver modules (irreducible composites). OCP and ISP are silent about unification (IVP-4). IVP’s four directives cover both separation and unification, pure and composite elements, with formal precision.
The question to ask when a SOLID heuristic appears to apply is not “how do I fix this code?” but “what causal domain knowledge is missing or incorrectly expressed such that this code structure emerged?” The code defect is a symptom. The knowledge defect is the cause.

title: SOLID Heuristics Reveal Incomplete Domain Knowledge — Nothing More
section: 9 A note on Robert C. Martin’s achievement
text:
9 A note on Robert C. Martin’s achievement
This article argues that SOLID heuristics are diagnostic patterns for incomplete knowledge, not design principles. That does not diminish Robert C. Martin’s contribution. Identifying five recurrent patterns across decades of practitioner experience — and giving them names that the entire industry adopted — is a remarkable feat of pattern recognition [Martin 1996a, 1996b, 2000, 2003]. The heuristics are not principles in the formal sense, but their identification was an act of genuine discovery.
Several authors have previously observed that SOLID’s five heuristics are not all independent. Henney [2016] argued that ISP becomes redundant if SRP is properly applied. Oldwood [2014] proposed that all five reduce to two concepts. Kaminski [2019] noted that SRP, ISP, and DIP rehash similar concepts around managing dependencies. Terhorst-North [2022] proposed replacing SOLID entirely with a different framework. None of these critiques identified the specific mechanism that IVP reveals: each heuristic is a diagnostic pattern for a particular way domain knowledge is incomplete or incorrectly expressed.
This interpretation is itself only possible because of a formal theoretical development of the matter. The Independent Variation Principle provides a fundamental, principled design practice — four directives derived from the Change Management Hypothesis — that determines a unique module partition from causal domain knowledge alone. Without this formal foundation, SOLID’s heuristics remain disconnected rules of thumb. Earlier critics could sense overlap and redundancy. They could not specify why each heuristic arises or what structural situation it addresses — because those answers require the apparatus of change drivers, driver assignments, and the IVP directives. IVP does not merely critique SOLID. It provides the formal framework within which SOLID’s contribution — and its limits — become legible.
Three of the five — OCP, ISP, and DIP — have been essential in module boundary design for roughly thirty years. They address what happens at the seam between modules: OCP says don’t modify existing code, extend through a boundary. ISP says segregate interfaces per client at the boundary. DIP says depend on abstractions owned by the high-level module, not on concretions from the low-level one. These three are the practical workhorses of boundary design. They converge on the same structural truth IVP formalizes: variation forces are independent, and module boundaries must honor that independence.
SRP is different. It addresses internal cohesion — what belongs inside a class — not boundary structure. Its prescription (“one reason to change”) is correct for reducible composites but wrong for irreducible ones. LSP is also different: it addresses behavioral contracts within a type hierarchy, not boundaries between modules. The three boundary heuristics are where SOLID’s lasting value lies. The other two diagnose real problems but lack the generality of the boundary principles — and the formal foundation that IVP provides.

title: SOLID Heuristics Reveal Incomplete Domain Knowledge — Nothing More
text:
10 Further Reading
The formal theory is developed in Volume 1 of the IVP book series, with Chapter 9 providing the full IVP–SOLID analysis and Chapter 3 developing the structural formulation.

IVP formalization (preprint): DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18024111
ISP Is a Conditional Corollary of DIP Applied Per Client - An Asymmetric Relationship Gated by Interface Evolution Origin: DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20350293 — a formal proof that ISP is a conditional corollary of DIP applied per client, and that the two heuristics address the same structural constraint from different vantage points.

If this framing — SOLID as diagnostic patterns for incomplete domain knowledge — resonates, the ISP–DIP paper is the natural next read. It shows the same phenomenon at closer range: two heuristics that converge on one structure, differing only in which knowledge gap they are named after.

If you teach SOLID or use it daily in code reviews: does the “diagnostic pattern for incomplete knowledge” framing change how you apply these heuristics? I would value your perspective.

title: SRP’s Vocabulary Problem: Why Every Reformulation Failed
text:
I’ve just published SRP’s Vocabulary Problem: Why Every Reformulation Failed.
The Single Responsibility Principle has been criticized as vague, ambiguous, and arbitrary for thirty years. A companion paper shows it carries a demonstrable cardinality error — but that error was hiding in plain sight. Why did no one see it?
This paper answers that question. The vocabulary SRP inherited — “concern” from Dijkstra, “responsibility” from Martin — imports a cardinality assumption before any reasoning begins. The words make the right question unaskable.

title: IVP Has a Proof — The Γ-Equality Partition Is the Unique Cost-Minimizing Modularization
text:
How should software be modularized, and why that way? A new preprint answers both questions with a proof — and the answer is the Independent Variation Principle (IVP).
A change-driver is an external condition — a regulation, a contract, a protocol specification — whose change forces governed elements to change. The how is the rule itself; the why is that this exact grouping, and no other, minimizes the cost of change. For fifty years that second question — why these boundaries rather than those — had only well-motivated opinion behind it. This paper turns the answer into a theorem.

title: IVP Has a Proof — The Γ-Equality Partition Is the Unique Cost-Minimizing Modularization
section: 1 The proof is a counting argument
text:
1 The proof is a counting argument
Draw a bipartite incidence graph: elements on one side, change-drivers on the other, edges recording which drivers govern which elements. On that graph, two lemmas show that any modularization deviating from the IVP prescription pays a strictly higher cost — either by scattering same-driver elements across modules, or by mixing different-driver elements in the same module.
The Γ-equality partition — the one that groups elements by identical change-driver sets — is not one good option among several. It is the unique cost-minimizing modularization.

title: IVP Has a Proof — The Γ-Equality Partition Is the Unique Cost-Minimizing Modularization
section: 2 Why more than five decades of principles couldn’t settle this
text:
2 Why more than five decades of principles couldn’t settle this
Information hiding, the SOLID and package rules, layered and hexagonal architectures, domain-driven boundaries — each distilled real experience into advice about where to draw module boundaries, and each is a heuristic. They share one structural limitation: none was derived from a cost objective, or any other clearly stated objective, so none can prove its boundaries are optimal rather than merely reasonable, and where two of them disagree there is no principled way to say which is right.
Some are also internally inconsistent. Martin’s Common Closure and Reuse/Release principles, for instance, cannot both be satisfied under client-driven interface evolution — and the framework names no winner. The common root is the absence of a single objective to optimize against.

title: IVP Has a Proof — The Γ-Equality Partition Is the Unique Cost-Minimizing Modularization
text:
3 What the proof gives you
This paper supplies that objective and proves the consequence. Once the change-drivers are identified, the question “which elements change for the same reasons?” becomes the precise predicate Γ(e₁) = Γ(e₂) — grouping by the external conditions that govern an element, not by which changes happen to be probable or which have co-occurred in the commit history — and the optimal boundaries follow from it by counting. No competing rules to reconcile, no judgment, no taste, no appeal to accumulated experience.

Yannick Loth. The Independent Variation Principle: Deriving Optimal Module Boundaries from the Element–Change-Driver Graph. June 2026.
📄 Free preprint on Zenodo — DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20794332

title: Inheritance vs Composition: What the Independent Variation Principle Actually Tells Us
text:
“Favor composition over inheritance” is one of the most cited design guidelines in software engineering. It is tempting to read this as a rule IVP prescribes. It is not.
The Independent Variation Principle (IVP) is precise about what it governs and what it leaves open. This post uses a payment-processing example to show what IVP actually tells us about inheritance and composition — and, just as importantly, what it does not.

title: Inheritance vs Composition: What the Independent Variation Principle Actually Tells Us
section: 1 What IVP governs — and what it does not
text:
1 What IVP governs — and what it does not
IVP’s normative content is a module partition, not a mechanism choice [1]. Given a system’s elements EE and its set of change drivers CC, IVP assigns each element ee a set of change drivers Γ(e)\Gamma(e) — the change drivers whose state changes create a modification requirement for ee — and prescribes, in its structural formulation [1]:

Admissibility — every element has at least one change driver: ∀e∈E,|Γ(e)|≥1\forall e \in E,\ |\Gamma(e)| \geq 1.
Element Form — every element is either pure (|Γ(e)|=1|\Gamma(e)| = 1) or irreducibly composite: no proper subset of its driver set can achieve its purpose, and no decomposition into sub-elements with strictly smaller driver sets jointly preserves that purpose.
Separation — elements assigned different sets of change drivers reside in different modules: Γ(e1)≠Γ(e2)⇒M(e1)≠M(e2)\Gamma(e_1) \neq \Gamma(e_2) \Rightarrow M(e_1) \neq M(e_2).
Unification — elements assigned the same set of change drivers reside in the same module: Γ(e1)=Γ(e2)⇒M(e1)=M(e2)\Gamma(e_1) = \Gamma(e_2) \Rightarrow M(e_1) = M(e_2).

Equivalently, the modules of an IVP-compliant system are the Γ\Gamma-equivalence classes of EE [1]. The first two clauses are the ones the composition-vs-inheritance discussion must not skip. Admissibility says every element answers to some change driver. Element Form ties the assignment to purpose and to the domain knowledge the element embodies: Γ(e)\Gamma(e) is not an arbitrary label — ee embodies the knowledge governed by its drivers, so the assignment is grounded in what the element exists to realize [2]. Separation and Unification then say how those grounded assignments group elements into modules.
Inheritance and composition are both such mechanisms. The theory treats inheritance — class B extends A — as a structural dependency: a relation observable directly in the artifact, like a function call or an import. IVP does not have a “composition directive” and an “inheritance directive.” What it does have is a coupling criterion, and that is where the real guidance lies.

title: Inheritance vs Composition: What the Independent Variation Principle Actually Tells Us
section: 2 What IVP mandates: its own minimal coupling
text:
2 What IVP mandates: its own minimal coupling
IVP’s coupling criterion follows from its rule [1]. The partition induced by Γ\Gamma-equivalence is fixed by the change drivers; the coupling that survives a compliant partition is IVP’s minimal coupling — the necessary coupling: essential same-Γ\Gamma coupling inside a module, plus the essential cross-Γ\Gamma coupling between modules that is the irreducible cost of communication between Γ\Gamma-classes.
One thing IVP’s minimal coupling forbids:

Accidental coupling — coupling not required by any domain artifact. Two elements are coupled when one depends on something the other defines or maintains; that dependency is essential when a domain artifact (a statute, contract, standard, specification) requires it, and accidental when no domain artifact mandates it — a framework convention, a language limitation, a deployment detail.

The accidental coupling IVP is most concerned with is cross-Γ\Gamma accidental coupling — accidental coupling that connects elements assigned different sets of change drivers.
IVP also leaves no room for accidental coupling between elements that should be apart. If two elements with different change-driver sets sit in the same module and are accidentally coupled, the module is impure: the partition has co-located elements that Separation would keep in different modules, and the system does not faithfully embody the domain’s change structure [1]. IVP’s Separation directive eliminates this case by construction — cross-Γ\Gamma elements are never co-located in a compliant partition. The only accidental coupling that can remain inside a module is the same-Γ\Gamma kind — a concrete reference where an abstraction would do — and that is a code-quality defect, not a failure to embody the domain.
Because the coupling verdict is relative to the chosen rule, it is not a property of the code in the abstract — it is a property of the code under a given partition. IVP’s verdict is IVP’s because IVP picks Γ\Gamma-equivalence as its modularization rule. A different rule would classify the same dependencies differently.

title: Inheritance vs Composition: What the Independent Variation Principle Actually Tells Us
section: 3 The payment example: what IVP diagnoses

title: Inheritance vs Composition: What the Independent Variation Principle Actually Tells Us
section: 4 Why composition avoids that specific defect

title: Inheritance vs Composition: What the Independent Variation Principle Actually Tells Us
text:
5 What IVP does not say
IVP does not endorse “prefer composition over inheritance” as a universal rule. Three specific caveats:
Inheritance is not forbidden. Where the two sides genuinely share the same change driver — so IVP assigns them the same Γ\Gamma and the same module — the coupling inheritance creates is essential, not accidental, and IVP is satisfied. The composition example itself uses this: CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment implement PaymentMethod, an “is-a” relationship to an abstraction that genuinely shares the payment-method change driver. That inheritance is IVP-compliant. What the example removes is inheritance across the two change drivers — subclassing a base that pulls in infrastructure the payment-method domain does not mandate. A geometric-shape hierarchy is IVP-compliant if all its elements are Γ\Gamma-equivalent, so that every change modifying one also creates a modification requirement for the others. A framework’s intentional extension points are IVP-compliant only when the extension and the base are same-Γ\Gamma; a low activation frequency does not by itself make them compliant. The defect is coupling different change drivers, not using inheritance.
Composition can violate IVP too. Composition that couples elements assigned different sets of change drivers across a module boundary is just as much cross-Γ\Gamma accidental coupling. Mechanism alone does not determine compliance; the change-driver assignment Γ\Gamma does.
The verdict is rule-relative. “The hierarchy couples independent change drivers” is an IVP-specific diagnosis. It follows from choosing Γ\Gamma-equivalence as the modularization rule. Another rule would partition the elements differently and classify the same edges differently. IVP’s answer is the answer given its choice of rule, not a mechanism-independent fact.

title: Inheritance vs Composition: What the Independent Variation Principle Actually Tells Us
text:
6 The takeaway
IVP does not tell you to reach for composition and avoid inheritance. It tells you something more useful: start with the domain. Ask what the domain actually prescribes: what are the change drivers, and what does each element’s specification require it to embody and depend on? The change drivers determine the partition; then couple elements only where the domain requires the dependency, and never make an element embody knowledge its causal domain does not mandate. When you evaluate a design, ask not “inheritance or composition?” but “what does the structure of the causal domain knowledge dictate, and does this mechanism add coupling the domain never had?”
In the payment example, inheritance happens to manufacture accidental embodiment and cross-driver accidental coupling — through the knowledge the extends edge forces the subclass to carry — and composition happens to avoid it. That is why the classical guideline points the right way in this example. But IVP explains the reason: the best structure is derived directly from the structure of the causal domain knowledge, and the mechanism is faithful exactly when it adds no coupling the domain did not already decide.

title: Inheritance vs Composition: What the Independent Variation Principle Actually Tells Us
text:
7 Learn More
IVP formalizes the module partition a system’s change drivers prescribe and the coupling a compliant partition tolerates — giving a precise, decidable answer where classical heuristics rely on intuition. The formal development — the module partition and the coupling-floor argument — is proved in the paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1], with the change-driver partition and purity/completeness accounted for in Causal Cohesion [3] and the cohesion-as-correctness framework in On the Nature of Cohesion [2].
This site’s overview sections — IVP (software) and Software design — present the theory and its applications in more depth, and the language coupling analysis applies the coupling lens across 65 programming languages.

title: Architecture
text:
Architecture is the part of software design concerned with module boundaries and the decisions that are hard to change — the system’s skeleton. Architecture is a subset of design; not all design is architecture.
The change-management criterion for module boundaries that distinguishes architecture from lower-level design is developed in the published paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1]. The criterion is the missing piece two design notions openly defer to. Cohesion is correctness relative to a partitioning rule, assessed as a purity-completeness pair per rule, so a cohesion judgment is only as definite as the rule behind it [2]. Coupling is access to a shared resource, and telling couplings a domain artifact mandates (essential) from the rest (accidental) needs a criterion grounded in the domain; without one, module boundaries are arbitrary [3]. The change-driver partition closes both gaps at once: grouping by the full change-driver set is the common refinement of the modularisation principles, so one partition answers to all of them together [2].

title: Architecture
text:
1 What architecture is
The usual answers describe the occupation, not the discipline. One says architecture is what architects do — an activity. Another says it is “the important stuff, whatever that is” [4] — a judgment, not a criterion. A third says it is the set of decisions that are hard to change — a cost correlate that misfires exactly where a criterion is needed. None of the three can say, for a concrete design question, whether the question is architectural at all.
The change criterion completes the significance answer instead of leaving it a shrug: “important” becomes definite once it is read as whatever materially shapes how the system varies under change. Significance is then a fact about the domain, not a consensus of experts.
One criterion does the classifying: derivability.

A question the design must answer is architectural exactly when the domain’s causal knowledge bears on the answer by restricting which answers the system may take.

The domain’s causal knowledge is the knowledge required to realize the system’s purpose within the obligations its governing artifacts impose — regulations, contracts, specifications, service-level commitments. Two separations carry the weight:

Domain obligations are facts about the domain. The architect has no authority over them; the architect’s derivation is a fallible estimate of them.
Machine and cost knowledge are not second sources of authority. They enter the derivation only through the obligations that depend on them: a latency SLA in the platform contract, not a taste for speed, forces the cache; a seven-year retention statute, not caution, forces the durable store.

The architecture of a system is then the set of its answers to architectural questions, together with their admissible sets. Given jointly satisfiable obligations, the criterion classifies each answer:

Derivable core — the obligations admit exactly one answer. The design transcribes it; no selection occurs, because a decision is a selection from two or more admissible answers, and a singleton leaves nothing to select.
Feasible region — the obligations admit several answers. Judgment operates here, and must be presented as judgment: reasoned, challengeable, never dressed up as necessity.
Provisional — the available knowledge does not settle the admissible set. The gap is a defect to repair, not a preference to push through quietly.
Infeasible — the obligations cannot be jointly satisfied. No realizable design exists, and the remedy is a governing act on the artifacts, not a design choice.

A payment system runs all four classes in one place. The acquiring contract requires settlement deduplication, and a seven-year tax statute makes that storage durable: derivable core, no design debate left. Confirmation by push or by polling admits several admissible answers: feasible region, and the choice is recorded as judgment. Whether capture must close within seven days is settled by no artifact at hand: provisional, a gap to repair. A new erasure duty within thirty days collides with the seven-year retention statute: infeasible, and resolved above the design when the statute prevails.
Checkability has a stated scope: the governing artifacts must be identifiable, the obligations expressed in them, and the knowledge required to realize the purpose within them available. Within that scope a third party can decide whether the derivation holds, given only the artifacts and the recorded material. Checkable does not mean true — a claim can be checkable and false — but it means the argument never rests on the architect’s private word.

title: Architecture
text:
2 The architect enables everyone else
Architecture is instrumental. It is a means to delivery, not an end in itself, and it is judged by whether it enables the delivery system around it to function. This is the central claim of the account:
Enablement. Every role the product’s obligations require — product managers, builders, testers, sponsors — must be able to do the job those obligations make necessary: with satisfying quality, in time, and in budget.
Three consequences follow:

Enablement is a property of the whole delivery system, and the architect is answerable for it even though many hands achieve it. Which roles are necessary is itself derived: a role is necessary exactly when some obligation makes its work necessary. Both errors are derivation defects — omitting a role some obligation requires leaves work that must be done with no one accountable for it; inventing a role no obligation supports smuggles a preference into the delivery system under the name of architecture.
The accountability is held by a single role. This is an organizational commitment, not something the criterion derives. The organization decides what fills the role — one individual architect, a team, or a committee whose members share the architecture tasks. Whoever fills it is answerable for the whole of enablement.
The duty is dischargeable. One accountability, four duties: derive (identify the causal domain knowledge and extract the design from it), document (express the one derivation so each role can act on it), validate (check the built system against the recorded derivation), and re-examine (re-derive when the knowledge moves).

Why the role must exist at all has a structural answer. Apply the change criterion recursively to the organisation itself: modules sit in deployment units, deployment units in organisational domains, and at each level the units below become elements with their own change-driver structure. A team that applies the criterion flawlessly inside its own modules is blind to the level where its whole module is one element among many. Cross-team and cross-system drivers therefore have no owner at the team level. The failure looks mundane. A module set one team owns is legitimate: all coordination is internal. The day a second team takes authority over half of it, nothing in the domain changes, but internal coordination silently becomes inter-team coordination — interface contracts, synchronised releases, shared pipeline ownership. No team can see the misalignment from inside. The role exists to hold what no team can see: a system whose change drivers cross team or system boundaries needs an architect — not a decision-maker, but the reader and steward of the drivers no single team can see.
The role account also corrects Fowler’s aphorism that an architect’s value is inversely proportional to the number of decisions made [4]. That metric can only describe what a good architect avoids. The value is three positive readings: identify the change drivers; decide when a hard constraint — security isolation, regulatory separation, deployment topology, a real-time budget — should dominate the change-cost axis; and choose the tools whose constructs let the domain knowledge be embodied faithfully. The rest is read off the domain, not decided.
Enablement is not the satisfaction of every local preference. A tester’s wish to bypass an audit trail is a local preference when the domain forces the trail; the correct answer is no, together with a way for the tester to do the real job — verifying behaviour — within the constraint. Only a blockage the architecture produced, or could have removed at a cost the domain permits, counts against the architecture.
Two tests make the claim operational rather than aspirational:

The documentation test. Documentation is one derivation expressed per audience, not a set of artifacts: milestones for product management, testable quality attributes for testers, contracts for builders, risk posture for the sponsor. Each role must be able to act on its view without interviewing the architect; under-documentation fails one way, and a view no required role consumes fails the other.
The validation test. When something fails, the process must be able to attribute the failure to the derivation and not only to the builders. A validation process that can only ever blame the builders is quality theater: it performs assurance while protecting the one thing that most needs to be challengeable.

The failure test turns the definition into three checkable predicates, each with an observable condition:

Blocking an artifact-derived job. A role cannot do the job its governing artifacts require because of a decision the causal knowledge does not admit.
Incoherent combinations. Every choice is admissible alone, but combinations fail — either behaviourally (no single behaviour of the system can exhibit two answers together, such as synchronous fraud review against a one-second latency SLA) or in delivery (a decision taken to satisfy one role defeats the required job of another, such as an hourly data-funnel rebuild that blocks the daily regression run).
Validation that attributes every failure to the builders. There is no recorded derivation to check the build against, or no step in the process that can blame the derivation.

Refusal follows the same pattern. The architect may refuse a demand that contradicts the derivable core, but only by showing why — citing the obligation the demand violates and the artifact that imposes it. An architect who cannot show why a demand violates the domain’s obligations has no authority to refuse it.
Re-examination closes the loop. The knowledge moves — an obligation is amended, a latency ceiling shifts, pricing changes — and every derivation built on it is in question. An architecture correctly derived from yesterday’s knowledge is today a derivation from a false premise, and it fails exactly as if it had been wrong from the start.

title: Architecture
text:
3 Architecture is derived, not designed
The account sharpens into a partition criterion, and the consequence is stark:

A decision is architectural exactly when its answer constrains the assignment of elements to modules — the partition of the system into modules — and therefore, wherever module and team boundaries align, which future change-work falls to which team. A decision the causal knowledge forces but that determines only itself — which database is named, which integer width is used — is derived but not architectural.
The class diagram is recovered, not designed. The classes, the coupling, the cohesion, and even the kind of relationship between two classes — parameter, association, or event — are transcribed from the domain’s temporal and identity semantics. Where the shape varies across developers, the variation traces to a convention the language underdetermines, not to a choice over the structure of knowledge.
Modularisation is derived too: the objective it serves is itself domain knowledge, read from the domain’s economics, and the cost-minimising partition is read off the forcing conditions. That the partition minimising change propagation minimises lifetime maintenance cost is a proved result, not a preference [5]; the optimal modularization is derivable from coupling [6], and the partition it produces is the change-driver partition [1] — the common refinement of the modularisation principles, so one decomposition answers to all of them at once [2].
Most apparent trade-offs dissolve once demands carry numbers and scopes. The irreducible remainder is resolved by a business commitment made above the system, not by the architect: the architect surfaces the conflict with its prices attached, and stops.

Within the design there is no choice: only the value choice above the system and the reading beneath it remain. The value choice has a number attached and is made above the design — committing to one card scheme’s fees over another’s, or accepting a 200 ms p99 to halve infrastructure cost. Everything else is arithmetic, and arithmetic does not have taste.

title: Architecture
text:
4 Styles assume; the domain decides
Read as hypotheses about which parts change for different reasons, the styles get a uniform diagnosis. Each style fixes a structural proxy — rings, layers, slices — and succeeds where the proxy tracks the domain’s actual variation. Where it does not, the style fails silently: nothing in the diagram tells you the assumption broke.
The shared prescription behind the core-protecting styles — that business logic can always be made independent of infrastructure — does not always hold. Achievability is a structural property of the domain. Where the domain’s drivers require infrastructure-level knowledge, no reformulation of the domain eliminates that knowledge, enforcing the style forces a falsified model, and abstraction that removes load-bearing drivers is domain substitution, not purification. A pricing module whose rounding rules a tax statute fixes shows the substitution: route the statute’s rounding into an infrastructure adapter, and the adapter now embodies domain knowledge wherever the diagram places it. What counts as infrastructure is relative, too — a payment processor is infrastructure to a client system, and a first-class, regulation-driven domain to its own operators. The practical test is driver completeness: after the abstraction, are all original drivers still represented and independently testable?
Clean Architecture decomposes into a partition criterion (group by ring role) plus a dependency-direction constraint. The partition criterion diverges from the optimal partition whenever ring role does not track the change drivers [1], and stability by ring position corrupts the stability ordering, because genuine stability is a property of an element’s governing authorities, not its ring membership. The conclusion is not to apply the rings more carefully, but to apply the change-driver partition directly and invert dependencies only where the domain grants substitutability.
Boundary ownership has its own grammar: who controls an interface specification, who implements it, and who uses it. Of the ownership configurations that grammar allows, three are stable — bilateral control, provider-driven control, shared governance; four degenerate to simpler forms; two are structurally contradictory.
Architecture Styles examines the styles one at a time: Hexagonal Architecture, Onion Architecture, Clean Architecture, Layered Architecture, and Vertical Slice Architecture. Each asks whether the style embodies the domain’s knowledge or invents structure the domain never mandated.

title: Architecture
section: 5 Splitting services trades a coupling space, it does not shrink one
text:
5 Splitting services trades a coupling space, it does not shrink one
The monolith-to-services split has a reputation for reducing coupling, and a habit of disappointing it. The analysis:

Coupling is access to a shared resource, and it does not depend on where the elements run [3]. A split therefore cannot remove coupling in general; what it does is replace one kind of coupling space with another.
The co-location family — shared mutable state, implicit initialisation order, cache and configuration bleed, concurrency, shared transactions — is unbounded, bespoke to each system, largely written nowhere, and therefore unmanageable.
The remote-deployment family a boundary installs is short, fixed, and manifest by construction: latency, availability and partial failure, serialisation and versioning, delivery and ordering, consistency, transport security, discovery, and boundary observability. It is handled largely by organisational discipline — timeouts, retries, idempotency, contract tests, service-level objectives — with a small named residue of genuine technical complexity, consistency above all.
Coupling grounded in what two sides share, not where they run, survives any seam. The coupling paper names it essential: a domain artifact — a statute, a contract, a standard — requires the elements to share the resource, so no deployment can remove it [3]. Where a seam strands such a genuinely-shared resource across the boundary, the split adds the fixed remote set on top of the surviving domain-imposed coupling [7]: the distributed monolith, which is not a botched decoupling but the predictable cost of a seam that ignores the shared-resource structure. The canonical case is two services and one database: the seam splits the code, but both sides still write the same orders table, so every schema change now crosses the very boundary the split was meant to remove.
Because one side’s coupling is invisible and never priced while the other’s is tangible and fully counted, the choice cannot rest on a cost estimate. It rests on the preconditions: whether a favourable seam exists, whether what crosses it is thin, and whether the organisation can bear the fixed remote set.

title: Cohesion: Core Conclusions
text: The cohesion series reworks one of the oldest and most abused concepts in software design. Cohesion entered the field with Stevens, Myers, and Constantine in 1974 and was codified by Yourdon and Constantine. Five decades of research and measurement followed. This page collects what the cohesion series concludes.

title: Cohesion: Core Conclusions
section: 1 Cohesion is correctness relative to a partitioning rule
text:
1 Cohesion is correctness relative to a partitioning rule
The central definitional result: cohesion is correctness relative to a partitioning rule.
A partitioning rule sorts the element set into equivalence classes — the elements that belong together. Against such a rule, a module deviates in exactly two ways:

Impurity. The module contains elements that belong to a different class.
Incompleteness. Some element of the module’s class resides outside the module.

So cohesion is assessed on two axes: purity and completeness. A module that is both pure and complete is fully cohesive: it holds exactly the elements its class requires, and nothing else.

title: Cohesion: Core Conclusions
section: 2 One pair per rule — the cohesion profile
text:
2 One pair per rule — the cohesion profile
A system is partitioned by many rules at once: logical code structure, deployment packaging, temporal grouping, security, platform. These are not separate things being partitioned. There is one element set EE, and each rule groups it by some of the change drivers acting on its elements.
For a system assessed under kk partitioning rules, cohesion is the 2k2k-tuple of (purity, completeness) pairs — one pair per rule. A module is fully cohesive when it scores maximally on every component.

title: Cohesion: Core Conclusions
section: 3 Structural proxies do not define cohesion
text:
3 Structural proxies do not define cohesion
The series argues that published definitions of cohesion overwhelmingly specify structural properties of code — method-call overlap, shared-field density, connected components.
These are not cohesion as defined by a modularization principle. They are structural proxies: observable patterns that correlate with cohesion but do not define it. A survey of 24 cohesion metrics spanning five decades shows that each measures structural coupling, not principled cohesion, reporting at most one axis and only as a proxy.
The distinction matters: a metric that counts structural overlap cannot detect the actual failure mode — whether a module holds elements the domain says belong elsewhere, or scatters the elements the domain says belong together.

title: Cohesion: Core Conclusions
section: 4 The Γ-equivalence rule is the coarsest change-containing partition
text:
4 The Γ-equivalence rule is the coarsest change-containing partition
Among all partitioning rules, one is special. Grouping elements by their full change-driver set — the Γ-equivalence rule — is the coarsest partition that still contains every change to one module.
Every modularization principle groups by a subset of the change drivers. Therefore every principle’s classes are unions of Γ-classes, and the Γ-decomposition is a refinement of every principle’s partition. A single Γ-decomposition is correct under all the principles at once.
This is the bridge from cohesion to the Independent Variation Principle: Γ-equivalence is the change-driver concretization of the general cohesion schema.

title: Cohesion: Core Conclusions
text:
5 The causal cohesion metric
When the partitioning rule is change-driver-assignment identity — elements belong together iff they share the same change-driver set — cohesion becomes causal cohesion.
For a single rule, causal cohesion is the two-dimensional metric
Hcausal(M)=(purity(M),completeness(M)) H_\text{causal}(M) = (\text{purity}(M), \text{completeness}(M)) 
in (0,1]×(0,1](0,1] \times (0,1]. It is one slot of the full cohesion profile, not the whole profile. Both axes are directly interpretable and map to design actions: low purity says separate elements of impure modules into distinct modules; low completeness says merge the scattered elements of a class into one module.
The metric satisfies the six necessary conditions the schema imposes on any admissible cohesion metric, and it has an operational computation procedure.

title: Cohesion: Core Conclusions
section: 6 The four conditions are necessary and exhaustive
text:
6 The four conditions are necessary and exhaustive
Under the change-driver hypothesis and the objective of minimizing change propagation, four conditions are necessary and structurally exhaustive:

Admissibility — every element has at least one driver.
Element Form — every element is pure or irreducibly composite.
Separation — different-driver elements belong in different modules.
Unification — same-driver elements belong in the same module.

The first two constrain the element set; the last two constrain the partition. These are exactly the four conditions of IVP. The causal (purity, completeness) pair is the two-axis criterion these conditions reduce to when k=1k = 1.

title: Cohesion: Core Conclusions
text:
7 Where the proofs live
The derivations — that the four conditions are necessary and exhaustive, that Γ-equivalence is the unique minimizer, that the knowledge-embodiment theorem holds — are proved in the published cohesion papers: cohesion as correctness relative to a partitioning rule in the paper on the nature of cohesion [1], the four necessary and exhaustive conditions in the paper on cohesion and change propagation [2], and the causal cohesion metric in the paper on causal cohesion [3].
The knowledge-embodiment theorem — the result that maximal cohesion is maximal embodiment of domain knowledge — is treated on its own page.

title: Cohesion and Knowledge Embodiment
text: This page covers a central result of the cohesion theory: the knowledge-embodiment theorem. It is placed here, under design, rather than under the IVP core theory, because it is a theorem about cohesion, not a theorem of IVP itself.

title: Cohesion and Knowledge Embodiment
text:
1 Cohesion, briefly
Cohesion is correctness relative to a partitioning rule. Under any modularization principle that groups elements, a module has two properties:

Purity. The module contains no element from outside its correct class.
Completeness. The module contains every element of its correct class.

A module that is both pure and complete is maximally cohesive: it holds exactly the right elements and nothing else. When the partitioning rule is the change-driver rule, this recovers the IVP notion of maximal cohesion — but cohesion itself is the more general idea, defined for any rule, not only for IVP’s change-driver rule.

title: Cohesion and Knowledge Embodiment
text:
2 The knowledge-embodiment theorem
The theorem connects this structural measure to an epistemic one.
cohesion(M)=(1,1)⇔Knowledge(M)=KP(Ci) \text{cohesion}(M) = (1, 1) \iff \text{Knowledge}(M) = K_P(C_i) 
A module has maximal cohesion under a rule PP if and only if it embodies exactly the knowledge its PP-class must hold — every knowledge piece its class requires, and no knowledge piece its class must not hold.
In words: maximal cohesion is maximal knowledge embodiment. Get the structure exactly right, and the module’s knowledge is exactly right, with no separate effort.
This is why the result lives in the cohesion theory. It is a statement about cohesion — it says what maximal cohesion means epistemically. IVP supplies one particular partitioning rule (the change-driver rule); the theorem itself is about cohesion in general.

title: Cohesion and Knowledge Embodiment
text:
3 What maximal cohesion guarantees
A maximally cohesive module has four structural properties.

The module is epistemically self-contained. No knowledge its class must hold resides outside; no foreign knowledge resides inside.
The change radius is bounded. When a change driver governing the class’s knowledge activates, every affected element is in one module.
The module is independently verifiable. Correctness is checked against the class’s own knowledge, with no external consultation.
The module is independently replaceable. A replacement need only embody the same knowledge and answer to the same change drivers.

These are the structural conditions that underlie the benefits of modular programming under information hiding.

title: Cohesion and Knowledge Embodiment
text:
4 What it does not guarantee
The phrase “maximal cohesion is correct embodiment” is easily over-read as “maximal cohesion is total correctness.” It is not.
A system has three distinct properties that this phrase blurs:

Placement — the right knowledge sits in the right modules. This is what cohesion measures.
Faithful embodiment — each piece present is realized correctly. This is functional correctness.
Dependency parsimony — the dependencies among elements are the ones the purpose requires.

These three are independent. A module can score maximal cohesion and be wrong (one element computes its piece incorrectly). A module can be maximally cohesive and faithful yet carry an unneeded dependency. A system can be entirely faithful and badly placed.
Cohesion governs the cost of achieving and maintaining correctness — the scope that must be read and the radius that must change — not whether the system is correct. A correct system may be incohesive and expensive to keep correct; a cohesive system may be incorrect and cheap to repair.

title: Cohesion and Knowledge Embodiment
text:
5 The knowledge floor
At maximal cohesion across all partition-inducing rules, every knowledge piece resides in exactly one module, and the system’s relevant causal domain knowledge is partitioned across exactly as many modules as there are classes. This is a theoretical lower bound on module count — a structural minimum, not a practical recommendation. Subdividing within a class for readability or team structure is freely available.

title: Cohesion and Knowledge Embodiment
section: 6 Where this sits in the theory
text:
6 Where this sits in the theory
The knowledge-embodiment theorem is proved in the published paper on the nature of cohesion [1], where cohesion is defined as correctness relative to a partitioning rule and the equivalence between maximal cohesion and maximal knowledge embodiment is established.
IVP and cohesion are related but distinct. IVP is the principle that groups elements by change-driver assignment. Cohesion is the more general measure of correctness relative to any partitioning rule. The change-driver rule is one instance of that general idea — the instance IVP is built on.

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
text:
Design dashboards like one number per module. Complexity, coupling, cohesion — a single score, a colour, a flag. This page shows why, for cohesion, one number cannot decide whether an element is well placed. The failure is not a matter of precision or of a poorly chosen formula. It is structural, and it has four independent causes.
A module can deviate from its rule in two opposite ways — it can hold elements that do not belong, or it can be missing elements that do. These two defects call for opposite repairs, and no single number can tell them apart. The rest of this page proves that claim and its companions.
crumbs: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
text:
1 The setting
Cohesion is correctness relative to a partitioning rule [1]. A rule PP sorts the element set EE into equivalence classes [e]P[e]_P — the elements that belong together. A module M⊆EM \subseteq E complies when its boundary coincides with its class: M=[e]PM = [e]_P for every e∈Me \in M. Otherwise it deviates in one of two ways:

Impurity. MM contains elements from another class. The remedy is to remove them — to split.
Incompleteness. Some element of the module’s class lies outside MM. The remedy is to add it — to merge.

Assess a module MM against a class CC (the class it should realize). Write
purity(M)=|M∩C||M|,completeness(M)=|M∩C||C|.
\text{purity}(M) = \frac{|M \cap C|}{|M|},
\qquad
\text{completeness}(M) = \frac{|M \cap C|}{|C|}.

Both values lie in [0,1][0,1]. Purity is 11 exactly when MM has no foreign element; completeness is 11 exactly when MM is missing no member of CC. A module is fully cohesive precisely when both are 11.
The question of this page: can a single real number s(M)s(M) stand in for this pair and decide placement — issue the statement “this element is incorrectly placed”?
Two notions make the question precise.
Principled scalar. A function s(e,M,ℳ,E,R,P)→ℝs(e, M, \mathcal{M}, E, R, P) \to \mathbb{R} that may consult the principle PP as well as the structure — but whose output is one real number.
Verdict-deciding. ss decides placement iff there is an interpretation d:ℝ→{correct,incorrect}d: \mathbb{R} \to \{\text{correct}, \text{incorrect}\} with d(s(e,M))=VP(e,M)d(s(e,M)) = V_P(e,M) for every system and every element-module pair. (The module-level form s(M)s(M) is read the same way; the verdict is uniform across a module, so s(M)s(M) assigns one verdict to every element of MM.)
Four failure modes follow. They run from the strongest restriction on the metric — it cannot even see the rule — to the weakest — it sees everything and still adds nothing.
crumbs: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
section: 2 Failure mode 1 — the metric cannot see the rule
text:
2 Failure mode 1 — the metric cannot see the rule
Suppose the number is computed from the structure alone: from EE, RR, and the module MM, with no access to PP. Then it cannot decide placement, whatever its formula and whatever its precision.
Example. Let E={a,b}E = \{a, b\} and R=∅R = \emptyset, and let the module under test be M={a}M = \{a\}.

Under P1P_1 with a single class {a,b}\{a, b\}, we have [a]P1={a,b}≠M[a]_{P_1} = \{a,b\} \neq M, so aa is incorrectly placed (the module is missing bb).
Under P2P_2 with classes {a},{b}\{a\}, \{b\}, we have [a]P2={a}=M[a]_{P_2} = \{a\} = M, so aa is correctly placed.

The two systems present identical structural inputs — same EE, same RR, same MM — to any structural function, so such a function returns the same number for both. Yet the verdicts differ. No formula over the structure alone can be correct on both, at any level of precision.
This is the principle-blindness obstruction: the structure (E,R)(E,R) underdetermines PP, so “correct” — which is meaningless without PP — cannot be read off it. The constructive cell is also visible: give the metric access to PP and it can compare MM with [e]P[e]_P. But access alone is not enough, as the next three results show.

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
section: 3 Failure mode 2 — one axis collapses two opposite defects
text:
3 Failure mode 2 — one axis collapses two opposite defects
Grant the metric full access to PP, but let it return one number per module, built from the two-axis pair: s(M)=g(purity(M),completeness(M))s(M) = g(\text{purity}(M), \text{completeness}(M)) for some g:[0,1]2→ℝg: [0,1]^2 \to \mathbb{R}.

Proposition (aggregation ambiguity). (a) If gg is symmetric — g(p,c)=g(c,p)g(p,c) = g(c,p) — there are two modules with opposite defects and opposite remedies whose scores are exactly equal. (b) If gg is continuous and strictly increasing in each argument, the two classes of defect are indistinguishable to any measurement precision, and no threshold on the score separates them.

Proof. Fix a rule PP with a class CC of size 44, and four foreign elements x1,…,x4x_1, \dots, x_4 all belonging to another class.

Let M1=C∪{x1,x2,x3,x4}M_1 = C \cup \{x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4\}, so |M1|=8|M_1| = 8. Then purity(M1)=4/8=1/2\text{purity}(M_1) = 4/8 = 1/2 and completeness(M1)=4/4=1\text{completeness}(M_1) = 4/4 = 1: impure but complete — the remedy is to remove the four foreign elements.
Let M2={a,b}M_2 = \{a, b\} for two elements a,b∈Ca, b \in C. Then purity(M2)=2/2=1\text{purity}(M_2) = 2/2 = 1 and completeness(M2)=2/4=1/2\text{completeness}(M_2) = 2/4 = 1/2: pure but incomplete — the remedy is to add the two missing members.

Both modules can be realized in one system (E,R,P)(E, R, P).
(a) By symmetry, s(M1)=g(1/2,1)=g(1,1/2)=s(M2)s(M_1) = g(1/2, 1) = g(1, 1/2) = s(M_2): the scores coincide exactly, while the defects and the required repairs are opposite. The geometric mean g(p,c)=pcg(p,c) = \sqrt{pc} scores both modules at 1/21/\sqrt{2}.
(b) Consider the two boundary curves B1={(p,1):0<p<1}B_1 = \{(p, 1) : 0 < p < 1\} (impure-but-complete) and B2={(1,c):0<c<1}B_2 = \{(1, c) : 0 < c < 1\} (pure-but-incomplete). Because gg is strictly increasing, g(1,1)g(1,1) is the supremum of gg on both curves; because gg is continuous, each image g(B1)g(B_1), g(B2)g(B_2) is an interval with that same supremum. Two intervals with a common supremum overlap: there exist (p*,1)∈B1(p^*, 1) \in B_1 and (1,c*)∈B2(1, c^*) \in B_2 with g(p*,1)=g(1,c*)g(p^*, 1) = g(1, c^*). So an impure-but-complete module and a pure-but-incomplete module share the same score, and in their neighbourhood the two classes of module are indistinguishable to any finite precision. An interpretation that reads the failure mode off intervals of the score line therefore misclassifies achievable modules — there is no threshold that separates “remove foreign elements” from “add missing members.” ◼\blacksquare
The single number says something is wrong. It cannot say what, and the two repairs point in opposite directions.

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
section: 4 Failure mode 3 — a number cannot name the element
text:
4 Failure mode 3 — a number cannot name the element
Even a scalar that could read the defect from the score still could not say which element to move. Suppose ss is name-invariant: renaming the elements — carrying one system to another by a bijection σ\sigma with R′=σ(R)R' = \sigma(R), P′=σ∘P∘σ−1P' = \sigma \circ P \circ \sigma^{-1}, ℳ′=σ(ℳ)\mathcal{M}' = \sigma(\mathcal{M}) — leaves the score unchanged, sS′(σ(M))=sS(M)s_{S'}(\sigma(M)) = s_S(M). Any function deserving the name “measurement of the configuration” is name-invariant.

Proposition (no localization). A name-invariant module-level scalar cannot identify the repair target. There are two systems with the same element set, the same module MM, and the same score, whose minimal repairs move different elements.

Proof. Let E={a,b,c,x}E = \{a, b, c, x\}, let R=∅R = \emptyset, and let M={a,b,x}M = \{a, b, x\}.

System 1. P1P_1 induces classes {a,b}\{a, b\} and {c,x}\{c, x\}. Then MM is not a P1P_1-class, and the unique one-move repair is to remove xx: M\{x}={a,b}M \setminus \{x\} = \{a, b\} is a P1P_1-class, while no other single move produces one.
System 2. P2P_2 induces classes {a,x}\{a, x\} and {c,b}\{c, b\}. Again MM is not a class, and the unique one-move repair is to remove bb: M\{b}={a,x}M \setminus \{b\} = \{a, x\}.

Now take the transposition σ=(bx)\sigma = (b\ x), which exchanges bb and xx and fixes aa and cc. It carries system 1 to system 2: σ({a,b})={a,x}\sigma(\{a,b\}) = \{a,x\}, σ({c,x})={c,b}\sigma(\{c,x\}) = \{c,b\}, σ(R)=R\sigma(R) = R, and σ(M)=M\sigma(M) = M (the set {a,b,x}\{a,b,x\} is fixed as a set).
By name-invariance, sS2(M)=sS2(σ(M))=sS1(M)s_{S_2}(M) = s_{S_2}(\sigma(M)) = s_{S_1}(M): the score is the same in both systems. But the repair targets differ — xx in system 1, bb in system 2. A designer observing only the score cannot tell the two configurations apart. And the obstruction is structural, not a matter of resolution: a score fine-grained enough to point at xx rather than bb would have to change under the transposition σ\sigma — and would thereby cease to be name-invariant, that is, cease to measure the configuration. ◼\blacksquare

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
section: 5 Failure mode 4 — a scalar that decides is the rule in disguise
text:
5 Failure mode 4 — a scalar that decides is the rule in disguise
The first three results say a measurement-like scalar fails. The fourth closes the other direction: a scalar that does decide placement adds nothing.

Proposition (degeneracy). Any scalar that decides placement is threshold-equivalent to the rule’s own binary verdict.

Proof. Suppose ss decides placement via dd, in either the element-level form s(e,M)s(e,M) or the module-level form s(M)s(M). Let T={x∈ℝ:d(x)=correct}T = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : d(x) = \text{correct}\}, the preimage of the “correct” verdict. Then, using the definition of the verdict, s(e,M)∈T⇔d(s(e,M))=correct⇔VP(e,M)=correct⇔M=[e]P.
s(e, M) \in T \iff d(s(e,M)) = \text{correct} \iff V_P(e,M) = \text{correct} \iff M = [e]_P .
 So the indicator 1[M=[e]P]1[M = [e]_P] is recovered from the scalar by a single threshold test. (For the module-level form, the same unfolding gives s(M)∈T⇔Ms(M) \in T \iff M is a PP-class, since the verdict is uniform across a module.)
The real-valued structure — magnitude, ordering, continuity, distance from the threshold — contributes nothing to the decision. Any two verdict-deciding scalars induce the same partition of element-module pairs, the partition the rule already defines: one scalar might use [0,1][0,1] with threshold 0.50.5, another ℝ\mathbb{R} with threshold 00, but the partition is identical. ◼\blacksquare
crumbs: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
section: 6 The four modes cover every scalar
text:
6 The four modes cover every scalar
The results assemble into a trichotomy. Every scalar aimed at the placement verdict either lacks the principle, has it but fails to decide, or decides only degenerately.

Principle-blind. No measurement without PP decides placement (failure mode 1).
Non-deciding. With PP, a scalar may fail to decide. For the measurement-like classes the failure is provable: a scalar factoring through the purity/completeness pair cannot determine the failure mode (failure mode 2), and a name-invariant scalar cannot identify the repair target (failure mode 3).
Degenerate. With PP, any scalar that decides placement is threshold-equivalent to the rule’s binary verdict (failure mode 4).

In every case the placement verdict originates in the partitioning rule, not in a number. A number can repeat the rule’s verdict on a module; only the rule can say what is wrong and which element must move.
crumbs: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
section: 7 What the scalar is still good for — and what it is not
text:
7 What the scalar is still good for — and what it is not
The result is a limit on deciding. It does not by itself say that a scalar has no practical use — but the usual consolation is weaker than it sounds.
The consolation runs: even if a number cannot decide, it can rank modules for inspection — which to examine first, which grouping looks most suspect. But a ranking asks the scalar to do exactly what the proposition forbids: order modules by comparing an impurity defect with an incompleteness defect on a single line. Any such order presupposes an aggregate g(purity,completeness)g(\text{purity}, \text{completeness}) and, with it, an exchange rate between “an element that does not belong” and “a class member that is missing.” The two axes are independent and incommensurable; nothing in the rule or the domain fixes that rate. Change the aggregate — product, arithmetic mean, weighted sum — and the same modules are ordered differently: a designer ranking by pc\sqrt{pc} and one ranking by 0.7p+0.3c0.7p + 0.3c will name different modules as most suspect, and the rule adjudicates nothing between them.
So even the attention-directing use rests on a convention, not on cohesion. What survives without arbitration is only the degenerate bit: whether a module sits at (1,1)(1,1) or below it — the rule’s own verdict, reproduced by a threshold. Everything finer is a chosen weighting. A scalar score can therefore flag that a module is not a class, and a designer may adopt a heuristic order to decide where to look first — but the order is not grounded in the theory, is not invariant across aggregates, and two defensible scores need not agree.
A separate and weaker point concerns empirical use: structural scores have been reported to correlate with fault-proneness and maintenance effort, so they can serve as screening signals and change predictors. That is a statistical fact about a proxy for change, not a claim that the score measures cohesion — and it does not repair the arbitrariness of ranking by the score.
The impossibility still bites when the score is asked to issue the verdict — to declare an element misplaced from the number alone, without comparing the module against the rule. There, the score is not merely arbitrary; it is the rule in disguise.
crumbs: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
text:
8 Where this comes from
The cohesion schema — correctness relative to a partitioning rule, and the (purity, completeness) pair — is defined and developed in On the Nature of Cohesion [1]. The constructive alternative it points to is the per-rule pair for diagnosis, and the rule PP itself for the verdict. The companion page Why two metrics are necessary proves that the pair is the minimal adequate output for a single rule.


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

On the Nature of Cohesion: Cohesion as Correctness Relative to a Partitioning Rule — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21703193

title: Coupling: Core Conclusions
text: The coupling series supplies what the coupling literature has never had: an ontological account of what coupling is across all its manifestations. Five decades of dimensions, metrics, and measurement frameworks produced no such account. This page collects what the coupling series concludes.

title: Coupling: Core Conclusions
section: 1 Coupling is access to a shared resource
text:
1 Coupling is access to a shared resource
The central definitional result: two elements are coupled exactly when they access a shared resource.
A resource is anything whose definition, state, or capacity constrains the elements that share it — a module’s interface, a type definition, a database schema, a release pipeline, a team boundary, a deployment unit, a CPU core. A coupling is the ternary relation
(e1,r,e2) (e_1, r, e_2) 
— two entities together with the resource that links them. The resource is the medium of the coupling.
The definition is change-independent: coupling is a standing constraint that holds whether or not any change occurs. Interference and shared fate are couplings that need no change at all.

title: Coupling: Core Conclusions
section: 2 The recognized dimensions differ only in the resource
text:
2 The recognized dimensions differ only in the resource
Every recognized coupling dimension — structural, temporal, concurrency, semantic, platform — differs only in which resource is shared and how the sharing is enforced. There is no structural difference underneath.
The series provides a taxonomy of resource types organized by seven constraint-kinds (contract, store, medium, budget, authority, location, time) and three coupling modes (definitional, state, capacity). Each coupling dimension maps to its resource, its governing contract, and its enforcement mechanism.

title: Coupling: Core Conclusions
section: 3 Necessary coupling is to be made manifest, not minimized
text:
3 Necessary coupling is to be made manifest, not minimized
The visibility principle: coupling is not to be minimized but made manifest. Each shared resource is governed by an explicit contract whose violation is immediately detectable.
This reframes the classical imperative. The goal is not to eliminate coupling — coupling is a standing constraint of any system that shares resources — but to make it visible and governed. The directive applies to necessary coupling: the shared-resource edges the system genuinely requires. Accidental coupling is a different target, and it is removed, not merely made visible. The two directives are not in tension because they operate on disjoint edge sets — the visibility principle governs the edges the system needs, while the grouping result below removes the edges above the floor.

title: Coupling: Core Conclusions
section: 4 Grouping by identical resource-access minimizes accidental coupling
text:
4 Grouping by identical resource-access minimizes accidental coupling
From the coupling definition alone — without change drivers, Γ, or IVP — one result follows: grouping elements by identical resource-access sets
R(e1)=R(e2) R(e_1) = R(e_2) 
minimizes accidental coupling cost.
The series reveals a tripartite structure: E→ℛ→CE \to \mathcal{R} \to C. Every element accesses a set of resources; every resource is governed by a set of change drivers; the element’s change-driver set is derived, not primitive:
Γ(e)=⋃r∈R(e)D(r) \Gamma(e) = \bigcup_{r \in R(e)} D(r) 
This is why the coupling-side and cohesion-side derivations are two ends of the same refinement chain: the resource-set partition refines the Γ partition. Γ is derived from RR through the governance mapping.

title: Coupling: Core Conclusions
section: 5 Coupling is a consequence of cohesion
text:
5 Coupling is a consequence of cohesion
The classical imperative — “maximize cohesion, minimize coupling” — treats the two as independent objectives requiring a trade-off. The series proves otherwise: within any single dimension, coupling is a consequence of cohesion, and the coupling categories that modularization controls are diagnostic of cohesion defects, not independent design variables.
Coupling decomposes into eight mutually exclusive categories — the product of three binary partitions (internal/external, same-class/cross-class, necessary/not), parameterized by a partitioning rule. At maximal cohesion (purity = completeness = 1), all modularization-controlled coupling categories are empty.
The result: the normative decomposition simultaneously maximizes cohesion and minimizes avoidable coupling — one optimum, not two.

title: Coupling: Core Conclusions
text:
6 The coupling floor
There is an irreducible coupling the domain demands — the coupling floor. At correct boundaries, the floor equals the necessary dependency graph exactly; every edge above it is a boundary defect or an accidental edge.
Because coupling is measured against a partitioning rule, necessary coupling is rule-relative: the same edge that one concern demands be internal is, under another, demanded external. The imperative to “minimize coupling” has no fixed referent until the rule is fixed. A raw count cannot separate domain-mandated coupling from placement error.

title: Coupling: Core Conclusions
text:
7 Where the proofs live
The proofs — that coupling is access to a shared resource, that the resource-set partition uniquely minimizes accidental coupling, that coupling is a consequence of cohesion, the coupling floor — are in the published coupling papers: the definition of coupling as shared resource access in the paper on the nature of coupling [1], the derivation of the modularisation directive from coupling in the derivation paper [2], and the coupling floor and coupling-as-consequence-of-cohesion results in the decomposition paper [3].


The formal development. The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

On the Nature of Coupling: All Coupling as Shared Resource Access — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21925122
A Self-Contained Derivation of the Optimal Modularization from Coupling — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21925268
Coupling as a Consequence of Cohesion: Decomposition, the Coupling Floor, and Domain-Imposed Coupling — Zenodo, 2026 — doi:10.5281/zenodo.21925201
