title: MATLAB (R2026a)
text: This assessment applies the coupling account — coupling as access to a shared resource, and the coupling floor [1], [2] — and the knowledge-embodiment theorem [3]; the language is assessed against its official reference [4].

title: MATLAB (R2026a)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses MATLAB in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 39/100 · Ecosystem coupling 61/100 · Engineering readiness 42/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Dynamic typing with no static check (T1): A variable takes its type from the value assigned to it, so a type error is reported only when the statement runs
⚠️ A numeric value carries a class but no shape: double is the default for a literal, and a 1×1 scalar, a vector, and a matrix are the same class, so the type does not state the dimensions the algorithm needs
⚠️ Cell arrays and structs are weak structural types: They group heterogeneous values but declare no schema, so a consumer learns a struct’s fields from the code that fills it
⚠️ Only a package folder scopes a name: A +pkg folder gives its functions and classes their own namespace, but a plain function or script on the search path shares one flat name space with every other file on the path, so a collision is resolved by path order
⚠️ Argument validation is opt-in: An arguments block (R2019b+) checks class, size, and shape at call time, but a function without one accepts anything



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Toolboxes separate domain computation from the core language: Signal Processing, Control System, and Image Processing operations are ordinary function calls, so an algorithm does not embed its own filter or transform code
✅ A classdef file groups state with its operations: Properties and methods are declared in one unit, so a consumer binds to the class name
❌ Global mutable state by default (C1): The base workspace and every shared function workspace hold variables that running code can read and overwrite at any time
❌ No immutability by default (C2): Every array is mutable, and there is no const-like freeze for ordinary data
⚠️ Constructors are ordinary methods with no enforced invariant: A class defines its own Name(...) constructor, so a well-formed instance depends on the author’s validation
⚠️ Scripts run in the caller’s workspace: A variable a script creates stays in the caller after the script returns, so a script couples to every caller’s variable names



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Copy-on-modify protects the reader: An assignment copies a value only when the copy is modified, so a function that receives an array does not change the caller’s value
⚠️ The collector runs on its own schedule (M2): Memory returns when the interpreter decides, so release timing is not owned by the code
❌ No RAII (M3): There is no block-scoped destructor, so a file handle, timer, or instrument connection stays open until delete or an onCleanup object runs
❌ No ownership model (M4): No static lifetime or aliasing rule ties an array’s storage to one owner
⚠️ clear and pack are manual controls: Freeing a large array and defragmenting the workspace are explicit calls, so the memory strategy is the programmer’s



1.1.4 Error

✅ try/catch gives a structured recovery path: A catch block receives the MException object, with its identifier, message, and stack, so recovery need not parse text
✅ error takes a stable identifier: error('pkg:func:reason', ...) sets MException.identifier, so a caller can branch on the code rather than on the message
❌ Unchecked exceptions only (Er2): A raised MException travels up until something catches it or the program stops, and no caller is required to handle it
⚠️ An empty catch is common in legacy code: A catch block with no body discards the failure without a trace
⚠️ Many failures are detected only at run time: An out-of-bound index, a class mismatch, or a singular matrix is reported when the statement executes



1.1.5 Concurrency

⚠️ Manual synchronisation with no race detection (K3): parfor, spmd, and parfeval leave the shared-variable reasoning to the programmer, and the language reports no data race
✅ parfor separates loop iterations: An independent loop is split across workers, so iteration order is not part of the result
✅ labSend and labReceive pass data between spmd workers: A worker sends a value to a named peer instead of writing into shared memory
⚠️ The parallel constructs need the Parallel Computing Toolbox: parfor, distributed arrays, and parpool are a separate licensed product
⚠️ A captured variable is broadcast to every worker: A parfor body sees a copy of the outer variable, and a reduction must use a supported form or a temporary variable



1.1.6 Platform

✅ GNU Octave is a compatible open implementation: Most MATLAB programs run under Octave, so a project is not bound to one vendor’s binary alone
⚠️ A licence still governs the base product: An installation of MATLAB itself needs a licence, so deployment and continuous integration depend on MathWorks’ terms and pricing
⚠️ Toolbox coverage is proprietary: Domain functions come from licensed MathWorks toolboxes, so portability depends on which toolboxes the code calls
⚠️ A compiled component still needs the MATLAB Runtime: MATLAB Compiler builds a library callable from C, C++, .NET, or Python, but the component runs against a version-matched MATLAB Runtime



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

One-based indexing is a convention choice: Starting an array at index 1 is a documented decision, and the cost is re-learning for a user who comes from a zero-based language
The global workspace suits interactive work: A session-wide namespace is convenient at the command line, and the coupling it creates at scale follows from using session state as program state
Everything-is-an-array is a deliberate uniformity: One container for scalars, vectors, matrices, and N-D arrays keeps the language small, and the loss of shape in the type is the price
The filename rule is a lookup convention: A function file is named for its entry point, and local functions in scripts (a later addition) reduce the constraint
A proprietary platform is traded for an integrated toolchain: The licence buys one install, one editor, and one support channel
Scripts are for session-scale tasks: Converting a script to a function removes the caller-workspace coupling




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Matrix expressions call tuned BLAS and LAPACK libraries: A*B, A\b, and fft run in compiled libraries, so numerical throughput does not depend on hand-written loops
✅ Vectorisation removes per-element interpreter overhead: One array expression is one interpreted call, whatever the element count
⚠️ The interpreter performs no ahead-of-time compilation (R1): Base MATLAB executes an interpreted form, so a loop that cannot be vectorised is slower than its compiled equivalent
✅ The execution engine compiles eligible code just in time: The engine introduced in R2015b accelerates a repeated loop after warm-up
⚠️ Speed follows the shipped library, not the source: The cost of a signal-processing or control operation depends on the toolbox build and on the CPU it was tuned for



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is proprietary (Ec4): Toolboxes, the editor, and the reference documentation come from one vendor under licence
✅ The toolbox library covers most engineering fields: Optimization, Statistics and Machine Learning, Signal Processing, and Control System toolboxes are long-established products
✅ The Add-On Explorer installs packages by name: MathWorks and community add-ons are installed through one manager, so a project does not have to vendor source
✅ MATLAB Central File Exchange is a large community index: User-contributed functions and toolboxes are published together and searchable
⚠️ Toolboxes ship in lockstep with the release: A toolbox is versioned for the MATLAB release it targets, so an upgrade can require every toolbox to move
⚠️ Every tool in the chain assumes a licensed installation: Editors and continuous-integration integrations exist, but they resolve back to a licensed MATLAB



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Backward compatibility is a stated commitment: MathWorks keeps old syntax working and warns before a feature is removed, so a program from an earlier release generally still runs
✅ Two releases a year on a known cadence: R2026a and R2026b follow a predictable schedule, so an upgrade path can be planned
✅ verLessThan lets one source span two releases: A program can branch on the MATLAB version, so an old and a new release can be supported together
⚠️ An upgrade can change performance or a default: A new execution engine, a new library version, or a changed default can alter timing or output for code that relied on the old behaviour
⚠️ A deprecated function may stop working later: Deprecation is announced, but a function or toolbox marked for removal eventually goes away



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for numerical linear algebra: Matrix syntax, \ for a linear solve, and N-D arrays match the mathematics directly
✅ Signal processing, control systems, and image processing are first-class domains: Each ships as an endorsed toolbox with the reference algorithms
❌ Domain and vendor lock-in (D1): The language and its library set target one vendor’s platform, so adoption is also a procurement decision
⚠️ Simulink is a second modelling toolchain: A graphical model is not MATLAB source, so a control design that uses Simulink couples to a second product and file format
⚠️ General application work sits outside the design centre: File handling, text processing, and network code read as additions to a numerical language



1.2.5 Learning

⚠️ Moderate at the start and steeper later (L1): A\b and 1:n are learnable in days, while vectorisation, the workspace model, and copy semantics take practice
⚠️ The workspace model confuses newcomers: A variable a script creates persists in the caller, so a beginner cannot tell where state lives
⚠️ One-based indexing diverges from most languages: Code ported from a C-family or Python source needs every index checked by hand
✅ Documentation is uniform and complete: Every function has a reference page with examples, and the language is taught in standard textbooks
⚠️ Toolbox knowledge is separate from language knowledge: Finding the right function means knowing which toolbox owns the domain



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Matrix-oriented and compact: A(:, 2) = A(:, 1) * 3; expresses a whole-column operation in one statement
✅ Keyword-light and readable: Most statements are operations on data, with few punctuation-only constructs
⚠️ Element-wise and matrix operators differ by one dot: * versus .* and ^ versus .^ are distinct operations, so a missing dot silently changes the computation
⚠️ end is overloaded: It terminates a block and marks the last index inside a subscript
⚠️ The semicolon controls output rather than the statement: A missing ; prints every intermediate result, which clutters a long run



1.2.7 Testing

✅ A test framework ships in the base product: matlab.unittest.TestCase, functiontests, and runtests provide assertions, fixtures, and parameterised cases
✅ A failure reports the value and the assertion: The framework prints the constraint that failed and the observed value, so a failure is localised
✅ Mocking and coverage are part of the framework: matlab.mock creates replacement objects, and the code-coverage plugin reports unexecuted lines
⚠️ A test suite lives in function files beside the code: There is no separate test manifest, so a suite’s scope follows the folder layout
⚠️ Automated runs need a licence: Continuous integration needs a licence seat or a pre-built component with the MATLAB Runtime



1.2.8 Security

✅ No pointers and no manual memory access: The language offers no address arithmetic, so a buffer overflow cannot be written in MATLAB source
✅ External access is explicit in the source: fopen, readmatrix, and webread are visible calls, so a reader can see every file and network access
⚠️ eval, evalin, and str2func execute text as code: A string built from untrusted input can become a statement, which is the injection pattern
⚠️ load can introduce undeclared variables: Restoring a .mat file creates variables whose names the source does not state, and such a name can shadow a live variable
⚠️ Static proof of run-time error freedom needs a separate product: Polyspace Code Prover proves the absence of certain run-time errors, but it is licensed apart from the language




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

⚠️ One vendor decides the language’s direction.
⚠️ The specification is not public.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [5]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [6].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [7].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: MATLAB’s design yields moderate language-imposed coupling for numerical engineering work. Matrix operations remove per-element iteration from the source, and toolboxes separate domain algorithms from the core language. title: R (4.5)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses R in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 47/100 · Ecosystem coupling 50/100 · Engineering readiness 61/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Dynamic typing with no static check (T1): A value carries its type at run time, so a type error surfaces when the expression evaluates
⚠️ An atomic vector holds one type and coerces silently: c(1, "a") becomes a character vector with no error, so a mixed vector changes type
⚠️ A factor stores integer level codes behind printed labels: A comparison and an ordering can therefore differ from the text a reader sees
⚠️ library() copies a package’s exported names onto the search path: A package has its own namespace and pkg::name reaches any of its objects, but the habitual library(pkg) attaches the exports to the search path, so two packages that export one name collide and the later attachment masks the earlier
✅ A function is a first-class value with its own type: is.function, formals, and body expose a function as data
⚠️ Attributes travel with a value invisibly: A names, class, or dim attribute changes dispatch and printing, so two values that print alike can behave differently



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A data frame is the central structured-data abstraction: Named columns of one length form a table, and a model function accepts it without knowing how it was built
✅ Functions are first-class and an environment is a lexical home: A function can be stored, passed, and returned, and it closes over its defining environment, so deliberate state is possible as a closure instead of a global
✅ The formula interface separates a model from a caller’s data: y ~ x1 + x2 names the columns, so the same call works on any data frame that has them
❌ Global mutable state by default (C1): <- at top level writes into the global environment, and <<- writes into an enclosing environment, so a name is shared across the session
❌ No immutability by default (C2): A binding is assigned freely, and attr(x, "a") <- v, names(x) <- v, and a reference-class field change a value in place
⚠️ Many functions capture their arguments non-standardly: subset, with, and most modelling functions evaluate an argument inside a data frame, so the call does not follow the usual rule



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Copy-on-modify protects the reader: A value is copied only when the copy is modified, so a function that receives a vector does not change the caller’s value
⚠️ Copy-on-modify raises peak memory: Modifying a large object can duplicate it, so the footprint exceeds the logical size of the data
⚠️ The collector runs on R’s schedule (M2): Collection happens when R decides, and gc() reports heap use, but there is no block-scoped release
❌ No RAII (M3): There is no destructor at block exit, so a connection, a file, or a graphics device is closed by on.exit or explicitly
❌ No ownership model (M4): No static rule ties a value’s storage to one binding
✅ on.exit registers exit-time cleanup: An action runs when the function returns or raises, which is the R idiom for releasing a resource



1.1.4 Error

✅ Conditions are classed objects: stop, warning, and message signal a condition with a class, so a handler matches a class rather than a message string
✅ tryCatch separates recovery from cleanup: An exiting handler returns a value, and finally runs on every path
✅ withCallingHandlers allows a non-unwinding response: A handler can log a warning and let evaluation continue
❌ Unchecked exceptions only (Er2): A signalled condition propagates until something catches it, and no caller is required to handle it
⚠️ A warning is not an error: It prints and evaluation continues, so an ignored warning can leave a wrong result
⚠️ No composable result value: A failure is a thrown condition or a sentinel such as NULL or NA, so it does not compose through a call chain



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ parallel ships with the base distribution: mclapply forks workers on Unix, and makeCluster with parLapply runs across sockets, so independent work splits without a shared-memory protocol
✅ A socket cluster passes results, not shared state: A worker returns a value that is serialised back, so workers do not share an address space
✅ future and %dopar% give a declarative parallel surface: Code written for a sequential lapply is unchanged when it runs in parallel
⚠️ Base R evaluates one expression at a time: Vectorised operations are the usual substitute for a second thread
⚠️ A forked worker copies on write: mclapply shares the parent’s memory until a worker modifies it, and then it duplicates
⚠️ Reproducibility needs explicit seed handling: A parallel random stream requires clusterSetRNGStream or the future seed mechanism



1.1.6 Platform

✅ One open-source implementation with several distributors: The R Core Team maintains the interpreter under the GNU GPL, and CRAN ships source and binaries
✅ Official builds cover the three desktop platforms: Linux, macOS, and Windows binaries are published for each release
✅ The interpreter is not tied to one editor: RStudio, VS Code, Emacs ESS, and the plain console drive the same R
✅ Package installation is declarative: install.packages fetches from a named mirror, and renv records exact versions in a lockfile
⚠️ A source package with C or C++ needs a toolchain: The published binary avoids the compiler, but a source install needs headers and a linker



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Copy-on-modify is a deliberate trade: Immutability by copy protects callers and costs peak memory
Non-standard evaluation is a deliberate design: It makes subset(d, x > 1) and a formula interface readable and lets a modelling call record the variable names it was given, at the cost of evaluation that is not visible at the call site
The global environment is for interactive analysis: A session-wide namespace suits exploratory work at the console
A factor encodes categorical data: The hidden integer code is the price of ordered levels and of a compact representation
One-based indexing and <- are convention choices: They follow the S language and the statistics literature, so the cost is familiarity, not a forced dependency
R is for statistics, not general programming: The assumption of a data-analysis workload is a scope decision




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Vectorised and matrix operations call compiled C, C++, and BLAS/LAPACK code: colSums, %*%, and lm do their work in compiled libraries, so the interpreter is not in the inner loop
✅ A large set of compiled packages exists: data.table, Rcpp, and Matrix move hot paths into compiled code, and CRAN distributes them
⚠️ Interpreted with no ahead-of-time compilation (R1): Base R executes an interpreted form, so a scalar loop is slower than its compiled equivalent
⚠️ The just-in-time compiler helps only where it applies: The byte-code compiler (level 3, cmpfun) speeds up a loop, but the gain is bounded
⚠️ Memory pressure shows up as time: Copying and collection cost time that the source does not show



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ CRAN is a large, curated, central repository: Tens of thousands of packages pass an automated check before publication
✅ The RStudio IDE is a first-class environment: Console, source editor, plots, and a debugger sit in one window
✅ Reproducibility tooling is mature: renv records a project library, and a package manager can pin a date-based snapshot
⚠️ Package quality varies: The CRAN check verifies correctness and portability, not statistical validity, so a method needs its own reading
⚠️ A deployment needs the full environment: R, a build toolchain, and system libraries for compiled dependencies make a project heavier to ship than a single binary



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Backward compatibility is strong and documented: The Core Team publishes a NEWS file per release and keeps the language API stable, so an old script generally still runs
✅ A regular release cadence exists: An x.y.0 release appears each spring and a patch release follows in the same year
✅ The tidyverse and r-lib provide deprecation discipline: The lifecycle package marks a function as experimental, deprecated, or superseded before removal
⚠️ A third-party package can break across a major release: A package that used an internal API can fail after an upgrade, and the fix belongs to its maintainer
⚠️ A package can be archived from CRAN: An unmaintained package is removed from the index, so code that depends on it needs a replacement or a frozen snapshot



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for statistical computing: lm, glm, aov, and t.test are in the base distribution with a formula interface
✅ CRAN and Bioconductor cover the applied fields: Biostatistics, econometrics, time series, and genomics each have dedicated packages
✅ A report is generated from the analysis itself: knitr, rmarkdown, and Quarto run the code and place its output in the document
❌ Domain lock-in to statistics and data analysis (D1): The core value types, the formula interface, and the modelling packages assume a data-analysis workflow
⚠️ A production service in R is unusual: A service with a high request rate is usually written elsewhere and calls R for the model



1.2.5 Learning

⚠️ Steep (L1): The idioms — vectorisation, the apply family, environments, and S3 dispatch — take time for a programmer from an imperative language
⚠️ Non-standard evaluation surprises newcomers: An argument can be evaluated inside a data frame, so subset and dplyr code does not follow the usual call rule
⚠️ Factor semantics are unfamiliar: A factor compares by its integer level code, so an ordering or a comparison can differ from the printed text
⚠️ The apply family is confusing: sapply varies its return type with the input, so a result is not predictable from the call alone
✅ Documentation is generated, complete, and mandated: Every CRAN package must document every exported function, and ? reaches the reference page



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The formula interface and the pipe are compact: y ~ x and x |> f() read as a data pipeline
✅ Indexing follows one rule across atomic, list, and data-frame values: [, [[, and $ behave consistently, so a new structure needs no new syntax
⚠️ Two assignment operators exist: <- binds a name in the current environment, and = also assigns at top level but separates a named argument inside a call, so the meaning depends on position
⚠️ . is overloaded: It means every other variable in a formula and the piped value in a magrittr pipe
⚠️ A print method hides structure: Printing a data frame or a model object shows a summary, so str() is needed to see the actual shape



1.2.7 Testing

✅ testthat is the de facto standard framework: It provides expectations, a runner, and a per-file test structure
✅ A package must pass R CMD check: CRAN runs the check, which executes the tests and the examples, so a package is not published with a failing test
✅ Property-based and snapshot testing exist: hedgehog generates inputs, and a testthat snapshot records output for comparison
✅ Interactive debugging is available: browser(), traceback(), debug(), and the RStudio debugger stop at a line and inspect its environment
⚠️ Errors are runtime-only (G3): A type error appears when the line runs, so the test suite is what reaches the untested path
⚠️ A suite depends on the installed environment: The tests run through the package machinery, so the environment must be installed first



1.2.8 Security

❌ Known vulnerability/injection (Q3): eval(parse(text = ...)), do.call on a string, and system() turn text into code or a command, so concatenated input is an injection surface
❌ Dynamic typing carries its risk into security code: A check written for one class can pass an object of another class, and dispatch then runs a different method
⚠️ system2 reduces but does not remove shell risk: It passes arguments as a vector, yet a shell is still involved
⚠️ load and readRDS restore an object, not only data: A serialised object can carry an environment, so restoring untrusted state is a code-execution path
⚠️ The interpreter runs with the user’s full privileges: R has no sandbox of its own, so code in a session has the user’s access to files and the network
✅ CRAN policy limits what a package may do: Network access and writes outside the temporary directory are restricted during install and check




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

❌ Interpreted by default: the slowest class in the energy and time benchmarks [5]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [6].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [7].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

title: SQL (ANSI SQL:2023)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses SQL in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 85/100 · Ecosystem coupling 80/100 · Engineering readiness 76/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Static column typing: Every column, parameter, and result column has a declared type, checked when the statement is prepared or planned
✅ Schema is declared independently of queries: A table declares its structure once; queries consume it without redeclaring it
❌ No sum types: A column carries one scalar type, so alternatives are modelled with nullable columns or separate tables and the caller must know the encoding (T4)
❌ No generics: There is no type parameter, so reuse across types is done by generating DDL, not by the type system (T5)
❌ NULL is not type-safe absence: NULL is compatible with every domain, three-valued logic propagates through expressions, and NULL = NULL is unknown rather than true (T10)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Declarative query construction: A statement states the result set, and the engine chooses the access path, so construction does not couple to a storage layout or an algorithm
✅ Views separate consumers from the query behind them: A view exposes a stable relation whose defining query can change without changing its consumers
✅ Set-based composition: Joins, unions, and subqueries compose relations, so logic composes without imperative sequencing or shared cursors
✅ Schema and use are separated: Tables declare the data, and normalisation stores each fact once so a fact duplicated across columns cannot drift out of agreement
⚠️ Triggers fire implicitly: A trigger runs in response to a data change, so the writer of a statement cannot see from the statement which code will run
⚠️ Stored procedures couple construction to the engine: SQL/PSM standardises persistent stored modules (Part 4 of ISO/IEC 9075), but the dialects used in practice — PL/pgSQL, PL/SQL, and T-SQL — share little beyond the basics, so the code depends on one engine



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No manual memory management: The storage engine owns buffers, caches, and page allocation, and a statement never names an address or frees anything
✅ No explicit allocation in queries: The engine materialises or streams a result set, so query text does not couple to a memory layout
✅ Resource limits are declarative configuration: Work memory and temp-file behaviour are engine settings, not properties the query must manage
⚠️ Large intermediate results still cost memory: An unbounded sort, hash join, or SELECT * spool can exhaust the engine’s memory even though the language hides allocation
⚠️ Materialised views and temporary tables persist engine-side state: They pin storage and need a refresh policy, coupling the data to a refresh lifecycle



1.1.4 Error

✅ Standard SQLSTATE: An error carries a five-character SQLSTATE class and subclass, so a handler matches a portable code instead of a message string
✅ Structured handlers in SQL/PSM: DECLARE ... HANDLER and EXCEPTION blocks separate the normal path from the recovery path
✅ Constraint violations are errors, not silent writes: A primary-key, foreign-key, UNIQUE, or CHECK violation aborts the statement
⚠️ Vendor error codes extend SQLSTATE: PostgreSQL SQLSTATE codes, Oracle ORA- numbers, and SQL Server error numbers differ outside the standard classes, so handlers are not portable
⚠️ Some failures depend on the data: Name and type errors are caught at prepare time, but division by zero, overflow, and constraint violations are detected only at execution



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Transactions group statements atomically: BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK make a unit of work commit or abort as one, so a statement does not coordinate with others by hand
✅ Isolation is selectable: READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE let the application declare the visibility contract it needs
✅ MVCC in PostgreSQL and Oracle: Readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers, so read and write traffic decouple
✅ Set-based statements reduce explicit locking: One UPDATE moves many rows without a row-by-row lock protocol in application code
⚠️ Default isolation permits anomalies: READ COMMITTED is the default in PostgreSQL, so non-repeatable reads and write skew are possible unless the application raises the level
⚠️ Explicit locking couples code to the engine: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, LOCK TABLE, and advisory locks are vendor-shaped and must agree with the lock ordering of the whole application



1.1.6 Platform

✅ A standard core is portable: DDL, DML, and joins written to core SQL run on PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server, Db2, and SQLite with little change
✅ Standard call interfaces: ODBC and JDBC let one client reach many engines, so an application does not bind to one engine’s binary protocol
✅ Multiple independent implementations: No single vendor owns the language, so the standard cannot be changed unilaterally
⚠️ Dialects diverge outside the core: String functions, date arithmetic, LIMIT versus FETCH FIRST, and window-function details differ by vendor
⚠️ Vendor extensions bind queries to one engine: JSON operators, array types, regex syntax, and identity or sequence clauses are engine-specific



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Denormalisation is a modelling choice: Storing a value in two places trades redundancy for fewer joins; the language permits it but does not force it
NULL versus NOT NULL is a modelling decision: Making a column nullable widens its value set, and the three-valued-logic cost follows from that decision, not from a forced dependency
The optimiser owns the execution plan: A declarative statement gives up control of access paths, so plan hints are a choice about how far to override the engine
Schema migration is a process, not a mechanism: Changing a column couples deploy order to schema version, but the coupling follows from sharing one schema, which is the purpose of a relational store
Vendor-specific SQL may be worth the portability cost: Writing to one dialect buys features and performance; the loss of portability is a deliberate trade, not a property of the language
SQL is not a general-purpose language: The assumption of a database engine and a set-based workload is a scope decision, not a coupling defect




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Decades of query-optimisation research: Cost-based planners, index selection, join reordering, and predicate pushdown produce good plans without hand-tuning in the common case
✅ Set-based execution: One statement moves many rows, so per-row interpreter overhead is amortised by the engine
✅ Indexes and partitions are declarative: An index is declared once and then used by any matching query
✅ Engines are written in C or C++ with mature storage layers: Throughput and buffer management are the engine’s responsibility, not the query’s
⚠️ Plan quality is an engine property: The same query can be fast on PostgreSQL and slow on another engine, and the language guarantees no plan
⚠️ Plans can regress without a query change: New statistics, a version upgrade, or changed data volume can select a worse plan



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ Tooling is fragmented by dialect: ORMs, migration tools, linters, and formatters commonly target one engine’s dialect, and there is no single SQL toolchain (Ec2)
✅ The standard interfaces are universal: ODBC, JDBC, and ADO.NET drivers exist for nearly every engine and host language
✅ Mature, independently maintained engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server, Db2, and SQLite are all long-lived and actively developed
✅ A very large body of published knowledge: Standards documents, engine manuals, and books are abundant and stable over decades



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The standard evolves slowly: SQL:2023 appeared six years after SQL:2016, so a needed feature can wait years for standardisation (V4)
✅ The language is broadly backward compatible: New editions add features and rarely remove them, so decades-old queries keep running
✅ Vendor implementations lead the standard: PostgreSQL, Oracle, and others ship features before standardisation, which gives users early access
⚠️ Adoption lags publication: An engine may take years to implement a newly standardised feature, so code written to the standard may not run everywhere yet



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for relational data: The model of relations, tuples, and set operations matches tabular data directly
✅ One language spans several data domains: Analytics with window functions, transactional writes with DML, and semi-structured data with SQL/JSON all live in the same language
✅ SQL/PGQ in SQL:2023 adds property-graph queries: Graph patterns are expressible without leaving SQL
⚠️ Procedural logic is awkward: Row-by-row algorithms and complex control flow read poorly in SQL/PSM and are usually pushed to a host language
⚠️ It is not a runtime for arbitrary programs: SQL assumes a database engine and a set-based workload, which limits use outside data management



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Basic queries are gentle: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE is readable and learnable within days
✅ The declarative surface hides the hard part: A beginner writes a correct query without knowing the plan the engine will choose
⚠️ Advanced work is steep: Query optimisation, join ordering, and window semantics take years to master
⚠️ NULL semantics surprise newcomers: Three-valued logic makes an intuitive predicate such as a <> 5 fail to match rows where a is NULL
⚠️ Dialect knowledge is required in practice: Beyond the standard core, a developer must learn one engine’s functions, types, and plan output



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Keyword-based and readable: Statements read close to English and do not lean on punctuation or symbols
✅ Compact for the result produced: A join and filter over several tables fits in a few lines
⚠️ DDL is verbose: CREATE TABLE, constraints, indexes, and ALTER TABLE statements are long and repetitive
⚠️ Identifier quoting differs by engine: Double quotes, backticks, and square brackets each mark an identifier in a different dialect



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Plan inspection is standard practice: PostgreSQL and MySQL report the chosen plan and actual timings through EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and Oracle and SQL Server expose equivalent plan and runtime statistics
✅ Constraints are executable invariants: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK, and NOT NULL reject bad data at write time, so tests need not re-check them
✅ Transactions isolate a test: A test can run inside a transaction and roll back, leaving the database unchanged
✅ Standard schema introspection: INFORMATION_SCHEMA and catalog views let tooling verify structure
⚠️ No in-language test framework: Test harnesses live in the host language, so a suite couples to the driver and to a fixture loader



1.2.8 Security

❌ Injection is the canonical failure: Because a statement is text, building it by concatenating untrusted input lets that input become code (Q3)
✅ Parameterised statements remove the injection surface: Bind variables and prepared statements carry data out of band, so a value cannot change the parse
✅ GRANT and REVOKE express least privilege: Access is declared per object and per role
✅ Views and row-level security restrict visibility: A view, or PostgreSQL row-level security, limits what a statement can see
⚠️ Dynamic SQL re-opens the risk: EXECUTE IMMEDIATE, dynamic PL/pgSQL, and string-built queries defeat parameterisation where they are unavoidable
⚠️ Definer’s-rights procedures can escalate: A procedure that runs with its definer’s rights (SECURITY DEFINER) can grant more access than intended unless it is audited

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

⚠️ No maintained portable target.

Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

Verdict: SQL’s design yields low language-imposed coupling for the work it is built for. The declarative model separates what a result is from how it is computed, and the schema separates data structure from the queries that consume it. Views decouple consumers from the query behind them, and transactions decouple statements from each other’s timing. Main strengths: the standard core is portable across many independent engines, types come from the schema, and a mature optimiser takes on execution plans. Main weaknesses: NULL is not type-safe, no sum types or generics exist, the standard moves slowly, tooling fragments by dialect, and a string-built statement is a standing injection hazard unless parameters are used.

title: Groovy (5.x)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Groovy in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 38/100 · Ecosystem coupling 80/100 · Engineering readiness 81/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

⚠️ Dynamic typing is the default: A def declaration defers method resolution to the runtime metaclass protocol, so a mismatch is reported when the line runs rather than when the file compiles (T1, T3)
✅ @CompileStatic and @TypeChecked restore compile-time checking: Groovy 2 and later can compile a class to direct bytecode, and the annotated class is checked in the manner of Java
⚠️ Generics are erased on the JVM: List<String> is a List at runtime, so a cast or a reflection call can reach a type the declaration does not admit (T7)
✅ Traits compose behaviour without inheritance: A trait may carry default methods and state, so behaviour is mixed in rather than inherited from a superclass
✅ Safe navigation separates the test from the call: a?.b short-circuits to null at the point of use, so the absence test stands where the value is read
⚠️ Operator overloading is by method name: a + b may call plus and a[i] may call getAt, so a dense expression can invoke user code the syntax does not show (T8)



1.1.2 Construction

⚠️ Mutability is the default: A field is mutable unless it is final or the class is annotated @Immutable (C2)
✅ GroovyBeans generate the accessors: A property declaration is compiled with its getter and setter, so the boilerplate leaves the source
✅ Map constructors separate the arguments from their order: new Point(x: 1, y: 2) names each value at the call site, so the call does not depend on positional order
✅ @Immutable makes a value type in one annotation: It generates the tuple constructor, equals, hashCode, and a defensive copy of the fields
⚠️ AST transformations decide the shape at compile time: @Canonical, @TupleConstructor, and @Builder generate constructors whose signatures are not written in the source



1.1.3 Memory

❌ The JVM owns deallocation: There is no free operation, and a collection is scheduled outside the program’s control (M2)
⚠️ No RAII: @Cleanup and withCloseable release a resource at the end of a declared block, but nothing runs automatically at the end of an arbitrary scope (M3)
❌ No ownership model: A reference may alias or be shared freely, and the collector decides when the object dies (M4)
✅ withCloseable binds release to a closure: stream.withCloseable { ... } closes the resource when the block returns, including on an exception
✅ @Cleanup names the release point: A local annotated @Cleanup is closed at the end of its enclosing block
✅ Collection is invisible in the source: An allocation is a new, and no deallocation call is ever written



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked: Groovy requires no throws clause and the compiler does not check that a handler exists, so an exception may propagate from any call (Er2)
✅ try/catch/finally is the structured path: A catch clause names the type it handles, and finally runs on every exit
✅ @TypeChecked turns a type error into a compile error: A call to a method that does not exist fails the build rather than the run
⚠️ Dynamic dispatch failure is a runtime exception: A missing method or property raises MissingMethodException or MissingPropertyException at the call
⚠️ ?. and ?: suppress a failure by design: Safe navigation returns null where an exception would otherwise report the fault



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ The JDK concurrency library is available: Thread, synchronized, java.util.concurrent executors, and atomics are reached directly
✅ @Synchronized puts the monitor on the declaration: The annotation transformation wraps a method in the object’s monitor, so the lock is stated beside the method
✅ GPars adds dataflow, actors, and parallel collections: The abstractions are a library over the JDK, so a concurrent design is not limited to threads and locks
⚠️ Shared mutable state is the default: A field is reachable by every thread, and the compiler checks no access pattern (K2)
❌ No structured concurrency in the language: A task tree, a scope, and a join are the JDK executor’s responsibility, and Groovy adds no scope construct of its own (K4)



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Runs on the JVM and interoperates with Java: Any Java class is callable, and most valid Java is valid Groovy
✅ Compiles to standard JVM bytecode: The output is a class file, so any JVM accepts it and the JDK’s tools apply
❌ The JVM is the only target: There is no non-JVM implementation of Groovy, so a program couples to one runtime (P2)
✅ Gradle and Jenkins Pipeline give it a first-class host: The build and CI systems execute Groovy directly, which is why the language is present in most Java builds
⚠️ @Grab resolves a dependency from the script: The annotation fetches an artifact from a repository at compile time, so a script couples to a repository and a version



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Dynamic or static compilation is a per-file choice: @CompileStatic buys speed and checks at the cost of the metaprogramming forms it cannot compile
DSL-friendly syntax trades precision for brevity: Optional parentheses and dots make a DSL read well and a fragment ambiguous
def is a productivity trade: Less typing now, a later failure at run time
ExpandoMetaClass is a deliberate escape hatch: It is a scope and architecture decision, and its hidden reach is the price of the flexibility
Java source compatibility is a target: Most valid Java remains valid Groovy, which constrains the syntax as much as it helps
There is no fixed release cadence: The release schedule is the project’s own decision




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ @CompileStatic approaches Java: The annotation emits direct bytecode calls, so the dynamic dispatch cost is removed for the annotated class
✅ The JVM JIT optimises a hot path: The HotSpot compiler applies its full pipeline to the generated bytecode
⚠️ Collection pauses are inherited from the JVM heap: A stop-the-world or concurrent cycle is scheduled by the collector the program chooses, not by the program (R2)
⚠️ Dynamic dispatch costs in dynamic mode: A call site without @CompileStatic goes through the metaclass protocol, so the per-call overhead is higher than Java’s
⚠️ JIT warm-up precedes peak speed: A short script or a test run finishes before the compiler has optimised the hot path (R3)



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Apache top-level project: The language is governed by the ASF, so it is not owned by one vendor
✅ The whole Java library ecosystem is available: Any Maven artifact is usable from Groovy, resolved by the ordinary Java build tools
✅ Gradle and Jenkins Pipeline are built on it: The two most common build and CI systems make Groovy a mainstream presence
✅ Grails and Spock are established projects: The web framework and the testing framework are mature and maintained
⚠️ Groovy-specific libraries are few: Most dependencies are Java libraries, so a Groovy-only package is less likely to exist



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Apache governance with published release notes: A change is recorded in the release notes and the language documentation
✅ Java source compatibility is maintained: Most valid Java keeps compiling as Groovy
✅ Groovy 5.x improves performance and JDK support: The 5.x line raises the runtime baseline to the modern JDK
✅ @CompileStatic can be adopted file by file: A project migrates incrementally rather than all at once
⚠️ There is no fixed release cadence: The timing of a release is the project’s decision, so a needed fix has no promised date



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Build automation is a primary domain: Gradle’s build scripts are Groovy, and the DSL reads as a configuration
✅ CI pipelines are a primary domain: Jenkins Pipeline scripts are Groovy, in the Jenkinsfile form
✅ Web development is supported by Grails: The framework carries the persistence, routing, and view layers
✅ Testing is supported by Spock: The specification framework defines a given/when/then DSL in Groovy
❌ The host framework can own the architecture: A Gradle build script and a Jenkins pipeline run inside the host’s execution model and its conventions, so the code couples to that model (D3)
⚠️ Application code usually prefers Java or Kotlin: Groovy’s share of general JVM application work is smaller than its share of scripting and build work



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Gentle for a Java developer: Most valid Java is valid Groovy, so an existing file compiles
✅ Typing is optional: A script can start with def and add @CompileStatic later
✅ The closure and builder idioms read like the domain: each, collect, and the builder pattern remove loop and assembly boilerplate
⚠️ The dynamic model is a large corner: The metaclass protocol, method-missing dispatch, ExpandoMetaClass, and the differences of @CompileStatic from Java must each be learned
⚠️ Two compilation modes are two languages: Code that compiles under @CompileStatic is a subset of dynamic Groovy, so a developer must know which rules apply where



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Concise and Java-compatible: A statement needs no semicolon, no type, and often no parentheses
✅ Properties replace explicit accessors: x reads getX() and x = v calls setX(), so the accessor is not written
✅ GString interpolation is built in: "Hello $name" embeds an expression in a string literal
✅ Optional return and statement-value rules shorten a method: The last expression is the result
⚠️ Operator syntax invokes methods: a + b, a[i], and a << b may call plus, getAt, or leftShift, so the notation hides the call
⚠️ Parenthesis omission can be ambiguous: foo bar baz depends on the method-call rules, which the reader must resolve



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Spock is a first-class framework: given/when/then blocks, data tables, and mocks are a Groovy DSL over JUnit
✅ JUnit works directly: A plain JUnit test class is a Groovy class
✅ assert prints the intermediate values: A power assertion reports each subexpression of a failed assertion, which localises the failure without a debugger
✅ Metaprogramming builds test doubles: ExpandoMetaClass and map coercion can stub a method without a mocking library
⚠️ A dynamic failure appears only when the test runs the line: For a def call path the test is the first check
⚠️ @CompileStatic changes what a test can patch: A statically compiled class does not consult the metaclass, so a stub installed that way has no effect



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safety is the JVM’s responsibility: A buffer overflow or a use-after-free is not expressible in Groovy code
✅ The JDK security stack is available: TLS, the cryptography providers, and the access-control APIs are directly usable
⚠️ Metaprogramming can cause type confusion: ExpandoMetaClass, methodMissing, and invokeMethod change dispatch at runtime, so a call may reach code the source does not name
⚠️ Script execution is a code-execution surface: GroovyShell, Eval, and evaluate run arbitrary text, so untrusted input must never reach them
⚠️ An AST transformation executes at compile time: A build-time transformation runs code in the build, which is a supply-chain surface
⚠️ @Grab pulls code into the build: The resolved artifact is loaded onto the script’s class path from a remote repository

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.

title: Perl (5.42)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Perl in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 28/100 · Ecosystem coupling 53/100 · Engineering readiness 65/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ No type system: Dynamic, weakly typed
❌ TIMTOWTDI: “There’s More Than One Way To Do It” creates inconsistency
⚠️ Sigils: $scalar, @array, %hash provide some structure
❌ Context-sensitive: Same code behaves differently in scalar/list context
⚠️ Moose: Object system add-on provides types, not core
⚠️ A method call resolves on the run-time object: $obj->method looks the name up in the object’s class when the call runs, so a rename breaks a caller only at run time (T3)
❌ Regular expressions: Write-only code, couples understanding to expertise



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Bless: Primitive object system, bless {} is manual
❌ Core class syntax is experimental: use feature 'class' provides a core object system, but the implementation is still experimental, so a project cannot rely on it
⚠️ Moose/Moo: Modern OOP libraries improve this significantly
❌ Hash-based objects: No encapsulation enforcement
❌ Global variables: $_, @_, %ENV everywhere
❌ **Implicit $_**: Default variable creates hidden dependencies
❌ Package variables: Global state pervasive



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Reference counting: Deterministic deallocation
⚠️ Cyclic references: Leak unless broken manually
✅ Automatic: No manual malloc/free



1.1.4 Error

❌ Die/eval: Exceptions not typed, eval catches everything
❌ Return undef: Many functions return undef on error, silent failures
⚠️ $!: Global error variable couples error state
❌ Signatures declare parameters only: A sub’s signature does not state the errors it may raise, so the failure channel is invisible at the call



1.1.5 Concurrency

⚠️ Threads: Available but discouraged, heavyweight
⚠️ Fork: Process-based concurrency common
❌ No modern concurrency: No async/await, no actors
❌ Shared state: Manual locking, error-prone



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No company owns the language: Perl 5 is released by the Perl 5 Porters under the Artistic License and the GNU General Public License, and no vendor controls it
✅ The interpreter is portable: The same C source builds on Linux, macOS, the BSDs, Windows through Strawberry Perl, and OpenVMS
✅ CPAN is vendor-neutral: The archive is mirrored worldwide and serves any Perl distribution, not one vendor’s package service
✅ A base interpreter ships with most Unix systems: Many Linux distributions and the BSDs install perl as part of the base system, so a script needs no extra platform



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Regexes are woven into the grammar: Pattern matching is syntax rather than a library, which makes text handling concise and the language hard to read — a syntax decision, not a coupling mechanism
Sigils prefix every name: The leading $, @, or % encodes the noun in the identifier, a readability trade expressed in the name rather than in a type system
Scalars carry both a number and a string: The dual-valued scalar is why == and eq are separate operators, a convenience whose cost falls on every comparison
Backward compatibility is the default: Decades of behaviour remain in the language, and use strict and use warnings recover discipline one file at a time — a compatibility cost, not a forced dependency
The successor was released as another language: Raku was developed separately from Perl 5, so Perl 5 continues on its own line — a project decision, not a coupling




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Interpreted: Slower than compiled, and the reference interpreter has no JIT
✅ Regex engine: Very fast for text processing
❌ Memory usage: Higher than C, lower than Ruby/Python



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ CPAN: Comprehensive Perl Archive Network, massive
⚠️ Aging: Fewer new modules than modern ecosystems
⚠️ IDE support: Limited compared to modern languages
✅ CPAN minus: Great dependency testing
⚠️ Tooling dated: Perldoc, prove, but aging



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ Perl 6 → Raku: Split into separate language
⚠️ Perl 5 stable: Very conservative, few changes
❌ Declining use: Community shrinking



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for text processing: Regex, sed/awk replacement
✅ Good for system admin: DevOps, automation
⚠️ Web declining: CGI era passed, PSGI exists
❌ Not for applications: Modern alternatives better
✅ Bioinformatics: BioPerl still used



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Steep: Sigils, context, special variables
❌ Write-only code: Hard to read others’ code
⚠️ Good docs: Perldoc comprehensive
❌ Many gotchas: $_, context, references



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Sigils everywhere: $@% visual noise
❌ Context sensitivity: Same code different results
⚠️ Powerful: Can express complex logic concisely
❌ Punctuation soup: Special variables like $!, $?, $@



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Test::More: Good testing framework
✅ Prove: Test runner works well
⚠️ Debugger: Perl -d works but basic
✅ Testing culture: CPAN requires tests



1.2.8 Security

✅ Taint mode: Tracks untrusted data
⚠️ Type confusion: Dynamic typing allows anything
⚠️ Eval risks: Code injection if used carelessly
✅ No memory bugs: GC prevents use-after-free




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

❌ Interpreted by default: the slowest class in the energy and time benchmarks [5]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [6].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [7].



1.4.3 Safety certification

title: Python (3.14)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Python in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 32/100 · Ecosystem coupling 73/100 · Engineering readiness 81/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Dynamic typing: All coupling at runtime
⚠️ Duck typing: Any object with a matching method name is accepted, so the interface a call expects is an assumption at the call site
❌ match/case is not exhaustive (3.10+): A value that matches no case falls through without an error, so completeness is the programmer’s claim
✅ | union type syntax (3.10+): str | int cleaner than Union[str, int]
⚠️ Type hints (PEP 484) help: Gradual typing, but not enforced by the runtime; mypy/pyright provide enforcement at build time
⚠️ Protocols (PEP 544) declare a structure for the type checker: An object satisfies the protocol implicitly, and the runtime does not enforce it
❌ None everywhere: Couples to absence checking



1.1.2 Construction

⚠️ __init__ can have side effects: Constructors couple to initialization
✅ Dataclasses decouple: Auto-generated methods; kw_only, slots options improve control
⚠️ Multiple inheritance: Diamond problem; MRO (Method Resolution Order) couples resolution to inheritance order
✅ @override decorator (3.12): Catches broken overrides at check time
❌ Global mutable state common: Module-level variables couple
❌ Monkey patching couples: Can modify anything at runtime
❌ Import side effects: Module execution couples to import
❌ Mutable default arguments: def f(x=[]) couples calls together



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Reference counting + GC: Immediate deallocation for most objects
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free
⚠️ Reference cycles need GC: Cycle detector runs periodically
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Cycle collection can pause
❌ __del__ timing non-deterministic: Finalizers unreliable for resource cleanup
⚠️ Context managers cover the block they wrap: with releases a resource at block exit, but a resource acquired outside one has no automatic release
❌ Global references common: Module-level variables extend lifetimes



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions unchecked: No type tracking in signatures
✅ Exception groups + except* (3.11+): Can handle multiple concurrent exceptions without losing information
❌ Broad exception catching couples: except Exception catches too much
⚠️ Result types possible: Libraries exist but not idiomatic



1.1.5 Concurrency

⚠️ The GIL is still the default: Free-threaded mode is opt-in through a --disable-gil build or the python3.14t executable, and threads then use multiple cores at a single-thread cost of about 5-10%
✅ Async/await separates: Explicit async functions
⚠️ Multiprocessing decouples: Separate processes, but manual (less necessary with free-threaded mode)
⚠️ Free-threaded mode is new: Ecosystem still adapting; many C extensions need GIL


Note on concurrency: The coupling analysis gives Python partial credit for free-threaded mode (3.14+, officially supported). The GIL is still the default, but it’s no longer a permanent restriction. Teams deploying free-threaded Python 3.14 can eliminate GIL-based threading coupling entirely. The Concurrency dimension still counts the default GIL (K1); free-threaded by default would remove that mechanism.



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No company owns the language: Python is governed by the Python Software Foundation and released under the PSF Licence
✅ Several implementations exist: CPython is the reference implementation, and PyPy, GraalPy, Jython, and IronPython are independent runtimes
✅ The runtime is portable: CPython builds on Linux, macOS, Windows, and on many other platforms, including IBM z/OS
✅ The packaging tools are vendor-neutral: Pip, venv, and the Python Package Index are not tied to one vendor’s platform
✅ No vendor controls the roadmap: Language changes are public Python Enhancement Proposals (PEPs) decided by the Steering Council



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Dynamic Typing vs. Maintainability: All coupling invisible until runtime, couples correctness to testing — mitigated by mypy/pyright in CI
Free-threaded Mode vs. Ecosystem Readiness: GIL removal is real but opt-in; many libraries haven’t adapted
Monkey Patching: Can modify stdlib/libraries at runtime, couples code to load order
Mutable Default Arguments: def f(x=[]) shares state across calls, couples invocations
Import Side Effects: Modules execute on import, couples import order to behavior
Duck Typing vs. Protocols: No interface enforcement couples to runtime type checking — statically checked by type checkers




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

❌ Slow: Interpreted, dynamic (though free-threaded mode helps parallelism)
⚠️ Free-threaded mode: Opt-in removal of GIL (3.14+); ~5-10% single-thread overhead
⚠️ C extensions help: But couples to C ecosystem
❌ High memory: Object overhead significant
⚠️ PyPy, Cython: Improve but fragment ecosystem



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Massive ecosystem: PyPI has everything
✅ Excellent for data science: NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn
✅ Great tooling: Pip, venv, Poetry, uv
✅ IDE support: PyCharm, VSCode excellent
✅ Jupyter notebooks: Interactive development



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Python 3.x backward compatible: Post-2-to-3 migration resolved
✅ Type hints: Gradual typing without breaking
⚠️ Free-threaded transition: C-extension ecosystem still adapting
✅ Annual releases: Predictable cadence (3.13, 3.14, 3.15…)



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for data science: Industry standard
✅ Great for ML/AI: TensorFlow, PyTorch
✅ Strong for scripting: Quick automation
✅ Good for backend: Django, Flask, FastAPI
❌ Poor for systems: Interpreted overhead



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Extremely gentle: Easiest to learn
✅ Readable: “Executable pseudocode”
✅ Massive resources: Tutorials, courses everywhere
✅ Quick productivity: Write useful code day 1



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Clean, readable: Indentation-based
✅ Minimal boilerplate: Concise
✅ Expressive: List comprehensions, generators
⚠️ Indentation: Can cause issues



1.2.7 Testing

✅ pytest, unittest: Excellent frameworks
✅ pdb debugger: Built-in
✅ Type checkers: Mypy, pyright
⚠️ Runtime errors: No compile-time checks



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents memory bugs
⚠️ Type confusion: Dynamic typing allows anything
❌ Pickle vulnerabilities: Deserialization attacks
⚠️ Dependency vulnerabilities: Large attack surface




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain
