title: Fortran (2023)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Fortran in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 32/100 · Ecosystem coupling 68/100 · Engineering readiness 65/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

⚠️ Typing is static but implicit typing is the default: Without implicit none, a name beginning with I–N is an integer and every other name is a real, so a misspelled variable becomes a new one rather than an error (T2)
❌ There are no sum types: An alternative is encoded as an integer tag beside the payload fields, and select case or select type must decode it, so nothing checks that the right branch was taken (T4)
⚠️ There are no generics, and a generic interface overloads a name instead: An interface block binds one name to several specific procedures and the compiler resolves the call by argument type, which is overloading without a type parameter (T5)
⚠️ Operator and assignment overloading is expressible: interface operator(+) and interface assignment(=) redefine + and = for a derived type, so the work behind an operator is invisible at the call site (T8)
✅ A module is a namespace with a selective import: use mymodule, only: a, b brings in two names and nothing else, so no flat global namespace is imposed
✅ class(t) and select type give checked run-time polymorphism: A polymorphic dummy argument dispatches on the dynamic type of the actual argument, and select type narrows it in a checked branch



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Global mutable state is the default storage class: A module variable and a common block are shared by every procedure that names them, and a variable marked save keeps its value between calls (C1)
❌ There is no immutability by default: Only a parameter names a constant, and a module variable is writable by any user unless it carries the Fortran 2003 protected attribute (C2)
❌ A structure constructor validates nothing: t(a, b) fills the components in order or by keyword, and no invariant can be stated at the type, so a valid object exists only because the caller made it valid (C4)
✅ A pure procedure states the absence of side effects: It may not write a global, an intent(in) argument, or a saved variable, and the compiler enforces the rule
✅ intent(in), intent(out), and intent(inout) state the direction of an argument: The declaration says whether a routine reads, writes, or does both, and the compiler checks it at the call site
✅ elemental states an elementwise operation: An elemental procedure applies to each element of an array, so a scalar definition composes with array construction without a written loop



1.1.3 Memory

❌ allocate and deallocate are written by hand for a pointer: The language tracks no owner and no bound, so a pointer target is freed by an explicit statement and a missing one leaks (M1)
❌ There is no ownership model: A pointer may alias a target, dangle after deallocate, or be freed twice, and the compiler does not see the aliasing (M4)
⚠️ Release tied to scope is partial: An allocatable local and a derived-type component with a final procedure are released at scope exit, but a pointer is not, so the rule differs by variable kind (M3)
⚠️ An allocation failure must be tested: allocate(a(n), stat=ierr) returns a code the program has to check, and without stat= a failure aborts the program
✅ move_alloc transfers an allocation without a copy: call move_alloc(from, to) moves the storage and deallocates the source, so a result array is returned without duplication
✅ Allocatable locals are released at procedure exit: An allocatable array declared inside a procedure is deallocated when the procedure returns, which is a scope-tied release the language provides



1.1.4 Error

❌ There is no exception mechanism: A failure is reported through a stat=/iostat= code or an err= label, and the caller has to test it (Er1)
❌ A returned code can be ignored: Nothing obliges a caller to look at iostat, so a failed read, allocate, or deallocate proceeds as though it had succeeded unless the program checks (Er3)
❌ There is no composable result type: No value carries either a result or an error, so error state travels in an extra out argument or in a saved flag (Er4)
✅ error stop gives a defined abort: Since Fortran 2008, error stop stops the program with a message or an integer stop-code, and Fortran 2018 added the optional quiet= specifier, so a fatal failure is stated rather than inferred from a negative status
⚠️ IEEE exceptional values are inspected through an intrinsic module: ieee_arithmetic and ieee_exceptions let a program test ieee_is_nan and select a halting mode, but the checks are ordinary calls rather than a language guarantee
✅ A pure procedure cannot perform I/O: An I/O failure is outside a pure procedure by construction, so a computational kernel has no I/O error channel to handle



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Coarray images share memory by default: A coarray declared with codimension is written by one image and read by another, and nothing in the language prevents the race (K2)
⚠️ Synchronisation is manual: sync all, sync images, event post/event wait, and lock/unlock are image control statements the program must place at the right point
✅ do concurrent states an independent loop: The construct asserts that the iterations have no interdependencies, and Fortran 2018 adds local, local_init, and shared locality specifications, so the compiler may parallelise it
✅ atomic and critical give a defined atomic access: atomic define/atomic_ref and a critical construct express one update that must not interleave
⚠️ The practical parallel model sits outside the language: Coarray support varies across compilers, so most high-performance code uses OpenMP directives or MPI calls



1.1.6 Platform

✅ One standard source runs on every major compiler: gfortran, ifx, nagfor, Cray, and LLVM flang accept standard-conforming Fortran on Linux, Windows, macOS, and the large HPC systems
✅ iso_c_binding names the interoperable interface: c_int, c_double, c_ptr, and c_funptr let a Fortran routine be called from C and call C in return
✅ iso_fortran_env names the portable kinds and units: real64, int32, and input_unit state a portable choice where real(8) names one machine’s representation
✅ A compiled module is a binary interface: A module is compiled to a file a consumer imports, so the interface is checked when the consumer is compiled
⚠️ Vendor directives are common in working code: !DIR$ and !DEC$ directives, REAL*8, and STRUCTURE/RECORD appear in legacy HPC source, which binds it to one compiler
⚠️ Coarray support varies by compiler and platform: A coarray program depends on the compiler’s image implementation and its transport library, so its portability is weaker than that of a serial program



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

implicit none is the modern practice, not the standard default: A project chooses to require it, and the language permits implicit typing for the old source
Column-major order is a deliberate numerical choice: Array expressions follow Fortran’s storage order, which is what the linear-algebra kernels are written for
The aliasing rules are what the optimiser needs: The standard’s restrictions let the compiler vectorise a loop, which costs flexibility and buys speed
goto remains for compatibility: It is retained so that decades of code keeps compiling, and a new program need not use it
Whole-array syntax exists so the compiler chooses the loop nest: The programmer gives up per-loop control in exchange for vectorisation
The legacy corpus is working, tested numerical code: The aging ecosystem holds decades of validated physics and linear-algebra routines




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The program is compiled to machine code: gfortran, ifx, and flang emit native objects for the target CPU, and the performance of an array kernel rivals C
✅ Array syntax maps onto the machine’s loop nests: a = b + c over whole arrays lets the compiler fuse and vectorise the loops, and matmul and dot_product have library or instruction implementations
✅ Nothing between the source and the CPU interprets: A Fortran binary has no bytecode dispatch and no JIT warm-up
⚠️ The optimiser needs the aliasing facts: Without intent(in), contiguous, and pure, the compiler must assume a possible alias and cannot reorder the loops
⚠️ The floating-point contract is the compiler’s flags: -O3 with -ffast-math or -fp-model fast changes the order of the operations, so the measured speed depends on the build options



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ There is no standard package manager for the language: Dependencies are resolved by a language-agnostic manager such as Spack or Conda or by the system manager, and the fpm package manager is young and small (Ec3)
✅ The numerical libraries are mature and standard: BLAS, LAPACK, and the vendor-tuned kernels (MKL, ESSL) are callable from Fortran directly
✅ A compiler is available on every system: A Fortran compiler is installed on every HPC cluster and is packaged for every common Linux distribution
✅ Interoperation with the C and Python ecosystems is standard: iso_c_binding and the Python wrapper generators make a Fortran kernel callable from a Python array library
⚠️ Tooling beyond the compiler is thin: Formatting, lint, and documentation come from small community projects (fprettify, ford) rather than from a supported toolchain
⚠️ The community is aging: Adoption is declining and maintenance is concentrated in the HPC and numerical community



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The standard is backward compatible: Fortran 90 source mostly compiles with a Fortran 2023 compiler, and only a small set of features has been deleted
✅ The compilers retain the deleted features as extensions: arithmetic IF and PAUSE, both removed by the standard, are still accepted by the common compilers
✅ The intrinsic modules extend the language without editing it: iso_c_binding, iso_fortran_env, and the parallel features were added as modules and new syntax rather than as changes to existing syntax
⚠️ A revision takes about a decade: The editions are 2003, 2008, 2018, and 2023, so a needed feature waits years for the standard and lives as a compiler extension until then
⚠️ One program can hold several standards: A single codebase can mix a Fortran 77 common block with a Fortran 2008 module, so the version in use is a property of the file
⚠️ An extension can become load-bearing: A program that depends on a vendor directive cannot be moved to another compiler without an edit



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Numerical and scientific computing is the design target: Array syntax, complex arithmetic, real kinds, and the IEEE intrinsic modules fit it directly
✅ High-performance computing is the deepest adoption: Weather, climate, and physics codes are written in Fortran, so the language dominates legacy HPC codebases
✅ submodule fits a large numerical codebase: A module can declare the interface and a submodule hold the implementation, so changing a kernel recompiles only that submodule (Fortran 2008)
✅ Coarrays put a parallel program in the language: A distributed-memory program is written without a call from a separate parallel library
⚠️ The language assumes a numerical, batch-shaped workload: Text handling, dynamic data structures, and event-driven logic get little support, and the standard library is mainly the intrinsic procedures
⚠️ A new project often keeps Fortran for the kernel only: The language is used where the inner loop must be native, and the orchestration moves to Python or C++



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The core is small once implicit none is in place: The statement forms, the intrinsic procedures, and the array expressions are a modest set
✅ The authoritative material is stable and complete: The ISO standard, the compiler references, and Modern Fortran Explained cover the language in one place
✅ The array idiom has a direct mathematical reading: A whole-array expression reads as the equation it computes
❌ Legacy syntax quirks create friction: Fixed-form source with its column rules, implicit typing, and common blocks must be read to work on an existing codebase (L1)
⚠️ The array and parallel idioms take practice: Array sections, where, and do concurrent read differently from an explicit loop, and the cost of a temporary array is easy to miss



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ Fixed-form source is column-sensitive: In a .f file a label sits in columns 1–5, a continuation mark in column 6, and a statement starts in column 7, so the layout carries meaning
⚠️ The language is verbose: Kind, intent, and dimension accumulate on every dummy argument, and the internals of a procedure need their own contains block (S1)
✅ Whole-array expressions are compact: c = matmul(a, b) + alpha * c states a matrix update in one line
✅ Free-form source is line-oriented and readable: With implicit none and use, only:, a modern module reads close to the mathematics
⚠️ A common block’s storage is positional: Two declarations of the same block must list the fields in the same order with the same types, and the block’s layout is a convention rather than a checked interface



1.2.7 Testing

✅ error stop gives a test program a defined failure status: A failing check stops the program with a non-zero status that a harness can read
✅ Run-time checks can be compiled in: -fcheck=all (gfortran) and -check all (ifx) raise on an out-of-bounds subscript, an unassociated pointer, and a shape mismatch
✅ The numerical libraries ship their own test suites: LAPACK and BLAS carry a published suite that exercises each routine, which is the numerical community’s model
❌ There is no test framework in the language: A test is a program that runs and compares, and a runner such as pFUnit or test-drive is a third-party library
⚠️ There is no assertion intrinsic: A check is an explicit if (cond) error stop, so its presence is a written decision
⚠️ The result depends on the flags and the hardware: The summation order, -ffast-math, and the fused multiply-add change the last bits, so a test must fix the build and compare with a tolerance



1.2.8 Security

⚠️ Memory safety depends on a checked build: An out-of-bounds subscript, an unassociated pointer, and a mismatch between an actual and a dummy argument are found only when the compiler is asked to check them, and the standard requires no run-time check
✅ There is no dynamic evaluation of source text: The language has no eval, no reflective call by name, and no string-to-code path, so a value cannot become code
✅ intent(in) prevents a write through the callee: The compiler refuses an assignment to an intent(in) dummy argument, so the read-only direction is enforced
⚠️ The C interface hands safety to the neighbour: c_ptr and type(c_funptr) are raw addresses, and the guarantees of the C code on the other side become part of the program
⚠️ There is no capability model and no sandbox: A program runs with the authority of the process, and the mitigations come from the operating system and the linker
✅ A pure procedure cannot corrupt state through I/O or a global: The effect set of a pure procedure is empty by construction




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.

1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].

Verdict: Fortran’s design produces a low core score, because the constructs that make the numerical work fast are the constructs that couple. Array expressions and pure procedures are real separations, and a module with a submodule separates an interface from its implementation. But implicit typing hides a misspelled variable, common blocks and module variables are global mutable state, a pointer is freed by hand with no owner, and an error is a code the caller may ignore. Main strengths: the fit to numerical computing is exact, array performance rivals C, and one standard source runs on every major compiler. Main weaknesses: the ecosystem is small and aging, the revision cycle is slow, and the syntax of a legacy file depends on column positions.

title: Lua (5.5)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Lua in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 43/100 · Ecosystem coupling 84/100 · Engineering readiness 61/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ There is no static type check: Every value is a tagged variant and type() answers at run time, so a wrong shape is found when the operation runs rather than when the file loads (T1)
❌ Dispatch is a lookup, not a declared type: obj:m() reads the field m through the metatable chain, so which function runs depends on the table’s metatable rather than on a declared receiver type (T3)
❌ There are no sum types: An alternative is a tag field beside the payload ({kind = "circle", r = 1}), and nothing checks that the branch matches the tag (T4)
❌ There are no generics: Reuse across element types is a naming convention or a documented contract, because the element type of a table is declared nowhere (T5)
❌ There is no namespace (T6): require returns a value and every global name lives in one shared table, so two modules that define the same name collide
⚠️ Metamethods overload the operators: __add, __eq, __lt, __concat, __len, and __call redefine the notation for a table, so an operator at a call site may run a function the reader cannot see (T8)



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Globals are the default, so a construction site can write shared state: x = 1 without local creates a field in the global table that every chunk sees (C1)
❌ Nothing is immutable: There is no const and no frozen table, so any code that holds a table can change it (C2)
✅ A table constructor and a closure are values: {1, 2, 3} and function(x) return x * 2 end are built where they are written, with no class or factory in the way
✅ A metatable gives construction its own meaning: setmetatable(t, {__index = proto}) decides how the value answers a missing field, so the object-like behaviour is installed rather than inherited by the syntax
✅ __call makes any table callable: A table with a __call metamethod can be used as a function, so a design need not wrap it in one
✅ An upvalue is private by construction: A variable declared local outside a nested function is reachable only through that function’s closure, so a private field needs no keyword



1.1.3 Memory

❌ Collection is non-deterministic in its timing: The collector runs on its own schedule, so the moment a table’s storage is reclaimed is not the moment the last reference to it goes out of scope (M2)
❌ There is no ownership model: The collector sees reachability rather than ownership, so nothing states which part of a program is responsible for dropping a reference (M4)
⚠️ Most values have no destructor: A table’s __gc metamethod runs only if its metatable already carried __gc when it was set, so release is not tied to a scope by default (M3)
✅ A to-be-closed variable releases deterministically: local f <close> = res calls the value’s __close metamethod when the block ends, including on an error (Lua 5.4)
✅ A weak table lets the collector take an entry: With __mode set to "k", "v", or "kv", an entry whose key or value is otherwise unreachable is removed, so a memo table does not pin its values
✅ The collector can be inspected and driven: collectgarbage "count" reports the footprint in kilobytes, and a program can request a step or select the incremental or generational mode (Lua 5.4)



1.1.4 Error

❌ An error carries no declared type: error accepts any value and pcall returns it unchanged, so there is no error type a handler can be checked against (Er2)
❌ A nil result is easy to leave unchecked: io.open and os.remove report a failure by returning nil plus a message, and nothing requires the caller to look (Er3)
✅ pcall and xpcall state the protected call: A call is placed in a protected region and its status is returned, so the recovery path is an explicit second call
✅ A message handler is attached in the language: xpcall(f, handler) passes the error through a function, which is where a traceback from debug.traceback is added
✅ assert states a precondition with its message: assert(cond, "msg") raises when the condition fails, so the check and its text are one call
✅ An error value can be a table: A structured error with a code and a message is an ordinary table, because error raises the value it is given



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Coroutines are the only concurrency in the core: coroutine.create, resume, yield, and status give a cooperative task, so there is no lock, no shared-memory race, and no preemption to reason about
✅ A yield point is explicit: Control returns to the resumer only at a coroutine.yield, so the interleaving is visible at the line it happens
✅ A generator is a coroutine and a call site: An iterator is a function that yields, and for x in gen() do consumes it, so the producer does not know its consumer
✅ coroutine.wrap and coroutine.close complete the protocol: wrap returns a callable that propagates the error, and close closes a suspended coroutine and runs its pending to-be-closed variables (Lua 5.4)
⚠️ There is no scheduler and no parallelism: A coroutine runs only when it is resumed, so one blocking call stops the whole interpreter and parallel work needs a host with several interpreter states
⚠️ A table shared between coroutines is still shared mutable state: The language treats the state as one, so the discipline of not yielding mid-update is the programmer’s



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The reference implementation is portable C: The interpreter builds from one small C library on any platform with a C compiler, and the embedding API (luaL_newstate, lua_pcall, the lua_push* and lua_to* stack functions) is the intended interface
✅ The host controls a script’s environment: A chunk can be loaded with a table as its _ENV, so the set of names a script can see is the host’s decision (Lua 5.2 and later)
✅ Several independent implementations exist: PUC-Rio’s lua, LuaJIT, Luau, and hosted implementations in other languages each provide the language or a near variant
✅ A compiled chunk is data the host decides to load: load and lua_load take text or a binary chunk, so the host chooses what code runs and in which environment
⚠️ The implementations diverge: LuaJIT implements Lua 5.1 with extensions and Luau diverges for its host, so a script that uses goto, integer division, or <close> needs the reference implementation or a recent alternative
⚠️ The default library reaches the operating system: os.execute, os.remove, and io.open are in the standard library, so a host that needs a sandbox must remove them



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

One compound structure is a deliberate economy: The language trades a declared type for one constructor that covers arrays, records, objects, and modules
Metatables are an opt-in object model: The core has no classes, and the idiom that adds them is chosen by the program rather than imposed
Embedding is the primary use, so the host owns the runtime: The small library and the C API are the reason to choose the language, not a defect
Cooperative scheduling is a design decision: With no preemption there is no thread of the language’s own, and the host decides about parallelism
The global table is a scripting convenience: It keeps a short script short and lets a host inject functions, and avoiding it is a discipline
A version pin is an adoption cost, not a mechanism: A library written for one version does not load on another, which follows from separate version lines rather than from a coupling in the language




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The reference implementation is a compact register-based virtual machine: The compiler emits bytecode for a small instruction set (luac -l prints it), so start-up is immediate
✅ LuaJIT traces a hot loop into machine code: The tracing compiler specialises the recorded path, which is why a numeric or table loop runs far faster than in the interpreter (the implementation is Lua 5.1 with extensions)
✅ Strings are interned, so a string key hashes once: Every string is hash-consed and its hash is cached, so a table lookup by string is cheap
✅ Tail calls are proper and do not grow the stack: A tail call reuses the frame, so a state machine written as tail recursion runs in constant space
✅ The collector takes bounded steps: The incremental mode does a small amount of work between bytecodes, and Lua 5.4 adds a generational mode for the allocation-heavy case
⚠️ The array part and the hash part of a table are a performance fact of its shape: The same logical sequence is a fast array or a slow hash depending on how it was built, so a hot path must keep the dense part dense



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The library pool is small: LuaRocks carries many small modules and few large frameworks, so a project writes its own glue (Ec3)
✅ LuaRocks is a standard package manager and build tool: A rockspec declares a module and its dependencies, and luarocks install and luarocks make build and install it
✅ The language server and the linter are mature: lua-language-server checks the code against annotations such as ---@param and ---@type, and luacheck reports unused variables, globals, and a module’s public surface
✅ The C API is documented and versioned: The manual’s C API chapter and lua.h/lauxlib.h state the stack protocol, and bindings exist for C++, C#, Go, Rust, and Java
✅ The language runs wherever a C library runs: The interpreter is embedded in web servers, editors, games, and network equipment, which is why it is the standard embedded scripting layer
⚠️ The implementations split the ecosystem: A binding written for the LuaJIT foreign function interface or for Luau does not work in the reference interpreter, and the reverse



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ A release is a deliberate, documented step: Each version has its own manual and a changes list, and the reference implementation is small enough to read
✅ The C API of a version line is stable within that line: A program builds against one set of headers and the matching library
✅ Feature additions are small and conservative: goto, integer division, the <close> attribute, and the generational collector were added as syntax or library functions rather than as a redesign of the language
⚠️ Source compatibility is not kept across minor versions: 5.2 replaced setfenv, getfenv, and loadstring with _ENV and load, and 5.3 introduced the integer subtype, so a codebase is usually pinned to one version
⚠️ The implementations lag the reference: LuaJIT remains at 5.1, so a program that wants the newer syntax gives up the tracing compiler
⚠️ A dialect can move the language forward on its own: Luau adds gradual typing and performance annotations to its host’s variant, which is not the standard language



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Embedding a scripting layer in a host program is the design point: The interpreter is a C library with no external dependency, and the host decides the API it exposes
✅ Game scripting is the widest adoption: The language is the scripting layer of World of Warcraft, Roblox (as Luau), and many engines
✅ Configuration and data description work by construction: A table literal is a data format, and load or dofile evaluates it into a value
✅ Prototype-style objects are expressible with __index: The object model is a library idiom over tables rather than a language feature
⚠️ It is not a systems language: There is no pointer, no placement control, and no unchecked array, so work at that level belongs to the host C code
⚠️ A CPU-bound kernel needs LuaJIT or C: The interpreter is fast for a scripting language and is not a substitute for compiled numerical code



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The core syntax is small and regular: About two dozen keywords, one compound structure, and no declaration ceremony, so the language itself is learned quickly
✅ One document is the complete specification: The reference manual covers the syntax, the standard library, and the C API in a single short text
❌ The advanced layer is a second subject: Metatables, __index chains, closures over coroutines, and the C API are where the difficulty is, and the core syntax does not announce them (L1)
⚠️ The types live in the programmer’s head: With no declaration and no annotation, a reader infers a table’s shape from its uses unless the language server’s annotations or Luau types are added
✅ The interpreter reports the line and the call stack: An uncaught error prints its message with a Lua traceback, so a failure is located from the output



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The syntax is small and uses words as delimiters: local, if ... then ... else ... end, for ... do ... end, and function ... end, with no braces and no required semicolons
✅ A table constructor is a compact data notation: {x = 1, y = 2} is a record and {1, 2, 3} is an array, in the same brackets
✅ Short forms carry the common idioms: #t is the length, a .. b concatenates, t:k() calls a method, and ... is the variable argument list
✅ Multiple assignment and multiple return are one form: local x, y = f() and return a, b pass several values without a tuple type
⚠️ A missing local is a global write: x = 1 inside a function writes a field of the global table, and the mistake is invisible at the line
⚠️ The notation does not state the structure: The same {} is an array, a record, an object, or a module, so the intent is a comment rather than a declaration



1.2.7 Testing

✅ busted gives a describe/it suite with matchers: A third-party runner with luassert matchers runs a spec/ directory from the command line
✅ luaunit gives a single-file test framework: One file supplies the assertions and the runner, which suits an embedded project
✅ A test can substitute a chunk’s environment: load(src, name, "t", env) runs the module against a table the test supplies, so a dependency is replaced without editing the source
✅ The debug library can instrument a run: debug.sethook counts calls and samples, and debug.getinfo reports the source line, so a profiler or a coverage tool is written in Lua itself
✅ Static checks catch mistakes before a run: The language server reports an annotation mismatch and luacheck reports an unused variable and a global leak
⚠️ Testing is not part of the standard library: assert is the only built-in check, so the runner and the fixtures are dependencies



1.2.8 Security

⚠️ A binary chunk from an untrusted source is unsafe: The manual states that load does not check the consistency of a binary chunk and that a crafted one can crash the interpreter or run arbitrary machine code
✅ _ENV gives a chunk a restricted global table: A sandbox loads a chunk with an environment that holds only the functions the host allows, and the chunk has no other path to the host’s state
⚠️ The debug library defeats a sandbox: debug.setupvalue, debug.getregistry, and debug.sethook reach past the environment, so a sandbox must remove the library and the host must not reopen it
⚠️ The standard library includes file and process access: io.open, io.popen, and os.execute are available unless the host removes them from the environment
✅ A pure Lua value cannot be a forged pointer: A value is a tagged variant, an out-of-bounds access is a table miss rather than an address, and there is no pointer type or pointer arithmetic in the language
✅ The interpreter imposes no host dependency of its own: It makes no call outside the C library unless the program does, so the attack surface of a script is the surface the host exposed




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

❌ Interpreted by default: the slowest class in the energy and time benchmarks [5]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [6].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [7].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Lua’s design yields the low core score of a dynamic scripting language, with the coupling concentrated in its data model. One table type serves as array, record, object, and module, so the shape of the data is a convention and every structure error waits for a run time; the global table is the default and errors are unchecked. The counterweight is that the language is small, orthogonal, and easy to embed, and that its separating constructs are real: __index decouples object-like behaviour from syntax, a coroutine makes every interleaving explicit, <close> and weak tables tie release to a block or to reachability, and the C API decouples the language from its host. Main strengths: exceptional performance for a scripting language, a very small footprint, and mature tooling. Main weaknesses: no static type check, globals by default, an unchecked error channel, and a library pool that is small beside the language’s adoption.

title: OCaml (5.4)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses OCaml in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 58/100 · Ecosystem coupling 84/100 · Engineering readiness 61/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Variant types declare a checked case distinction: type shape = Circle of float | Square of float is a closed sum, and the compiler checks that a match covers every constructor
✅ Types are static and inferred: The Hindley–Milner algorithm gives a principal type without annotations, and no value is untyped
✅ A signature hides a type behind an interface: A .mli file can export type t as abstract, so a consumer binds to the operations and not to the representation
✅ A functor makes a type a parameter: Set.Make(String) builds a set module for a given ordered type, so one algorithm is reused across types without run-time dispatch
⚠️ Operators are rebound in scope rather than overloaded (T8): + is int addition and +. is float addition, and a module-qualified form such as Int64.(a + b) or a local let (+) = ... changes which operator is in scope, so the reader must track the binding
⚠️ The object layer is a second type system: Classes and row-polymorphic object types sit beside the core types, so a codebase can mix two paradigms



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Mutable state is the natural default container for shared data (C2): The idiomatic way to hold module state is a ref cell, an Array, or a Hashtbl, each mutable, so any caller of the interface can change what the module holds
✅ A variant constructor is the only way to build a value of the type: Node (l, x, r) names the construction path, so every construction is visible in the type declaration
✅ A record literal states every field: { x = 1.; y = 2. } must be complete unless with is used, so a field cannot be left unset silently
✅ A signature can hide the constructor of an abstract type: With type t abstract and val create : unit -> t, construction goes through the module, so the invariant holds by construction
✅ A let binding evaluates its right-hand side once: let x = expensive () evaluates at that point, and the result is a value rather than a re-evaluable expression
⚠️ A mutable field relaxes the invariant: A record field declared mutable can be assigned at any time, so an invariant over the record is maintained by the code rather than by the type



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Collection is automatic with no manual free: The collector reclaims an unreachable block, and a program never calls free
⚠️ Collection is not tied to the last reference (M2): A block stays allocated until the collector decides, so a latency-sensitive path is coupled to a component it never calls
❌ There is no RAII (M3): There is no scope-bound destructor, so a file descriptor, a Unix.file_descr, or another non-memory handle is released by an explicit call or a bracket such as Fun.protect
❌ There is no ownership model (M4): No static lifetime or aliasing rule ties a value to an owner, so a mutable structure that escapes its module is shared without a trace
✅ Fun.protect brackets a resource: Fun.protect ~finally:close body runs the release on the normal path and on the exceptional path, so the release need not be repeated at every exit
⚠️ The major heap is measured and tuned by hand: Gc.set and Gc.stat control and report space_overhead and the major cycle, so a latency-sensitive program reads collector statistics itself
⚠️ C stubs and Marshal sit outside the collector’s view: A value held in a C global must be registered with caml_register_generational_global_root, and Marshal.from_string builds a value the collector then owns, so the boundary is the programmer’s to manage



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked (Er2): raise, Failure, and Not_found are not declared in the type of a function, so a caller cannot see the failure set from a signature
✅ result is a composable value: ('a, 'b) result is Ok of 'a | Error of 'b, and Result.map, Result.bind, and Result.fold chain operations without a match at every step
✅ A variant closes the failure set: type error = Not_found | Permission_denied makes the cases finite, so a match over the failure is checked for exhaustiveness
✅ try ... with separates the abnormal path: A handler can match an exception constructor such as Sys_error _ | Unix.Unix_error _ and re-raise cheaply with raise_notrace
✅ Option carries an absence without an exception: Some x and None give a missing result a value, and Option.map and Option.get compose it
⚠️ A wildcard handler hides a fault: try f () with _ -> default catches every exception, including Out_of_memory and an unintended bug, so the cause disappears



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ OCaml 5 runs OCaml code on several cores: Domain.spawn starts a second domain, so the global runtime lock that serialised all code in earlier versions no longer applies
✅ Effects express a scheduler in the language: An effect handler such as Effect.Deep.try_with or Effect.Shallow defines what an effect does, so a concurrency library is ordinary OCaml
✅ Eio supplies structured concurrency: Eio_main.run gives a scheduler with fibers, cancellation, and capability-scoped resources, so a program names a scope rather than a thread
✅ Atomic, Mutex, and Condition are primitives of the runtime: A shared cell of type 'a Atomic.t has defined operations, and Mutex.lock guards a critical section
✅ A channel passes values between domains: Domainslib.Chan with Domain.spawn gives a message-passing design instead of a shared one
⚠️ A library written for one domain must be revisited: Code that relied on the single runtime’s atomicity now shares state across domains, so the migration is a review rather than a recompile



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The native compiler emits machine code for many targets: ocamlopt produces a native executable for x86-64, ARM64, RISC-V, and Power, and ocamlc produces bytecode wherever the virtual machine runs
✅ A C stub reaches any system library: An external declaration plus a small C stub links a C library, so the language’s reach follows the reach of C
✅ MirageOS links an OCaml program into a unikernel: A set of modules builds a freestanding image, so the target needs no operating-system process
✅ The JavaScript backends target the browser: js_of_ocaml compiles bytecode to JavaScript, and Melange compiles OCaml to JavaScript modules
⚠️ The foreign-function interface is manual: An external declaration and its C stub must be kept in step by hand, so the boundary carries the correctness burden of both sides



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The object layer is opt-in: Classes and objects are separate from the module system, so a project can ignore them entirely
Inheritance instead of a functor is a design decision: Using class inheritance where a functor would do is a choice the language permits and does not require
Terse syntax is a stated preference: let f x = x + 1 and the ;; toplevel separator are stylistic, and the adjustment period is not a forced dependency
Persistent structures trade space for sharing: A version-keeping data structure retains the older versions, which is a space cost rather than a coupling mechanism
Interface files are a convention: A project can omit the .mli file, and the abstraction benefit follows from the discipline rather than from the language
Effect handlers are opt-in: A program can ignore effects and write plain code, so the paradigm adds no dependency unless it is used




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ ocamlopt compiles ahead of time to native code: There is no interpreter and no warm-up, so a program starts at full speed
✅ The core type system erases at compile time: An abstract type and a generic function carry no run-time dispatch, so the abstraction costs nothing to execute
✅ A functor is specialised at compile time: Set.Make(String) produces a module whose calls are direct, so the reuse costs no dynamic dispatch
✅ An unboxed representation is available per declaration: An all-float record and an [@@unboxed] declaration avoid a heap indirection, so a numeric structure can be dense
⚠️ A mixed record boxes its float field: type t = { n : int; x : float } stores x in a box, and only an all-float record or an annotation removes it, so the representation is a per-declaration detail
⚠️ Allocation rate drives the collection schedule: A high allocation rate fills the minor heap often, and the program cannot schedule that collection itself



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The library ecosystem is small next to Haskell or Rust (Ec3): Fewer general-purpose packages exist, so some work starts from a blank module
✅ opam is a mature package manager: opam resolves versions, pins a package to a revision, and keeps per-project switches, and the opam repository index is curated
✅ dune builds, tests, and documents a project: One file describes a library, an executable, and a test, so no external build system is needed
✅ merlin and ocaml-lsp give editor support: Type-directed completion, jump-to-definition, and error reporting are available in Emacs, VS Code, and others
✅ Substantial systems are written in it: The Rocq (Coq) proof assistant, the Frama-C analyzer, Jane Street’s trading systems, and the Tezos blockchain are OCaml codebases
⚠️ A niche language means fewer answers: The community is smaller, so a team depends on the members it can find



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ OCaml 5 keeps the single-domain case working: A program that ran on 4.x recompiles on 5.x, and the multicore runtime is the same source language
✅ Version changes have been additive in practice: The core syntax and the standard library have stayed stable across decades
✅ A switch pins a compiler version per project: opam switch keeps an old compiler and a new one side by side, so a project upgrades on its own schedule
✅ The multicore change has a migration path: Code that used Threads can move to Domain and a scheduler library such as Eio, with Domainslib bridging the two
⚠️ A single-domain library needs a review for OCaml 5: A global mutable structure that was safe under one runtime becomes shared state when several domains run



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for compilers and static analysis: Algebraic data types, pattern matching, and a module system match a syntax tree and a typed pass directly, and the OCaml compiler itself is written in OCaml
✅ Proven in proof assistants and verification: Rocq (Coq) and Frama-C are OCaml programs, and their term representations are OCaml variants
✅ Proven in finance: Jane Street’s trading systems are OCaml, and the language is used for typed, low-latency systems
✅ A strong fit for parsers and interpreters: menhir generates a parser, and a variant-based abstract syntax tree keeps the grammar’s cases explicit
⚠️ Numeric and tensor work needs a library: Dense array and tensor programming depends on a package such as Owl or on a C binding, not on the core language
⚠️ The object layer is rarely the right tool: Most OCaml code uses modules and variants, and the object system is a separate, optional design



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The abstraction layer is steep even when the syntax is not (L1): A newcomer learns inference, the module and functor system, and pattern matching together, although the language is generally considered easier to approach than Haskell
✅ Inference removes annotation work: let rec fact n = if n = 0 then 1 else n * fact (n - 1) is accepted without a type written by hand
✅ The error messages point at the mismatch: The compiler prints the inferred type and the conflicting type, and Merlin shows the type under the cursor
❌ The module language is a second language: Functors, signatures, and module type of are a topic of their own beyond the expression language
⚠️ Reading an inferred signature is a skill: val f : ('a -> 'b) -> 'a list -> 'b list must be read fluently before an interface is easy to write



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ let, match, and type share one shape: A binding, a case analysis, and a declaration all need no braces, and the toplevel ends a phrase with ;;
✅ Pattern matching is written as data: match xs with [] -> 0 | x :: _ -> x states the cases directly
✅ The keyword set is small and consistent: The same |-case form serves a variant declaration, a match, and an exception handler
✅ Terse for the type information it carries: One line declares a record, and inference fills in the annotations
⚠️ Integer and float operators differ by a character: + is not +., and = is structural while == is physical, so a sign or a repetition changes the meaning
⚠️ Extensions extend the notation: let* binding operators, ppx rewrites, and [@@deriving] attributes are not core syntax, so a reader must know which extensions a file uses



1.2.7 Testing

✅ A test framework lives in the package repository: alcotest and ounit2 provide assertions and runners, and dune runtest runs the suite
✅ Inline and expect tests sit beside the code: let%test and let%expect_test (ppx_inline_test and ppx_expect) keep the expected output in the source and diff it on a run
✅ The type checker catches faults before a test does: An exhaustiveness check reports a missing match case at compile time, which removes a whole class of test
✅ bisect_ppx measures coverage: An instrumented build reports which points were executed
⚠️ A hand-written module is the usual stand-in: There is no dynamic mocking of a module, so a seam must be a functor parameter or a signature
⚠️ An effectful path needs its handler installed: A test of a scheduler runs the effect handler, which is a different setup from a test of plain code



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safety is the default: The collector and the type system prevent use-after-free, and an out-of-range a.(i) raises Invalid_argument instead of reading adjacent memory
✅ A signature hides the representation: With type t abstract in the .mli, a consumer can neither forge a value nor read its internals
✅ A typed function cannot receive a value of another type: A value that reaches a typed parameter is of that type, so a string cannot become a program structure at that boundary
✅ The runtime bounds an array access: The bounds check is part of the language, so an off-by-one index is a defined exception
⚠️ Marshal.from_string trusts its input: A crafted byte string can build a value that the type system then trusts, so untrusted input must not be unmarshalled
⚠️ Obj.magic and a C stub break the type system: Obj.magic reinterprets a value without a check, and a stub can return an ill-typed value




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

Verdict: OCaml’s design yields low core coupling (72/100) because its abstraction is checked at compile time. A variant type closes a case set, an abstract type in a .mli hides its representation, a functor makes a type a module parameter, and the inference engine reports a mismatch before the program runs. The coupling that remains is mostly about state and lifetime: there is no ownership rule and no block-scoped release, exceptions are unchecked, and mutable containers are the natural way to hold module state. On the platform side, the small library ecosystem and the concepts of the module language are the real cost, while observation of the collector is a matter of tuning rather than of correctness.

title: Racket (8.17)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Racket in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 62/100 · Ecosystem coupling 84/100 · Engineering readiness 57/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Typing is dynamic with no static check (T1): A value carries its type at run time, so a wrong-typed use fails when the expression executes
❌ Dispatch is resolved at run time (T3): (send obj 'msg) and a generic method resolve when called, so a missing method fails there rather than at compile time
❌ There are no sum types and no core generics (T4, T5): An alternative is a struct, a symbol, or a tagged list plus a contract, and no type parameter exists in the core language
❌ The numeric operators dispatch on a hidden type (T8): +, *, and = accept any number, and the exact or the inexact result follows the values at run time, so the arithmetic is overloaded without a declared type
✅ A contract checks the module boundary at run time: (provide/contract [f (-> integer? integer?)]) and define/contract reject a wrong call at the boundary and name the module at fault
⚠️ #lang typed/racket types part of a program: A typed module imports an untyped one through require/typed and a contract, so static and dynamic code meet at a checked boundary



1.1.2 Construction

✅ struct declares the constructor with its invariant: (struct posn (x y) #:transparent #:guard check) creates the constructor, the predicate, and the accessors together, and the guard rejects a bad argument
✅ A macro extends the language at compile time: A define-syntax form sees its syntax objects and expands to core forms, so a construct is added without a run-time library
✅ Hygiene prevents accidental name capture: A binding the macro introduces cannot collide with a name at the use site, so the expansion does not depend on the caller’s names
✅ A module scopes what it defines: A binding is private until it is provided, so a helper constructor stays invisible outside the module
✅ #lang fixes the whole surface of a file: A module states its language on the first line, so a DSL and the base language do not mix by accident
⚠️ set! reaches any binding in the core language: A variable can be reassigned unless the language of the file forbids it, so immutability is not enforced by the core



1.1.3 Memory

✅ A call-with-* form brackets a resource: (call-with-input-file path proc) opens and closes around the call, and with-handlers covers the exceptional path
✅ A place collects its own heap: A place runs on a separate thread with a separate store, so parallel work does not extend one collection pause
❌ Collection is non-deterministic (M2): The collector runs on its own schedule, and (collect-garbage) or the PLTSTDERR collection log is the only control a program has
❌ There is no RAII (M3): There is no scope-bound destructor, so a port, a TCP listener, or a subprocess is released by an explicit close-input-port or by a bracket the author writes
❌ There is no ownership model (M4): No static lifetime or aliasing rule ties a value to an owner, so a shared mutable structure escapes its module without a trace
⚠️ A custodian groups resources only when it is created: make-custodian and custodian-shutdown-all shut down a group of threads and ports together, and the code must ask for that grouping



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked (Er2): raise, error, and raise-user-error are not declared in a signature, so a caller cannot see the failure set from the definition
✅ with-handlers selects the recovery by predicate: (with-handlers ([(lambda (e) (exn:fail? e)) handler]) body) chooses the handler from the exception’s type rather than from a code number
✅ An exception is a struct with fields: (exn-message e), (exn:fail:contract? e), and the continuation marks of exn:fail make a failure an inspectable value
✅ A failure can be a value instead of a throw: A struct with an ok and an error variant, or a pair of values, carries the outcome without an exception
✅ A contract violation blames a party: An exn:fail:contract carries the offending value, the contract, and the module blamed, so a boundary fault is localised
⚠️ A catch-all handler hides the cause: (with-handlers ([void void]) ...) discards the reason, and any cleanup must be arranged with dynamic-wind rather than by the handler



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ A place gives shared-nothing parallelism: place runs a computation on its own thread and store, and place-channel-put and place-channel-get pass values, so several cores are used without shared memory
✅ A future parallelises an expression: (future expr) runs on a thread from the pool and (touch f) forces the result, and the runtime keeps a future’s computation safe on its own
✅ A thread is a lightweight green thread: (thread proc) starts one, (sync evt) waits on an event, and channel-put and channel-get pass values between threads
✅ Non-blocking I/O composes through events: sync on a port or on an async-channel waits for whichever is ready, so no callback pyramid is needed
✅ A custodian bounds a thread group: A supervisor custodian shuts down its threads and ports together, so a group of tasks is torn down as a unit
⚠️ A shared box still needs a lock: A box or a vector written from two threads needs a semaphore or box-cas!, and the runtime reports no race



1.1.6 Platform

✅ A program compiles to a native executable: raco exe produces a standalone binary and bundles the runtime and the libraries it needs
✅ The runtime runs on the major platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux, and the BSDs are supported from one source
✅ Racket CS builds on Chez Scheme: The default runtime compiles with Chez’s compiler, and the earlier bytecode runtime with its JIT remained available as the alternative
✅ raco covers install, build, and delivery: raco pkg, raco exe, and raco distribute are one tool family for a project’s whole lifecycle
⚠️ The runtime must be present unless it is bundled: A source program needs an installed Racket, and raco distribute is the step that removes that dependency
⚠️ Cross-compilation is limited: An executable targets the platform that built it unless a cross build is arranged



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Language-oriented programming is the premise: Building a DSL is the design centre of the language, and the work of designing the notation is the price of a task-specific language
Contracts are opt-in: A module can leave a boundary unchecked, and the per-call cost of a contract follows from asking for the check
#lang fixes the language for a whole file: A module cannot change its language halfway, which is a deliberate uniformity rather than a coupling defect
A macro can obscure its expansion: A macro is powerful, and the readability cost of an unusual expansion is a style decision
A linked list is the core sequence type: cons, car, and cdr model a sequence as a pair chain, so the cost in memory locality is a representation choice
The λ-calculus core is deliberately small: The core language is tiny because a macro expands to it, which is a design decision




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Racket CS compiles through Chez Scheme: A module is compiled to native code ahead of time, so an interpreted step is not in the hot path
✅ Hot code is compiled rather than interpreted: The compiler and the JIT of the runtime remove repeated interpretation of a loop
✅ A future and a place use several cores: A computation split across futures runs on the available threads and places
⚠️ Numeric code is moderate: A boxed number and a generic arithmetic operation over the numeric tower cost more than unboxed arithmetic in a compiled language
⚠️ A contract adds a check per boundary crossing: A contract on a hot function is a run-time check on every call
⚠️ A continuation capture does real work: call/cc and dynamic-wind save and restore the control state, so a control abstraction is not free



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The package ecosystem is small (Ec3): The count of published packages is well below a mainstream language’s, so a project may write what it cannot find
✅ raco pkg is a first-class package manager: raco pkg install takes a package name, a file, or a Git URL, so a dependency needs no manual vendoring step
✅ The distribution ships a large library: racket/base, racket/list, racket/contract, racket/class, racket/draw, and racket/gui come in one installation
✅ DrRacket is an IDE for both beginner and expert: The editor, the REPL, and the stepper are part of the distribution, and the stepper shows one reduction at a time
✅ Scribble documents a package in the language itself: Scribble writes prose with Racket syntax and produces HTML, PDF, and the reference pages from one source
⚠️ The community is small: Questions are answered, but by fewer people than in a mainstream ecosystem



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ The language is stable and backward compatible: Racket 8.x runs code written for earlier releases, and the compatibility promise covers the core
✅ #lang isolates a change: A DSL fixes the language of its own files, so a change to the base language does not reach a #lang that pins it
✅ The change of runtime kept the language: Racket CS replaced the bytecode runtime beneath the language, and existing source recompiled
✅ A package can be held at a version: An installation can be pinned to a version or to a repository revision, so a build can be made reproducible
⚠️ A library API can change between releases: The core is stable, and a library outside it may change, so an upgrade needs a test run



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for language research and DSLs: Macros, #lang, and the reader produce a new language from a module, as the paper “Languages as Libraries” documents
✅ Strong fit for teaching: DrRacket, How to Design Programs, and the teaching languages such as #lang htdp/bsl are built for a first course
✅ Good for compilers and interpreters: #lang plus raco makes a language implementation a package, and the Beautiful Racket book builds several
✅ racket/gui covers a desktop application: The GUI toolkit and racket/draw ship in the distribution, so a windowed program needs no external dependency
⚠️ Commercial adoption is small with notable exceptions: Naughty Dog’s game scripting language and the Arc dialect behind Hacker News run on Racket, but the general production footprint is small
⚠️ Heavy numeric work belongs in a library: Array and tensor computation depends on a package rather than on the core language



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The concepts are many even when the syntax is small (L1): Macros, continuations, modules, and contracts are separate topics, and each takes practice
❌ A macro is a topic of its own: Writing a macro requires the syntax-object model and the phase distinctions, which are separate from ordinary programming
✅ DrRacket and the stepper make evaluation visible: A beginner steps an expression and sees each reduction of the program
✅ A complete curriculum exists: How to Design Programs and its teaching languages are free and aligned with the IDE
✅ The documentation is comprehensive: The Racket Reference and the Racket Guide cover the language and each library with examples
⚠️ A Scheme background helps and misleads: The parentheses and the λ-calculus core transfer, while the module system, structs, and #lang differ from a bare Scheme



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The syntax is uniform: Every form is a parenthesised list, so a reader learns one shape and applies it everywhere
✅ A user form looks like a built-in form: A macro-defined form has the same shape as let or define, so no new grammar is needed
✅ A reader extension can change the surface: #lang plus a readtable defines a different notation for one file without changing the language
✅ Prefix notation removes precedence rules: (+ (* a b) c) states the order of operations in its nesting, so no precedence table must be learned
⚠️ The parentheses are dense: A deeply nested expression needs careful counting, and most editors use a paredit or rainbow-paren mode to help
⚠️ A quoted form blurs data and code: '(a b) is a list and (a b) is a call, so one character changes the meaning of a form



1.2.7 Testing

✅ rackunit ships with the language: check-equal?, check-true, and test-case are in the distribution, and raco test runs a directory of tests
✅ A test can live in the module it tests: A (module+ test ...) submodule holds the tests, so no separate test file is needed
✅ A contract is an executable invariant: A contract on an exported function rejects a wrong call, so a test need not re-check the boundary
✅ A failure reports both values: A failed check-equal? prints the expected value, the actual value, and the source location
✅ The debugger and the stepper inspect a real run: DrRacket’s debugger steps the evaluation, and the stepper shows the reduction sequence
⚠️ Dynamic typing defers a fault to the executed path: A wrong-typed call passes the build and fails a run, so the covered paths matter



1.2.8 Security

✅ The runtime is memory-safe: No pointer arithmetic and no manual free exist, so a use-after-free or a buffer overflow cannot be written in Racket source
✅ A contract guards a trust boundary: A contract on a value that arrives from outside rejects a wrong shape at the boundary and names the party at fault
✅ racket/sandbox runs untrusted code with limits: A sandboxed evaluator carries its own language, a memory limit, and a custodian that bounds its run time
✅ eval is explicit and scoped: eval and dynamic-require are visible calls, and the namespace decides what the evaluated code can reach
⚠️ eval on a term built from input is the injection pattern: (eval (read input)) executes the text, and read itself can allocate on a crafted input
⚠️ Two places share the file system: A place shares no memory with another, but two places can still corrupt one file, which the language does not prevent

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.

Verdict: Racket’s design yields moderate core coupling (62/100) and better platform and ecosystem coupling (84/100). The language-oriented model is a real decoupling device: a macro expands to core forms without a name from the use site leaking in, a struct carries its own guard, a module hides what it does not provide, and a contract checks a boundary and names the party at fault. The cost sits in the type system and the heap, where typing is dynamic, dispatch resolves at run time, there are no sum types or core generics, and memory has neither an ownership rule nor a block-scoped release, with collection decided by the runtime. Around the language, the package ecosystem is small and the concept load is heavy, while the toolchain, the documentation, and the debugging support are complete.
