title: Scheme (R7RS)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Scheme in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 62/100 · Ecosystem coupling 84/100 · Engineering readiness 57/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ No static type check: A binding has no declared type and a call is resolved when it runs, so a type error is reported at run time rather than at load time (T1)
❌ Dispatch is dynamic: An application checks its argument count and its operands’ types when it executes, so an over-application or an under-application is an error then (T3)
❌ No sum types and no generics in the core: An alternative is a tagged list whose tag the code must test by hand, and a reusable procedure accepts any object and documents its expectation in a comment (T4, T5)
⚠️ + and the other arithmetic procedures are ordinary bindings: A redefinition changes what (+ a b) means, so an expression can invoke code the syntax does not show (T8)
✅ Hygienic macros decouple a macro from its use site: syntax-rules renames the identifiers a template introduces, so a macro cannot accidentally capture a name from the caller
✅ Lexical scope is one small rule: A lambda binds its parameters and its internal definitions, and nothing else is visible



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Constructors are ordinary procedures: A record constructor or a lambda that returns a list is built with the same mechanism, so construction does not couple to a class system
✅ define-record-type declares the shape once: The R7RS form generates the constructor, the type predicate, and the field accessors from one declaration
✅ Proper tail recursion is a language guarantee: A tail call reuses the current frame, so a loop written as a tail-recursive procedure runs in constant stack space
✅ let confines a binding to its body: A construction can build its state inside a let and expose only what it returns
⚠️ set! lets a construction mutate a captured binding: A closure can change state that its caller still holds, so a value built by a procedure is not automatically immutable
⚠️ A plain program has one top-level environment: R7RS define-library with explicit export confines a set of bindings, but a program’s top-level defines share a single scope



1.1.3 Memory

❌ A garbage collector reclaims memory: The implementation chooses the collector, and the program cannot free an object or predict when it dies (M2)
❌ No RAII or scope-exit destructor: A resource is released by an explicit call, and dynamic-wind can wrap that call in a dynamic extent, but nothing runs automatically at the end of an arbitrary scope (M3)
❌ No ownership or borrow model: A reference is an untracked alias, and the collector alone knows when an object is unreachable (M4)
✅ No manual deallocation: There is no free operation in the language, so a program cannot release a live object by mistake
✅ dynamic-wind binds a release to the dynamic extent: Its after thunk runs on every exit, including a non-local one
✅ R7RS pairs acquisition with release in the common cases: call-with-port, with-input-from-file, and with-output-to-file close what they open



1.1.4 Error

❌ A failure is raised and is not described by a signature: A procedure promises nothing about the conditions it may raise, so the failure set is not readable from the call (Er2)
✅ guard gives a structured handler: An R7RS guard clause names a condition and a recovery expression, and the handler returns a value to the guard
✅ with-exception-handler installs a handler for a dynamic extent: The handler is bound where it is installed, not at the raise point
✅ Condition types form a small hierarchy: error-object?, file-error?, and read-error? distinguish a raise by kind
✅ error carries a message and irritants: The offending values travel with the condition
⚠️ raise and raise-continuable differ: A non-continuable raise does not return to the raise point, so a handler must transfer control explicitly



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ The core defines no shared-memory concurrency: R7RS specifies no threads, so the standard makes no promise about a race the language does not create
✅ Continuations separate control flow from the call stack: call/cc captures the current continuation as a procedure, so a coroutine, a generator, or a backtracking search is a library over it
⚠️ Parallelism is an implementation extension: SRFI-18 supplies threads and SRFI-21 supplies synchronisation, and an implementation may support neither
⚠️ A thread extension fixes no memory model: SRFI-18 defines a mutex and a condition variable, but the report it extends states no ordering guarantee for a shared object
✅ A cooperative scheduler is expressible in the language: A queue of continuations plus a trampoline gives green threads without a runtime thread



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No single implementation owns the language: The language is a published report, and Chez, Guile, Racket, CHICKEN, Gambit, MIT, and Chibi all implement it
✅ define-library is the portability unit: An R7RS library with explicit import and export moves between implementations with its source
✅ The core is small enough for a small runtime: The report’s language fits a microcontroller interpreter and an embeddable one
✅ A program runs under several evaluation strategies: A compiler such as Chez and a simple interpreter both accept the report’s subset
⚠️ The standard is a family of reports, not one: R5RS, R6RS, and R7RS are not fully compatible, so the name “Scheme” alone does not say which report a program targets
⚠️ The library set beyond R7RS-small is the implementation’s: Each dialect ships a different collection, so portability in practice follows the chosen implementation



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The minimalist core is a deliberate trade: The report defines a small language and leaves libraries to the SRFIs, so a program chooses its extensions
The report split is a standards history: R5RS, R6RS, and R7RS followed a disagreement about how large the language should be
Dynamic typing is a design choice: No type declaration is required, so the discipline is the programmer’s
call/cc is a powerful and uncommon operator: Full continuations make control flow harder to reason about, and the expressiveness is the return
The REPL-first workflow is a choice: A program is developed at the prompt, which suits exploration and is not required by the language
Niche adoption is a scope outcome: The language targets education and research rather than industry




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Native compilers are available: Chez Scheme, Gambit, and CHICKEN compile Scheme to native code, so a program need not be interpreted
✅ The core is small enough to compile well: A compiler sees the whole language, so a straightforward optimiser covers it
✅ Tail calls do not consume stack: A recursive loop compiles to a jump
✅ Numeric code is fast in the strong implementations: A fixnum loop compiles to machine operations when the compiler proves the operands are fixnums
⚠️ Performance varies significantly by implementation: The same program can be fast under Chez and much slower under a simple interpreter
⚠️ A dynamically typed call is a checked call: The compiler inserts checks the program did not write, and their cost depends on how well it can eliminate them



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is small and spread over implementations: R7RS-small ships no library set, and the shared material is the SRFI collection plus each implementation’s own packages (Ec3)
✅ The SRFIs are a portable library standard: A program requests a library by number, and an implementation reports the SRFIs it supports
✅ The implementation distributions are mature and maintained: Guile, Chez, Racket, Gambit, and CHICKEN are long-lived projects with their own package collections
✅ snow and the implementation indexes collect R7RS libraries: A portable library can be published for several implementations at once
⚠️ Package management is implementation-specific: raco pkg, chicken-install, and Guix each serve one dialect, and the report fixes no package manager
⚠️ A library that uses a dialect extension is not portable: A program written against one implementation’s collection usually needs editing for another



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ SRFIs extend the language without changing the report: A new facility arrives as a numbered request, and each implementation adopts it independently
✅ A program written to R7RS-small keeps its meaning: The small report is stable, so its subset does not move under the program
✅ define-library localises a change to its importers: An exported name is the interface, and a change inside a library is invisible to the code that imports it
⚠️ Three reports are in circulation and they differ: R5RS, R6RS, and R7RS disagree on libraries, on the details of syntax-rules, and on some standard procedures
⚠️ An improvement reaches a program when an implementation adopts it: There is no single body that ships the language, so the timing is the implementation’s decision



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent as a teaching language: A dozen special forms cover the core, and SICP uses the language as a complete course
✅ Excellent for programming-language research: A small core with hygienic macros and first-class continuations is a substrate for experiments
✅ A real scripting and extension language: Guile is the extension language of GNU packages, including the Guix package manager
✅ Embedding is a real use: A small Scheme interpreter is embedded in applications for configuration and scripting
⚠️ Commercial application work is rare: Adoption is niche, so a team that picks Scheme for a product finds few precedents



1.2.5 Learning

❌ The distinctive abstractions take real effort: call/cc, continuation-passing style, and hygienic macro writing are each a skill that takes time (L1)
✅ The core is small enough to learn quickly: The special forms are few, and a complete course in them exists
✅ A REPL returns the value immediately: The read-eval-print loop gives feedback on each expression
✅ The report is precise about the language it defines: The specification states the required behaviour of each procedure
⚠️ The report is a specification, not a tutorial: A beginner needs a text such as SICP alongside it
⚠️ A continuation is easy to use outside its intended extent: Control that re-enters a captured continuation can surprise the programmer



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The syntax is uniform: A program is a sequence of S-expressions, so there is almost no grammar to learn
✅ Prefix notation removes precedence rules: (+ 1 (* 2 3)) states the order in brackets, so no operator-precedence table is needed
✅ Quasiquotation makes a template readable: `(a ,b ,@c) builds a list with holes at the point of use
✅ The reader recognises the literal syntaxes directly: #\a is a character, #(1 2) is a vector, and #; comments out the next datum
✅ A macro can add a readable form: define-syntax with syntax-rules introduces surface syntax without changing the core
⚠️ A deeply nested expression needs the editor’s indentation: The reader balances the brackets, and the human eye follows the layout



1.2.7 Testing

✅ SRFI-64 defines a portable test framework: test-begin, test-equal, and test-end run under any implementation that supports the SRFI
✅ error makes a check cheap to write: (unless test (error "..." x)) fails a check and reports the offending value
✅ The REPL is the first test loop: An expression is evaluated and its value is compared at the prompt
✅ The implementation supplies a tracer and a debugger: Chez, Guile, and Racket each expose a trace facility and an inspector
⚠️ No test framework is in the standard: A project depends on its implementation’s SRFI coverage rather than on the report
⚠️ A test exercises the paths it runs: An unexecuted branch is unchecked, and a dynamic error in it appears only when the branch is reached



1.2.8 Security

✅ The implementation manages memory: The language exposes no pointer and no manual free, so a buffer overflow or a use-after-free is not expressible in Scheme source
✅ Hygienic macros remove a class of capture defect: A macro cannot bind a name it did not intend to bind
✅ The core has no unsafe memory operation: The report defines no pointer arithmetic and no address
⚠️ eval and read execute data as code: (eval (read port)) runs whatever the input contains, so untrusted input must never reach it
⚠️ A continuation can cross an intended check: A continuation captured before a permission test can be re-entered after it
⚠️ A foreign-function interface leaves the safe subset: An FFI in an implementation reaches native code, and the memory-safety guarantee stops there




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

title: SPARK (Pro 25)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses SPARK in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 73/100 · Ecosystem coupling 69/100 · Engineering readiness 42/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ The static type system is Ada’s: Every object, parameter, and function result has a declared type, and the compiler checks every assignment and call
✅ Subtypes carry range constraints: subtype narrows a base type with a range or a predicate, and in the proved subset a violation is a proof obligation rather than a run-time check
✅ Enumeration and discriminated record types express alternatives: An enumeration gives a finite value set, and a variant record’s discriminant states which branch is active
✅ Generics are checked at each instantiation: An Ada generic is analysed where it is instantiated, so a reusable abstraction is verified at its use site
✅ Type_Invariant states a property of a private type: The invariant is an obligation on every value of the type
⚠️ Access types are admitted only under an ownership policy: SPARK allows a pointer when its owner is declared, so indirection is available but constrained



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Contracts are part of the subprogram declaration: Pre, Post, and Contract_Cases state the obligation beside the parameters, so a caller reads it with the signature
✅ Flow contracts state what a subprogram reads and writes: Global, Depends, and Refined_Global make the data flow a declared artefact
✅ Abstract states confine a package’s state: Abstract_State declares the state as an abstraction, Refined_State binds it to concrete variables, and Initializes states what a package sets up
✅ Separation is proved rather than advised: The ownership policy, the flow aspects, and the contracts are analysed by GNATprove, so a declared separation is verified and not merely recommended
⚠️ The declarations carry more than the code needs: A proof requires a contract for every subprogram on the path, so construction carries an annotation burden
⚠️ A unit can opt out with SPARK_Mode => Off: An analysed region and an unchecked region can sit in the same program



1.1.3 Memory

✅ An ownership policy governs any access type: SPARK’s data-ownership regime gives a pointer a stated owner, so a dangling or duplicated reference is a proof failure rather than a run-time defect
✅ No manual deallocation in the subset: Unchecked_Deallocation is outside SPARK, so a program never frees memory by hand
✅ No garbage collector: SPARK compiles to native code and runs without a collector
✅ Bounded containers remove the heap: Ada.Containers.Bounded_Vectors and its siblings hold their storage in the object
✅ A local object’s lifetime is its scope: A stack variable’s extent is fixed by the block that declares it
⚠️ An owned access type still allocates at run time: The allocation is allowed and proved, but the allocator’s behaviour remains a run-time fact



1.1.4 Error

✅ A failure is a proof obligation: GNATprove reports an unproved check, so a fault is found in the toolchain rather than in a test run
✅ A raise is stated in the contract: Exceptional_Cases names the exceptions a subprogram may propagate, so the failure set is declared
✅ Run-time checks are proved impossible rather than disabled: Once GNATprove proves that an index, a range, or a division cannot fail, the check costs nothing
✅ Assert becomes a proof obligation: pragma Assert states a property that the analysis must establish or report
✅ Assume records an unproved fact explicitly: An assumption is written in the source and appears in the analysis report
⚠️ The proof is no stronger than its assumptions: An Assume, an unproved check, or a SPARK_Mode => Off unit leaves a gap in the guarantee



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Ada tasking is available and analysable: A task and a protected object are language constructs, and SPARK analyses the data flow of the supported subset
✅ A protected object is the synchronisation boundary: A protected operation enforces mutual exclusion and a barrier, so the lock is not written by hand
✅ The Ravenscar profile gives a static task set: No task is created dynamically, and the ceiling-locking protocol prevents priority inversion
✅ Shared state must be declared: A variable shared between tasks appears in a Global or Depends aspect, so the sharing is visible
⚠️ The analysed subset of tasking is smaller than Ada’s: An entry family, a dynamic rendezvous, or an unrestricted task is outside the analysed subset



1.1.6 Platform

❌ SPARK is a subset of Ada and a program is an Ada program: GNAT compiles the code, and the language has no existence apart from the Ada platform (P1)
❌ A foreign call leaves the proved region: An interface to C or another language is declared outside SPARK, so it cannot be analysed with the rest
✅ GNAT is a mature and portable Ada compiler: The same source compiles for x86-64, ARM, and the embedded targets used in avionics
✅ The qualified toolchain targets the certificated platforms: GNAT Pro supports VxWorks, LynxOS-178, and bare metal with a qualification for DO-178C
⚠️ Full support is a commercial subscription: GNATprove is available in the community toolchain, and SPARK Pro adds support, libraries, and qualification
⚠️ The build is a GNAT project: gprbuild and a project file describe the build, so the project couples to the Ada toolchain



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The proved subset is smaller than Ada: A feature outside SPARK is left out or isolated behind a SPARK_Mode => Off boundary
The restriction on pointers is a deliberate exchange: Aliasing is removed in return for an ownership regime and an array or a bounded container in place of a linked structure
The annotation burden is the price of the proof: A contract, an invariant, and a flow aspect are written for each unit on the path
The target domain is high-assurance by design: Aviation, space, and medical devices are the intended context, and the domain mark records that scope
Verification effort is a project decision: Zero-defect software is achievable given sufficient effort, which is a budget choice
The proof checks the contract, not the requirement: A verified program can implement the wrong specification, which no toolchain detects




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The compiled output is an Ada program’s native binary: SPARK compiles to the same native code, so the verification adds no run-time cost
✅ A proved check need not execute: A check that GNATprove established can be suppressed at that point, so the verified code does not pay for the guard
✅ No collector and no interpreter: The run-time has neither a garbage collector nor a JIT, so the timing is the Ada run-time’s
✅ The Ravenscar profile bounds the run-time behaviour: The task set, the priorities, and the locking are static, which makes the timing analysable
⚠️ The run-time is the Ada run-time: Tasking, the secondary stack, and exception propagation cost what GNAT’s run-time costs
⚠️ The proof is a build-time cost: GNATprove can take far longer than the compilation, which delays the build but not the program



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The SPARK ecosystem is a subset of Ada’s: A library must itself be in the SPARK subset to be analysed with the program (Ec3)
✅ Ada’s tooling serves the project: Alire supplies packages and gprbuild builds the project
✅ GNATprove and SPARK Pro are purpose-built and mature: The analyser and the commercial support layer are actively developed
✅ The industrial community sustains the toolchain: The requirements of the certificated industries drive the analyser and the library work
✅ A verified library base exists: SPARK’s own libraries and verified components ship with the toolchain
⚠️ A library that uses pointers must be isolated: An Ada library outside the subset is reached through an unproved boundary



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ SPARK tracks a published Ada standard: The subset is defined against Ada 2012 and Ada 2022, so a language change follows the standard revision
✅ Successive SPARK releases widened the subset: The ownership policy, the functional contracts, and the proof of type invariants were added over several releases
✅ Ada’s compatibility record is strong: An older Ada program generally compiles under a later revision
⚠️ A new feature arrives with a toolchain release: The analyser states the subset it supports, so adoption follows the release
⚠️ A proof depends on the toolchain version: A check proved under one GNATprove release can need a new annotation under another



1.2.4 Domain

❌ The language exists for high-assurance systems: Aviation, space, and medical devices, where DO-178C, EN 50128, or IEC 62304 applies, are the intended domains (D1)
❌ Outside those domains it is rarely chosen: A general application gains little from the proof and pays the toolchain cost (D1)
✅ The fit in the intended domain is excellent: The tools, the libraries, and the certification evidence all target it
✅ DO-333 credits the proof against the certification objectives: The formal-methods supplement to DO-178C lets the analysis substitute for some test objectives
✅ The shipping uses are real: Airbus, Thales, and Lockheed Martin build critical software on it
⚠️ The labour pool is small: An engineer with both Ada and formal-methods experience is hard to find



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Two skills must be learned, not one: SPARK requires Ada fluency and formal-methods practice, so contracts, invariants, and the proof tool must all be mastered (L1)
❌ A proof failure must be read as a counterexample: GNATprove reports an unproved check with a path, and turning the report into a fix takes experience
✅ The analysis report is actionable: The tool names the check, the path, and the assumption that blocks the proof
✅ The learning material is complete: AdaCore’s tutorial and the SPARK course material cover the language and the proof method
⚠️ The learning curve is very steep: A first proved subprogram is quick to write, and a first proved package with an abstract state is not



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The syntax is Ada’s: A package, a subprogram, and a loop read as they do in Ada, and a contract appears as an aspect or a pragma
✅ The block structure is explicit: A begin/end pair closes a block, and the end repeats the name it closes
✅ Contracts sit beside the parameters: Pre =>, Post =>, and Global => are part of the subprogram declaration
✅ Quantified expressions are first-class: (for all I in A'Range => A (I) > 0) states a property in the source
⚠️ An aspect clause can be long: A Depends aspect over much state is a long expression that needs careful reading



1.2.7 Testing

✅ The proof covers the property the contract states: An obligation is discharged for every value it quantifies, not for a sample
✅ The test suite no longer has to trigger every check: A bounds or range check proved impossible needs no test to reach it
✅ gnattest generates a unit-test harness: It reads a package specification and emits AUnit test stubs
✅ AUnit covers the behaviour a contract does not state: The proof and the test suite answer different questions
⚠️ A property that no contract states is not proved: The analysis reaches exactly the contracts and invariants that are written



1.2.8 Security

✅ The classic memory-safety faults are proved absent: A buffer overflow, a use-after-free, and a null dereference are removed by the subset and the proof, so the vulnerability class does not exist in the analysed code
✅ Input validity is stated and checked: A range constraint or a Pre aspect states what the caller must guarantee, and the proof covers the rest
✅ Unchecked_Conversion and pointer arithmetic are outside the subset: The unsafe operations are not available to analysed code
⚠️ The guarantee stops at the SPARK_Mode => Off boundary: An imported C function, a device driver, or an unchecked allocation is not proved
⚠️ The trusted base includes the prover and the compiler: A defect in GNATprove or in the code generator is outside the proof




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.5 Interop

⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

⚠️ One vendor decides the language’s direction.
⚠️ The specification is not public.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

✅ A standards-qualified toolchain or an established safety standard covers this language.

Verdict: SPARK’s design yields low core coupling for the work it is built for, and its platform cost is the price of a narrow domain. The static type system is Ada’s, the contracts and flow aspects make every global dependency explicit, an ownership policy removes coupling through shared references, and the toolchain proves the run-time checks that other languages leave to a test suite. The only scored core loss is P1: the language is a subset of Ada and does not exist apart from that platform. Main strengths: GNATprove, a toolchain qualified for DO-178C, DO-333 credit for the proof, and industrial use at Airbus, Thales, and Lockheed Martin; main weaknesses: an ecosystem that is a subset of Ada’s, a domain lock-in to high-assurance systems, and one of the steepest learning curves here.

title: Turbo Pascal (7.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Turbo Pascal in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 39/100 · Ecosystem coupling 54/100 · Engineering readiness 42/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Strong static typing is enforced at compile time: Every variable, parameter, and function result has a declared type, and an assignment between incompatible types is rejected
✅ Enumerated and subrange types state a value domain: type TDay = (Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri) and a subrange such as 1..31 narrow the domain in the declaration
✅ A typed pointer names what it addresses: ^T is a pointer to T, so an assignment between pointers of different types is an error
❌ A variant record is an unchecked union: record ... case Tag: T of ... end names the alternatives, but the compiler does not require the tag to be tested before a field is read (T4)
❌ No generics: A container is written for one element type, or it stores Pointer values and casts them, so reuse across types is untyped (T5)
✅ A unit is the namespace and a real module boundary: The interface section is what a uses clause sees, and the implementation section is private to the unit



1.1.2 Construction

✅ A uses clause states each dependency: The compiler rejects a call into a unit that is not listed, so the dependency edge is written in the source
✅ interface and implementation separate the contract from the code: A caller compiles against the declarations only
✅ An object declares its own construction and destruction: An object type declares constructor Init and destructor Done, and New(P, Init) runs the constructor together with the allocation
✅ Unit initialization and finalization run in dependency order: A unit’s startup code runs before the program body and its shutdown code runs after it
❌ Mutability is the default: A var is writable and reassignable, and only a const marks a value fixed (C2)
⚠️ A class hierarchy couples a derived object to its base: Object-oriented programming arrived in version 5.5, and an object type derives from one base, so shared behaviour is reached through that single-inheritance chain



1.1.3 Memory

❌ Every heap allocation is manual: New and Dispose, or GetMem and FreeMem, are the ways to use the heap, and the programmer writes the matching release (M1)
❌ Nothing runs when a variable leaves its scope: There is no release tied to scope, and a destructor is a method the programmer must call (M3)
❌ No ownership model: A typed pointer may alias, dangle, or be disposed twice, and the compiler does not track it (M4)
✅ The run-time library owns the heap: New, Dispose, Mark, and Release give a defined heap with a stack-like mark and release discipline
✅ A String value carries its own length: A String[255] short string stores its length in the first byte, so a string operation needs no terminator
⚠️ Real-mode addressing bounds the heap: In the 16-bit memory models the heap lies in the data segment, so the model’s segment limit caps one allocation



1.1.4 Error

❌ The default failure path is a halt or an error code: An unhandled run-time error stops the program with a run-time error number, and an I/O failure is reported through IOResult when checking is off (Er1)
❌ No composable result type: A failure cannot be carried in the type of a function’s result, so the caller learns of it from an error code or an exception (Er4)
✅ try/except/finally is a structured path: Version 7 added exception handling, and the finally block runs on every exit from the statement
✅ raise names the failure: raise EDivByZero.Create raises an object from the SysUtils exception hierarchy
⚠️ The exceptions are unchecked: Nothing in a signature states which exceptions a routine may raise, so the recovery path depends on a convention
⚠️ Two error styles coexist: {$I-} with IOResult checks one call at a time, while try/except covers a block, so a program mixes both



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ The language has no concurrency construct: There is no thread type, no task, and no synchronisation primitive; concurrent work in DOS is expressed with an interrupt procedure (K5)
⚠️ The only shared state is a global variable: With no concurrency construct in the language, a global variable is what the main code and an interrupt procedure both reach, and nothing guards the access
⚠️ A thread-local variable needs a successor compiler: threadvar gives a variable one copy per thread in Delphi and Free Pascal, but Turbo Pascal creates no thread and the DOS target has none
⚠️ An interrupt procedure must be declared as such: The interrupt directive saves the registers, and the protection is a declaration rather than a checked protocol
⚠️ Reentrancy is the programmer’s concern: An interrupt procedure that calls a library routine can corrupt state the interrupted code was using
⚠️ Cooperative concurrency came from an add-on: A terminate-and-stay-resident program or a library simulated multitasking outside the language



1.1.6 Platform

❌ The main target is 16-bit DOS: The compiler produces real-mode DOS executables, and version 7 was the last release of the line (P3)
❌ A compiled unit is a private object format: A .TPU file is Turbo Pascal’s own unit format, and no other language’s linker consumes it
✅ Free Pascal and Delphi compile the same source: Both accept Turbo Pascal units, so the source is not frozen to the original compiler
✅ The compiler is a self-contained toolchain: One executable compiles a program, and the IDE runs the edit-compile-run cycle
⚠️ The memory model is a compile-time choice: {$M} selects tiny, small, compact, large, or huge, and the model bounds the code and the data segments
⚠️ Real-mode addressing shows in the source: near and far pointers and segment arithmetic appear once a program leaves the small model



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The one-pass compiler is a deliberate speed choice: Compilation is nearly instant, and the price is a modest optimiser
The integrated IDE is the intended way to work: The compiler, the editor, and the debugger are one program
The 16-bit limit belongs to the target machine: The segment size is a property of the processor mode, not only of the language
Turbo Vision is supplied and not required: The text-mode GUI library is an optional dependency of the program
The goto statement remains in the language: A jump is available for the case where a structured form is awkward
Pascal is a teaching language by design: The readable syntax and the strong typing were written for instruction




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The compiler emits native 8086 machine code: There is no interpreter and no run-time compiler between the source and the processor
✅ Compilation is very fast: The one-pass compiler makes the edit-compile-run cycle take seconds
✅ A compiled program starts immediately: A DOS .EXE needs no runtime initialisation beyond the loader
⚠️ The optimiser does little global work: The algorithm and the data layout dominate the result
⚠️ The 16-bit target caps the work: The real-mode segment limit bounds the data one program can address
⚠️ A far pointer costs extra cycles: A segment override and a far access element are slower than a register operation



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ The ecosystem is legacy and discontinued: Borland ended Turbo Pascal after version 7 in favour of Delphi, so the tool and package field is historical (Ec3)
✅ Free Pascal, Delphi, and Virtual Pascal continue the language: Each is a compatible implementation, so much Turbo Pascal code still compiles today
✅ A large body of published material exists: The era’s books, tutorials, and the Turbo Vision source remain available
✅ The compiler is a single small program: Nothing else must be installed to build a program
⚠️ Reuse is by source: A unit is shared as .PAS source rather than as a resolved package with a version
⚠️ The tooling runs in DOS or an emulator: The IDE and the debugger need a DOS machine or an emulator on a current computer



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The language is discontinued: Borland ended the line in 1995 and moved it to Delphi and Object Pascal, so no version followed 7.0 (V3)
❌ The definition is frozen at 7.0: The language does not change, so a missing feature or a defect is permanent (V2)
✅ The reach of the tool was historically large: Over 400 000 copies were sold in the first two years, which made Pascal accessible to a generation of programmers
✅ The successors accept the source: Delphi and Object Pascal keep the unit, the static typing, and most of the syntax
✅ A port is an adjustment rather than a rewrite: Free Pascal compiles a unit with little change outside the platform-specific code
⚠️ The platform-specific part is real work: DOS interrupts, direct video memory, inline machine code, and .TPU linkage have no direct counterpart on a current target



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Structured programming instruction is the native domain: The readable syntax and the strong typing were designed for teaching
✅ DOS application and tool development fit the target: A compiled .EXE needed no runtime and ran on any PC of the era
✅ Turbo Vision covers text-mode GUI work: The bundled library provides windows, menus, and dialogs on a character screen
✅ A small number-crunching utility is a natural use: A scientific or engineering program was a common Turbo Pascal program
⚠️ New development does not choose it: The domain today is legacy maintenance and education
⚠️ Hardware access sits outside the language: A program that drives a device uses the BIOS, a DOS interrupt, or inline code



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The syntax is small and readable: begin/end, var, procedure, if/then/else, and for/to cover the language
✅ The compiler reports an error immediately: The short edit-compile-run cycle makes a mistake cheap to find
✅ The IDE integrates a debugger: Step, watch, and breakpoint are keystrokes away
⚠️ Pointers and manual memory are the hard part: The syntax is gentle and the heap discipline is not
⚠️ Real-mode addressing is a second subject: Near and far pointers and segments must be learned for system work
⚠️ The semicolon rule catches a beginner: A semicolon separates statements, so the last statement of a block takes none



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ The syntax is verbose: begin/end, unit/interface/implementation, try/except/end, and every declaration keyword are spelled out (S1)
✅ Keywords are words rather than symbols: if, then, do, of, and end carry the structure
✅ Blocks are bracketed consistently: begin/end closes every compound statement, including the body of a procedure
✅ A declaration names the variable before its type: var Count: Integer reads in one direction
⚠️ A statement separator, not a terminator: The semicolon rule is a rule to learn rather than a decoration
⚠️ A nested field needs its qualifier or a with: Reading a record inside a record is verbose without the with statement



1.2.7 Testing

❌ There is no test framework in the toolchain: A test is a program that runs and compares, and nothing in the distribution runs a suite (G1)
❌ The debugger is the era’s tool: The IDE steps and watches variables, with no assertion or coverage support (G2)
✅ A failed run-time check reports the detail: The run-time library prints the error number, the address, and the register contents
✅ A check is a few lines of Pascal: A comparison and a halt write a test without a framework
⚠️ A test suite is a program the programmer writes: No runner, no fixture loader, and no report come with the toolchain



1.2.8 Security

✅ The type system rejects a mismatch at compile time: A pointer to one type cannot take a pointer to another without a written cast
✅ The dangerous cast is one written site: Pointer and a type cast put the risk where the programmer wrote it
✅ A check can be switched on: {$R+} adds range checking to an array index and to a subrange assignment
⚠️ Manual memory management admits the classic faults: An overrun and a use-after-free are possible, and the compiler does not check them
⚠️ {$I-} disables an I/O check: After that directive a failed file operation must be tested through IOResult
⚠️ inline machine code bypasses the type system: An inline(...) statement writes raw opcodes into the compiled program




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

⚠️ No fast in-editor analysis.



1.3.5 Interop

⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

⚠️ One vendor decides the language’s direction.
⚠️ The specification is not public.

Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

Verdict: Turbo Pascal’s core score is held down by the mechanisms of its era rather than by a missing idea: the heap is manual, no release is tied to scope, and a failure is a run-time error number or an unchecked exception. Its one strong structural feature is the unit, where interface and implementation draw a real boundary and the uses clause writes each dependency into the source. Main strengths: strong static typing, near-instant native compilation, a gentle readable syntax, and a live path to Free Pascal and Delphi. Main weaknesses: no generics, unchecked variant records, no concurrency construct in the language, and a 16-bit target whose toolchain, ecosystem, and platform are all historical.

title: Visual Basic 16 (.NET)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Visual Basic .NET in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 46/100 · Ecosystem coupling 69/100 · Engineering readiness 88/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Option Strict Off is the default: Under it an implicit narrowing conversion and a late-bound Object call compile, and the type is resolved when the statement runs (T2)
✅ Option Strict On removes the late-bound path: The same code does not compile until the conversion or the reference is written explicitly
✅ Interface and Implements separate a contract from its implementation: A class names the interface members it supplies
✅ A nullable value type states an absence: Integer? is Nullable(Of Integer), and HasValue and Value test and read it
❌ Nothing is compatible with every reference type: A reference may be Nothing, no declaration requires a test before use, the language offers no nullable reference annotation, and for a string "" = Nothing is True (T10)
⚠️ A class hierarchy couples a derived class to its base: Inherits binds a class to the base’s virtual members, and an Interface with Implements is the alternative that avoids the chain



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Sub New is a real constructor: A class declares it, Overloads gives several signatures, and MyBase.New runs the base constructor
✅ ReadOnly and Const mark a fixed value: A ReadOnly field is set once, and a Const is fixed at compile time
❌ Mutability is the default: A Dim variable and a property are writable, and only an explicit ReadOnly or Const changes that (C2)
✅ A Structure is a value type with its own constructor: A copy of a structure is a copy of its values, and it is not collected
✅ Using bounds the life of a resource: The block calls Dispose on every exit path
⚠️ WithEvents binds the handler object to its source: A WithEvents field is tied to the events of one declared type, and Handles lists the events it answers, so the subscription is written into the declaration



1.1.3 Memory

❌ The garbage collector decides when memory returns: A reference is reclaimed after it becomes unreachable, and a collection pause is possible (M2)
❌ No release runs at the end of a scope: A class has a finalizer at best, whose time is not defined, and there is no deterministic destructor (M3)
❌ No ownership model: A reference may alias, and nothing in the type states who releases the object (M4)
✅ Using gives deterministic release for an IDisposable: The block calls Dispose on every exit, including the exceptional one
✅ IDisposable is the stated protocol for a native resource: A type that holds a handle states its release method
⚠️ A finalizer delays the collection of its object: The object survives one extra collection while the finalizer queue is drained



1.1.4 Error

❌ The exceptions are unchecked: No method signature states the exceptions it may raise, so a Try is a convention (Er2)
❌ A failure can be discarded by design: On Error Resume Next and an empty Catch both let a failure pass with no effect (Er3)
✅ Try/Catch/Finally is a structured path: The Catch block holds the recovery code and Finally runs on every exit
✅ The failure is selected by type: Catch ex As IOException chooses by exception type, and ex.InnerException carries the cause
⚠️ The legacy On Error GoTo form remains: It binds the recovery to a line label and a sequence, beside the structured form
⚠️ An Async failure arrives at the Await: An exception in an awaited task surfaces at the await, so the Try block must span it



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ Synchronisation is manual with no race detection: SyncLock guards a block, and the compiler analyses no program for a race (K3)
✅ SyncLock is a language construct: It takes a lock on an expression and releases it at the end of the block
✅ Async and Await state the suspension point: An asynchronous call reads as a sequence, and the language marks where it yields
✅ The task and thread types come from the runtime: Task, Thread, and the thread pool are .NET types the language uses directly
⚠️ The lock order is not stated: SyncLock names a lock and not an order, so a deadlock is a design concern outside the language
⚠️ An event handler runs on the raising thread: An event raised on a worker thread runs the handler there, and the UI-thread rule is a framework convention



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The compiler emits a portable .NET assembly: The resulting .dll or .exe runs wherever the .NET runtime runs
✅ The runtime runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS: The same assembly runs on each, so the language is not bound to one operating system
✅ The class library is reachable: An assembly with a public surface can be consumed from Visual Basic
✅ The project system is the common one: A .vbproj is an SDK-style project built by dotnet build
⚠️ A few newer features have no Visual Basic form: Nullable reference annotations and static abstract interface members have no equivalent syntax, so a consumer of a library that requires them needs a wrapper
⚠️ Windows Forms and WPF target Windows only: A GUI project on either framework runs on Windows



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Late binding is the pragmatic COM path: Option Strict Off around an Office object model avoids an interop reference, which is why the setting survives
The Visual Basic 6 heritage is deliberate: On Error, My, and the forms designer are continuity choices for the existing developer base
Verbosity buys explicitness: End If and End Sub are redundant, and the end of every block is visible
The design-time form designer is a tool: The layout is a tool feature rather than a language mechanism
A port to C# is mechanical: The constructs map closely, and the effort is the trade for leaving the language line
A frozen language is stable for existing code: No feature churn reaches a maintained program




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ The compiler emits IL and the runtime compiles it: The hot path becomes machine code through the just-in-time compiler
✅ The collector is generational: A short-lived object is reclaimed cheaply
✅ The runtime library supplies the fast paths: StringBuilder and the asynchronous I/O APIs are available to a Visual Basic program
⚠️ The first call of a method is the slowest: Compilation happens on first use, so start-up includes a warm-up
⚠️ Boxing and string concatenation allocate: An Object-typed value and a repeated & produce garbage on the heap
⚠️ A collection pause is possible on a large heap: The collector’s pause is outside the program’s control (R2)



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ NuGet is the package manager: A dependency is declared in the project and restored by dotnet restore
✅ The IDE is Visual Studio: Editing, refactoring, debugging, and the designer are integrated, and the free edition supports Visual Basic
✅ The class library is large and documented: I/O, networking, collections, and UI are covered by the runtime
✅ The compiler ships with the platform: vbc is maintained with the .NET SDK
⚠️ The published example is usually C#: A library’s documentation and samples are C#, and a Visual Basic consumer translates them
⚠️ New libraries are rarely written in Visual Basic: The language’s share of new code is small



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The language line is closed to new features: Microsoft has stated that Visual Basic will not be evolved for new workloads, and the language receives no new syntax (V3)
✅ The language remains supported for existing code: The compiler is maintained with the .NET SDK for bug fixes and platform compatibility
✅ The runtime advances under the language: An existing assembly runs on a current .NET, so the platform moves even though the language does not
✅ A migration path to C# exists and is close: The language improved substantially from Visual Basic 6, and the constructs and the object model map almost one to one onto C#
⚠️ A new framework feature can be C#-only: Nullable reference types and static abstract interface members arrived without a Visual Basic form



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Office and COM automation is a native domain: Object and late binding make an Office object model usable without an interop assembly
✅ Windows Forms is the rapid-desktop domain: The designer and the event model fit a business form application
✅ Console tools and services are straightforward: A short program builds into an .exe in the .NET toolchain
✅ The .NET library ecosystem is reachable: Any assembly with a public surface can be consumed
⚠️ Modern .NET UI frameworks are not offered for Visual Basic: The .NET MAUI and Blazor templates are C#, so a new Visual Basic GUI is a Windows Forms or WPF project
⚠️ It is not the choice for new development: The language remains less expressive than C# on the newer features, and the direction of the ecosystem is C#



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The syntax is readable and close to English: If ... Then, For Each ... In, and End Sub read as their meaning
✅ The curve is gentle from BASIC or Visual Basic 6: The surface carries over, and the runtime supplies the rest
✅ The reference documentation is complete: Microsoft documents every statement, keyword, and option
✅ The IDE guides a new user: IntelliSense and the compiler’s messages explain a construct as it is written
⚠️ Four Option statements change the language: Strict, Explicit, Infer, and Compare each alter what compiles or what a comparison means
⚠️ The large subject is the class library: The framework, not the syntax, is the bulk of the work



1.2.6 Syntax

❌ The syntax is verbose: Every block closes with its own keyword pair such as End If, End Sub, and Next, and a declaration repeats Dim and As (S1)
✅ Keywords are words: The reading is close to English
✅ A line ends a statement: Continuation is explicit with _
✅ Attributes are written in angle brackets: <Serializable> and <Obsolete("...")> attach metadata to a declaration
⚠️ A file-level Option changes the parse: Option Strict On at the top of a file changes which lines compile
⚠️ The language is case-insensitive: myValue and MyValue name the same variable, so a rename is not caught by the case



1.2.7 Testing

✅ A test framework is available from NuGet: MSTest, NUnit, and xUnit all run against the .NET test SDK
✅ dotnet test runs the suite: Discovery, execution, and the report come from the platform
✅ A test is written in Visual Basic: Attributes such as <TestMethod> mark a test method
✅ The debugger is integrated: A failed test can be stepped through in Visual Studio
✅ An assertion or mocking library is a package: NUnit’s assertions and Moq are consumed from NuGet
⚠️ The default Option Strict Off weakens the test itself: A test project with the default setting can pass a value of a wrong type and notice only at run time



1.2.8 Security

✅ The runtime is memory-safe: No use-after-free and no buffer overrun occurs in safe code, and the language has no pointer type
✅ No unsafe context exists in Visual Basic: The unverifiable memory operations of the runtime are out of reach
✅ The exception path keeps the failure in a value: ex.Message and ex.InnerException carry the detail to a handler
✅ Option Strict On removes the late-bound call: The member is resolved by the compiler rather than by name at run time
⚠️ On Error Resume Next can hide a failure that matters: A suppressed failure leaves the program in a state the next statement does not expect
⚠️ A COM interop boundary is outside the runtime’s checks: A late-bound call crosses into unmanaged code that the type system does not verify

Verdict: Visual Basic .NET reaches a mid-range core score by inheriting the .NET runtime’s separation of interface from implementation, its collected memory, and its checked types, while keeping the older Visual Basic defaults beside them. The losses are those defaults: Option Strict Off, a Nothing that fits every reference type, unchecked exceptions, a failure a caller may discard, and manual synchronisation. Main strengths: interfaces, Option Strict On, Using for deterministic release, the whole .NET class library, and a mechanical path to C#. Main weaknesses: Option Strict Off defers a conversion to run time, Nothing is not a checked absence, the collector decides when memory returns, a race has no detector, and the language line is closed to new features.

title: Eiffel (ECMA-367 / ISO/IEC 25436:2006)
text:
Analysis against the Eiffel language standard (ECMA-367, approved June 2005; ISO/IEC 25436:2006) and EiffelStudio 25.12 (January 2026). Eiffel, created by Bertrand Meyer, is the language that introduced Design by Contract.
This assessment applies the coupling account — coupling as access to a shared resource, and the coupling floor [1], [2] — and the knowledge-embodiment theorem [3]; the language is assessed against its official reference [4].

title: Eiffel (ECMA-367 / ISO/IEC 25436:2006)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Eiffel in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 46/100 · Ecosystem coupling 46/100 · Engineering readiness 57/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Design by Contract (DBC): require (preconditions), ensure (postconditions), and invariant (class invariants) make an element’s change conditions explicit. This is the coupling-relevant feature: contracts name the requirements an element realizes, so a change in one element’s requirements that forces another element’s contract to change is visible at the boundary
✅ Void safety (attached types): x: attached T vs x: detachable T separates non-null from nullable at compile time (Eiffel 6+). Eliminates the null-checking coupling class at compile time
✅ Strong static typing: No implicit coercion, no unchecked casts as escape hatches
✅ No argument overloading: Each feature name within a class maps to exactly one feature — “one name, within one class, means one thing.” This eliminates method-resolution ambiguity coupling and is what makes Eiffel’s multiple inheritance safe
✅ Command-Query Separation: Queries (which return information) must not modify the instance — a Meyer design rule that prevents side effects hidden in value retrieval from coupling unrelated elements
✅ Generics with constraints: LINKED_LIST [G -> COMPARABLE] decouples containers from element types
⚠️ Multiple inheritance: Supported with rename, redefine, and select — powerful feature reuse but creates hierarchy coupling and diamond complexity
⚠️ Inheritance still available: Class hierarchies couple behavior to the inheritance tree



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Creation procedures (create): Separate allocation from initialization; create x.make(...)
✅ Invariants validate object state: invariant clauses check well-formedness after every feature call
⚠️ Creation procedures can have side effects: Nothing enforces pure construction
❌ Once routines create global singleton state: once routines run once (per thread by default, configurable per process or per object) and cache their result — a memoized shared-state coupling across the system



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Automatic GC: No manual deallocation, no use-after-free, no dangling pointers
✅ No pointers: Memory safety by construction; expanded types give value semantics
⚠️ GC pauses: Non-deterministic, couple timing-sensitive code to runtime
⚠️ Void references possible (legacy code): Without attached-type discipline, dereferencing a void reference raises a Void_call exception at runtime



1.1.4 Error

✅ Rescue/retry: Structured exception handling where rescue + retry separates error recovery from error detection — failure handling decoupled from the code that triggered it
✅ Contract-driven exceptions: Exceptions arise from precondition/postcondition/invariant violations, making failure points explicit and first-class rather than accidental
⚠️ Exceptions not used for control flow: Eiffel treats exceptions as contract failures, so error recovery is limited to what the contract model supports
⚠️ Contracts can be disabled at compile time: EiffelStudio can compile an executable to include or exclude any set of contracts (workbench vs. deployment modes), coupling correctness to build configuration



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ SCOOP (Simple Concurrent Object-Oriented Programming): Separates concurrency from logic via processor- and handler-oriented design; decouples “what runs concurrently” from “how it synchronizes” (e.g. multiple threads without explicit mutex management). Available in EiffelStudio, though not yet part of the official language definition
✅ Agents: Wrap operations into objects, closely connected with closures and lambda calculus — decoupling callbacks from the calling code
⚠️ SCOOP is complex and niche: Correct concurrent design requires deep expertise; low adoption
⚠️ Shared mutable state possible: No compiler-level race detection



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Native compilation without a runtime: EiffelStudio compiles to a native executable, so a deployed program does not depend on a vendor runtime
✅ Portable across the major desktop platforms: EiffelStudio targets Windows, Linux, and macOS
⚠️ One vendor owns the ISO-conforming implementation: EiffelStudio is the ISO-conforming implementation and is commercial software from Eiffel Software, so the platform’s evolution depends on that single vendor



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Contract vs. Runtime Cost: Contract checking adds overhead; disabling it (deployment mode) removes the enforcement
Inheritance vs. Composition: Eiffel encourages inheritance as its primary reuse mechanism; multiple inheritance couples but enables precise feature reuse via renaming
SCOOP vs. Pragmatism: The concurrency model is elegant and low-coupling but hard to adopt in practice
Once Routines vs. Independent Units: Memoization decouples repeated computation but couples the element to global shared state that other elements may depend on
Contract Depth vs. Discipline: DBC only helps if teams actually write contracts; without them Eiffel degenerates to a plain typed OOP language




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Compiled to native code: EiffelStudio generates efficient native executables
⚠️ GC pauses: Non-deterministic, though modern GCs keep them short (R2)
⚠️ Contract overhead: Runtime checks add cost; disablement improves performance but removes guarantees
✅ Deterministic when contracts disabled: Predictable execution in deployment mode



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ Small ecosystem: Far fewer libraries than the JVM or .NET, so a solution couples to the few that exist and to a niche community
✅ EiffelStudio is a complete IDE: Integrated compiler, debugger, and contract-aware tooling
⚠️ Dated tooling: Modern build systems and package managers are weak relative to mainstream
⚠️ Niche community: Limited third-party support and resources
⚠️ Fragmented implementations: EiffelStudio, “The Eiffel Compiler” (tecomp), Gobo Eiffel, SmartEiffel, and LibertyEiffel differ; the GNU implementations track an older language version and do not fully implement the ISO standard



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ ISO/ECMA standard: Eiffel is an ISO/IEC standard (ISO/IEC 25436:2006, ECMA-367), giving a stable language core
⚠️ Slow, conservative evolution: The standard is stable but innovation is glacial
⚠️ Implementations diverge: EiffelStudio and the GNU-based implementations have drifted on language features
❌ Niche survival concern: Long-term support depends on a small commercial base



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for high-integrity and contract-heavy domains: DBC is ideal where correctness is paramount and reliability is the design goal
✅ Good for teaching design-by-contract: The language enforces the discipline
⚠️ Poor for mainstream web/systems: GC, niche ecosystem, dated tooling
⚠️ Little adoption in modern development: Hard to hire for



1.2.5 Learning

✅ DBC is a clear mental model: Contracts make intent explicit
⚠️ Multiple inheritance + renaming complexity: Advanced Eiffel is hard to master
⚠️ SCOOP adds a second learning curve: The concurrency model is non-trivial
⚠️ Fewer modern resources: Documentation is dated relative to mainstream languages



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Readable, English-like: if x then ... else ... end, require/ensure/invariant read naturally
✅ Explicit contracts: The syntax makes specification a visible part of every feature
⚠️ Verbose: end clauses and full declarations add ceremony
⚠️ Non-standard keywords: Keywords (e.g. feature, deferred, attached) are unfamiliar to most programmers



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Contracts enable automated testing: preconditions/postconditions/invariants act as built-in test assertions
✅ EiffelStudio debugger: Contract-aware, can inspect invariant violations
✅ Exception handling tools: rescue/retry makes error paths debuggable
⚠️ Few third-party test frameworks: The ecosystem is thin



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC, no pointers, no use-after-free, no buffer overflows
✅ Void safety: Prevents null-pointer vulnerabilities by default (with attached types)
✅ Strong typing: No type-confusion bugs
✅ No argument overloading: Unambiguous feature resolution reduces surprising dispatch
⚠️ Once-routine shared state: Can create hidden shared-state vulnerabilities




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

⚠️ No fast in-editor analysis.



1.3.5 Interop

⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

❌ Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: Eiffel’s Design by Contract is the strongest contract-based coupling tool any mainstream-adjacent OOP language offers: it states each routine’s obligations and guarantees in the source, so a boundary change is detected at the contract level rather than hidden in implementation. Void safety removes a whole null-checking coupling class that Java and C# still carry. The no-argument-overloading rule and Command-Query Separation eliminate two specific coupling hazards (ambiguous dispatch, hidden side effects). Main strength: DBC + void safety expose and prevent coupling better than almost any OOP language. Main weakness: niche ecosystem, once routines create shared state, and contracts are only as good as the discipline that writes them.

title: Java (Java 26)
text:
Analysis against Java 26 (March 2026). Earlier Java releases carry more of the mechanisms below; modern Java (17+) dramatically improves the coupling profile.
This assessment applies the coupling account — coupling as access to a shared resource, and the coupling floor [1], [2] — and the knowledge-embodiment theorem [3]; the language is assessed against its official reference [4].

title: Java (Java 26)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Java in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 50/100 · Ecosystem coupling 61/100 · Engineering readiness 85/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Interfaces decouple specification from implementation: Can program to interfaces
✅ Generics enable type parameterization: List<T> decouples from concrete types
✅ Sealed classes (Java 17): Controlled inheritance hierarchies — the class author decides which subclasses exist, decoupling from unknown extensions
✅ Records (Java 16): Immutable data carriers with auto-generated equals/hashCode/toString — construction decoupled from mutation
✅ Pattern matching (Java 21): switch expressions + sealed types enable exhaustive, compositional dispatch
❌ No higher-kinded types: Can’t abstract over generic types
⚠️ Type erasure couples generics: Runtime loses type information
⚠️ Inheritance still available: Unchecked class extension possible (unless final or sealed)
❌ Null still exists: NullPointerException possible (no non-nullable types in the language)
⚠️ Module system (Java 9+) limits reflection: Strong encapsulation of non-exported packages became the default in Java 16, so reflective access to them now needs an explicit --add-opens — reflection is no longer a free-for-all
❌ Package-private couples to package structure: Visibility tied to organization



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Records are immutable by default: record Point(int x, int y) — no mutation coupling, auto-generated components
✅ Immutable collections (Java 9+): List.of(), Set.of(), Map.of() produce unmodifiable collections
✅ Copy-with-change without mutation: Records have no withers or copy constructors, so a copy-with-change is a hand-written call that supplies the new value and copies the rest
✅ Dependency injection frameworks: Spring/Guice decouple construction from usage
⚠️ Records eliminate builders for simple cases: Complex multi-step construction may still need builders
⚠️ Constructors couple creation to initialization: Not eliminated, but records and patterns reduce the problem
❌ Static methods couple to global state: Singleton pattern creates hidden dependencies



1.1.3 Memory

✅ JVM GC decouples memory: Modern GCs (ZGC, Generational ZGC, Shenandoah) provide sub-millisecond pause times
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have dangling pointers
✅ Foreign Function & Memory API (Java 22): Safe memory access without JNI, decoupling native interop from unsafety
✅ AOT object caching with any GC (Java 26): Ahead-of-time object caching reduces startup time and memory pressure regardless of GC choice
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Minimized by modern GCs but not deterministic
❌ Memory leaks from static references: Static collections couple to application lifetime (still possible)



1.1.4 Error

✅ Checked exceptions separate error paths: throws IOException makes errors explicit
✅ Pattern matching for switch + sealed types (Java 21): Exhaustive error handling — compiler verifies all error cases covered
✅ Primitive types in patterns (preview, Java 26): Extends pattern matching to primitive types, enabling exhaustive switching over numeric domains
❌ Try-catch doesn’t compose: Can’t map/flatMap over exceptions without wrapping
⚠️ RuntimeException bypasses checks: Unchecked exceptions defer error-coupling detection to runtime (sealed hierarchies with pattern matching help)



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Virtual threads (stable, Java 21+): Lightweight threads — each task gets its own thread, eliminating callback coupling
✅ Structured concurrency (preview, Java 21+): StructuredTaskScope — subtask lifetimes scoped to lexical block, preventing thread leaks
✅ Scoped values (final, Java 25+): Thread-local data with guaranteed cleanup, decoupling context from global state
✅ CompletableFuture: Composable async primitives when needed
⚠️ Shared mutable state still possible: synchronized, volatile, and manual lock patterns remain available



1.1.6 Platform

✅ Open specifications: The Java Language Specification and the JVM Specification are public standards that any conforming implementation may implement
✅ Multiple vendor runtimes: OpenJDK, Oracle JDK, Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Azul Zulu, and GraalVM run the same class files
✅ Open-source core: OpenJDK is developed in the open under the GPL with the Classpath Exception
✅ Portable bytecode: Compiled classes run unchanged on every platform that hosts a JVM



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Checked Exceptions vs. Composition: Explicit errors don’t compose natively (no monadic operations), though sealed types + pattern matching provide exhaustive error handling
Backward Compatibility vs. Modern Features: 30 years of legacy — old codebases can lag behind modern idioms
Null as Default vs. Safety: Everything nullable by default couples all code to defensive checks — records and pattern matching help but don’t solve the root issue
Type Erasure vs. Runtime Types: Generics erased at runtime couples generic code to raw types
Inheritance vs. Composition: Hierarchy coupling possible when teams choose extension over composition




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ JVM optimization: Excellent JIT, fast steady-state
✅ Virtual threads: Low-overhead concurrency scales to millions of threads
⚠️ GC pauses: Tunable; ZGC offers sub-millisecond pauses (R2)
⚠️ Startup time: JIT warmup (mitigated by AOT object caching (Java 26), GraalVM native image, CDS archives, and CRaC)
✅ G1 throughput improvements (Java 26): Reduced synchronization overhead in G1 GC improves throughput
✅ HTTP/3 client (Java 26): Native HTTP/3 support decouples networking from legacy protocol constraints
✅ Mature profilers: Excellent performance tooling



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Massive ecosystem: Maven Central has everything
⚠️ Enterprise monoculture: Spring dominates the server stack, so the alternatives are not really alternatives (Ec6)
⚠️ Legacy burden: The enterprise stack keeps a 1999-era API in service next to a 2026 one, so a library supports both (Ec7)
✅ Standardized build: Maven/Gradle industry standard
✅ Excellent IDEs: IntelliJ, Eclipse, NetBeans
✅ Mature tooling: Debuggers, profilers, monitoring
✅ Cross-platform: Write once, run anywhere (mostly true)



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Strong backward compatibility: Rarely breaks
✅ Regular releases: 6-month cadence, LTS every 2 years
✅ Preview features: Opt-in features decouple experimentation from production stability
⚠️ Legacy burden: Old APIs accumulate (though deprecated-for-removal process is active; applet API removed in Java 26)
✅ final mutation now warns (Java 26): Deep reflection that mutates a final field reports a warning, ahead of a future release that blocks it



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for backend/enterprise: Industry standard
✅ Good for Android: Primary language (with Kotlin)
✅ Strong for distributed systems: Mature frameworks
⚠️ Poor for frontend: Applet API removed (Java 26); JavaFX remains niche
⚠️ Not for systems programming: GC, overhead



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Gentle: Widely taught, lots of resources
⚠️ Modern Java is growing in surface: Records, sealed types, pattern matching, virtual threads, modules — more to learn than Java 8
✅ Excellent docs: Javadoc, tutorials, books
⚠️ Legacy/Modern split: Learning the “right” modern way requires guidance



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Records eliminate getter/setter boilerplate: record Person(String name, int age) replaces 50-line POJO
✅ Pattern matching reduces verbosity: switch expressions + sealed types
⚠️ Still verbose compared to Kotlin/Scala: Type erasure, generics syntax
⚠️ Checked exception syntax: Verbose, couples signatures



1.2.7 Testing

✅ JUnit industry standard: Mature testing
✅ Excellent debuggers: Step-through, breakpoints, virtual thread debugging
✅ Mocking frameworks: Mockito, EasyMock
✅ Profiling tools: VisualVM, YourKit, JFR



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents memory bugs
✅ Type safe: Static typing
✅ Module system: Restricts reflective access to non-exported packages by default (Java 16+)
⚠️ Null: NullPointerException still possible
⚠️ Serialization vulnerabilities: Deserialization attacks (mitigated by records + modern serialization frameworks)




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.

1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.
