title: Rust (1.96 / 2024 edition)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Rust in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 85/100 · Ecosystem coupling 84/100 · Engineering readiness 68/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Traits decouple without inheritance: Interface + implementation separate
✅ Zero-cost abstractions: Monomorphization prevents abstraction coupling to runtime cost
✅ No null: Option<T> makes absence explicit
✅ Ownership prevents aliasing: Can’t have multiple mutable references, eliminates coupling
✅ Associated types in traits: Decouple trait from concrete types
⚠️ Orphan rules couple trait implementations: Can’t impl external trait on external type



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Constructors are just functions: new() is convention, not special
✅ Builder pattern zero-cost: Type-state pattern at compile time
✅ No shared mutable state: Construction can’t couple to globals
✅ Drop trait separates cleanup: Destruction logic separate from construction



1.1.3 Memory

✅ Ownership system prevents memory coupling: Compiler prevents use-after-free and double-free at compile time
✅ No GC, no pauses: Deterministic deallocation via RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization, via the Drop trait)
✅ Lifetime tracking decouples: References can’t outlive referents
✅ Zero-cost abstractions for memory: Box, Rc, Arc explicit about allocation strategy
✅ Allocator parameter support: Can decouple allocation strategy from data structures
✅ No implicit copies: Move semantics by default prevent accidental copying
⚠️ Reference cycles with Rc: Rc<RefCell<T>> cycles require Weak to break
⚠️ Lifetimes can couple: Complex lifetime constraints create dependencies between regions
⚠️ Unsafe blocks bypass memory-safety guarantees: Can violate all guarantees, but explicit



1.1.4 Error

✅ Result<T, E> makes errors explicit: Can’t ignore errors without .unwrap()
✅ ? operator composes: Error handling doesn’t obscure logic
✅ No exceptions: All errors in type system
✅ Panics are rare: Explicit unwrap/expect, or Result



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Ownership prevents data races: Compiler enforces Send/Sync
✅ Async/await with explicit futures: Concurrency in types
✅ Channels separate communication: Message passing decouples concurrent tasks
✅ No shared mutable state without explicit synchronization: Arc/Mutex make coupling visible



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No vendor lock-in: Compiles to native code for every major platform
✅ Broad target support: Linux, macOS, Windows, WebAssembly, and bare-metal no_std
✅ Static linking by default: A binary does not couple to a platform’s runtime or shared libraries



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Safety vs. Flexibility: Borrow checker rejects valid programs that don’t fit ownership model
Lifetime Complexity: Complex lifetime bounds couple function signatures to caller context
Async Colored Functions: async fn creates two function worlds (sync/async), couples call sites
Trait Coherence vs. Modularity: Orphan rules prevent implementing external traits on external types
Compile Times vs. Zero-Cost: Monomorphization couples build time to generic instantiation count
Learning Curve vs. Productivity: Steep learning curve couples team productivity to expertise




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Zero-cost abstractions: No runtime overhead
✅ No GC: Deterministic performance, no pauses
✅ Predictable: WYSIWYG performance model
✅ Compile-time optimization: LLVM backend
⚠️ Binary size: Can be large without optimization



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Cargo is excellent: Best-in-class package manager
✅ Great IDE support: Rust-analyzer, IntelliJ, VSCode
✅ Strong ecosystem: crates.io growing rapidly
⚠️ Smaller than JVM/npm: Fewer libraries than established ecosystems
✅ Excellent docs: Rustdoc, The Book



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Editions system: Breaking changes isolated to editions
✅ cargo fix: Automated migration
✅ Strong stability: Post-1.0 stability guarantee
⚠️ Async runtime: Tokio is the de facto standard; async support has stabilized at the language level (2024 edition)
❌ An edition can change what existing code means (V1): Edition 2024 rewrote the capture rules of impl Trait, required unsafe extern, and reserved gen, so a crate that adopts it must be revisited



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for systems: Memory safety without GC
✅ Great for embedded: No runtime, predictable
✅ Strong for CLI tools: Single binary, fast startup
✅ Good for WebAssembly: First-class WASM support
⚠️ Backend less common: Growing but smaller than Java/Go



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Very steep: Ownership, lifetimes, borrowing
❌ Compiler fights you: Borrow checker takes time to internalize
✅ Excellent docs: The Book, Rustlings, error messages
❌ Lifetime complexity: Advanced patterns very difficult



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Expression-oriented: Everything returns a value
⚠️ Lifetime annotations: <'a, 'b> syntax noisy
✅ Pattern matching: Powerful, expressive
⚠️ Macro syntax: ! and #[] can be confusing



1.2.7 Testing

✅ cargo test: Built-in testing
✅ Integrated benchmarking: Cargo bench
⚠️ Debugging async code: Can be challenging
✅ gdb/lldb support: Standard debuggers work



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: Ownership prevents use-after-free, double-free
✅ Thread safe: Send/Sync prevent data races
✅ No null: Option prevents null pointer derefs
⚠️ Unsafe blocks: Can bypass safety (but explicit)




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.
⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ A change pays a slow build.



1.3.5 Interop

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [8].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

✅ A standards-qualified toolchain or an established safety standard covers this language.

title: TypeScript (6.0)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses TypeScript in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 28/100 · Ecosystem coupling 73/100 · Engineering readiness 96/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Structural typing decouples from concrete types: Can pass any object with right shape
✅ Union types separate cases: string | number makes alternatives explicit, and a discriminated union is a checked sum type
✅ Generics enable parametric polymorphism: Decouple from concrete types
✅ strictNullChecks makes absence a checked case: string and string | null are different types, so a possibly-absent value must be narrowed before use, and T10 is absent
⚠️ any is an explicit opt-out: strict bans an implicit any, but a written any still drops the check at that spot
❌ Type assertions couple to implementation: as Type forces coupling
❌ The artifact carries no types: Types are erased at run time, so a consumer recovers a type by convention (T7)
⚠️ A method call dispatches on the run-time value: An interface declares the method, but the call reaches the prototype’s implementation at run time (T3)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Object literals decouple construction: { name: "Alice", age: 30 } without classes
⚠️ Class constructors can have side effects: Nothing prevents coupled initialization
⚠️ Dependency injection requires manual wiring: No built-in mechanism
❌ Module side effects: Imports can execute code, coupling load order
❌ Global namespace pollution: window, global create hidden coupling
❌ Objects are mutable unless marked readonly (C2): readonly is opt-in, so any holder of a reference can change the object



1.1.3 Memory

✅ JavaScript GC decouples memory: Generational GC (V8, SpiderMonkey, etc.)
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free
⚠️ Closure captures extend lifetimes: Closures hold references, prevent collection
⚠️ Event listeners create memory leaks: Forgotten listeners couple to DOM/event system
⚠️ Circular references with DOM: Can create leaks if not careful with event handlers
⚠️ Collection follows the JavaScript runtime’s schedule (M2): A value stays allocated until V8’s collector decides, and the pause is non-deterministic, so the heap’s release schedule is not the program’s to name
✅ using ties a release to the scope (M3 absent): TypeScript 5.2 adds using and await using, so a value with a Symbol.dispose method releases at block exit



1.1.4 Error

❌ Exceptions are unchecked: No throws clause, errors hidden from type system
⚠️ Result types exist but not idiomatic: Libraries like neverthrow exist but uncommon
❌ Promise rejection is unchecked: Async errors not tracked by types



1.1.5 Concurrency

✅ Async/await separates sync from async: async function makes concurrency explicit
❌ Promises don’t track errors: Promise<T> doesn’t show failure type
⚠️ The event loop is the only unit of work (K1): Single-threaded, so a long callback blocks every other task and no second core is available for CPU-bound work, and callbacks create order coupling
⚠️ Shared module state has no concurrency discipline (K2, K3): A module-level binding is reachable from every callback, and nothing detects a race across interleaved tasks



1.1.6 Platform

✅ The compiler is open source and emits a standard target: tsc is developed in the open under Apache 2.0, and its output is ECMAScript, so no proprietary runtime is required
✅ The emitted code runs on every major engine: The output runs on V8, SpiderMonkey, and JavaScriptCore and on Node.js, Deno, and Bun alike
✅ Several tools compile TypeScript: tsc, esbuild, swc, and Node.js type stripping all accept .ts source, so the build step is not locked to one implementation
✅ No language runtime is deployed: Type checking happens at build time and the artifact is JavaScript, so nothing of TypeScript ships to the platform
✅ The compiler runs on all three desktop platforms: One npm package covers Windows, macOS, and Linux



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Type Safety vs. Runtime Reality: Types are documentation only, no runtime enforcement couples safety to discipline
Gradual Typing vs. Type Holes: any escape hatch couples strict code to untyped code
JavaScript Compatibility vs. Type Safety: Must support all JS patterns, even unsafe ones
Type System Complexity vs. JavaScript Simplicity: Advanced types (conditional, mapped) couple to TS-specific knowledge
Build Step vs. Simplicity: Compilation adds complexity, couples deployment to build tools




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ JavaScript runtime: Inherits JS performance characteristics, JIT optimization
⚠️ Type erasure: No runtime cost but also no runtime enforcement
✅ Event loop: Single-threaded simplifies reasoning
❌ Unpredictable GC: No control over pause times (R2)
⚠️ Bundle size couples to libraries: Frontend deployment couples to dependency graph



1.2.2 Ecosystem

✅ Massive ecosystem: Npm has everything
✅ Excellent IDE support: VSCode, IntelliJ, WebStorm
✅ Build tools mature: Webpack, Vite, esbuild, tsc
⚠️ Too many build tools: Choice couples to toolchain complexity
✅ TypeScript compiler fast: Incremental compilation



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Strong backward compatibility: Breaking changes rare
✅ Regular releases: Predictable cadence
✅ Gradual adoption: Can upgrade incrementally
⚠️ Lib versioning: @types packages couple to library versions



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for frontend: Industry standard for React, Angular, Vue
✅ Great for backend: Node.js/Deno with types
✅ Full-stack: Shared types between frontend/backend
⚠️ Systems programming: Not suitable, GC/interpreted



1.2.5 Learning

✅ Gentle for JS developers: Incremental adoption
✅ Good documentation: Official handbook is excellent
⚠️ Type system complexity: Conditional types, mapped types can be confusing
✅ Familiar to C#/Java devs: Similar type system concepts



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ JavaScript syntax: Familiar, minimal new syntax
⚠️ Type annotations can be verbose: Generics get noisy
✅ Type inference: Often don’t need explicit types
⚠️ Any escape hatch: Too easy to bypass types



1.2.7 Testing

✅ Jest, Vitest, Mocha: Mature testing frameworks
✅ Debugging tools: Browser DevTools, VSCode debugger
✅ Source maps: Debug TypeScript directly
⚠️ Runtime vs compile-time gap: Types don’t catch runtime issues



1.2.8 Security

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents memory bugs
⚠️ Type erasure: No runtime validation
❌ Prototype pollution: Object mutation can create vulnerabilities
⚠️ Dependency vulnerabilities: Npm ecosystem size couples to attack surface




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ The package registry is a flat name space.

Verdict: TypeScript keeps less of JavaScript’s type coupling than JavaScript does: strict makes absence a checked case, structural typing and discriminated unions remove the dynamic-typing and sum-type mechanisms, and using ties a release to the scope. What its type layer cannot remove is the JavaScript runtime’s: a single-threaded event loop, a collector the program cannot schedule, unowned mutable objects, and failures that no type tracks. TypeScript therefore scores above JavaScript — 31 against 28 — and both stay in the lowest band, because the runtime coupling dominates.

Companion to: The Great Language Smackdown · the Criteria · the Scoring Model

This page holds every number in the comparison. Every table responds to the controls above it: type to filter, and choose a key to re-rank. The first table ranks all 65 languages by the ranking score — coupling, lifted by at most 15% for readiness — with the star band that follows from Core coupling, and shows Ecosystem coupling alongside. The next three give the per-dimension sub-scores that produce those totals. The last table gives the mechanism-presence data behind every score, so any number can be reproduced from first principles. The criteria are on the Criteria; the arithmetic, the presence rules, and the ranking rule are on the Scoring Model.


Scores from the model (capped-sum-per-dimension), analysis date June 2026. Versions are the latest stable as of that date. Rank is the Ranking score: core  (1 - LIFT + LIFT * readiness / 100). Coupling is primary; readiness is a modifier capped at 0.15, so a full 0-to-100 readiness swing is worth 15 coupling points at the top of the scale — the weight of one High mechanism. Readiness can therefore settle a close call, and it can never overturn a large coupling gap. Higher is better: each score is 100 minus priced cost, not a general quality measure. Each column has its own scale and its own band; do not compare across columns. The star rating reflects the Core Coupling score: 90+ = ★★★★★, 75–89 = ★★★★, 60–74 = ★★★, 45–59 = ★★, below 45 = ★. Ecosystem coupling is a lens and does not enter the ranking, because it is a dependency context rather than a quality. The table sorts by any column, so a reader who wants pure coupling sorts by that column.*

Low score = Fragmented build systems, limited libraries couple to toolchain

Language Evolution (Coupling to Language Versions)

High score = Backward compatible, stable, no breaking changes
Low score = Frequent breaking changes couple codebase to specific versions

Domain Suitability (Coupling to Problem Domains)

High score = Works well across multiple domains
Low score = Couples to specific domains, struggles outside comfort zone

Learning Curve (Coupling Productivity to Expertise)

High score = Gentle, quick to productivity
Low score = Steep, productivity couples to deep expertise

Syntax & Ergonomics (Coupling Intent to Verbose Expression)

High score = Concise, readable, minimal boilerplate
Low score = Verbose, boilerplate couples intent to ceremony

Testing & Debugging (Coupling Understanding to Manual Inspection)

High score = Excellent tools, easy to test/debug
Low score = Poor tools couple understanding to manual inspection

Security (Coupling Correctness to Security Concerns)

High score = Memory safe, type safe, prevents vulnerabilities
Low score = Unsafe, couples correctness to security awareness

title: C shell (csh 8.2 / tcsh)
text: This assessment applies the coupling account — coupling as access to a shared resource, and the coupling floor [1], [2] — and the knowledge-embodiment theorem [3]; the language is assessed against its official reference [4].

title: C shell (csh 8.2 / tcsh)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses the C shell in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 43/100 · Ecosystem coupling 57/100 · Engineering readiness 64/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Every value is a word list: set binds a list of words to a name, and no declaration states what the name holds, so the same variable carries a path on one line and a number on the next (T1)
❌ No sum types: An option that may be absent, numeric, or textual is one string, and the reader must decode the convention (set flag versus set flag=0) to tell them apart (T4)
❌ No generics: A command is specialised only by the words passed to it, so the same logic is written again for each shape of data (T5)
❌ Arithmetic is a second grammar: @ and if ( expr ) evaluate C operators over words, so a number is a word that is re-parsed at each use, a null or missing argument counts as 0, and a non-numeric word raises Badly formed number
❌ One flat namespace: set variables and setenv environment variables form two flat spaces with no lexical scope, so a sourced file cannot hide a name from its caller (T6, T11)
❌ An unset name expands to empty: Csh has no nounset option — its letters are -bcefimnstVvXx — so a misspelled variable becomes an empty argument instead of an error (T10)



1.1.2 Construction

❌ No function scope: A variable set in a script is visible to every command the script runs, and a sourced file writes directly into the caller’s namespace (C1)
❌ No immutability by default: Every name is writable everywhere, so a value read at the top of a script can change before it is used (C2)
❌ Aliases are the only reuse mechanism: An alias is textually substituted with \!* arguments, so its body is expanded in the caller’s context instead of a protected one
❌ Recursion re-enters the script: With no function call, a recursive routine re-invokes $0, which couples the logic to the script path and to the positional parameters
⚠️ tcsh can freeze a variable: set -r marks a name read-only, but this is a tcsh extension and it is never the default
✅ path is tied to PATH: Assigning the path word list re-exports PATH, so the search path is edited as a list rather than by string editing



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No allocation syntax: The language has no pointer, no address, and no free, so word lists are allocated by the interpreter on assignment
✅ No deallocation to manage: unset drops a name and the interpreter reclaims the words, so a script has no free order and no double free to avoid
⚠️ Assignment copies the list: set b = ($a) duplicates every word, so a large list is held twice while the assignment runs
⚠️ Global scope extends lifetime: Because every variable is global, data created early in a session stays resident until it is explicitly unset
✅ Word lists are the only aggregate: There are no user-visible buffers or arenas, so memory layout never enters a script



1.1.4 Error

❌ No structured error path: Csh gives onintr for interrupts and $status for the last exit code, but there is no exception, no error value, and no handler that can return a result (Er1)
❌ $status is lost by the next command: Any command resets it, so a test placed between a failure and its check silently discards the error (Er3)
❌ Errors do not compose: A failure is a global word rather than a value that can be returned, combined, or stored, so recovery cannot be factored into a routine (Er4)
⚠️ Diagnostics are short and late: The parser is ad hoc, so a fault such as 0: Event not found. reaches the user only when the line runs and names nothing beyond the command
⚠️ The parser reads a command at a time: A syntax error later in a file is reported when execution reaches it, so earlier side effects are already committed
⚠️ onintr couples cleanup to a label: The handler is a named target in the script rather than a scope, so cleanup cannot be attached to the thing it cleans up



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ No concurrency primitives: & and job control start and steer jobs, but there is no lock, channel, or await, so coordination is done by signals and exit codes (K5)
✅ Processes are the unit of parallelism: The language models concurrency as separate processes joined by pipes, so no shared address space has to be reasoned about
✅ Job control isolates the terminal: Csh introduced job control, so a foreground or background decision does not require the script to manage the terminal itself
⚠️ wait is the only join: wait blocks for all jobs or one named job and returns no value, so a result must travel through a file or a pipeline
⚠️ Background jobs inherit the whole environment: A & job shares every global variable and the current directory, so ordering between jobs is unspecified unless the script waits
⚠️ No coprocess: Unlike ksh’s |&, csh offers no supported two-way conversation with a child, so a pipeline stage cannot be driven interactively



1.1.6 Platform

❌ Two implementations of one lineage: The language is defined by the frozen BSD csh 8.2 and by tcsh, so there is no third implementation to check behaviour against (P2)
⚠️ The frozen and maintained dialects differ: set -r, bindkey, and the completion system are tcsh additions, so a script that uses them is not a csh script
⚠️ No standard to be portable to: The POSIX committee chose KornShell, so csh has no specification and its contracts live in two manuals
✅ tcsh is packaged nearly everywhere: Tcsh ships on the BSDs, Linux, and macOS, where csh normally resolves to tcsh, so an interpreter is usually present
✅ Interactive configuration transfers within the family: alias, history, !!, tilde expansion, and the directory stack behave the same in csh and tcsh
⚠️ Scripting support is frozen: New portable automation targets other shells, so csh is maintained rather than extended



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Interactive first, scriptable second: The design targets the terminal, so a weak scripting surface is a priority choice rather than a defect in the language
The C-like expression grammar is a deliberate borrowing: @ and if ( expr ) give a C programmer a familiar evaluation model; the cost is a second grammar, not a forced dependency
The 1993 freeze is a maintenance decision: Original csh is complete and unmaintained while tcsh continues the line, so the freeze is a project decision rather than a coupling mechanism
set and setenv are two commands by history: The split mirrors the shell-variable and environment-variable distinction that every shell must represent somehow
The ad-hoc parser is one implementation’s shortcut: A different implementation could parse the same language properly, so the parser defect is not part of the language contract
csh is not a general-purpose language: An interpreter plus a set of external commands is the assumed platform, which is a scope decision




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Interpreted with no compilation step: Every command line is parsed and evaluated as text at run time, so a loop over files pays parser cost per iteration (R1)
⚠️ Builtins are a short list: cd, set, @, and echo avoid a process, and almost everything else forks and executes
✅ Path hashing avoids repeated search: rehash and hashstat keep a table of resolved command paths, so command lookup does not rescan PATH
✅ Scripts start without interactive configuration: Tcsh reads .tcshrc for interactive shells only, so a script pays no start-up cost for prompt and completion setup
⚠️ Arithmetic is re-parsed per evaluation: @ evaluates its expression each time it runs, so a numeric loop is far slower than compiled code
⚠️ The shell is rarely the bottleneck: Time goes to the external commands it spawns, so interpreter overhead matters mainly in arithmetic-heavy loops



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ No package manager: There is no distribution channel for csh code, so shared routines are copied between scripts or vendored as files (Ec1)
⚠️ The user base is small and narrowing: Csh survives as a login-shell option on the BSDs and macOS, and new scripting rarely targets it (Ec3)
✅ Documentation is complete and stable: The csh and tcsh manuals describe the language fully and have changed little in decades
✅ Interactive tooling is mature in tcsh: bindkey, complete, and the set toggles are documented and widely configured
⚠️ No static analysis: ShellCheck does not analyse csh or tcsh, so a csh script has no mainstream linter
✅ Scripts are the interchange format: csh is invoked from make, cron, and login configuration without a binding layer



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Backward compatibility is total: Tcsh runs csh scripts unchanged and adds behaviour through new builtins and set variables
✅ No version treadmill: No breaking change can arrive for frozen csh, and decades-old scripts still run
⚠️ Fixes arrive only in tcsh: A defect or an unhelpful message in csh stays, and the remedy is to install tcsh and let csh point at it
⚠️ Two dialects share one manual: The tcsh manual marks tcsh-only behaviour with (+), so a reader must know which shell they have
⚠️ No standardisation track: With POSIX committed to KornShell, no committee can modernise the language



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Adequate as an interactive login shell: History, aliases, tilde notation, the directory stack, and job control cover terminal work
⚠️ Weak as a scripting language: foreach, while, if, and switch cannot be piped into one another, so a data-processing script must be rebuilt around that limit
⚠️ Text handling calls out to other tools: There are no associative arrays and no substring operators beyond the :r, :e, :h, and :t modifiers, so sed and awk do the work
⚠️ Arithmetic is integer only in csh: @ and expr cover integers, so floating-point calculation leaves the shell
✅ Configuration files are the native domain: .cshrc, .login, and .logout express an interactive environment directly
⚠️ Legacy maintenance persists: Csh remains a login shell on some BSD and macOS accounts, so its configuration files still need care



1.2.5 Learning

✅ The interactive surface is gentle: History substitution, aliases, and tilde notation are learnable in an afternoon
✅ The grammar resembles C: if ( $#argv > 1 ) and @ arithmetic read as expected to a C programmer
⚠️ The scripting limits are learned by failure: A beginner discovers that a control structure cannot be piped only when the pipeline fails
⚠️ Word modifiers must be memorised: :r, :e, :h, :t, :g, and :q are a compact but unguessable syntax for path and quoting work
⚠️ set and setenv confuse newcomers: Two binding commands with different rules produce silent mistakes when the wrong one is used



1.2.6 Syntax

⚠️ Block terminators disagree: if closes with endif, switch with endsw, and foreach and while with end
⚠️ set, setenv, and alias follow different rules: Three ways to bind a name use three argument conventions
⚠️ No separate stderr redirection: >& merges the two streams and |& pipes both, so a stream cannot be redirected on its own
✅ Terse for its work: foreach f (*.c) with if (-e $f) expresses a loop and a test in a few characters
✅ Word modifiers are short and local: $file:r.c and $path:h perform path surgery inline
⚠️ @ and if ( expr ) add a second reading of a line: The same word is a string in one place and an expression in another



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No test framework in the language: A test is a script that calls the code and compares $status, with no assertion, fixture, or reporting facility (G1)
❌ Debugging is echo and set -x: Csh prints commands with set echo and the -x option, but has no breakpoint, no state inspection, and no debugger (G2)
❌ Faults appear only in the branch that runs: With no static check, a mistyped variable or a bad foreach pattern is found during the test run (G3)
⚠️ A hand-built harness is possible: $status and onintr allow a script to record an outcome and report it
✅ Exit status is a usable oracle: After a command, if ($status == 0) tests the one outcome the language reports reliably
⚠️ Interactive behaviour needs a terminal: History, completion, and prompt behaviour are tty-driven, so they resist automated checks



1.2.8 Security

❌ Unquoted expansion is re-parsed: Because a value is a word list, an unquoted $var splits and globs, so untrusted text can change the number of arguments a command receives (Q2)
⚠️ eval and $< feed outside text to the parser: Both re-enter the interpreter with text that is not validated
⚠️ No restricted mode: Csh offers no sandbox and no capability model, so a script’s protection is the file permissions of its user
✅ set noclobber protects existing files: The option makes > refuse to overwrite, so a mistake cannot silently destroy data
✅ Environment changes are explicit: setenv and unsetenv are named builtins, so a script’s effect on its children is visible in the text
✅ No memory-safety surface: There are no pointers and no manual allocation, so memory defects belong to the programs csh runs




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

⚠️ No fast in-editor analysis.



1.3.5 Interop

❌ No general foreign-function interface.
⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.

Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Every operation starts a process: time, and therefore energy, is dominated by process startup.



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

⚠️ Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [5].

What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

⚠️ No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

Verdict: The C shell gives the coupling profile of a word-based shell: values are words, names have one global scope, and an error is a global status word rather than a composable value, which puts a floor of 43 under the core score. Its own contributions are interactive — history, aliases, tilde notation, the directory stack, job control, and path hashing — and none of them separates concerns inside a script. The original shell has been frozen since 1993 and tcsh carries the line forward, so the language is stable but small, and tcsh-only extensions such as set -r and the completion system sit outside what a csh script may rely on.

title: Ksh (kSH 93u+)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses Ksh in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 43/100 · Ecosystem coupling 68/100 · Engineering readiness 64/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ Values are strings with run-time attributes: typeset -i, -F, -E, -l, and -u decide how a name is read and written, but the parser performs no static check and the attribute is enforced when the value is used (T1)
❌ No sum types: A tagged alternative is a word plus a convention, because typeset -T gives a named structure rather than a choice between variants (T4)
❌ No generics and no dispatch by type: A routine is specialised only by its positional parameters, and behaviour is selected by the string in $0 or by the command name, never by a declared type (T5, T9)
❌ One flat global namespace: typeset inside a function body makes a name local, but a plain assignment writes the global, and no module boundary hides anything from the process (T6, T11)
❌ An unset name reads as empty by default: set -o nounset turns a reference to an unset name into an error, but the option is off by default and nothing forces a variable to be initialised (T10)
⚠️ typeset -T defines a real named type: A type can own discipline functions (.get, .set, .unset) and a create routine invoked for each instance, which is more than text binding — yet an instance is still a compound of words with no static check



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Global by default and mutable by default: A plain assignment writes the global namespace, and no binding is immutable unless readonly or typeset -r is applied (C1, C2)
⚠️ Validation is not attached to a plain variable: A name accepts any word, and the checking that exists comes from an attribute or from a discipline function added with typeset (C4)
✅ function bodies get local variables: A variable declared typeset in a function body is local, so a routine keeps its working state out of the caller’s namespace
✅ Discipline functions are real set and get hooks: x.set, x.get, and x.unset run on assignment and reference, so a rule about a value is attached to the value’s name instead of to every write site
✅ Name spaces and FPATH separate a library’s names: namespace lib { ... } keeps internal names out of the flat space, and a function on FPATH is loaded on first reference
✅ typeset -n gives a nameref: A function can operate on a caller’s variable by name without string concatenation and eval



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No allocation or free in the language: There is no pointer, no address, and no deallocation builtin; the shell owns every value
✅ Scope and unset bound a lifetime: A local variable disappears when its function returns, and unset drops a name, so working state does not persist by accident
✅ Associative arrays are managed by the shell: typeset -A allocates and grows its own storage, so no capacity handling is written
⚠️ Assignment copies compound values: A typeset -T instance and a compound variable are copied on assignment, so a large structure is duplicated in full
⚠️ Parsed functions stay resident: ksh93 compiles a script to an internal tree and caches it, so a long session keeps the parsed definitions in memory
⚠️ typeset -E, -F, and -X choose a representation, not a lifetime: The attribute pins a value to double, float, or long-double storage, which couples the number to a precision decision made once



1.1.4 Error

❌ No structured error path: $? and trap ... ERR are the whole apparatus, with no exception and no error value (Er1)
❌ The ERR trap is global and undifferentiated: One handler covers the whole script, it receives no description of the failure, and it fires only where an explicit check or set -o errexit applies (Er3)
❌ Errors cannot be returned: A function’s outcome is its exit status, so an error carries no payload and cannot be combined with another (Er4)
⚠️ set -o errexit is fragile: The option does not fire inside && and || chains, in conditions, or after a negation, so a wrapper that suppresses it changes error behaviour
✅ trap covers named signals and EXIT: Cleanup can be attached to EXIT and to specific signals, so a script releases resources on any exit path
✅ $? is unambiguous at the test, and pipefail extends it: The status of the last command is read directly, and set -o pipefail makes a mid-pipeline failure visible



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ No concurrency primitives: There is no lock, channel, or await; the only parallel construct is a background job (K5)
✅ Coprocesses give two-way communication: cmd |& with print -p and read -p keeps a child in conversation without a named pipe or a temporary file
✅ Processes are the unit of parallelism: Concurrency is expressed with pipes and background jobs, so no shared address space has to be reasoned about
⚠️ Background jobs inherit the global environment: A & job shares every global variable, the umask, and the current directory, so ordering is unspecified unless the script waits
⚠️ wait returns a status, not a value: The join exists, but a result must travel through a pipe, a file, or a coprocess
⚠️ No structured concurrency: Nothing guarantees that a job started inside a function finishes before the function returns



1.1.6 Platform

❌ One lineage defines ksh93: The language comes from AT&T’s KornShell and its maintained fork ksh93u+m, while the BSD-derived pdksh and mksh implement an older dialect, so behaviour is not interchangeable (P2)
✅ POSIX with extensions: A script written to the POSIX shell language runs under ksh93, so it can move between systems that have a KornShell
⚠️ Two dialects share the name ksh: mksh and pdksh lack associative arrays, discipline functions, and floating point, so #!/bin/ksh means different things on different systems
⚠️ Availability is not uniform: ksh93 ships on AIX and Solaris and is packaged for Linux, but it is not the default shell on any mainstream Linux distribution
✅ A manual and a test suite define the language: The ksh93 manual and the AT&T test suite, now maintained in ksh93u+m, are the reference for behaviour
⚠️ One implementation carries the extensions: With no standard covering them, an omission or a defect in ksh93 is a property of the language as practised



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

The ksh88 lineage is a separate language: mksh and pdksh continue the older design on BSD and Android, and that divergence is a history of implementations rather than a coupling mechanism
Rich builtins are a deliberate choice: print, typeset, and the .sh.* variables lengthen the learning curve to remove whole categories of external command
The floating-point attribute is a representation choice: typeset -E, -F, and -X select storage precision, which is a modelling decision about the numbers a script handles
Discipline functions are a heavy mechanism: A .get hook runs on every reference, so encapsulation is paid for with an unpredictable per-access cost
namespace is not a module system: It prevents name collisions inside one script but hides nothing from the process, which is a scope decision
POSIX mode is available but not the goal: set -o posix narrows ksh to the standard, and a script that wants the extensions rightly leaves it off




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Interpreted with an internal compile step: A script is parsed into a tree and cached, so a function body is not re-parsed on every call, but there is no artifact to precompile (R1)
✅ A native implementation with an optimised parser: ksh93 was designed with performance in mind, and the maintained fork continues to fix hot paths
✅ Coprocesses avoid repeated process creation: A child started once with |& is driven with print -p and read -p, so a loop does not fork per iteration
✅ Builtins cover most text work: print, printf, [[ ... ]], and ${var/pat/rep} avoid an external process for common operations
⚠️ Path hashing and tracked aliases are opt-in: alias -t records a resolved command path, so a script without it rescans PATH
⚠️ A .get discipline runs on every read: A hook on a variable adds work to each reference, so encapsulation has a per-access price



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ No package manager: There is no dependency resolver or module registry for ksh, so shared code is sourced from a directory on FPATH (Ec1)
⚠️ The ecosystem is smaller than Bash’s or Zsh’s: Few libraries and completions target ksh93 specifically
⚠️ The user base is declining: Bash is the default on Linux and absorbed most of ksh’s ideas, so new ksh93 code is rare
✅ The maintained fork revived the project: ksh93u+m restarted development and fixed defects that had stood for years
✅ Documentation is complete: One manual documents the language, the builtins, and the discipline mechanism
✅ The historical influence is documented: Ksh is the source of [[ ... ]], $'...', select, typeset, printf, and pipefail in other shells



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ No breaking-change culture: New features arrive as extensions, and a ksh88-style script still runs
✅ set -o posix pins the dialect: A script can fix POSIX behaviour so that a change in an extension does not silently alter it
✅ The extensions are stable to the point of immobility: A construct such as typeset -A has behaved the same way for decades
⚠️ The 93v- development line was abandoned: The ksh2020 line never reached a stable release, and ksh93u+m carried the language instead
⚠️ Development rests on a small group: The maintained fork is a volunteer effort, so the pace of change is outside user control
⚠️ The older dialect is frozen in place: AIX and other systems ship a ksh88-era shell, so the language as practised is fragmented



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Good fit for POSIX system scripting with extras: ksh93 covers portable shell code and adds associative arrays, floating point, and coprocesses where the standard stops
✅ Strong for text and record processing: ${var/pat/rep}, ${var:offset:length}, [[ ... =~ ... ]], and printf keep string handling inside the language
✅ Associative arrays fit lookup and configuration work: typeset -A and compound variables model keyed data without a temporary file or an external tool
✅ Coprocesses suit long-running children: A child started once can be driven from a loop instead of through a named pipe
⚠️ Not a general-purpose language: The model is a shell over external commands, so a program with real data structures belongs elsewhere
⚠️ The most advanced features are not portable: Discipline functions, name spaces, and typeset -T exist only in ksh93



1.2.5 Learning

✅ POSIX knowledge transfers: A Bash or sh user can write ksh on the first day
✅ Functions are more capable than in sh: function name { } with typeset locals is a familiar and predictable form
⚠️ The surface is large: typeset has many attributes, and [[ ... ]], (( ... )), print, whence, and the .sh.* variables each need their own reference
⚠️ The documentation is a specification, not a tutorial: There is little introductory material for the ksh93-specific features
⚠️ The dialect trap is invisible: A script written for ksh93 runs under mksh until it reaches an associative array or a float



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ POSIX surface with familiar extensions: if, case, for, and while are the standard forms, and (( ... )) and [[ ... ]] read like C
✅ ${var/pat/rep} handles substitution inline: A replacement no longer needs sed in a pipeline
⚠️ $'...' and typeset attributes add notation: Quoting, justification, case conversion, and numeric attributes each add their own spelling
⚠️ function and name() differ quietly: The two definition forms have different scoping behaviour, so the choice of syntax changes the semantics
⚠️ print and printf overlap: Two output builtins with different escape handling coexist



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No test framework in the language: A test is a script that checks $?, with no assertion, fixture, or report facility (G1)
❌ Faults appear only on the branch that runs: With no static check, a mistyped variable or a bad attribute is found during the run (G3)
✅ The DEBUG trap gives a command-by-command trace: trap ... DEBUG runs after each command, which makes a failure locatable in a long script
✅ A syntax check runs without execution: ksh -n parses a script and reports errors without running it
✅ set -o xtrace shows the expansion: set -x prints the expanded command, so an argument built from several variables can be inspected
✅ typeset -f and whence -v inspect the loaded program: A test can assert on a function’s definition and on how a name resolves



1.2.8 Security

❌ Unquoted expansion is re-parsed: A word is split and globbed again, so untrusted text can change the argument count unless it is quoted (Q2)
⚠️ eval and indirect expansion re-enter the interpreter: Text assembled from data and passed to eval, or a name resolved through a nameref, becomes code or a name the parser decides
⚠️ No memory-safety defect class, but no confinement either: Values are interpreter-managed, yet the shell has no capability or sandbox model beyond its restricted mode
✅ [[ ... ]] does not word-split: The test construct evaluates its operands directly, so a value cannot become extra operands or a pattern
✅ A restricted mode exists: rksh93 blocks cd, redirection, and assignment to SHELL, ENV, and PATH, so an untrusted script can be run with fewer powers
✅ readonly and typeset -r freeze a value: A name can be fixed against later assignment and against unset

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ No stable tracing and metrics standard.
⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.

⚠️ No fast in-editor analysis.

⚠️ No maintained portable target.

title: Sh (POSIX.1-2024)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses sh in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 43/100 · Ecosystem coupling 57/100 · Engineering readiness 64/100

1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

❌ All values are strings, and numbers live in a second grammar: x=1 and x=abc are the same assignment, and $(( ... )) evaluates a signed-integer expression that is re-parsed at each use (T1)
❌ No arrays and no associative arrays: A list is a string split on IFS, and the specification provides no indexed or keyed aggregate (T4)
❌ No generics and no dispatch by type: A routine is specialised only by its positional parameters, and behaviour is selected by the command name (T5, T9)
❌ One flat namespace: The specification gives a function no local scope, so a function’s working variables are the caller’s variables (T6, T11)
❌ An unset name and an empty name are indistinguishable: set -u turns a reference to an unset name into an error, but it is off by default and an empty value still passes (T10)
✅ Default and alternate expansions are part of the language: ${var:-default} and ${var:+alternate} carry the missing-value case in the expansion itself, so many ad-hoc checks disappear



1.1.2 Construction

❌ Global by default and mutable by default: An assignment writes the single namespace, and only readonly fixes a value (C1, C2)
❌ No constructor or validation at the point of assignment: Nothing checks a value when it is bound, so validation is written as a separate case statement or test (C4)
❌ Functions share the caller’s variables: The standard provides no local declaration — local is a ksh and Bash extension, and shells that offer it differ in detail — so a helper must save and restore every name it touches, or run in a subshell
✅ A subshell is a scope: ( ... ) runs in a child process, so a subroutine is isolated from the parent’s values by wrapping it
✅ Positional parameters are the argument list: A function or a sh -c string reads its inputs as $1, $2, and so on, so a routine consumes its arguments instead of reading a global
✅ ENV separates interactive setup from scripts: An interactive shell reads its personalisation file from $ENV, so a non-interactive script starts with none of it



1.1.3 Memory

✅ No allocation or free in the language: There is no pointer and no deallocation builtin; the shell owns every string
✅ A subshell releases its memory at exit: ( ... ) ends and its environment is discarded, so temporary state does not survive it
✅ unset drops a name: The shell reclaims the storage, so no free order and no double free can arise
⚠️ Assignment copies the value: b=$a duplicates the string, and there is no way to reference a value without copying it
⚠️ A pipeline is a set of processes: The shell forks each stage, so the memory cost of a pipeline is the sum of its parts
⚠️ Command substitution is buffered whole: $(cmd) collects the entire output before the enclosing command runs, so the whole result is held in memory and then split



1.1.4 Error

❌ No structured error path: The entire apparatus is $? and trap, with no exception and no error value (Er1)
❌ $? is lost by the next command: Any command resets it, so an interposed test discards the failure (Er3)
❌ Errors do not compose: A failure is an exit status, so it cannot carry a payload, be returned as data, or be combined with another (Er4)
⚠️ set -e is not a reliable policy: errexit does not fire in && and || chains, in conditions, or after a negation, so a wrapper that suppresses it changes the behaviour of the whole script
⚠️ There is no ERR trap in the standard: Reporting and cleanup must be attached to EXIT, to a named signal, or to an explicit check after each command
✅ trap ... EXIT runs on every exit path: Cleanup can be attached once and will run on a normal exit or on a handled signal



1.1.5 Concurrency

❌ No concurrency primitives: No lock, channel, semaphore, or await exists; the only parallel construct is & (K5)
✅ Pipelines are a first-class composition: The pipeline is a core operator of the language, so stages are connected without the script manipulating file descriptors
✅ wait and $! make a job addressable: cmd & records the process id in $!, so a script can wait for one job rather than for all of them
✅ A subshell isolates concurrent state: ( ... ) & gives a job its own copy of the environment, so the job cannot change the parent’s values
⚠️ Background jobs share files and the working directory: A & job inherits the environment, the umask, and the current directory, so ordering is unspecified unless the script waits
⚠️ No value comes back from a job: A status arrives through wait, and a result must travel through a file, a pipe, or a named pipe



1.1.6 Platform

❌ sh is an implementable name, not an implementation: POSIX defines the language but not which program provides it, so /bin/sh is dash, ash, bash in POSIX mode, or a vendor shell depending on the system, and only the standard subset is portable (P2)
✅ POSIX guarantees that a shell exists: Every conforming system provides sh, so a script invokes an interpreter without installing anything
✅ The standard is written for maximum reach: The language contains no optional syntax that a conforming shell may omit
⚠️ Implementations are not equally complete: An older sh may lack behaviour added in Issue 8, so a script that uses pipefail or $'...' is portable only to newer systems
⚠️ sh -c is the universal entry point: system(), make, containers, and cron all use it, which makes the shell the assumed execution layer even when no script is written
⚠️ Extensions are common and not portable: local, [[ ... ]], arrays, and function are available in many sh implementations but are outside the standard



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

Minimalism is the point: The language is small because every construct must be implementable on every conforming system, so the absence of arrays is a scope decision
Portability costs expressiveness: Writing to the standard means doing without associative arrays, pattern-replacement expansions, and floating point
No interactive features is a deliberate omission: Line editing, history, and completion are terminal concerns and are kept out of the standard
/bin/sh is a policy choice on each system: A distribution links it to dash, bash, or another shell, and that choice is not the language’s
Integer arithmetic is the standard’s floor: A script that needs floating point calls an external tool, which is a design boundary rather than a defect
The specification is written for implementers: Its precision makes it slow to read, and that is the price of one text that many shells obey




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

⚠️ Interpreted with no compilation: Each command is parsed and executed as text, and there is no artifact and no JIT (R1)
✅ A minimal implementation starts fast: dash and ash reach the first command in a fraction of the time a feature-rich shell needs, which matters for the many sh -c calls in a build or a boot
✅ Builtins replace processes for common work: printf, read, test, getopts, and parameter expansion avoid an external command
⚠️ Every external command forks: The builtin set is small, so a loop that calls sed, grep, or basename per item pays a process per iteration
⚠️ Command substitution is buffered and re-split: $(cmd) reads the whole output and then splits it on IFS, so a large result is walked twice
✅ Scripts pay no start-up configuration: The ENV file is read only by an interactive shell, so a non-interactive script pays nothing for user setup



1.2.2 Ecosystem

❌ No package manager: There is no dependency mechanism for shell code, so shared routines are sourced from a directory or vendored (Ec1)
✅ Every UNIX-like system has an implementation: Dash, ash and BusyBox ash, FreeBSD sh, ksh, and bash in POSIX mode all provide an sh mode, so a script always has a host
✅ The standard is published and maintained: The Open Group Base Specifications define the language in one stable document with a change history
✅ Analysers target sh by default: ShellCheck and similar tools treat sh as the base case, so a minimal script is the best-supported one
✅ checkbashisms detects non-portable constructs: A script can be checked against the POSIX surface before it is released
⚠️ Most published shell libraries assume Bash: They use arrays and [[ ... ]], so they cannot be used in a strictly conforming script



1.2.3 Evolution

❌ The standard moves slowly: Issue 7 appeared in 2018 and Issue 8 in 2024, so a needed feature waits years for the committee (V4)
✅ The standard is backward compatible: Issue 8 adds features and removes only what was already marked obsolescent, so old scripts keep running
✅ Removals are signposted for years: test’s -a and -o primaries were marked obsolescent in Issue 7 before Issue 8 removed them
✅ The change history ships with the text: Every change from the previous issue is recorded in the specification rationale
⚠️ Adoption lags publication: A shipped sh may implement an older issue for years, so a script written to Issue 8 may not run on the host it is deployed to
⚠️ The committee decides on defect reports: A change enters the standard only through an accepted interpretation, so the process is deliberate rather than responsive



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent fit for its intended domain: Boot scripts, installers, container entrypoints, and configure scripts need the one interpreter that is always present
✅ Stop-gap automation is a native use: A two-line sh -c avoids a build step and a binary, which is why build tools, cron, and orchestrators embed it
✅ Portable text filtering composes well: Pipelines over grep, sed, and awk are the idiom the language was designed around
✅ Configuration and environment setup read cleanly: Exporting variables, setting umask, and changing directories is a few lines
⚠️ Data structures push the script elsewhere: Without arrays, a keyed or indexed collection becomes a temporary file and a series of awk invocations
⚠️ Not a general-purpose language: The model is a shell over external commands, so a program with real logic belongs in another language



1.2.5 Learning

✅ A small surface to learn: Assignments, if, case, and pipelines cover most scripts, and the standard is short compared with bash or zsh
✅ Skills transfer upward: Everything learned in sh applies to Bash, ksh, and zsh, which is why it is the usual starting point
✅ The specification is the reference: A precise description of every construct exists in one place
⚠️ Quoting and word splitting trap newcomers: $var unquoted splits and globs, so a space or an asterisk in a value changes the command
⚠️ [ is a command, not syntax: test parses its arguments, so an unquoted empty variable changes the argument count and can turn a test into an error or a truth
⚠️ The specification is written for implementers: It is precise about behaviour and thin on explanation, so learners need other material



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ The language is small and predictable: Assignments, if, while, for, case, and pipelines cover the whole grammar
✅ Here-documents handle multi-line input: << and <<- embed a block of text in a script without escaping
⚠️ Expansion has five forms to remember: %, %%, #, ##, and ${#var} are compact but each has its own rule
⚠️ Quoting rules are context-dependent: Single quotes, double quotes, and backslash escapes each treat $, backtick, and newline differently
⚠️ [ and test need the operands spaced out: The bracket form requires a space after [ and before ], which is easy to forget
⚠️ No [[ ... ]] in the standard: The construct was removed from the shell language description in an early POSIX proposal, so richer tests are written with case or with expr



1.2.7 Testing

❌ No test framework in the language: A test is a script that checks $?, with no assertion, fixture, or reporting facility (G1)
❌ Faults appear only on the branch that runs: With no static check, a mistyped variable or a missing file is found during the run (G3)
✅ A syntax check runs without execution: sh -n parses a script and reports errors without running it
✅ set -x shows the expansion: The traced command reveals how a value was split and quoted before it ran
✅ Exit status is a reliable oracle: $? after a command gives one unambiguous value to assert on
✅ A test can be isolated with a subshell: ( ... ) gives each case a fresh copy of the environment, so one case cannot leak into the next



1.2.8 Security

❌ Command construction from text is the classic injection path: A value expanded into a command line or passed to eval becomes code, so unquoted expansion of untrusted input is unsafe (Q3)
❌ Weak typing removes a check the shell cannot make: A value that should be a number, a path, or a flag is a string, and only the command that receives it can object (Q2)
✅ test can be made argument-safe: [ "X$response" = "Xexpected" ] or ${var:+...} expansion removes the ambiguity that an unquoted variable introduces
✅ set -f disables globbing: noglob stops an expanded * from becoming a path list
✅ umask is part of the language: File-creation permissions are set inside the script rather than left to the ambient environment
✅ No memory-safety surface: Strings are interpreter-managed, so a script has no buffer to overflow




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

1.3.5 Interop

⚠️ No maintained portable target.



1.3.6 Governance

1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

⚠️ Every operation starts a process: time, and therefore energy, is dominated by process startup.

title: C++ (C++23)
text:
Analysis against C++23 (ISO/IEC 14882:2024). Older C++ standards have substantially worse coupling properties; C++23 represents the best of what modern C++ offers.
This assessment applies the coupling account — coupling as access to a shared resource, and the coupling floor [1], [2] — and the knowledge-embodiment theorem [3]; the language is assessed against its official reference [4].

title: C++ (C++23)
text:
1 Assessment
This page assesses C++ in five parts: core coupling — what the language’s own constructs force; ecosystem coupling — what the surrounding platform, tooling, and community cost; engineering readiness — whether the artifact can be reproduced, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to other languages, and governed openly; the profile — the unscored facts a score cannot express; and the scoring detail — the mechanism marks and the arithmetic behind every score. A ✅ bullet marks a construct that helps. A ⚠️ or ❌ bullet marks a cost; the scoring model does not price every cost named here.
Core coupling 50/100 · Ecosystem coupling 61/100 · Engineering readiness 65/100

Note: The score reflects C++23 with modern idioms (smart pointers ≥ raw pointers, std::expected ≥ exceptions, modules ≥ headers, concepts ≥ unconstrained templates). Teams stuck on older standards or pre-modern coding styles will experience significantly worse coupling properties.


1.1 Core coupling

1.1.1 Type

✅ Templates enable generic programming: Decouple algorithms from types
✅ RAII separates resource management: Constructor acquires, destructor releases
✅ Concepts (C++20) constrain templates: Clean error messages, explicit constraints decouple interface from implementation
✅ Modules (C++20/23) decouple compilation: import replaces #include and removes header coupling, though headers remain for code not yet migrated
✅ Deducing this (C++23): Eliminates const/non-const overload duplication
⚠️ Multiple inheritance still available: Diamond problem possible (though final specifier helps)
⚠️ Template metaprogramming still complex: Despite concepts, advanced templates couple to expertise
❌ Macros couple: Preprocessor doesn’t respect scope (though modules reduce header macro issues)



1.1.2 Construction

✅ Constructors separate: Copy, move, default constructors are distinct
✅ Move semantics decouple: Transfer ownership without copying
✅ Designated initializers (C++20): Named initialization decouples from parameter order
❌ Constructors can throw: Exception during construction couples cleanup
⚠️ Two-phase initialization still possible: Though discouraged by modern idioms
❌ Global state common: Static variables, singletons (not enforced away)



1.1.3 Memory

✅ RAII decouples resource management: Destructors run deterministically, no GC needed
✅ Smart pointers eliminate manual delete: unique_ptr, shared_ptr are idiomatic (manual new/delete is a code smell in modern C++)
✅ std::span/std::mdspan (C++20/23): Non-owning one- and multi-dimensional views decouple algorithms from container types and memory layout
✅ Explicit lifetime management (C++23): std::start_lifetime_as for safe low-level patterns
⚠️ shared_ptr has atomic ref counting cost: And circular references need weak_ptr
⚠️ Raw pointer escape hatches exist: A raw pointer and a reference can alias the same object with no owner stated, though idiomatic C++23 uses spans and smart pointers (M4)
✅ No GC, deterministic: Full control over allocation timing
❌ Undefined behavior still exists: Buffer overruns, null derefs possible when using raw pointers/functions



1.1.4 Error

✅ std::expected and std::optional monadic operations (C++23): and_then, transform, or_else make error and absence handling composable and type-safe
❌ Exceptions still exist and remain unchecked: std::expected is idiomatic and preferred, but exceptions are still in the language and used in the standard library
✅ std::stacktrace (C++23): Provides unwinding visibility, addressing historical debugging pain
✅ std::variant: Type-safe discriminated union for error discrimination



1.1.5 Concurrency

⚠️ Shared mutable state default: Mutexes required, though lock-free patterns are achievable
✅ std::jthread (C++20): Auto-joining threads with cancellation via std::stop_token
✅ std::latch, std::barrier, std::semaphore (C++20): Higher-level synchronization primitives
✅ std::generator (C++23): Coroutine-based generator decouples producer from consumer
❌ Data races are undefined behavior: No compile-time prevention (unlike Rust)
⚠️ Memory model still complex: Atomic operations require deep understanding



1.1.6 Platform

✅ No vendor owner: The language is standardised by ISO/IEC and implemented independently by GCC, Clang, and MSVC, so no single vendor controls the standard
✅ No required platform runtime: A program compiles to native code and needs no C++-specific virtual machine or vendor service
✅ Every mainstream target is supported: Compilers and standard libraries exist for Linux, macOS, Windows, and embedded and bare-metal targets
✅ One source base for several implementations: Code that stays in the portable subset compiles under GCC, Clang, and MSVC, so the project is not bound to one compiler



1.1.7 Trade-offs (not coupling)

RAII vs. Exceptions: Exception during construction couples cleanup to unwinding, may leak
Zero-Cost Abstractions vs. Compile Time: Templates (and now concepts + modules) couple build speed to abstraction usage
C Compatibility vs. Modern Features: Legacy C patterns can couple to modern C++ code when used
Standard Versions: C++11/14/17/20/23 couple codebases to version choices; modern C++ is largely additive since C++11
Safety vs. Performance: std::span bounds-checking is opt-in; raw pointer escape hatches remain for performance




1.2 Ecosystem coupling

1.2.1 Performance

✅ Zero-overhead abstraction: Pay only for what you use
✅ No GC: Deterministic, predictable
✅ Manual control: Full optimization control
✅ Compile-time computation: Constexpr (expanded in C++23 — now covers std::bitset, std::unique_ptr, std::optional, std::variant, std::string, cmath functions)
⚠️ Binary bloat: Templates can explode size (mitigated by explicit instantiations, LTO)



1.2.2 Ecosystem

⚠️ No standard package manager: CMake + Conan/vcpkg are de facto standards, but fragmentation persists
⚠️ Compilation speed: Templates + concepts + modules improve but still slower than Go/Rust
✅ Excellent IDE support: CLion, Visual Studio, VSCode with clangd — all support C++23
✅ Vast library ecosystem: Decades of libraries, Boost, Qt, etc.
⚠️ Build system convergence improving: CMake dominates; vcpkg/Conan converging



1.2.3 Evolution

✅ Additive since C++11: Code from C++11+ largely compiles under C++23 (removed features are rare and deprecated first)
⚠️ Legacy C++98 burden: Old codebases still exist, but not a language-level problem for new code
✅ 3-year standard cadence: Predictable evolution (C++23 → C++26 → C++29)
⚠️ Feature complexity grows: Each standard adds more to learn



1.2.4 Domain

✅ Excellent for systems: Performance critical code
✅ Great for games: Industry standard
✅ Strong for embedded: (with care, constexpr + templates help)
✅ Good for high-performance: Finance, scientific computing
⚠️ Not for web: Rare use case



1.2.5 Learning

❌ Very steep: Massive language surface area accumulated over 40+ years
❌ C++23 idioms are learnable but the full language is not: Smart pointers, expected, ranges, modules add to surface
❌ Undefined behavior: Still exists and requires understanding to avoid
✅ Excellent resources: Effective Modern C++, C++ Core Guidelines, cppreference



1.2.6 Syntax

✅ Modules reduce header boilerplate: import std; replaces many #includes
⚠️ Template syntax: <> remains noisy, though concepts improve readability
✅ Designated initializers: Named member initialization improves readability
✅ auto, structured bindings (C++17): Reduce verbosity



1.2.7 Testing

✅ GTest, Catch2, doctest: Mature frameworks
✅ Static analyzers: Clang-Tidy, CppCheck, and MSVC Code Analysis find some undefined behaviour before runtime, though no analyzer is sound or complete
✅ Profilers: Excellent tooling (perf, VTune, Instruments)
✅ std::stacktrace (C++23): Runtime stacktrace capture improves debugging
⚠️ Template errors: Concepts (C++20) dramatically improve error messages, but edge cases remain



1.2.8 Security

⚠️ Memory safety depends on idiom: std::span, std::mdspan, smart pointers are memory-safe; raw pointers and pointer arithmetic are not
✅ Smart pointers + RAII eliminate most memory bugs in modern C++: unique_ptr prevents use-after-free, double-free
✅ AddressSanitizer, MemorySanitizer: Compiler instrumentation catches memory bugs at test time
❌ Unsafe escape hatches remain: reinterpret_cast, pointer arithmetic, manual new/delete still compile (Q1)




1.3 Engineering readiness

1.3.1 Reproducibility

❌ Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.
❌ Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.



1.3.2 Supply chain

⚠️ Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.



1.3.3 Observability

⚠️ The standard library has no structured logging.



1.3.4 Feedback

❌ A change pays a slow build.



1.3.5 Interop

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.



1.3.6 Governance

✅ No charged mechanism in this dimension.




1.4 Profile
Unscored, and kept separate from every score on purpose. The profile records what a mechanism price cannot express: what a running program costs, how well a coding model and an agent work in the language, and whether a safety-critical path exists.

1.4.1 Energy and cost
What this axis asks: what does a running program cost in energy and time?

✅ Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [5], [6]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [7].



1.4.2 AI and agent readiness
What this axis asks: how well does a coding model and an agent work in this language?

✅ A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [8], [9].



1.4.3 Safety certification
What this axis asks: is there a certified or standards-qualified path to a safety-critical system?

✅ A standards-qualified toolchain or an established safety standard covers this language.

Verdict: C++23 provides substantially better coupling than its reputation suggests. Modules decouple compilation units. std::expected provides composable error handling. Concepts eliminate template error message hell. std::span/std::mdspan provide safe non-owning views. Smart pointers are idiomatic and eliminate manual new/delete. Main strength: RAII + zero-cost abstractions + deterministic performance. Main weakness: the language retains unsafe escape hatches (raw pointers, macros, exceptions) and new features coexist with old ones, meaning teams must enforce modern idiom discipline. C++23 with Core Guidelines and static analysis is a different language from C++98.
